Drug Emporium cfo leaving 


COLUMBUS, Ohio — Drug Emporium cfo Stephen Pohlit is 
leaving to take a post with another firm, less than a year after 
joining the off-price drug chain to help spearhead an accounting 
and operations overhaul. Pohlit will ait hia post before mid-No- 
vember, according to the company. 

Drug Emporium ceo Gary Wilber said a search is under way 
for a successor. He praised Pohlit’s efforts, saying, “Steve 
came to us 10 months ago to play a key role in our continuing 
restructuring program and he has done just that. In 10 
months, the restructuring of our accounting operations is 
substantially complete. 

“While we continue to standardize and streamline these oper- 
ations, we now have a centralized accounting department and 
the people and procedures are in place for the future,” he said. 

Pohlit’s new corporate destination is not yet known. “He 
would prefer for his new company to release that information on 
[its] own,” said a Drug Emporium spokesperson. 


American’s Maher named 


LOS ANGELES — David Maher, 
chairman, ceo and president of American 
Drug Stores, Inc., has been selected as 
the 1992 Retailer of the Year by the Insti- 
tute of Retail Management at California 
State University. 

The award is given to the individual 
whose record of achievement and integrity 
serves as a role model for young people en- 
tering the retail industry.

Fay's to enter mail order, 


By Barbara White 

LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — 
Fay’s Inc. is planning to enter 
the mail order pharmacy busi- 
ness. The company announced 
the election of David Eilerman 
as vp and general manager of 
the company’s newly-formed 
mail order pharmacy services 
division. 

Before joining Fay’s, Eiler- 
man had been regional vp for 
America’s Pharmacy, the mail 
order pharmacy services sub- 
sidiary of Systemed, Inc. for 
over four years. Previously, he 
was employed by Blue Cross of 
California and Blue Cross and 
Blue Shield of New Mexico. 

Fay’s chairman and ceo 
Henry Panasci, Jr. said the 
appointment of Eilerman was 
the first step in establishing 
the chain in the mail order ser- 
vices business. 

Eilerman said the mail order 

harmacy service already has 
its first customer, but he de- 
clined to name the client. He 
expects the division to fill its 
first prescription on Jan. 2. 

To open its doors, Eilerman 
said the operation will need to 


names Ellerman to run division 


employ about 20 people—not 
only in pharmacist capacities. 

“We will need marketing 
suport services and a sales 
force,” he said. “Our sales reps 
will be regional [vps] and will 
cover a specific geographic 
area, since we are taking this 
business national.” He said he 
envisions employing about 
five to seven reps who will 
cover six to 10 states each. 

Fay’s is still scouting for the 
best location for its newest op- 
eration and will probably opt 
to take the operation out of 
New York state. 

“We need to set up the mail 
order pharmacy services divi- 
sion in a state that’s friendly to 
the corporate customer. That 
means the generic substitu- 
tion laws need to be liberal so 
that we can substitute as long 
as a physician permits. The cli- 
mate also needs to be liberal in 
terms of cost competitiveness. 
We need to be able to use techs 
to do routine tasks, such as 
pulling medications and count- 
ing pills, while the pharma- 
cists use their skills on other 
tasks,” he said. “New York 


state doesn’t represent the 
best environment.” 

New York state has strin- 
gent substitution laws and a 
1-1 tech-to-pharmacist ratio. 

Kilerman said Pennsylva- 
nia, with its close proximity to 
Fay’s warehouse, would be a 
desirable location, though the 
company would consider other 
states in which there is al- 
ready mail order competition, 
such as Ohio or Florida. 

Why is Fay’s taking on the 
mammoth mail order busi- 
ness? “There is a growing con- 
sensus among bill payers that 
mail order is less expensive 
than retail pharmacy,” said 
Kilerman. “The reality is that 
the drug bill in the U.S. will 
run over $60 billion this year; 
70 percent of that bill is main- 
tenance drugs. That’s where 
mail order comes in.” 

Eilerman said that mail or- 
der customers are loyal. 
“Once you get somebody into 
your program, they stay 
there,” he said. In a tough eco- 
nomic climate, Fay’s is betting 
that the investment in the mail 
order division will pay off.

guaranteeing free and open 
trade. The proposed legislation 
seeks to amend Robinson-Pat-

representatives and brokers 
the standing to sue for damages 
caused by large retailers [pow-

trust laws,” according to a

incide with its introduction.

were first aired.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 9, 1992 


In the world of baseball, Dennis Eckersley is the 
premier closer, perhaps the best the game has ever 
seen. Say goodnight to opponents when the Oakland 
As send him to the mound in the ninth. The sonic pop 
of his fastball into the catcher’s mitt marks his 
team’s cadence to victory almost every time. Sim- 
ply, he’s Eck. 

Less than an hour away in L.A. works another 
Eck who, instead of fast- 


balls, throws ideas at 
people to see what grabs 
hold. Fresh thinking is 
his arsenal against com- 
petition, and the Vons 
Companies’ operation un- 
der Dennis Eck, presi- 
dent and chief operating 
officer, embodies the 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


spirit of innovation. 

Since assuming his title in February 1990, report- 
ing to ceo Roger Stangeland, Eck, the former chair- 
man and ceo of American Food and Drug Stores, has 
used his directness and broad retail perspective to 
help Vons better secure its food store market share 
lead in Southern California. Since the merger with 
Safeway, Vons Companies now operates 342 stores 
pumping over $5 billion in volume. 

In New Orleans last week at the FMI GM/HBC 
Conference, I had the chance to speak with Eck 
about EDLP and his chain’s transition to category 
management. On the former: “It’s an overstated 
concept because the difference between EDLP 
.. . Land high-low] is smaller than it’s ever been. 
We all pass on trade allowances. And to build busi- 
ness, we want to run with the most consistent and 
complete suppliers. When we cut the bottom SKUs, 
that’s just good business—and it creates the next 
tier of slow movers.” 

On the latter: “Our buyers are taking one catego- 
ry at atime, while keeping our normal way of buying 
and going to market in place. We’ve improved the 
pay, position and prestige of our category manag- 
ers, keeping good people in these positions.” 

I got the distinct feeling that while these may be 
important issues to him, Eck’s eye is really focused 


OPINION 


Which Eck would you rather face? 


on products being pulled through by consumers— 
with retailer efforts aiaing that process. Volume 
building is crucial today given the price deflation in 
food, and the gross profit opportunities inGM/HBC. 

In Eck’s earlier presentation on the role of 
GM/HBC at Vons, he honed in on various themes: 
Fresh thinking. Densing up. Store-specific market- 
ing. Aggressive pursuit of GM/HBC business. 

Now densing up may have more applications for 
space-constrained drug stores, but Vons uses this 
concept of filling the cube more efficiently to full ad- 
vantage. Eck described how store managers 
thought “it was the stupidest idea” to use dead space 
on the side of dairy, freezer and produce cases for 
custom-built displays of school/home office, sewing 
notions, and other heavily SKUed, clutter-prone 
categories. 

He insisted and won their hearts and minds with 
such benefits as: 20 to 30 percent category sales 
gains; lower payroll costs since the staff works less 
in the backroom; and advances in turns, margins and 
in-stock positions, especially during coupon drops. 

“It only cost us $10,000 [in inventory] per store to 
dense up,” said Eck. He noted further that perma- 
nent displays cut out the clutter and added visual 
punch to many categories. 

He half-kidded with Ambassador’s Bill Marter 
about a greeting card fixture he’d like to see devel- 
oped that hangs from the ceiling. “Why not?” Eck 
posed. “Cards are light.” He’s also looking at a ser- 
vice party goods center. 

Other areas to watch: - 

@ Pharmacy, Vons’ second-fastest-growing depart- 
ment behind floral. Now at 108 counters, “it’s going 
into as many stores as we can put it in,” said Eck. 
The chain remodels 65 units a year, aiming for eight 
out of 10 stores to be redone “as completely as we 
can” every five years, he added. 

@ Photofinishing. Minilabs are going into its higher- 
volume stores. 

@ Stationery. Eck called it “an important category 
for us to dominate.” 

Eck and Eck. One on the mound, one in the board- 
room. One pitches baseballs, the other ideas. Both 
are equally powerful. 


Drugs may curb rising 


Back in 1965, a year before Medicaid emerged as a 
key element in Washington’s “War on Poverty,” $6 
billion was a lot of money. That’s what America was 
spending annually on drugs and other non-durable 
health care needs. 

Since then, spending on drugs has increased tenfold. 
This year government forecasters expect the nation’s 
drug bill to hit $63 billion. 

If the experts in Wash- 


ington are right, the cost of 
medicine should continue 
climbing significantly fast- 
er than the rate of inflation 
in the foreseeable future. 

Assuming that U.S. 
spending for drugs rises 
by an average of 7.5 per- 
cent annually—a rosy sce- 
nario in view of recent pharmaceutical price hikes— 
Americans will be spending $111 billion a year on 
drugs by the turn of the century. 

Even more disturbing is that this year federal experts 
expect spending on drugs to rise at almost twice the rate 
of increase in the entire U.S. Gross Domestic Product. 

Given these facts, it’s not surprising that Washing- 
ton 's taking a close look at the economics of the phar- 
maceutical marketplace. 

A new study by the Congressional Budget Office 
(CBO) confirms what people in the drug store industry 


we WASHINGTON 
"i, PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


health care costs 


knew: Despite a quarter century of federal, state and 
private cost containment initiatives, a steadily rising 
share of our national income is being spent on pharma- 
ceutical products and services. But there’s a positive 
twist to the CBO findings as well. Although government 
health policy officials don’t often acknowledge it, drugs 
are helping to hold down the rise in health care spending 
as a whole. 

Indeed, while drug spending is up tenfold since 1965, 
the cost of physician services is 19 times higher than it 
was then; hospital expenditures are 22 times higher; and 
spending on nursing home care is 32 times higher. 

Why are drug costs climbing at a more moderate rate 
than other health care expenditures? The conventional 
wisdom among third-party prescription program ad- 
ministrators is that they deserve the credit for slowing 
the rise in pharmaceutical prices through pharmacy re- 
imbursement ceilings and other cost-containment mech- 
anisms. 

But congressional researchers found a completely dif- 
ferent explanation. “Almost 75 percent of drug spending 
is paid out of pocket by consumers,” according to the 
CBO, concluding that this relative absence of third-par- 
ty coverage “has helped restrain drug spending in rela- 
tion to other, more heavily insured types of spending.” 

If the Congressional experts are right, maybe we 
should be looking at the third-party prescription crowd 
in a different light. Instead of being part of the solution 
to high costs, maybe they’re a big part of the problem.

with a cautious eye

Change was the hot buzz- 
word during the presidential 
election. Now that it’s here in 
the form of President-Elect 
Bill Clinton, chain drug retail- 
ers find themselves wonder- 
ing if it is for the best. 

Along with change comes 
uncertainty, and that is what 
has retailers scratching their 
heads. The new administra- 
tion’s impact on consumer 
spending, financial markets, 


health care delivery systems 
and environmental regulation 
will affect drug retailers. 
Many who were contacted 
by Drug Store News declined 
to comment. Those who did 
were cautiously optimistic.

change, but it remains to be 
seen how effective Clinton will 
be in getting his legislative 
agenda passed,” said Tim 
cAlear, president and chief

RxPlus stores sold 


to Osco, Walgreen 


By Allene Symons 

PHOENIX — RDS Acquisi- 
tion Corp., operating the 
RxPlus stores under Chapter 
11 bankruptcy protection since 
last November, was ordered by 
an Arizona court to sell the 66- 
store chain to American Drug 
Stores subsidiary Osco Drug, 
Walgreens, and several indi- 
vidual operators in separate 
transactions. 

The court order, handed 
down the second week in No- 
vember, approved the sale to 
Osco of 38 RxPlus stores in- 
cluding inventory, fixtures and 
prescription files. Osco will as- 
sume 18 of those store leases in 
a deal expected to close by the 
calendar year’s end. 

Walgreens acquired the 
pharmacy files and inventory of 
16 stores in El] Paso, where it 
now operates 13 Walgreens 
stores, and in northern New 
Mexico where it operates 36 
stores statewide. The acquisi- 
tion was effective as of Nov. 11, 
according to Walgreens 
spokesperson Michael Polzin. 


The demise of RxPlus 
marks the end of a year-lon 
build-down by parent RDS. 
The chain was formed in 1990 
when an investor group head- 
ed by chain drug veteran Al 
Towle aeouieet 146 Revco 
stores and 17 SupeRx units to 
form the 163-store RxPlus 
chain. By early summer of 
1992, six months after filing 
for bankruptcy protection, the 
chain was down to 78 stores, 
and 66 remained at the time of 
the recent court order. 


Strategy shift 


The Osco acquisition of 18 
RxPlus sites follows a shift in 
Southwest marketing strategy 
for the chain. Osco retreated 
from some markets, including 
Salt Lake City, but took a pow- 
er position in Phoenix with the 
rollout of its much-praised Vi- 
sion prototype last year. Osco 
now 35 stores in Phoenix 
and Tucson, according to Cal 
Drecksel, vp-investor relations 
for American Drug’s parent 
company, American Stores. 


The acquired stores aver- 
age 5,000 square feet and will 
be converted to Osco stores, 
according to Drecksel. In con- 
trast, a typical Osco is be- 
tween 18,000 and 20,000 
square feet and the new Osco 

ision stores are in the 14,000- 
to 15,000-square-foot range. 

Drecksel noted that a new 
name may be necessary to dif- 
ferentiate the smaller Arizona 
stores from full-size Osco 
stores. “I think we might 
eventually change the name,” 
said Drecksel. 

In California, American 
Drug’s acquisition early this 
year of CVS also meant ab- 
sorbing smaller sites and re- 
cently resulted in a new name, 
Sav-on Express. 

“In some areas we may build 
smaller stores. If the opportu- 
nity comes to get an acquisition 
at a good price and if they ha 
pen to be smaller—since we're 
trying to grow the 
business—we'll go after them. 
This adds to our pharmacy net- 
work,” Drecksel added. 


PLMA finds store brands in golden era 


CHICAGO — Consumer 
spending is sluggish and 
mired in a troubied economy. 
Brand loyalty is down. Moves 
by some key suppliers away 
from trade promotions in fa- 
vor of everyday low price 
have some retailers miffed. 
Price competition continues 
to erode gross 
margins. 

at do all 
these market 
forces portend? 
For one thing, 
they’re all light- 
ing a fuse under 
the private label 


So far, private label brands 
seem to be filling the bill. 
Done right—with the proper 
selection of me-too products, 
the right packaging, the 
right placement and the right 
price—they They remain a 
potent source of high hihi 
margins and image-building. 


What’s more, consumer ac- 
ceptance of store brands is at 
an all-time high, as demon- 
strated by last year’s Gallup 
Poll on consumer prefer- 
ences. And a sick economy 
has helped keep price and 
value at the top of their list.

3rd VIX off-pricer: Cleveland area 


PARMA HEIGHTS, Ohio — First National rmarkets 
has opened its third VIX deep-discount drug store in early No- 
vember in a bid to compete directly with Marc Glassman’s 
Cleveland-area off-price empire. a 

VIX stores are similar in merchandising concept, low-price 
image and advertising, with emphasis on steeply discounted 
brand names. The stores—all of which are located in Cleve- 
land’s suburbs—are similar to the VIX concept developed in 
New York by Topps Markets in New York. ee 

First. National also runs the Finast supermarket chain in 
Ohio. Company officials are mum on future plans for the new

Walgreen named in professorship 


ANN ARBOR, Mich. — An endowed professorship will be 
established at the University of Michigan College of Pharmacy 
in the name of Charles R. Walgreen, Jr., the retired chairman of 
the Walgreen Co. The professorship will be funded by a pledge 
of $1.5 million by Walgreen’s three children.

Study shows value of Couponing 


NEW YORK — Consumers are using more coupons to 
make their dollars stretch further in the poor economy. A new 
study by NCH Promotional Services, a Chicago-based mar- 
keting firm, showed that Americans are using cents-off cou- 
pons at record rates. For the first six months of 1992, the 
study showed that coupon use grew 10 percent and saved con- 
sumers about $2.3 billion on their grocery bills. If the trend 
continues, NCH predicts that consumers will save a record 
$4.7 billion this year.

By David Q. Mahler 

They came from far and 
wide to attend the third an- 
nual meeting of the National 
Association of the No-Name- 
Yet Club. 

“The what?” you ask. 

Well, it is not so much an 
association or a club. It is 
more of a fraternity of old 
friends, most of whom are 
now retired, who worked in 
the chain drug store vine- 
yards for 25 to 40 years. They 
are still looking for a more 
formal, fussy name—one 
whose acronym scans a little 
easier than NANNYC—but 
they are in no rush to find it. 

Some 21 members of the 
group, together with 
ge met last month at 
the Chatman Bars Inn on 
Cape Cod to share memories, 
tell tales of children and 
grandchildren, and talk of 
their travels, their golf 
scores, their aches and pains 
and what they are doing now. 

But besides reveling in 
friendship, the group has a se- 
rious side: to use the extensive 


management experience resi- 
dent in the group to do pro 
bono work with small busi- 
nesses, helping them to im- 
prove their management and 
operational skills. 

Wally McCurdy, former 
sales manager of Bristol-My- 
ers who also served as a dean 
of Fordham Graduate School 
of Business, is taking the lead 
in coordinating the group’s 
activities. 


Still going strong 


Although they’ve collec- 
tively accumulated almost as 
many years of work experi- 
ence as Methuselah lived, this 
is a youthful group, most of 
whom are still active in one 
business or another.

them are doing:

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 23, 1992 


This is a particularly special issue of the year be- 
cause it addresses the winning business practices 
shared by so many Retail Excellence Award winners. 

Large doses of perseverance and vision helped these 
companies and executives perform so impressively this 
past year that they earned industrywide ballotting, and 
were honored at a recent Drug Store News REX night 
at the Tatou restaurant in New York City. 

Festivities were pre- 


ceded by an afternoon of 
timely business sessions: 
a panel discussion on ev- 
eryday low pricing led by 
David Mahler, former edi- 
torial director at Lebhar- 
Friedman, who drew out 
incisive comments by pan- 
elists David Morocco of 
Brooks Drug, Terry Files of Rockbottom and consul- 
tant Win Weber. 

In separate presentations, Paco Underhill of Envir- 
osell, N.Y., spoke about how in-store environments 
affect shopper behavior and traffic flow, and Dan 
O’Connor of Management Ventures, Cambridge, 
Mass., discussed category management. 

The night belonged to the retailer, wholesaler and 
supplier award winners. The major awards went to: 
@ Large Drug Chain of the Year: F&M Distributors, 
an off-price pioneer that recently surpassed the 100- 
store mark and $700 million in annual sales. 

@ Regional Drug Chain of the Year: Big B, which has 
posted record earnings its past six quarters and has 
stuck through the most trying of times following a 
tragic plane crash in which family members and key 
company executives perished. 

@ Wholesaler of the Year: Drug Guild, the largest 
wholesaler in the N. Y.-N.J.-Conn. area, known for its 
tailored programs and broad offerings. 

@ Chain Design Format of the Year: Walgreens, for 
its prototype which upgrades cosmetics, expands 
greeting cards and refines many years of merchandis- 
ing study. 

@ Chain Drug Marketer of the Year: James Mastrian, 
executive vp of marketing at Revco, regarded as a 
driving force in that chain’s revitalization and emer- 
gence from bankruptcy. 

® Combo of the Year: Albertson’s, operator of 600 
stores in 19 states, aiming at 800 by 1996, with an in- 
creasing emphasis on pharmacy and HBC. 

More REX coverage begins on page 29. Kudos to all.

Congratulations to all the REX winners 


The following two letters were sent to Drug Store 
News regarding the REX awards: 


Dear Editor: 

I'd like to thank you for the honor of being named 
Drug Chain Marketer of the Year. 

I have always felt that personal performance alone 
does not produce results. This award symbolizes the 
dedication of the Revco organization and its suppliers 
working toward a single purpose. 

Everybody—our marketing staff, our store organi- 
zation and our vendors overcame a lot of adversity this 
past year. And to be recognized for our successes by. 
Drug Store News makes this award very special. 

Revco, today, is an exciting company. It is a compa- 
ny driven to be a leader and innovator within the chain 
drug industry. It is a company with a well-defined 
strategy for the future. I am proud to be a part of this 
outstanding organization. I am also proud to be associ- 
ated with so many fine companies and individuals in 
our industry. I can’t think of any honor more humbling 
than being recognized by key industry executives. 

The REX Marketer of the Year is the highlight of 
my many years in the chain drug industry. My sincere 
thanks to you and to Drug Store News. 

James P. Mastrian, R.Ph., sr. vp, Revco 


Dear Editor: 

Special thanks for once again including the fight 
against multiple witveu on the agenda of your spe- 
cial REX Awards evening. It is an honor and a privi- 
lege to be a part of such a wonderful event. 

Our appreciation is not only for the generous finan- 
cial support that you, Lehhar-Friedman, and so many 
of your industry’s leaders provide to our work, we are 
also tremendously grateful for the time that you give 
us to share our message with all of the good friends of 
Drug Store News who you assemble for the evening. 
It is an enormous asset for us to have access to that 
special forum to let people know a little more about 
this often misunderstood disease. 

As always, you did an absolutely spectacular job with 
the awards. Because the room was so cozy this year, 
there seemed to be a tremendous warmth and camara- 
derie among all of those attending, which must be a won- 
derful asset for the industry. Congratulations on anoth- 
er terrific event—and many, many thanks for 
continuing to include us. 

Carol M. Kurzig, executive director

Next to George Bush, the biggest loser in this year’s 
elections just might be the pharmaceutical industry. 

Here in Washington, brand name drug manufactur- 
ers have become accustomed to frequent broadsides 
from Congress. But next year, with Bill Clinton in the 
White House, they’ll be on the receiving end of some 
major-league bashing from the Administration, too. 


Clinton has made no secret of his disdain for the way 

the pharmaceutical indus- 
try prices its products. 
During the campaign he 
vowed to end manufactur- 
er “drug price gouging” 
by taking away the indus- 
try’s carrots and replacing 
them with sticks. 

For openers, the Presi- 
dent-Elect will support proposals by his home state 
senator, David Pryor (D-Ark.), to eliminate federal 
tax breaks for pharmaceutical companies that raise 
drug prices faster than incomes of American workers. 
Clinton has also voiced support for schemes to pres- 
sure pharmaceutical manufacturers to reduce spend- 
ing on product marketing and divert the “savings” to

Tougher controls of drug prices ahead 


research and development. 

There’s no telling how far Clinton’s new federal 
board of health regulators will push the drug industry, 
but there’s little doubt that key Congressional Demo- 
crats will be demanding outright government controls 
over pharmaceutical prices. 

House Health Subcommittee Chairman Henry 
Waxman (D-Calif.), for one, has already called for the 
United States to follow Canada’s lead in bringing 
down prescription drug prices through tougher regu- 
lation of the pharmaceutical industry. 

A General Accounting Office study conducted for 
Waxman found that the prices charged to drug whole- 
salers in the United States on more than 100 of the na- 
tion’s most widely prescribed drugs average 32 per- 
cent higher than in Canada. | 

Look for Waxman to hold hearings early next year 
on why Americans must pay more for drugs than con- 
sumers in other countries. 

But suppose President Clinton taps his fellow Ar- 
kansan for a key role in his new Administration? The 
industry could wake up one morning to find David 
Pryor at the controls of a Clinton health care steam- 
roller as Secretary of Health and Human Services!

Among the other baking 
soda introductions of late is one 
from CCA. Known for its anti- 
stain/whitener products, CCA 


introduced its Plus+ White 
Baking Soda Toothpaste this 
spring (along with its new Plus- 
+ White Anti-stain Fluoride 
Toothpaste and Gel). 

It’s no surprise that drug 
chains are adding baking soda 
formulas to their — label 
offerings. Arbor Drug’s Mar- 
kus Ernst says the chain’s pri- 
vate label baking soda tooth- 
paste “is doing very well.” 


Beyond baking soda 


For decades, dentists have 
recommended the oral care 
home remedy of baking soda 
and hydrogen peroxide. 

Mentadent, a “two-phase” 
hydrogen peroxide and baking 
soda toothpaste, is pump deliv- 
ered from two separate cham- 
bers so the chemical reaction 
doesn’t occur before applica- 
tion. Currently it’s being tested 
in the New England market. 

Gary Fraser, marketing 
manager of oral care for Che- 
sebrough, says “We are trying 
to meet a consumer need by 
providing baking soda and hy- 
drogen peroxide in a conve- 
nient system with fluoride and 
great taste.” The premium- 
price a provides mar- 
gins of 25-30 percent. 

A similar new product with 
fluoride is Zila’s PeriGel, 
which is being tested in 11 
western states and in Eckerd 
stores in the Southeast. 

PeriGel comes in a single 
box with two tubes and the 
consumer applies equal 


amounts on the toothbrush. 
One of the first new forms 
since gel is Check-Up Liquid 
Fluoride Toothpaste, intro- 
duced this summer, which 
claims faster dispersal. It also 
comes in a new t of dis- 
penser, a squeeze-bottle de- 
signed to maximize facings 
due to its squared design. 


Several alternatives 


There’s no data yet on mar- 
riages saved by avoiding 
toothpaste tubes, but consum- 
ers now have several alter- 
nate delivery forms includin 
pumps, stand-up tubes aa 
the neat squeeze. Tubes still 
lead the pack with 83.1 per- 
cent, down fractionally as a 
format but up in dollars since 
high-ticket specialty denti- 
frice is mainly in tubes so far. 

Crest’s neat squeeze and 
new stand-up tubes from Col- 
gate and Check-Up mean less 
outer packaging while gravity 
assists the consumer in get- 
ting out the last drops. Col- 
gate will repiace pumps in fa- 
vor of the stand-up tube, says 
Colgate’s Nigel Burton, add- 
ing “We wanted to make a 
very proactive point about 
what we thought this new 
product would do.” 

When partnering with re- 
tailers, he notes, it’s impor- 
tant to “improve category 

rofitability, making sure that 

KUs don’t just proliferate. 
When reasonable, you should 
offer replacement.’ 


Retailers are banking on whiter teeth 


Consumers want whiter 
teeth and they’re willing to 
pay for it. Michele Arnault of 

cKesson reports that “peo- 

le are trading up to Rem- 
aon It has a professional 
recommendation, and because 
it doesn’t have hydrogen per- 
oxide, people are using it. It 
appeals to baby boomers who 
can afford to pay $5.99-$7.99 
to look better.” 

The technical difference be- 
tween anti-stain toothpaste 
and teeth whiteners is lost on 
most a Rembrandt 
Whitening Toothpaste, with its 
anti-stain ingredient citroxain, 
is broadcasting the safety mes- 
sage to consumers, reassuring 
them with its upbeat ad cam- 

aign,and has even added a new 

avor. Like Oral-B’s Indicator 
ae such visibility can 
boost the whole category. 


Different approaches 


While an increasing number 
of anti-stain products are posi- 
tioning as a complete denti- 
frice s adding fluoride and 
promoting daily use—like 
Check-Up Zact Stain Control 
Wieesiie Wants cthers, 
like Topol Smokers Tooth- 
paste and Caffree, stick to 
their specialties. 


Some manufacturers have 
diversified. This summer, 
Natural White, which offers 
the three-step teeth-whiten- 
ing system, added Natural 
White Whitening Toothpaste 
to its line. This fall, it intro- 
duced Old Farmer’s Almanac 
Baking Soda Toothpaste. 


Whitener issue cools off 


The “whitener” issue has 
cooled off since the FDA flur- 
ry of recent months, when 
whiteners with hydrogen per- 
oxide were first challenged as 
unapproved new drugs rather 
than cosmetics. 

FDA spokesperson Mike 
Shaffer told Drug Store News 
that the FDA recently issued 
letters to around a dozen teeth 
whitener manufacturers, noti- 
fying them that it is permissi- 
ble to market their products 
(the kind with hydrogen per- 
oxide) until a final determina- 
tion had been made. “It’s an 
ga age lag thing,” said 
Shaffer. “The agency is going 
to be somewhat taking a wait- 
and-see kind of attitude. 
There really isn’t enough evi- 
dence to make it go one way or 
the other.” 

“We hope to pick up the 
pace we had before the FDA 


” 


started its campaign,” says 
Ira Berman, chairman of 
CCA, maker of Plus+ White 
one-step gel and three-step 
(rinse, gel and toothpaste). 
“For a while, we laid low—we 
really stopped advertising. 
Now we're going back on TV. 
We didn’t think there was a 
problem to begin with. The 
consumer will realize that if 
it’s on TV, then it’s alright.” 

Dep has also taken an ag- 
SS position with = na- 
tional ad campaign in August 
for Topol Mega White. 

Other teeth whitener manu- 
facturers are marketing more 
ee naively now that the 
FDA seems to be backing off, 
but the term “whitener” is be- 
ing downplayed. 

ental Concepts’ Stay 
White—which has new up- 
scale pen with red and 
gold foil and is promoting its 
safety benefit to consumers— 
is promoting the benefit of 
unique cleansing action. “We 
don't have to use this termin- 
ology, but we think it’s more 
comfortable,” said Dental 
Concepts Econ rson Gene 
Wagner. “We’re changing our 
position. It’s still maximum 
whiteness but we're getting 
away from ‘whitening.

@ At last, the Health Care Fi- 
nancing Administration has 
issued “Interim Final Rules” 
to implement OBRA 90 with 
less than two months remain- 
ing before pharmacists will be 
required to comply with new 
Medicaid patient counseling 
and DUR requirements. 

In translating the new fed- 
eral regulations for state 
Medicaid agencies, HCFA 
stressed that “ancillary per- 
sonnel may make the offer to 
counsel,” and may also “col- 
lect, record, and obtain pa- 
tient profile information.” 
The dhatcanbiat, however, 
must personally counsel 
Medicaid patients who re- 

uest it, and must personally 
“review and interpret patient 
profile information.” 

Each state will decide 
whether pharmacists may use 
written materials to extend 
the offer to counsel, but the 
federal rules make it clear 
that “the content of the coun- 
seling is governed solely by 
the professional judgment of 
the pharmacist.” 


® President-elect Bill Clinton 
vows to “stop drug price goug- 
ing’ by pharmaceutical man- 
ufacturers by eliminating 
federal tax breaks for manu- 
facturers who raise drug 
prices faster than the rise in 
income for American work- 
ers. Clinton also plans to dis- 
courage pharmaceutical 
firms from spending more on 
marketing than R&D. For 
more on how the Clinton Ad- 
ministration will impact phar- 
macy, see “The Clinton Pre- 
scription,” page 76. 


Age of counseling 
Stirs design changes 


pharmacy facelift is now underway at chains and inde- 
pendents. Patient and pharmacist interaction and the 
counseling requirements of OBRA ’90 are the driving forces 
behind a nationwide pharmacy redesign effort that repre- 
sents a significant shift in how we will communicate with pa- 
tients. Cover story begins on page 15.

have to rely on sexual lubricants.

cists now have something the 
can recommend that doesnt 
carry the stigma of a sex aid and

pause or post-menopause, 
nursing mothers and women

HSI taps Urquhart 
as vp-marketing 


CINCINNATI — Former Wellby Super 
Drug Stores president Margaret Urquhart 
has joined Hook-SupeRx Inc. as corporate 
vp-marketing, a new post which reflects 
the growing consolidation of the two drug 
chains. 

Urquhart will have overall corporate re- 
sponsibility for marketing, advertising and 
buying, and will report to Michael Moore, 
senior vice president and chief operations of- 
ficer. In addition, she will serve on HSI’s ex- 
ecutive management committee. 

Urquhart will also be in charge of — ng the company’s fu- 
ture marketing organization, Moore said. 

The executive comes to HSI after a long career at the 
Weliby division of Hannaford Brothers. She rose through the 
ranks as store manager, general merchandise buyer, director 
of merchandising and director of advertising before taking 
the top spot at Wellby in 1989.

Walgreens’ 300th in Florida 


surpasses Illinois count 


TAMPA — Walgreens opened its 
300th Florida store with little fanfare, 
but customers in the neighborhood 
where it opened certainly noticed. 

An almost unheard of 100 prescrip- 
tions were filled the first day the store 
was open and that volume is expected 
to grow, according to pharmacist Mar- 
guerite Reghanti. Walgreens encour- 
aged the transfer of prescriptions by 
placing on the pharmacy and cosmetics 
counters flyers explaining the transfer 
process. An exterior sign also promot- 
ed prescription transfers. 

e new store, a freestanding unit in 
an established neighborhood, is char- 
acteristic of the chain’s attitude to- 
ward expansion. Walgreens hopes to 
open 145 stores in 1993 and as many as 
200 a year by 1997. To accommodate 
that aggressive expansion, more free- 
standing units are being built since 
there aren’t adequate retail centers 
under development. 

Recent years have seen Walgreens 
expand rapidly in Florida. Since 1990, 
the retailer has added 30 stores in 
Florida. Illinois is now number two in 
terms of store count with 297 stores. 
However, a company spokesman said 
Illinois will probably have 300 stores 
by February or March of 1993. 

Despite Walgreens’ rapid expansion 
in Florida, the Sunshine State is still 
home to Jack Fickerd Corp. Eckerd has 
about 535 Florida stores.

Publix elbows into Atlanta market 


ATLANTA — It’s a face-off 
of two different shopping 
hing ct Will consumers 

ere trade low prices offered 
by Winn Dixie, Big Star and 

ub Foods for the pleasurable 
shopping experience empha- 
sized by Publix? 

Shoppers have that choice 
now, with Publix having 
opened its second store here 
and with plans for another 50 
Southeastern sites in the com- 
ing decade. 

e 400-store chain is also 
negotiating for a 200-acre site 
on the outskirts of Atlanta 
where a distribution center 
will be built. Its opening is 
scheduled for late 1994. Publix 
officials wouldn’t comment on 
the chain’s expansion outside 


Florida, but the combo opera- 
tor clearly will weigh response 
to its service-skewed format 
here before expanding 
throughout the Southeast. 

“Publix has attractive store 
formats, so [it is] probably go- 
ing to get [its] share of busi- 
ness,” said Lee Wilder, a su- 
permarket analyst with 
Atlanta-based Robinson- 
Humphry Co. “[It is] not going 
to market the stores on the 
competitiveness of its HBC 
prices. [It is] going to market 
them on freshness, presenta- 
tion and selection. Then, while 
[it has] people in the store, [it] 
will get them to- meander 
down the HBC aisle and back 
to the pharmacy.” 

Publix has been adding and 


building stores with pharma- 
cies since 1986 and now has 66. 
The Atlanta expansion is a 
big step for Publix and one 
it hopes to finance with in- 
ternal funds and through the 
leasing of stores. Publix has 
seen sales increase to more 
than $6 billion in 1991 from 
$3.85 billion in 1987. During 
the same time period, net 
earnings increased from about 
$90 million to $160 million. 
The new Savannah, Ga., 
Publix store sits across the 
street from a similarly sized 
65,000-square-foot Kroger that 
opened a year ago, said a local 
source, who noted the two com- 
petitors slug it out for market 
share by tempting customers 
with triple coupon promotions. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, December 14, 1992 


OPINION 


The O’Hare Expo Center in Chicago was a hotbed 
of retail activity in recent weeks, as more than 1,500 
buyers and chain execs swooped to the Private La- 
bel Championship Trade Show in unprecedented 
numbers. 

“They’re pumped about private label prospects. It’s 
an optimism based on fact,” PLMA president Brian 
Sharoff told me. 

On their minds: use of 


private label as a strate- 
gic weapon to rebuild 
gross profit dollars erod- 
ed by the economy, in- 
tensified trade class com- 
petition and the loss of 
trade allowances due to 
manufacturer introduc- 
tions of everyday low 
price (EDLP) programs. 

As merchandise which retailers totally control, 
private label is a malleable tool that chain brains are 
promoting, pricing and assorting smarter—while 
largely raising the overall quality of their lines. Re- 
tailers are growing more astute about how store 
brands give them a competitive edge and a clear 
point of distinction. 

Coverage on pages 2 and 6 of this issue reflect the 
increasing importance of private label and the more 
sophisticated tactics needed to market it effectively 
today. Note especially the PLMA research study on 
“The Future of Store Brands: The Retail Perspec- 
tive,” conducted by Willard Bishop Consulting, Bar- 
rington, Ill., and Model Resources, Syosset, N.Y. 
Bishop presented major findings at the show, but 
PLMA will make the full report available this month. 

This show is always a great time to catch up with 
chain presidents and chairmen to discuss trade issues 
and challenges. To better relate what’s on the minds of 
these top execs and protect their identities, [’ll syn- 
thesize their comments here. What they say is worth 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


Store brands & strategy on execs’ minds 


considering, as it speaks to future viability of the drug 
trade class: 

e “The U.S. population will grow 2-5 percent in the 
next 10 years, but ethnic groups 15-20 percent a year.” 
This speaks to the need for store-specific marketing to 
meet the needs of diverse neighborhoods, even within 
the same general trading areas. 

@ “What will hapyen to drug stores when pharmacy 
inflation of 15 percent a year ends? The new guy in the 
White House will end that.” Chains are increasingly 
vulnerable when pharmacy drives sales dispropor- 
tionately, especially with third-party pressures erod- 
ing margins. 

@ “New OBRA regulations are eating up productivi- 
ty in pharmacy. We just invested in state-of-the-art 
pharmacy computers, and now we have to spend an- 
other $250,000 to upgrade software. We’re obsolete 
according to OBRA. That’s just dollars flying out 
the door.” Drug chains will grapple with OBRA 
compliance as the screws tighten on the heart of 
their business. 

e “What are drug stores doing going up to 35,000 
and 40,000 square feet? So they get 82-foot aisles 
and 42 feet of hosiery. Shoppers have changed. They 
want value. If you have a smaller-store formula that 
works and you have to get growth numbers, many 
fall into the trap of making stores larger to grow 
sales. What happens when the new or expanded cat- 
egories fail to produce?” 

@ “There’s no such thing as a level playing field. They 
[Procter & Gamble] sneeze and everybody else has a 
cold. Why don’t they have EDLP on everything, not 
just on brands where they have to compete with pri- 
vate label?” 

@ From a wholesale club exec: “We start looking at 
private label in a category when it accounts for about a 
20 percent national share. Nineteen percent of our 
shoppers buy private label; it accounts for 9.5-10 per- 
cent of our total SKUs, 30 percent of gross profit in 
sundries and 23 percent in HBA.” 


_Pharmacy execs torn on 


Optimistic pharmacy leaders expect the new OBRA 
’90 Medicaid Drug Use Review/Patient Counseling re- 
quirement to open new opportunities for pharmacists. 

Once OBRA ’90 takes effect on Jan. 1, they believe 
that third-party payors in and out of government will be 
forced to recognize that pharmacists who counsel pa- 
tients on drug use, maintain detailed patient profiles and 
perform DUR screens before filling each prescription 
will measurably enhance 


therapeutic outcomes and 
reduce health care costs. 
The next step, they be- 
lieve, will be for third-par- 
ty payors to encourage 
even more pharmacist-pa- 
tient communication by 
reimbursing pharmacy 
practitioners for cognitive 


KEN RANKIN 


services. 

That may well happen. Someday. 

But no one in the drug store industry who has read 
the Health Care Financing Administration’s new “in- 
terim” final rules implementing OBRA ’90 has any 
reason to be optimistic. 

If anything, the HCFA’s long-delayed regulations 
confirm the worst suspicions of OBRA ’90 critics who 
have been warning that these new Medicaid DUR/pa- 
tient counseling requirements are going to be a costly 
new burden for pharmacy. ; 

According to the HCFA’s own “regulatory impact 
analysis” of the rules, “most of the work and responsi- 
bility for implementing a meaningful DUR program 
will fall upon the estimated 58,000 retail pharmacists 
in the U.S.” A lot of the out-of-pocket costs, too. 


OBRA ’90 issues 


New computer software programs capable of han- 
dling the extensive DUR and patient profiling chores 
mandated by new law will cost the “average pharmacy” 
between $1,000 and $2,000, according to the agency. 

If the store’s existing computer system is not so- 
phisticated enough to handle the new prospective 
DUR software, additional hardware may be neces- 
sary—at an “initial cost” to the pharmacy of $12,000 to 
$15,000, says the administration. | 

The counseling and profiling requirements of 
OBRA 1990 will also prove costly for pharmacists, ac- 
cording to HCFA officials. 

“Our best estimate is that making the offer to coun- 
sel, reviewing a patient profile and conducting coun- 
seling [exclusive of establishing a patient profile and 
interventions where the pharmacist takes an action 
such as telephoning the physician] could take two to 
four minutes at a cost of $1 to $2 per prescription.” 

But even if only one-fourth of the estimated 280 
Medicaid prescriptions dispensed annually require 
such a consultation, the cost of pharmacists’ time to 
provide these patient services could run as much as 
$140 million a year. 

The $140 million question for pharmacy is whether 
practitioners will be reimbursed for these services. 
The HCFA’s answer: don’t count on it. 

Although the cost of providing OBRA ’90 services 
“may result in pressure to raise dispensing fees,” there’s 
not much chance of that happening, the agency said. 

Indeed, the HCFA predicted that “given the cur- 
rent budget climate and the states’ likely resistance to 
granting [pharmacy reimbursement] increases, the 
net impact on Medicaid program expenditures is not 
expected to be large.”

Drug stores get bigger share 


Another key trend this year 
is that drug stores are captur- 
ing a larger share of last pur- 
chases for most of the items 
asked about. 

Comparing 1992 to 1991, 
more consumers report buy- 
ing an item in a drug store in 13 
of the 21 categories tracked. 

The survey cites a decline 
in purchaser activity in only 
six categories. 

The trend to shopping 
more in drug stores was par- 
ticularly strong for consum- 
ers buying men’s cologne. 
Over 30 percent of the re- 
spondents reported buying a 
men’s cologne in a drug store 
in 1992 compared to just 21 
percent in 1990. 

In the last few years, more 
and more drug stores have 
started to stock the more ex- 

ensive prestige men’s co- 
ognes like Polo and Drakkar 
Noir, and this is probably one 
of the main reasons why con- 
sumers are shifting their pur- 
chasing habits.

Survey 
methodology 


The 1992 Consumer Top 
Brands Survey is based on a 
national sampling of 1,000 
households. 

The sample is projectable 
to all households in the conti- 
nental U.S. who are tele- 
phone subscribers, whether 
or not their number is listed 
in the directory. 

The study was conducted 
over the telephone with the 
“chief shopper” in the house- 
hold. Interviews were done in 
July, 1992. 

Sampling error ranges 
from plus or minus 1 percent 
to plus or minus 3 percent.

Unfortunately, drug stores 
only capture a small part of 
these purchases. Just 25 per- 
cent of the women in this 

ear’s survey reported they 
last bought a lipstick from a 
drug store, not much change 
from the 26 percent who last 
reported making such a pur- 
chase back in 1990. 

By looking at the brands 
that the .ajority of women 
say they prefer using, one can 
see why it has been hard for 
drug stores to capture a larger 
share of the lipstick business. 

The most-preferred brand 
is Revlon—which is widely 
available in department and 
specialty stores as well as 
drug stores. 

The second most-favored 
brand is Avon—only available 
through direct door-to-door 
sales or a mail order catalog. 

This year, Cover Girl, May- 
belline and Estée Lauder all 
showed similar levels of popu- 
larity, but that isn’t great 
news for drug stores either. 

Cover Girl and Maybelline 
are in wide distribution, avail- 
able in food stores, discount 
department stores and in deep 
discount drug stores, where 
they are usually featured for a 
percent off their list price. 

Clinique, the sixth most-fa- 
vored brand, is a popular de- 
"plea store brand. Mary 

ay, ranked seventh, is a pop- 
ular door-to-door brand. 

It is clear that the lipstick 
category, which used to be 
much more exclusive to drug 
stores, has evolved into a mar- 
keting challenge. 

If drug stores want to grow 
their lipstick sales, they have 
to find new ways to attract the 
consumer. It may mean that 
drug stores will have to work 
harder to broaden their prod- 
uct mix to include more up- 
scale, department store 
brands, or it probably means 
they will have to offer the con- 
sumer more than just low 
prices to attract them. 

Today’s women are value 
conscious, but they also need a 
pick-me-up sometimes. When 
asked by Drug Store News re- 
porters and other research- 
ers, they say they want stores 
to be “fun” to shop. This 
means that products are dis- 
played imaginatively, that 
new products are constantly 
available, and that salespeo- 
ple are friendly and helpfui. 

Although these findings may 
disappoint chain drug store oP 
erators, new strategies could 
fortify their share. That can be 
expensive, however. But at 
ieast the findings give manag- 
ers a feeling for their options.

Retail drug and proprietary stores were slightly ahead of the average for all retail sales gains. 


| fs 


as 


Drug stores beat average retail gains 


n 1991, Americans were 

struggling through a 

tough year, and in 1992 
the U.S. Department of Com- 
merce’s tracking of U.S. retail 
salee trends says the situation 
is cata 

The U.S. Department of 
Commerce, Bureau of the 
Census, reports that U.S. re- 
tail sales, for the first half of 
1992, were up 4.3 percent to 
$920 billion, compared to a 
mere 0.9 percent gain for the 
first half of 1991. 

The strongest gains were 
racked . by the hardware 
and lumber retail industry, 
whose sales were up 9.4 per- 
cent for the first six months; 
auto dealerships, up 8.6 per- 
cent for the same period; and 
general merchandise stores, 
up 6.7 percent. 


Retail drug and proprietary 
stores were slightly ahead of 
the average for all retail sales 
gains. For the first six 
months, retail sales for drug 
and proprietary stores were 
up 4.9 percent compared to a 
4.3 percent rise for all U.S. re- 
tail sales. 

However, drug and propri- 
etary stores were able to gen- 
erate growth in the first half of 
the year because of inflation, 
which drove up the cost of 
both prescription and over- 
the-counter : 

The Bureau of Labor Statis- 
tics reported that prescription 
drugs were up 8.9 percent for 
the first half of 1992 while 
over-the-counter drugs were 
up 3.8 percent. 

Retail sales in food stores, 
for the first half, were up only 1 


percent, while volume in res- 
taurants and bars grew 4 per- 
cent. 

Inflation has been moderate 
in the food industry. The De- 
partment of Commerce re- 
ported that the cost of foods 
meant for home consumption 
was flat, up just 0.1 percent, 
while the cost of foods con- 
sumed away from home was 
only up 2.5 percent 

etail sales trends for the 
first half of 1992 seem to hold 
some encouraging news about 
the economy. Sales for some 
retailers of high-ticket dura- 
ble goods and general mer- 
chandise stores were up rath- 
er dramatically, 8.6 percent 
and 6.7 percent respectively, 


while sales for hardware and 
lumber retailers were up a 
hefty 9.4 percent.

Drug stores must stir up HBA sales 


hen Nielsen com- 
pares compound 
growth in HBA dol- 


lar sales by trade class, it ap- 
that the drug store in- 
ustry’s dependency on 
pharmacy as its core business 
seems to be hurting the indus- 
try’s ability to generate at- 
tractive growth in toiletry and 
remedial product sales. 

In all but one of the catego- 
ries in Nielsen’s HBA index, 
drug stores have underper- 
formed the industry in terms 
of dollar sales growth. 

This means that, in many 
HBA categories, the drug 
store industrv’s share of sales 
is, and has been, shrinking. 

Chain drug stores do bet- 
ter, but they still have not 


been able to grow sales in the 
HBA categories as aggres- 
sively as mass merchandisers 
‘have. 

Here’s an example. The 
five-year annual average per- 
cent change for skin care sales 
is 7.3 percent; with just a 6.5 
percent five-year annual aver- 
age increase, all drug stores 
were underachievers. Chain 
drug stores, on the other 
hand, did a better job, gener- 
ating an 8.6 percent five-year 
annual average. But mass 
merchandisers did an even 
better job, racking up a five- 
year average of 10.5 percent 
compound growth. 

In remedial products 
where drug stores should 
have a clear competitive ad- 


vantage, the five-year annual 
average growth for drug 
stores was only 5.1 percent 
compared to 8.2 percent for 
chain drug stores, and 13.7 
percent for mass merchandise 
stores. 

As the mass merchandise 
chains such as Kmart, Wal- 
Mart and Target continue to 
Saphire strong growth in 

BA categories, they contin- 
ue, of course, to expand their 
share of total HBA sales. 

For 1991, for example, mass 
merchandisers enjoyed a 12 
Sa cg increase in total HBA 

ollar sales while food stores 
squeaked by with a slim 1 per- 
cent increase, and drug stores 
were flat with a 0.3 percent in- 
crease.

Mass merchandisers have

percent per year.

increased 4.2 points from five 
years ago, and in 1991, their 
dollar share was up 1.7 points 
from the year before.

ear. Their dollar sales share

Food store’s share 


Total HBA sales in food 
stores were up 1.1 percent in 
1991 vs. 1990. Over the past 
five years, HBA sales have in- 
creased 20 percent, an average 
rate of 3.8 percent per year. 

Food store’s 1991 share of 
HBA dollar sales is down 0.8 
— from the prior year. 

eir HBA sales share has de- 
creased 2.7 points from five 
years ago. 


Share sales trends

industry's share of the catego- 
ry sales measured declines a 
few points for almost every 
segment. Mass merchandis- 
ers’ share, on the other hand, 
continues to grow. 

For 1991, out of the 42 prod- 
uct segments measured, drug 
stores lost share on 25.

sales go down and as dollar 
sales grow soft, drug stores 
find it harder and er to at- 
tract the traffic that helps them

American’s Maher wins retailer award 


American Store chairman David L. Maher has been 
named 1992 Retailer of the Year by California State Universi- 
ty’s Institute of Retail Management. Maher is a member of the 

ational Association of Chain Stores board of directors, 
where he also serves on its executive committee. 

The award is presented each year to an individual whose re- 
cord of achievement and integrity serves as a model for young 
people entering the retail industry.

beat the recession: 
Sales up 7 percent 


NEW YORK — Chain drug stores increased - 
their bottom line by 10-12 percent in 1992, . 
NACDS chairman Harvey Rosenthal reported 
at an NACDS press conference here last month. 

Rosenthal estimated that total industry 
sales will be nearly $52 billion for 1992, an in- 
crease of 7 percent over the previous year. 

In the days ahead, he said chain drug stores 
will continue to stress their “core strengths of 
pharmacy, service and consumer convenience. 

Rosenthal said the industry has been re- 
sponding to the recent economic challenges by 
continuing to institute new systems “to keep us 
on the cutting edge of retailing in America, 


even in recessionary times. 


“This year saw greater emphasis on chain 
drug store companies investing their resources 
in ways to enhance operations. These range 
from store remodeling to new electronic sales 
tracking systems, and to inventory control and 


patient profile systems.

Hook-SupeRx consolidating 
data processing operations 


INDIANAPOLIS — Hook- 
SuperRx Inc. (HSI) has be- 
gun to consolidate all of its 
data processing into a single 
location in Lexington, Ky. 

The 1,150 store chain, which 
operates stores under the 
names Hooks, SupeRx and 
Brooks, has signed a 10-year 
services agreement with The 
Integrated Systems Solutions 
Corporation (ISSC), a wholly 
owned subsidiary of IBM. 

The agreement provides for 
outsourcing HSI’s data pro- 
cessing operations to ISSC 


and the implementation of an 
IBM point-of-sale system 
within all HSI stores. 

Undex the agreement, ISSC 
will consolidate HSI’s three 
data processing centers in Indi- 
anapolis, Cincinnati and Paw- 
tucket, R.I. into a single center 
located in Lexington. 

Consolidation and migra- 
tion of the data center opera- 
tions is expected to be com- 
pleted by the fall of 1993. 

In addition, SupeRx is hav- 
ing ISSC install and maintain 
an IBM 4780 point-of-sale sys- 


tem in each of its stores. 

HSI plans to develop what a 
source called “advance infor- 
mation programs” to better im- 
plement marketing tactics and 
strategy through use of its POS 
technology. Joseph Benario, 
ISSC’s director of marketing, 
said using the IBM POS system 
will enable HSI to immediately 
use “existing POS technology 
to develop advanced uses.” 

HSI stores are located in 
22 states, but their primary 
markets are in the Didwedt 
and Northeast.

and Rock Bottom. But he says 
the settlement is so financially 


exorbitant that Rite Aid “can’t 
even consider signing it.” 
“Local 1199 is taking a total- 
ly unrealistic position in an at- 
tempt to strongarm the drug- 
store industry in New York 
City. This action is an attempt 
to coerce the company with a 
media campaign comprised of 
half truths, out-right false- 
hoods and emotional appeals 
designed to disguise the 
union’s true objectives.” 
Some months ago, the union 
began boycotting Rite Aid 
stores in select regional mar- 
kets; now union leader Mike 
Rifkin—who’s also chairman 
of the National Rite Aid Boy- 
cott Committee—says it’s es- 
calating the boycott to include 
a print campaign, radio an- 
nouncements in select mar- 
kets like New York, Philadel- 
phia and Baltimore and a 
national mailing to 6,000 cler- 
gymen and political leaders. 
Rifkin says the actions were 
triggered by Rite Aid’s “unilat- 
eral decision to reduce health 


care benefits to a group of its 
employees following a year in 
which [its] profits increased 16 
percent to $124 million.” 

Souder says the union’s as- 
sertion that Rite Aid plans to 
reduce benefits for its New 
York City employees is a 
“bold, bald-faced lie.” 

Rite Aid spokes**oman Su- 
zanne Mead says the boycott so 
far has had absolutely “no im- 
pact” on Rite Aid stores. She 
says that the 115 members of 
Local 1199 “do not support the 
boycott action. They are not on 
strike, and in fact have been 
working without a contract 
since October 1991.” She adds 
that Rite Aid has no outstand- 
ing disputes with any other 
unions. “Our employees have 
refused to go on firike. which 
leaves the union with limited 

ining power, which is 
probably why they have de- 
cided to escalate the boycott.” 

Souder says Rite Aid has no 
immediate plans to counter 
the media campaign. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, January 4, 1993 


OPINION 


More than ever, the marketplace dictates that our 
drug chain readers be armed with as much detailed 


product information as we can uncover. Surveys tell 


us that our trade class—beset by competition from 
discounters, combos and wholesale clubs—needs to 
judge new products with savvy; carve-out high identi- 
ty areas for hot categories; assess planograms often to 
make the most of their relatively small shelf space; and 

create excitement about 


the products they sell to 
build incremental sales. 
They need to be super- 
productive merchants be- 
cause their stores are 


AL HELLER 
petitors, they aren’t 


treated as primary outlets 
by certain manufacturers, 
and they need to stem their share slippage in many 
front-of-store categories. 

All of which brings us to this, our first issue of 1993. 
On pages 15 and 16, we launch one component of our 
intensified product coverage: New Product Watch, 
drawn up exclusively for Drug Store News by Towne- 
Oller, a subsidiary of Information Resources, Inc. 
This will be a regular feature showing the impact of 
new items on specific core categories. The way we pre- 
sent the information will help readers cut through the 
data mass quickly and identify the vital must-haves 
- that drive categories. 

Throughout the year, Nielsen and IRI will pro- 
vide us with unique tables on category and item per- 
formance, the effectiveness of promotions, trade 
class share trends, and the purchase pattern of var- 
ied demographic groups. We value our special rela- 
tionships with both companies and will work togeth- 
er with each to bring our readers current, actionable 
data to help them manage categories and their busi- 
nesses better. 

Moreover, our team of veteran staff editors is now 
charged with category management responsibil- 
ities. They’ll bring to category coverage the same 
expertise and enthusiasm as they’ve shown in re- 


smaller than most com-- 


New products get fresh charge at DrSN 


porting news. We’ll be as vigorous in our coverage of 
significant new items as in our reports of mergers, 
profits and prototypes. 

Our staff editors will speak regularly with manu- 
facturers, wholesalers, and distributors even more 
so than before to gain a truly balanced perspective 
on category dynamics: intros, promotions, buying, 
pricing and packaging trends, test markets, and re- 
gional differences. Our staff will continue to speak 
often, of course, with chain merchandising execu- 
tives, wich the goal from this broad contact being to 
become highly useful information sources for our 
readers. 

We intend for our trade communications to be 
valuable information exchanges. Far more than us 
calling to probe about any single source’s particular 
business, we believe we best serve the trade when 
we share specifics such as new product launches, a 
discounter’s health and beauty aids strategy, a com- 
bo’s merchandising approach in cosmetics, or a 
wholesale club’s venture into pharmacy or private 
label. 7 

We feel deeply that we are partners in this trade, 
and one of our major goals as editors is to enhance the 
competitiveness of drug store operators through the 
rapid dispatch of useful information. 

We want our trade executives to be involved with 
us, to know they can call and get a knowledgeable 
opinion from our category management editors. 

They are: : 

@ Toiletries—Barbara White in New York (212) 756- 
5231. 

@ Pharmacy—Dianne Tharp in Tampa (813) 664-6946. 
@ OTCs—Mike Troy in Tampa (818) 664-6946. 

® General merchandise—Allene Symons in Los Ange- 
les (213) 464-8321. — 

@ Consumable/environmental/technology—Jim 

Frederick in Cleveland (216) 642-3420. 

We all look forward to greater exchanges with the 
trade on products. As the wisest chain presidents 
have told me, “No cash registers ever ring at head- 
quarters.” Know that we’re here for you, and this is 
one front we can shore up together. 


What can the drug store industry expect from the 
incoming Clinton Administration? That remains to be 
seen, but retail pharmacy won’t get anything unless it 
asks for it. Here’s what chains and independents alike 
should be demanding from the Clintonites: 

@ A health care reform plan guaranteeing patients ac- 
cess to the community pharmacy of their choice. Clin- 
ton has pledged that during his first 100 days in office 
he will advance legislation 


to extend health care cov- 
erage to all Americans. 
However that program 
develops, it should cover 
out-patient prescription 
drugs; it should offer con- 
sumers the right to select 
the pharmacy of their 
choice; and it should offer 
all pharmacies an opportunity to participate on an 
equal basis. 

@ A more equitable approach to third-party pharmacy 
reimbursement. Although pharmacists are being 
asked to provide costly and time-consuming new DUR 
and patient counseling services under the new OBRA 
90 rules, federal Medicaid officials have made no pro- 
vision to ensure that pharmacy reimbursement levels 
are adjusted to reflect these new duties. Worse yet, 
Medicaid drug program officials in many states are 
itching to reduce the already inequitable pharmacy re- 
imbursement levels as soon as the OBRA moratorium 
on such cuts expires in 1994. This situation is a ticking 


A Clinton wish list from drug stores 


time bomb that the Clinton Administration must ad- 
dress quickly. 

@ A new system offering pharmacy incentives to help 
hold down health care costs. Bill Clinton recognizes 
that runaway health costs are threatening to bank- 
rupt the nation—it’s important that he also recognize 
that pharmacists can play a pivotal role in helping to 
reduce the cost of health care. It’s time, too, for Wash- 
ington to recognize the simple logic of reimbursement 
incentives that encourage pharmacists to enhance 
therapeutic outcomes. 

@ A recognition that government over-regulation can 
kill the industry’s ability to create jobs. Federally man- 
dated employee benefits, heavy-handed OSHA enforce- 


ment practices, costly new wage and hour require- - 


ments, and other well-intentioned initiatives often 
backfire on the people they are supposed to help. The 
best social program is the opportunity for a secure job. 
e An immediate end to intrusive FDA attempts to 
regulate the practice of pharmacy. Federal Food and 
Drug bureaucrats have no business interfering with 
the historic right of pharmacists to compound drugs, 
and the incoming Clinton health team should make 
that clear to FDA officials from Day 1. 

@ Aneconomic climate that encourages consumer con- 
fidence. They used to call the drug store industry “re- 
cession-proof,” but don’t sing that song to the chain 
and independent drug store operators who struggle to 
stay afloat in today’s chilly economic waters. No sus- 
tained recovery can take place until retail cash regis- 
ters start ringing.

6 


ew items are the life- 

blood of a product cate- 

gory. They drive sales, 
stimulate growth and create 
profit opportunities for both re- 
tailers and manufacturers. 

To understand how some 
recent new products are per- 
forming in several important 
beauty care categories, Drug 
Store News, working with food 
and drug store sales informa- 
tion data supplied by Towne- 
Oller & Associates—a subsidi- 
ary of Information Resources, 
Inc.—created two new types 
of product performance track- 
ing charts: category impact 
and category staying power. 

The first column shows 
how many months this prod- 
uct has been in the 43,000 
store data base as of July 
1992. The second column 
shows its rank within the cat- 
egory as of July 1992, and the 
third column shows what per- 
cent of other items within its 
category it outsold. 

The category impact charts 
are based on a 12-month rank- 
ing for new items added to the 
Towne-Oller data base be- 
tween July 1991 and March 
1992, with at least three 
months of activity in the drug 
store tracking service as of 
April 1992. They show how 
each of these products ranked 
for the 12-month period end- 
ing July 1992 in drug stores. 

he new products ranked in 
these charts have performed 
well enough to enter the ranks 
of the top 30 percent to 50 per- 
cent of all items in their re- 
spective categories. 

Our staying power catego- 
ry charts show how well 
these new products have 
been able to maintain the 
strength of their initial 
launch. They use Towne- 
Oller data to look at how new 
products performed for the 
three-month period between 
May 1992 and July 1992. 

If a new product ranks high- 
er in the three-month period 
than it did in the 12-month peri- 
od, it generally means that 
stores sold through their first 
shipments and are continuing 
to reorder. 

These charts identify those 
new products that achieved 
strong “trial” sales and now 
seem to be satisfying enough 
consumers that shoppers are 
i Sock these products. 

n very active categories 
such as bath, the staying pow- 
er charts show that most of the 
new items have improved in 
rank based on sales for the 
most recent three months vs. 
sales for the 12 months. 

You will also see some shifts 
as some products move up in 
rank and others fall off. These 
charts give those of us who 
study new products a chance 
to see how they compare to 
one another as time goes by.

to automatic restock system 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Moving to eliminate much of 
the guesswork in stocking its 
stores for the B-T-S season, 
Revco D.S. recently used the 
event to test its new automatic 
a eg system. 

e shift to computer-gener- 
ated reorders went relatively 
smoothly, raising hopes for a 
more profitable Christmas sell- 
Ing season. 

“The main difference: we 
didn’t have to physically order 
each school supply item, and 
the sellthrough was much bet- 
ter than last year,” said Ches- 
terland store manager Ron 
Maurer. “We came through 
with very few holes on our 
shelves.” 

The automated reorder 
system, one of the most ad- 


vanced reorder systems yet 
ectings or is based on daily 
sales data provided by Rev- 
co’s chainwide POS scanning 
capabilities. 

canners are linked directly 
with Revco warehouses and 
billing systems so that reor- 
ders on school supplies are 
automatically generated for 
any product based on actual 
sellthrough at the check- 
stands. Revco let the scanner 
system take over B-T-S in late 
summer. 

It has since converted other 
merchandise segments to 
automatic replenishment, in- 
cluding fragrances, tobacco 
and seasonals for Halloween 
and Christmas. The tests put 
Revco close to a true perpetu- 
al inventory system. 


Such a system is a goal for 
many drug chains as they con- 
vert to scanners and see’ to 
harness the product move- 
ment information that scan- 
ners provide. But few chains 
have come as close as Revco to 
eliminating the labor costs and 
guesswork involved in man- 
ually reordering inventory. 

“It’s a way to try to maxi- 
mize sales, grow a category 
and increase our sell- 
through,” said Jim Mastrian, 
senior vp of marketing. 

“The key point is that we 
weren't buried with merchan- 
dise that we later would have 
had to mark down... and 
ship back to the warehouse for 
redistribution,” said Maurer. 
“You're able to sellthrough 
what you have.” 


Thrifty plans to leave Arizona 


LOS ANGELES — Thrifty 
Corp. will sell or close its 18 
remaining stores in Arizona. 

“We do not have a time yet, 
but we have made the decision 
to leave the state,” said execu- 
tive vp of administration 
Chris Bement, who noted the 
Thrifty has not yet found buy- 
ers for the stores. 

Bement said Thrifty is still 
in the preliminary stage of ne- 
gotiation with a potential buy- 
er, which could result in the 
sale of either all, or a just a 
few, of its 18 Arizona stores. 

Most likely, some stores 
will be liquidated while others 
will be sold. “We prefer to 
have them sold, so initially we 
will try to sell as many as pos- 
sible,” he said. 

Like many of its competi- 
tors, Thrifty has found Arizo- 
na retailing a tough, low-mar- 

in business in recent years. 

hoenix, where most of its 
stores are clustered, has be- 
come arguably the most com- 
petitive and overstored drug 
and supermarket arena in the 
U.S., with a slew of powerful 


competitors waging war with 
ever-lower prices and ever-in- 
creasing numbers of outlets to 
choose from. 

The result has been a down- 
ward spiral on prices and 

oss margins that is squeez- 
ing even the best operators. 

‘Almost nobody is making 
money here now,” noted one 
combo store veteran of the 
Phoenix price wars recently. 
“I predict we'll see a lot of 
store closings here in the next 


year or two.” 

For Thrifty, the decision to 
leave Arizona also springs 
from company efforts to focus 
on core markets on the West 
Coast, where the chain retains 
the bulk of its stores and its 
most advantageous leases. 

That is where the company 
is concentrating its store re- 
models and marketing efforts 
since its buyout last fall by 
Leonard Green & Partners 
and inside managers.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 18, 1993 


OPINION 


Innovation will carry the drug store industry 
through its toughest competitive period ever, as it 
transforms operators in this trade class into more 
sophisticated users of technology, bolder and more 
precise marketers and more efficient distributors of 
merchandise. 

New directions taken by chains in recent months 
are cause for optimism in an adverse period marked 
by: Wholesale clubs, more 


efficient at reducing oper- 
ating costs, are price jab- 
bing drug stores without 
mercy in many markets; 
the nation’s most power- 
ful discounters are mak- 
ing great strides in ex- 
panding and enhancing 
their pharmacy and health 
and beauty aid operations; food/drug combos are 
steadily adding one-hour photo finishing, pharmacy 
and expanded cosmetics areas to their stores. 

And now pharmaceutical price increases—the en- 
gine that has driven much of drug chain sales gains in 
recent years—will slow to a near halt, as manufactur- 
ers seek to avoid President-elect Clinton’s anticipated 
price controls. 

Drug chain reaction will have to be fast and creative 
to assure continued growth in a tough marketplace. 
Pharmacy executives can look at new pharmacy ser- 
vices, OTCs, private label and other directions to ex- 
pand profits, as they maintain their dominant share of 
U.S. prescriptions filled. 

But upstairs executives have to be concerned on a 
broader scale. Operating at an extreme space disad- 
vantage to other trade classes, drug chains have 
largely abdicated a great deal of front-of-store busi- 
ness to competitors. 

In part, one could argue, their stand today is a re- 
action to what happened a decade ago when many 
drug stores went so wild with general merchandise 
that they risked losing their distinctive health care 
image. 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


Chain operators steer in new directions 


Today they’re trying to adopt a more moderate 
approach by focusing the bulk of their energies on a 
few highly important core categories: photo, statio- 
nery, cosmetics, greeting cards and, of course, 
health care. 

As NACDS president Ronald Ziegler and Perry 
Drug Stores ceo Jack Robinson stated strongly to me 
in two recent separate conversations, drug chains are 
well positioned just because pharmacy accounts for 
such a large share of their business. 

Indeed, Walgreens, the industry pacesetter, has 
said that it intends to generate 50 percent of its vol- 
ume from pharmacy within a few years. Many other 
chains are also in the 35 percent to 50 percent neigh- 
borhood. 

Still, ’'m glad to see innovations that help chains 
shore up other key areas, such as: 

@ Perry’s new and novel ad campaign that targets eth- 
nic consumers with brand name products made by 
general market suppliers as well as ethnic manufac- 
turers. VP-merchandising Stephen Lund expects the 
program to generate $10 in sales for every $1 invested 
in advertising. 

@ PayLess’s development of an in-house television net- 
work that is raising sales, lowering travel costs, mini- 
mizing computer downtime and data transmission prob- 
lems. It also makes staff training, CE lessons and 
merchandising videotapes immediate and interactive. 
@ Genovese’s recent commitment to electronic tax fil- 
ing for customers in all of its 98 stores in New York, 
New Jersey and Connecticut. VP-marketing Donald 
Gross expects the chain to file 5,000 to 10,000 returns 
in 19938. Filers can expect refunds within 10 to 17 days 
by using the service. 

@ Revco’s automatic order replenishment system, 
based on daily sales data provided by POS scanners 
chainwide, eliminates labor costs and inaccuracies 
that are part of manual reorders based on weekly 
shelf audits. It improves sellthrough and minimizes 
markdowns. 

Steps such as these are invaluable in heightening 
drug stores’ competitiveness. 


Twenty years ago, when Jimmy Hoffa and his 
Teamsters were unionizing the nation’s pharmacists, 
the NACDS would have never considered creating an 
organization to represent pharmacists employed by 
the nation’s chain drug stores. 

In those times, such a group would have been re- 
garded as a magnet for every malcontent working be- 
hind a chain prescription counter. 

. At best, it would offer a 


soapbox to pharmacists 
who—in those days—con- 
sidered retail practice to 
be a less than professional 
pursuit. 

At worst, an organiza- 
tion of employee pharma- 
cists might become the 
industry’s Trojan 
Horse—a vehicle for union activists to invade chain 
pharmacy. 

But that was then, and this is now. 

The NACDS is moving ahead full tilt to establish a 
“National Council of Chain Pharmacists” to represent 
the views of the more than 65,000 pharmacists who 
practice in chain drug stores. 

And if there’s any concern at the NACDS that the 
proposed new pharmacist group could somehow back- 
fire on the chain drug industry, it isn’t showing. 

What has changed in the past two decades? The role 
of the community pharmacist, for one thing. 

While academics and clinical pharmacists debate 
the murky intricacies of “pharmaceutical care,” 


WASHINGTON 
) PERSPECTIVE 


Council to give chain R.Ph.s a voice 


community pharmacists are making real inroads 
into improved “patient care” through computerized 
DUR screening techniques and pro-active counsel- 
ing iniatives. 

Today’s chain pharmacists are on the cutting edge 
of pharmacy practice. They don’t have to take a back 
seat to any segment of the profession. And that alone 
should justify the creation of a new organization that 
will reflect their views on professional issues. 

There are, however, other reasons why the time is 
ripe for an organization of chain pharmacy practitioners. 

According to the NACDS, chain pharmacists con- 
stitute the largest single branch of American pharma- 
cy. Today they total well over half of the nation’s 
112,000 community pharmacy practitioners. And 
nearly four of every 10 U.S. pharmacists practice in a 
chain setting. 

But while chain pharmacists constitute a plurality 
of the country’s pharmacy practitioners, they have 
been a silent plurality. 

Independent pharmacists have never been bashful 
about making their views known, while pharmacists 
in academic and clinical settings have long exercised a 
degree of influence over professional affairs that far 
exceeds their numbers. 


It’s high time that rank-and-file chain pharmacy 


practitioners have an opportunity to express their 
views on issues such as Medicaid patient counseling 
standards, the all-Pharm.D. degree, third-party pa- 
perwork and state pharmacy board rules. 

If it works the way it should, the new NACDS coun- 
cil will give chain pharmacists that opportunity.

nour Jan. 4, 1993 issue, Drug Store News introduced a new reader service: 
a series of new product performance charts based on food and drug store 
sales information data supplied by Towne-Oller & Associates, a subsidi- 
ary of Information Resources Inc. (IRI). Drug Store News worked closely 
with Towne-Oller to develop these charts because we know how important 
new products are to our readers. "6 
The life-blood of a product category, new items drive sales, stimulate 
growth and create profit opportunities for retailers and manufacturers. 
For each category, we have developed two performance charts: a category 
wae chart and a category staying power chart.

Towne-Oller data base between July 1991 through March 1992 with at least 
three months activity in the drug store tracking service as of April 1992. It 
shows how each of these products ranked for the 12-month period ending July 
1992 in drug stores.

the ranks of the top 30 to 50 percent of all items in their respective categories.

in the 43,000 store data base as of July 1992. The second column shows the 
item’s rank within the category as of Tube 1992, and the third column shows
