Walgreen stalks new 
market for blitzkrieg 
entry in mid-’90s 


CHICAGO — Walgreen Co. is preparing for an 
all-out assault on a major new market in the mid- 
1990s, president and chief operating officer L. 
Daniel Jorndt revealed at the company’s annual 
meeting of shareholders here Jan. 13. 

Walgreens is keeping a closed lid on the loca- 
tion, but Jorndt described the target city as hav- 
ing a “two million-plus” population and no current 
Walgreens stores. He described the project as 
“well under way,” with many store sites already 
under scrutiny or in lease negotiations. 


To open 20 stores at once 


Jorndt also made clear that the planned entry, 
in 1995 or 1996, would be the most aggressive 
and rapid in Walgreens’ modern history. “We 
plan to open 20 stores on the first day, all at 
once,” he said. 

“It was a challenge to open seven stores at once 
in Indianapolis [in 1992], so you can imagine what 
kind of challenge this will present,” Jorndt said in 
a press conference following the meeting. 

However, he said, the logistical headaches in- 
volved in scouting, leasing and developing sites, 
staffing the stores and managing 20 simultaneous 
grand openings would pay off in rapid market 


share gains and o 


rating efficiencies. 
Jorndt added that the company would reveal

Walgreen keeps tight grasp on No. 1 spot 


Walgreen President Dan Jorndt outlines plans to keep the 
chain at the top of the industry through the 1990s. 


‘The best times are 
still to come,’ Jornat 
tells shareholders 


By James Frederick 

CHICAGO — Walgreen Co. will keep a sharp 
focus on self-renewal and disciplined operating 
principles to remain the undisputed leader of the 
chain drug industry in the 1990s, its two top ex- 
ecutives told a near-capacity crowd of company 
snareholders last ieth. 

“I believe we will end the tumultuous 1990s as 
we began them: in the No. 1 position,” president 
and chief operating officer L. Daniel Jorndt said 
at the company’s annual meeting here Jan. 13. 
“It’s not easy staying in first place in this com- 
petitive retail world, but we’re doing it. And 
we'll continue to do it because we don’t take any- 
thing for granted. Nothing.” 

Thus, he added, “despite our very successful 
past several years, our best times still lie ahead.” 


Sales up again 


Those predictions were borne out by the lat- 
est in a long and largely unbroken string of re- 
cord-breaking fiscal results. Sales advanced 12 

ercent to $1.9 billion for the first quarter ended 
ov. 30, 1992, with same-store results ahead an 
Se Gopi 8.1 percent. Pharmacy sales again 
led the way, rising 13.8 percent. The advances

13.6 percent to $40.2 million.

Douglas Maxi starts home delivery 


NORTH PROVIDENCE, R.I. — Douglas Maxi Drug has 
joined a number of other chains offering home delivery. Begin- 
ning last month, Douglas is offering free home delivery of pre- 
scriptions through Mr. Messinger, Inc., a local delivery con- 
cern, to customers anywhere in Rhode Island. The chain will 
deliver other products along with any prescription order. 


Cincotta goes to CDMA 


NEW YORK, N.Y. — John Cincotta has 
been named the cosmetics and health & beau- 
ty aids merchandise manager for Chain Drug 
Marketing Associates. 

Cincotta had previously been with Eckerd 
Drug Stores as as corporate buyer and plano- 
gram administer for eight years. 


One-unit deep discounter expands 


NEWARK, N.J. — One-unit deep discounter Gordon’s has 
opened a larger, second site in Staten Island, N.Y. The second 
store totals 25,000 square feet, with 21,000 square feet of selling 
space, a leap from the orb ag Newark store which is 16,000 
square feet, 14,000 of which is selling space. A third store will 


soon follow. 


BIZ KID$ gives kids a taste of retail 


ORLANDO, Fla. — It seems everyone is getting into the 
HBA business these days. Now, Orlando, Fla. fifth- ers are 
involved in an innovative educational program which allows 
them to operate a retail drug store. 

The new pro , called BIZ KID$, will run throughout 1993 
and is desi to give students a real-life economics lesson. 
Students apply for positions at the store and are responsible for 
collecting and paying sales taxes, special promotions and order- 
ing merchandise. Two percent of the store’s profits are paid to 
the mail as rent. 

In addition to HBA, there are home and office supplies and 
convenience foods departments. Who knows? A trip to the BIZ 
KID$ store might provide enlightening strategies for reaching 
tomorrow’s drug store customer.

DENVER — Retailers 
are beginning to take a 
“strategic approach” to 
store closing, evaluating 
the decision to close stores 
on the basis of maximizing 
their profitability, market 
share and leadership posi- 
tions, according to the re- 
sults of a study by Coopers 
& Lybrand and G.A. 
Wright, Inc. 

The study showed that 
an over-stored industry, 
fierce competition and lag- 


ging consumer spending 


are all contributors to the 
slimming of store counts. 
The study also suggested 
that the trend is expected 
to accelerate for the re- 
mainder of the decade. 
The two firms initiated a 
major study focusing on 
store closings and retail 
downsizing which hinged 
on interviews conducted 
with department, dis- 
count, specialty, drug, 


Retailer study evaluates 
Strategies for store closings 


convenience and super- 
market retailers. 

Retailers decided to close 
stores based on changing 
demographics, new com- 
petitive forces and the op- 
portunity to relocate to 
more desirable locations. 
That criteria suggests that 
retailers are already begin- 
ning to take a strategic ap- 
proach to assessing the cur- 
rent store base, rather than 
viewing store closings as a 
defensive move. 

Many retailers surveyed 
viewed store closings as a 
way of strengthening their 
businesses. In fact, retail- 
ers who closed stores in 
1991 revealed that not all of 
the stores they closed were 
necessarily performing at a 
loss, although most were. 

The firms claim that 
store closings, when care- 
fully planned and with the 
right financial controls in 
place, can result in strong- 


er, more efficient retail or- 
ganizations. 

Both food and general 
merchandise retailers cited 
underperformance as the 
No. 1 reason they decided 
to close stores in 1991 and 
1992. Competitive pres- 
sures were cited as the sec- 
ond most important reason 
contributing to their deci- 
sion to close stores. 

The desire to improve 
cash flow and the desire to 
redeploy assets in a more 
profitable way was another 
often-cited reason that re- 
tailers gave for closing 
stores. 

Coopers & Lybrand and 
G.A. Wright speculate that 
the findings reflect the con- 
tinuing trend of larger retail- 
ers—particularly in the food 
sector—taking over the lo- 
cations of smaller players 
who find they can no longer 
compete successfully in cer- 
tain markets.

DRUG STORE NEWS, February 1, 1993 


Top drug chain executives are baring more teeth 
this year. Most snarl at the low-cost discount store and 
wholesale club operators who take a big bite out of the 
health and beauty care business. 

By comparison, Walgreen president L. Daniel 
Jorndt and ceo Charles R. Walgreen III are smiling. 
And why not? 

The company they lead is on a roll, securely in the 
No. 1 trade class position 


at $7.5 billion sales gener- 
ated by more than 1,750 
stores. That roster is 
fresh, with 70 percent 
having been opened or re- 
modeled within the past 
five years. 

The chain’s lower oper- 
ating costs, driven by ma- 
jor investments in systems, make Walgreens a sharp- 
er competitor. 

Examples include its comprehensive Strategic In- 
ventory Management System (SIMS), which took five 
years and $50 million to develop; since its September 
rollout, the chain has been able to slash $53 million of 
inventory from its distribution centers. And Wal- 
greens is “committed to taking three-tenths of a per- 
cent out of our cost of doing business every year to the 
year 2000,” Jorndt disclosed recently. 

Equally important to the company’s growth is its 
dramatic jump into mail-order pharmacy, a national 
business segment that is growing 20 percent annually 
in new prescriptions and 30 percent in dollars. Pre- 
scriptions already account for 37 percent of Wal- 
greens’ volume, and will grow to 50 percent by the 
year 2000. 

“Only the Catholic Church in America has more 
members than AARP [American Association of Re- 


MARKET 
PULSE

OPINION 


Walgreen deserves leadership mantie 


tired Persons]. Older people need drugs,” Jorndt 
stressed to the annual meeting crowd at the Art Insti- 
tute of Chicago. 

Charles Walgreen told everyone that the chain’s 
$15 million Healthcare Plus mail service facility in 
Orlando, Fla. has already signed on 70 accounts, in- 
cluding USA Healthnet, the nation’s largest pre- 
ferred provider organization. Jorndt said later the 
unit “is engineered to handle up to 15,000 scripts a 
day. At an $80 average, that’s $1.2 million daily busi- 
ness potential.” 

This new distribution will help Walgreens offset the 
pressures on retail pharmacy, whose growth is no 
longer fueled by 10 percent annual prescription price 
inflation, and whose operating costs will likely rise 
due to OBRA ’90 compliance. 

Even as pharmacy accounts for more of Walgreens’ 
sales, Jorndt detailed for me how over-the-counter 
medicine, stationery and convenience foods are the 
front-of-store departments helping to fuel estab- 
lished-store sales growth of 6.9 percent in the first 
quarter of fiscal’93. Established stores are an internal 
measure of units opened 2’ years, more conservative 
than comparable stores opened one year. 

News coverage on page one of this issue details 
the renewal of Walgreens: satellite linkage of phar- 
macies and also stores with each other, distribution 
centers and headquarters; precise inventory man- 
agement systems to maximize turns; new market in- 
vasions; and flexibility on freestanding sites, which 
pump $500 to $600 in sales per square foot in densely 
populated areas. 

Jorndt joked to stockholders about how Wal- 
greens took over a Chinese funeral home in San 
Francisco: “We move the cold bodies out and the 
warm bodies in.” | 

That sounds like a rallying cry with bite for the 90s. 


Will Medicaid pick up the tab 
on counseling, DUR services? 


Who’s going to pay for all the new patient counsel- 
ing and drug utilization review services that pharma- 
cists have to provide as a result of OBRA 90? 

“Don’t look at us,” say the gnomes at the Health 
Care Finance Administration (HCFA)—that gang of 
tar-heeled bureaucrats who took two years to prepare 
federal OBRA ’90 ground rules, and then dumped 
them on pharmacy’s lap late last year just eight weeks 
before the requirements 


took effect. 

Don’t look for state 
Medicaid programs to 
pony up any additional re- 
imbursement for these 
services, either—certain- 
ly not in view of “the cur- 
rent budget climate and 
the state’s likely resis- 
tance” to paying more for prescription services, the 
HCFA says. 

Retail pharmacy will just have to absorb these 
costs, which some sharp-penciled HCFA-ite esti- 
mates at $1 to $2 per prescription—or a minimum of 
$70 million to $140 million a year. 

Not so fast, though. There are some folks who be- 
lieve that Medicaid has an obligation to cover these 
costs. Not just a moral obligation, but a legal one. 

Rob Waspe, NACDS senior vp and general counsel, 
for one, maintains that failure to pay pharmacists for the 
additional cost of counseling and DUR services would 
violate both the spirit and the letter of federal Medicaid 


“~™e WASHINGTON 


law provisions that require states to pay “reasonable” 
reimbursement for prescription services. 

“For the HCFA to continue to find state Medicaid 
agency payment to pharmacies ‘reasonable,’ those 
payment rates must be increased to reflect the new 
costs generated by OBRA ’90,” NACDS says in for- 
mal comments to the agency. 

In order to comply with federal law, the HCFA, 
therefore, must “assure that state Medicaid agen- 
cies increase reimbursement to community pharma- 
cies at a minimum to reflect all additional costs asso- 
ciated with the new” OBRA ’90 mandate, the chain 
group says. 

Since the HCFA rarely allows legal obligations to 
stand in the way of expediency, NACDS will almost 
certainly have to advance its “reasonable” reimburse- 
ment arguments in the courts. 

It doesn’t take a legal scholar to tell right from 
wrong on this issue, however. 

As NACDS put it in the association's comments to 
the HCFA, paying pharmacists for new counseling 
and DUR responsibilities is a matter of simple fair- 
ness. 

The “federal government cannot continue to pass 
laws that add costs to the services they have agreed to 
buy, without paying their fair share of those costs,” 
the chain group says. 

“Since the federal government has interjected itself 
as a business partner in health care service delivery, 
both patients and providers should be able to expect 
the government to act in good faith.”

Sales, income, revenues 
rise at Rite Aid Corp. 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Sales 
for the 13 weeks ended Nov. 28, 
1992 at Rite Aid Corp. in- 
creased 8.6 percent to $1.01 bil- 
lion from $929.83 million for the 
same period the previous year. 

Net income for the corpora- 
tion rose 4.2 percent to $26.38 
million from $25.33 million for 
the comparable period one 
year ago. 

Revenues for the 39 weeks 
advanced 8.7 percent to $2.98 
billion compared to $2.74 bil- 
lion one year earlier. Earnings 
increased to $86.61 million 
from $79.32 million last year. 

The drug store division of 
the corporation posted sales 
of $946.49 million, an in- 
crease of 8.4 percent over 
last year’s $873.42 million for 
the 13 weeks. Net income in- 
creased 7 percent to $24.50 
million from $22.90 million 


one year earlier. 

For the year-to-date period, 
drug store sales rose 8.2 per- 
cent to $2.80 billion from $2.58 
billion and net income advanced 
9.5 percent to $79.83 million 
compared to $72.88 million the 
previous year. 

Comparable drug store 
sales increased 4.7 percent for 
the quarter and 5.3 percent for 
the 39 weeks. 

Other Rite Aid divisions 
showed strong sales increases 
for the third quarter. The cor- 
poration’s American Discount 
Auto Parts division posted a 
sales increase of 14.1 percent 
for the third quarter (from 
$22.64 million in 1991 to 1992’s 
$25.84 million) and Encore 
Books posted a sales increase 
of 25.3 percent for the quarter 
(from $33.50 million in 1991 to 
$41.98 million in 1992). 


PayLess sales up 34.5% 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — PayLess, a wholly-owned sub- 
sidiary of Kmart Corp., posted sales of $608 million for the 
third quarter ending Oct. 28, 1992, compared with $452 mil- 
lion for the same period in 1991. Operating income for the 
quarter was $22 million, up 14.5 percent from $19 million. 

For the 39-week period, sales were $1.587 billion, up 21 per- 
cent vs. $1.312 billion for the same period in 1991. Comparable 


stores showed a 0.8 


percent increase. PayLess operating in- 


come was up 19.6 percent to $63 million, compared with $53 mil- 
lion for the same period last year. 


Revco sets new debt offering 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Reveo D.S. and its under- 
writers have set a price for a 
new series of senior unse- 
cured notes due Jan. 15, 
2000. The chain has also in- 
creased the amount of the 
debt issue from $125 million 
to $140 million due to strong 
demand. 

Revco will issue the notes 
at par with an interest rate of 
9.125 percent. The issue is 
underwritten by three firms 


led by Merrill Lynch & Co. 


Morgan Stanley & Co. and 
Jefferies & Company are co- 
managers. 

Under terms of the finan- 
cial overhaul, the chain will 
refinance its existing credit 
line and redeem its three out- 
standing public debt issues, 
using proceeds from a sale of 
$110 million in common stock 
pursuant to a rights offering 
to stockholders, as well as 
the $140 million in new notes 
and new credit lines totaling 
$300 million.

Osco stores, and one in Boul-

leases, fixtures and inven-

Chris Bement.

er stores were recently sold to

in some locations allowed

in merchandising changes over

Eckerd merges Florida DCs 


ORLANDO, Fla. — Jack Eckerd Corp.’s five Florida distri- 
bution centers will be closed and consolidated into a single Or- 
lando-based facility by next fall. eee 

It “will include a highly automated merchandise distribution 
system that will not only better serve the inventory manage- 
ment needs of Eckerd’s existing 539 Florida stores, but enhance 
the company’s continued growth in Florida,” said Stewart Tur- 
ley, Eckerd chairman and president. as 

Eckerd is acquiring the lease of the property and buildings 
from Super Foods Inc. for an undisclosed sum. Renovation and 
equipment installation at the nearly 600,000-square-foot facility 


is expected to begin soon. 


Thrifty to rebuild riot-ravaged stores 


LOS ANGELES — Thrifty Corp. will rebuild three of four 
stores destroyed in last spring’s riots here, and has announced 
that African-American contractors will get at least 50 percent of 
the reconstruction work. 


Neuman acdquires H.K. Hineline 


RIDGEFIELD, N.J. — Neuman Wholesale Drug Co. has ac- 
uired H.K. Hineline, a regional wholesaler based in Utica, 
N.Y. which has $20 million annual sales. Neuman, at $500 mil- 
lion in sales last year, an to double Hineline’s sales by the 
end of 1993. Hineline will operate as a wholly owned subsidiary 
of Neuman, and president Richard Hineline will stay in his post, 
said Neuman chairman Samuel Toscano. 


Ontario plans drug store tobacco ban 


TORONTO — Following through on an earlier warning, the 
government of Ontario said it will try to halt the sale of tobacco 
products in all stores in the province. 

The Ontario legislature will introduce the proposal to ban 
drug store tobacco sales in the spring, after Shoppers Drug 
Mart and other retailers refused to comply with an earlier re- 
quest from the Ontario College of Pharmacists for a voluntary 
end to cigarette sales. Shoppers president David Bloom has ar- 
gued that the proposed ban would unfairly target drug stores 


and constitute restraint of trade. 


Bergen-Durr renew VHA deal 

ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen Brunswig Corp. and its subsidiary, 
Durr-Fillauer Medical Inc., announced that they and Voluntary 
Hospitals of America (VHA) have extended the existing agree- 
ment for distribution of pharmaceutical products. Bergen esti- 
mates the extensions to April 1997 will generate $3 billion in sales.

DRUG STORE NEWS, February 15, 1993 


OPINION 


Healthy chain drug consolidation is pruning the least 
efficient stores and turning over doors to the more inno- 
vative, technologically savvy, low-cost operators. 

Chain stores aren’t diminishing—only the number 
of chains. In the midst of this turnover—competing 
not only against larger chains, but combos, discount- 
ers and wholesale clubs as well—is a particularly ef- 
fective tier of small regional powerhouses. 

By NACDS definition, 


they have 50 or fewer 
stores and less than $100 
million in annual sales. 

Execs in the trade will 
rightly portray them as 
feisty, agile, armed with 
local market knowledge, 
in tune with regional cul- 
tures and less afraid to 
take chances because of corporate hierarchies. Speed 
is their currency, and home-town relations are their 
bargaining chips, as they fend off continued encroach- 
ment by larger operators. 

Perhaps Alan Levin, ceo of 26-store Happy Har- 
ry’s in Delaware, summed it up best for me: “Small 
chains have to be on the cutting edge or on the cut- 
ting room floor.” 

How does he live out his motto? Consider these 
quotes: 

@ “Our organizational chart has the customer on 
top.” 

@ “If I don’t run on a customer’s problem, then I 
might as well get a check sent to me in Florida.” 

OK, that part of him is carried down from his dad, 
Harry Levin, who succeeded by putting people first. In- 
deed, says Wayne Nelson, vp-operations, “Alan is just 
like Harry. Harry would go 10 feet into a store, and 
you're done for two hours. He had a mind like a steel 
trap, and always remembered customers’ names.” 

The younger Levin has leveraged this approach 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


Regional powerhouses stake out turf 


with an employee incentive program based on custom- 
er service. A mystery shopper visits each store once a 
month to rate staffers on greetings, willingness to 
help, thank-yous, attitudes and cleanliness. Quarterly 
awards range from $500 for assistant managers down 
to $25 for part-timers. 

He has also borrowed a program from Douglas Drug 
to certify their own pharmacy technicians and give them 
a chance to raise their earnings and self-esteem. 

These aren’t altruistic programs. Levin is fully 
aware that shoppers draw their image of the stores 
from the store clerks and pharm techs they interact 
with. 

On the buying front, Levin was willing to be the 
first small chain head to invest heavily in E-3 buying 
software. This led to a 50 percent inventory invest- 
ment cutback, more free cash and a far greater ability 
to focus on the fastest turners. 

At Horton & Converse, in Newport Beach, Califor- 
nia, prime locations near medical centers and tailored 
merchandise mixes for patients and visitors, doctors 
and nurses are part of a winning formula. The chain 
has also decided not to indiscriminately chase the 
third-party pharmacy buck, preferring instead to de- 
velop cash business. 

In New York City, the super-productive Duane 
Reade stores are primed for another adrenaline boost. 
New president and ceo Bruce Weitz is examining how 
EDI and scanning will help the 37-store chain lower 
acquisition costs and identify movers rapidly. The 
chain already turns goods at twice the industry pace 
and sells at the rate of $1,300 per square foot. Prime 
sites on many of Manhattan’s busiest streets continue 
to be a foundation for this regional operator. 

Across the U.S., strong regional operators find 
ways to keep an edge in their markets and make life 
unpleasant for large chains. For more on how regional 
powerhouses work their strategies, see the special 
section in this issue starting on page 31. 


Whenever a politician offers you something for 
nothing, grab your wallet. 

Remember George McGovern’s plan to give every- 
body in the country $1,000? Or Ronald Reagan’s 
scheme to reduce the deficit by cutting taxes? 

Here in Washington, if a legislative solution 
sounds too good to be true, it probably is. But that 
doesn’t stop the politicos from making outlandish 
claims that, in any other 


context, would invite a 
deceptive advertising 
complaint from the 
FTC’s Bureau of Con- 
sumer Protection. 

This year, the some- 
thing-for-nothing crowd 
on Capitol Hill is honing in 
on health care. Long be- 
fore Hillary R. Clinton’s health care task force will be 
able to produce a single recommendation for reform- 
ing the system, Congressional word processors will 
have cranked out dozens of too-good-to-be-true pro- 
grams to overhaul the nation’s health delivery sys- 
tem. 

Some of these Voodoo health reform bills are al- 
ready in the hopper. Rep. Fortney “Pete” Stark, the 
California Democrat who masterminded the ill-fated 
Medicare “Catastrophic” prescription drug program a 
few years back, wasted no time coming up with his 
new “Health Care Cost Containment and Reform Act 
of 1993.” 

Under his bill (H.R. 200), some 70 percent of the 35 
million Americans with no health insurance would re- 
ceive government-paid coverage by bringing them in 
to the Medicaid prog..am for the indigent. 


» WASHINGTON 
) PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


There’s no such thing as a free lunch 


In addition to providing prescription benefits for 25 
million people in families with incomes up to double 
the poverty level, the legislation would resurrect the 
heart of Stark’s earlier “Catastrophic” drug plan for 
the elderly. 

Like the program that was ultimately repealed by 
Congress because senior citizens didn’t want to pay 
for it, Stark’s new proposal would provide prescrip- 
tion coverage under Medicaid Part B, subject to a stiff 
$850 annual deductible. But unlike the “Catastrophic” 
scheme, Medicare beneficiaries would not be asked to 
shoulder the cost of this coverage beyond paying “the 
usual 25 percent premium,” he says. 

Rather, Stark explains, the cost of these new pre- 
scription drug benefits would be “funded with savings 
achieved from cost-containment,” such as reducing 
“fraud and abuse.” Wow! Why didn’t we think of that 
the first time around? 

Similarly, Stark says we won’t have to pay for the 
cost of health care for those 25 million new Medicaid 
recipients currently without health insurance. “It 
should be emphasized that H.R. 200 includes no new 
taxes,” he explains. “All cost provisions are fully fund- 
ed with savings achieved from cost containment, rath- 
er than taxes.” | 

The cost controls envisioned by Stark include a cap 
on national health spending and, ultimately, limits on 
payments to health care providers. 

Assuming Washington is no better at eliminating 
waste, fraud and abuse than it ever was, the entire 
cost of these new health benefits will be achieved by 
squeezing pharmacists and other providers. And 
pharmacists, in turn, will have to pass these increased 
costs on to—you guessed it—us. 

Thanks again for the free lunch.

McKesson ups revenues 


10% in 3rd quarter 


SAN FRANCISCO — In its third quarter report, McKesson 
Corp. cited strong improvement over the first half in the profit- 


ability of its Health 


are Services segment, which comprises 


around 97 percent of McKesson’s revenues and 80 percent of its 


operating profit. 


Health Care Services—which includes McKesson Drug 
Co., the company’s Canadian pharmaceutical and health care 
distribution businesses, Service Merchandising and PCS 
Health Systems—was flat in the first two quarters, but the 
company reported a third-quarter gain of 11 percent operat- 
ing profit to $57.8 million on a 10 percent rise in revenues to 


$2.92 billion. 


PCS Health Systems posted a 6 percent increase in revenues 
to $28 million. Both Medis, the Canadian pharmaceutical busi- 
ness, and McKesson Service Merchandising were flat in the lat- 
est three months. McKesson Drug’s direct store delivery sales 
were only up 4 percent in the quarter, but operating profit 
reached “double digit,” according to the company. 

The company reported that for the third quarter, McKesson 
Corp. revenues, excluding sales to customers’ warehouses, 
would have been up 4 percent and 12 percent for the nine 


months. 


Chairman and ceo Alan Seelenfreund said that the low rate of 
sales growth in the quarter “reflects the company’s continuing 
focus on a credit-worthy, high-quality customer base.” 


Smith’s sees earnings gain 
despite flat store sales 


SALT LAKE CITY — Ad- 
justing to a weak economy and 
tight consumer spending, 
Smith’s Food & Drug Centers 
managed healthy net earnings 
increases for the fourth quar- 
ter and full year of fiscal 1992. 

Smith’s drove earnings 
ahead 13 percent for the quar- 
ter ended Jan. 2, to $13.1 mil- 
lion, on sales of $687 million 
vs. $593 million the previous 
year. For the year, net earn- 
ngs rose 19 percent to $53.6 
million on sales of $2.65 billion. 

The growth in profit came 
despite anemic same-store 
sales gains of 2 percent for 
the quarter and 1 percent for 
the year. “Comparable store 
sales were affected by mod- 
est deflation, consumer trad- 
ing down and the weak econo- 
my in general,’ noted 
Smith’s in a statement. 

However, the company re- 
ported, “Gross margins con- 
tinued to improve during 
1992. . . as a result of more 
efficient operations in matur- 
ing stores, distribution econ- 
omies and higher private la- 
bel sales.” 

The gain in margins was 

artially offset, however, by 
mith’s “aggressive efforts 
to improve sales in a very 
competitive market,” and by 


“higher operating costs from 
the entry into California.” 
Indeed, Smith’s has spent 
heavily in its bid to gain mar- 
ket share in Southern Cali- 
fornia and in Phoenix, Ariz., 
where lease costs are often 
exhorbitant and competition 
is white-hot. 

As aresult, net margins as a 
percent of sales decreased 
slightly to 2.02 percent from 
2.03 percent a year ago, the 
company announced. 

Nevertheless, Smith’s has 
pursued an aggressive growth 
strategy to position itself for 
future market strength in key 
Western regions. 

The combo chain opened 12 
large-scale food/drug stores 
last year, including stores in 
nine Southern California com- 
munities and additional units 
in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Al- 
buquerque, N.M.—the latter 
two to replace smaller Smith’s 
stores which were closed. 
Smith’s also completed two 
major store remodels, and 
ended the year with 119 
stores. Of these, 103 are large 
food/drug combos. 


Construction has also ote a 
on a new, million-square-foot 
automated distribution center 


in Riverside, Calif. to support 
Smith’s westward push.

R.U. READY FOR 
RU-486? 


The biggest roadblock to 
U.S. marketing approval for 
the controversial “French 
abortion pill” RU-486 now 
appears to be the reluctance 
of the drug’s manufacturer, 
Roussel-Uclaf, to submit an 
NDA. Hours after taking of- 
fice, President Clinton or- 
dered the FDA to re-evaluate 
the drug’s status—a move 
that could put RU-486 on an 
NDA fast track within the 
agency. But, despite a poten- 
tial $500 million market for 
the drug in this country, 
Roussel-Uclaf may not re- 
quest marketing approval— 
unless specifically asked to 
do so by the FDA.

What have 
I gotten 
myself into? 


As I write this, I have two days remaining 
before the NABPLEX exam. I am much too 
old for this. It seems like it was in a past life 
when I first sat for the licensing exam short- 
ly after graduation. As I recall, it was ex- 
tremely difficult then, even with all that 
education fresh under my hat. What am I to 
expect now? 

My preparation for this go ‘round seems 
weeks y inadequate at this point. It con- 
sists of a review course, which hopes to 
cram four years of professional education 
into four days. Thats it! 

Some of my fellow pharmacists hoping to 
get a Florida license have brought along 
Facts & Comparisons, have read the Rem- 
ington, have completed various printed re- 
view courses, are making tape recordings to 
play under pillows at night—and they re in 
their rooms studying right now while I 
write this editorial. 

My goal was admirable. I had hoped to 
be able to work occasionally in the commu- 
nity to “keep in touch” with community 


harmacy. But pharmacy practice must 
ave seal changed. I can't recall a single 
instance from my past pharmacy experi- 
ence when I needed the Henderson Has- 
selbalch Equation or used a Body Surface 
Area Nomogram to calculate dosage. I’ve 
also personally never had to calculate the 
kcal per TPN or needed to determine mil- 
liosmoles, assuming complete disassocia- 
tion, of course. I just hope I don’t complete- 
ly disassociate during the exam! 
If I really want to do this (and I do), I 
guess I'd better keep the fourth Tuesday in 
June (the next NABPLEX date) open.

The Food and Drug Admin-

new drugs last year, including

represent a measurable thera- 
peutic advance over drugs that 
are already on the market. 

Although this puts the FDA a

decade.

NDA backlog and streamline 
the FDAss drug approval pro-

headway in shorting the aver- 
age review time for new pre- 
scription medicines last year.

with 23.4 months the year be- 
fore. Significantly, however, 
among the 11 “priority” NMEs

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, February 15, 1993 


Biotechnology and the retail pharmacy 


consider it an entirely new and 
foreign discipline.”’ Yet, biotech- 
nology—the use of living organ- 
isms or their components to pro- 
duce useful products—has 
touched the human way of life for 
well over 1,000 years. 
Biotechnology is not a revolu- 
tionary technology, but rather an 
evolutionary one. Beer brewing, 
leavened bread baking, cheese 
making, selective breeding of 
plants for certain desirable char- 
acteristics and the discovery and 
production of penicillin are all ma- 
jor contributions of biotechnolo- 
gy. An extension of this technol- 
ogy, what we think of as today’s 
biotechnology, is the application 
of a collection of techniques aris- 
ing primarily out of developments 
in cell and molecular biology, ge- 
netics, biochemistry, microbiolo- 
gy and immunology in the 1970s to 


the generation of useful producti: 
and basic scientific knowledge.” 

Research achievements in each 
of these basic science areas have 
provided an apparent futuristic 
pharmaceutical technology, that 
yet remains very practical and 
conceptually simple. 

Applications of biotechnology 
are found in medicine, the phar- 
maceutical sciences, agriculture, 
environmental science, food sci- 
ence and forensics. The practice 
of pharmacy in all settings is now 
realizing the impact of pharma- 
ceutical biotechnology with the 
arrival on the pharmacist’s shelf 
of improved pharmaceuticals, 
novel therapeutic drugs and more 
specific diagnostic agents. 

Pioneering strategies for new 
drug design are also products of 
pharmaceutical biotechnology.

Continued from page 31 

Nearly two-thirds of the 273 
products registered with the 
FDA in 1989 contained biological- 
ly-derived ingredients. A 1991 
survey report of biotechnology 
medicines presented by the Phar- 
maceutical Manufacturers Asso- 
ciation found that 132 new phar- 
maceuticals are in testing, a 63 
percent increase over the past 
four years as seen in Figure I. 

Biotechnology continues to 
shape the future of the pharma- 
ceutical industry.‘ 

Wade and Levy state that 
“these pivotal developments may 
catapult the pharmacy profession 
into new roles and may provide 
many opportunities for pharma- 
cists to enhance the professional 
dimension of their practice—but 
only if they are prepared.” 

Pharmacy is poised to be one of 
the greatest beneficiaries of the 
current advances of biotechnolo- 
gy. The day-to-day functions of 
the drug store pharmacist will not 
necessarily change with the in- 
creasing introduction of more bio- 
tech drugs into the marketplace. 

However, the pharmacist’s 
base of knowledge necessary to 
acquire, store and dispense bio- 
technology-produced pharma- 
ceuticals will differ somewhat 
from that required to perform 
the same functions with most of 
today’s products. The pharma- 
cist’s confidence in and knowl- 


32 


edge of biopharmaceuticals will 
influence the delivery of phar- 
maceutical care. 


Community R.Phs., bio. drugs 


The traditional role of the phar- 
macist in the drug store is chang- 
ing from primarily drug prepara- 
tion and distribution to provision 
of quality total pharmaceutical 
care. The pharmacist has always 
served as a primary source of in- 
formation to the patient. This is 
especially true for those patients 
with questions concerning the na- 
ture of their apparently sophisti- 
cated and costly medications. 

The introduction and predicted 
continued expansion of biotech- 
nology pharmaceutical products 
have presented the pharmacist 
with new responsibilities and a 
unique opportunity for innovation 
in their pharmacy business in clin- 
ical services as well as drug infor- 
mation. With the evolution of 
knowledge necessary to compete 
in the modern biotechnology era 
comes phenomenal practice op- 
portunities for the innovative 
pharmacist, both today and into 
the next century. 


Historically 


In the past, pharmacists met 
the challenge of improving their 
base of knowledge necessary to 
acquire, store, handle, dispense 
and provide patient information 
about biopharmaceuticals such as 


the protein drugs insulin, gluca- 
gon, and growth hormone. Pa- 
tient counseling and education, 
cost containment management, 
intervention in financial reim- 
bursement and the handling, pre- 
paring, dispensing and monitor- 
ing of novel drug delivery 
systems affected everyday prac- 
tice of community pharmacy. 

Home diagnostic kits, such as 
pregnancy test kits, became 
available in the late 1970s at a 
reasonable cost. Careful coun- 
seling was required to assure 
that the patient understood the 
reliability of the tests and per- 
formed the tests to obtain the 
correct results. Thus, communi- 
ty pharmacists successfully met 
the challenge of biotechnology 
and improved their practice. 

The FDA approval of products 
derived from modern pharmaceu- 
tical biotechnology simply means 
that we now use different technol- 
ogies to produce the protein 
drugs and home diagnostic kits. 
Modern biotechnology also adds 
other dimensions: creation of 
more specific pharmaceuticals, 
lower cost to produce larger 
quantities of biopharmaceuticals 
and the ability to produce prod- 
ucts previously unattainable or 
even unknown. Although the 
pharmacist again has had to un- 
dergo another evolution of knowl- 
edge, the new products still re- 
tain some similarity to the older 
biopharmaceuticals. 

Opportunities for the communi- 
ty pharmacist in the dispensing 
and clinical use of the new bio- 
technology-derived products ex- 
ists if the pharmacist takes ad- 
vantage of them. Pharmaceutical 
care is the responsible provision 
of drug therapy with the goal of 
achieving definite outcomes to- 
ward improving a patient’s quali- 
ty of life.°,° 

Therefore, the pharmacist 
must serve not only as the drug 
expert for biotech drugs, but 
also as an educator of the total 
health care team by supplying 
drug information services that 
will satisfy a patient’s pharma- 
ceutical care. To take advantage 
of the opportunities presented 
by biotechnology, it is essential 
for the pharmacist to better un- 
derstand the nature of biotech- 
nology drug products. 

As a class of pharmaceuticals, 
biotechnology drug products are 


expensive and thus can represent 
a financial challenge for the com- 
munity pharmac. _t.' 


Financial considerations 


The availability of new and 
mechanistically-novel methods of 
therapeutic intervention are of- 
ten associated with substantial 
costs. The expense of research 
and development and, conse- 
quently, the cost of supplying the 
biotech pharmaceutical to pa- 
tients is quite high. In most cases, 
human insulin being a notable ex- 
ception, the lack of a competitive 
product may also be reflected in 
the price of the pharmaceutical. 

Many biotechnology drug prod- 
ucts currently on the market 
were manufactured under the Or- 
phan Drug Act. The first compa- 
ny to win FDA approval for such 
an orphan drug for a particular in- 
dication is granted seven years of 
market exclusivity. 

Pharmacists’ concerns over the 
increased expense inherently as- 
sociated with biotechnology 
drugs, coupled with the need to 
assume a greater responsibility 
for the provision of pharmaceuti- 
eal care utilizing these biotechnol- 
ogy products, has created some- 
what of a dilemma for many 
community pharmacists. 

Kane and Kuhn have nicely sum- 
marized many of the financial con- 
siderations facing an ambulatory 
care pharmacist becoming in- 
volved in the provision of biotech- 
nology-produced pharmaceuti- 
cals.° (Some of these financial 
considerations are found in Table 
1.)The twomost challenging finan- 
cial considerations for a community 
pharmacist involved with biotech 
drugs are the large initial invest- 
ment in stock and reimbursement 
issues. 


Inventory investment 


The pharmacist must decide if 
they want to make the large capital 
investment necessary to stock the 
biotechnology drug products. 
Should this be the case, additional 
considerations such as installing a 
sufficiently large refrigerated stor- 
age area become important. As will 
be described later, the biotechnolo- 
gy-produced biopharmaceuticals 
require storage in carefully tem- 
perature-controlled refrigeration 
units in order not to destroy the po- 
tency of an expensive product.

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, February 15, 1993 


continuing education 


Continued from page 32 

Ifthe pharmacist chooses not to 
invest a large amount of capital in 
shelf stock, the pharmaceuticals 
could be acquired on an as needed 
basis. Many wholesalers and 
pharmaceutical companies deliv- 
er biopharmaceuticals as needed. 

However, such an arr*nge- 
ment requires careful planning. 
The pharmacist must anticipate 
in advance the needs of the pa- 
tient necessitating closer patient 
follow-up to help determine when 
to order. Kane and Kuhn have 
also suggested that innovative fi- 
nancial management options for 
obtaining shelf stock could be de- 
vised. These might include some 
form of consignment or banking 
programs with wholesalers.® 


Reimbursement 


Pharmacists, as individual 
pharmaceutical care providers 
and as members of professional 
organizations, must become pro- 
active when dealing with the re- 


- Imbursement issue. 


As tighter budgetary restric- 
tions are placed upon the health 
care dollar, actively working 
with third-party payers will be 
of paramount importance to bet- 
ter assure a fiscally sound prac- 
tice involved in the provision of 
biotechnology-produced phar- 
maceuticals. 

Pharmacists should use their 
knowledge of biopharmaceuticals 
and pharmaceutical care to help 
educate third-party organiza- 
tions about key issues such as the 
medical versus economic benefits 
of a particular biotech drug. 

Many pharmaceutical compa- 
nies providing biotechnology- 
produced drugs have developed 
programs to assist with reim- 
bursement matters. Pharmacists 
should consult with the compa- 
nies providing the drugs they are 
dispensing to determine availabil- 
ity of such an approach. 

Patient counseling must in- 
clude discussions of reimburse- 
ment issues and determination of 
payment. This can become a very 
invaluable service to your pa- 
tients during a difficult time in 
their lives. 


Modern biotech. techniques 


An in-depth knowledge of the 
basic science and sophisticated 
supportive technology involved 
in the manufacture of biotech- 


nology pharmaceutical products 
is certainly not important for the 
successful practice of communi- 
ty pharmacy. 

However, a general under- 
standing of the technologies in- 
volved helps the pharmacist gain 
better insight into and compre- 
hension of biotech a drug’s use, 
stability and handling, side ef- 
fects and potential toxicity; in 
other words, how it differs from 
traditional drugs. 

Also, such an understanding 
will aid in appreciating the new 
biotech drugs in the pharmaceuti- 
cal companies’ development pipe- 
line. These are the so-called “mir- 
acle drugs” that your patients 
often read about while waiting in 
grocery store checkout lines, and 
later come in to ask you about. 

It’s not uncommon for a com- 
munity pharmacist to be asked by 
a patient “Is there a biotech drug 
available to treat... ?” This re- 
sults from the patient’s misunder- 
standing that a biotechnology- 
produced pharmaceutical must be 
better. In order to better respond 
to customer inquiries, all pharma- 
cists, no matter what their prac- 
tice, must become more knowl- 
edgeable about biotechnology 
pharmaceutical products. 

The basic sciences fueling the 
tremendous advances in pharma- 
ceutical biotechnology have made 
available a number of techniques 
that have proven or will soon 
prove valuable in the discovery, 
development and production of 
useful pharmaceuticals. The two 
techniques most commonly 
thought of as pharmaceutical bio- 
technology are hybridoma or 
monoclonal antibody (MoAbs) 
production and recombinant 
DNA (rDNA) or, more broadly, 
genetic engineering. 


Hybridoma technology 


Antibodies are proteins. As 
part of the normal immune sys- 
tem, each body can produce as 
many as a hundred million anti- 
body proteins directed against 
bacteria, viruses and other for- 
eign invaders. 

The B-lymphocyte, a plasma 
spleen cell, produces a wide range 
of structurally diverse antibody 
proteins with varying degrees of 
specificity in response to a given 
single antigen stimulus. 

These antibodies are called po-

lyclonal antibodies. Mono- 
clonal antibodies are homoge- 
neous, ultrasensitive, hybrid, im- 
mune system-derived proteins 
produced by a selected single 
clone of an engineered B-lympho- 
cyte.*-!! They are desig» ad to rec- 
ognize specific sites, or epitopes, 
on substances known as antigens 
that are uniquely associated with 
chemicals found in foreign organ- 
isms and/or humans. 

Hybridoma technology, the 
technology to produce monoclonal 
antibodies, consists of combining 
or fusing two different cell lines: a 
myeloma cell, generally from a 
mouse, and a plasma spleen cell 
(B-lymphocyte) capable of pro- 
ducing an antibody that recog- 
nizes a specific antigen. 

The resulting fused cell, or hy- 
bridoma, possesses some of the 
characteristics of both original 
cells: the myeloma cell’s ability to 
survive and reproduce in culture, 
and the plasma spleen cell’s abili- 
ty to produce antibodies to a spe- 
cific antigen. 

Hybridomas can be grown in 
large quantities, and clones pro- 
ducing antibodies with the appro- 
priate specificity for the original 
antigen can be isolated from cul- 
ture and put into the manufacture 
of monoclonal antibodies. 

Monoclonal antibodies are 
more attractive than polyclonal 
antibodies for diagnostic and 
therapeutic applications because 
of their increased specificity of 
antigen recognition. 

Monoclonal antibodies can be 
prepared with tremendous speci- 
ficity for antigens such as the pro- 
tein coat of an invading organism, 
a surface protein of a tumor cell, 
or the protein receptor regulating 
a key biological process. Thus, 
they can serve as site-directed 
“homing devices” to find and at- 
tach to the targeted antigen. 

Developments in hybridoma 
technology have led to highly spe- 
cific diagnostic agents for home 
use in pregnancy testing and ovu- 
lation prediction kits, laboratory 
use in colorectal and ovarian can- 
cer detection (awaiting FDA ap- 
proval), and in the design of site- 
directed therapeutic agents such 
as Muromonab-CD3 for kidney 
transplant rejection. 

Probably the pharmacist’s first 
exposure to a pharmaceutical bio- 
technology drug product was the 


34 


home pregnancy test kit. While 
home pregnancy test kits became 
available in 1977 with the intro- 
duction of the e.p.t. Pregnancy 
Test Kit from Warner-L2mbert, 
monoclonal antibody technology 
contributed to a second-genera- 
tion of more specific tests in the 
early 1980s.!7,13 | 

Human chorionic gonadotropin 
(hCG), the hormone that is pro- 
duced if fertilization occurs and 
continues to increase in concen- 
tration during pregnancy, serves 
as the “antigen” being detected 
by the monoclonal antibody. It’s 
because of monoclonal antibody 
technology that these second- 
generation test kits are more spe- 
cific for hCG, and therefore less 
prone to give false positives 
caused by interference from other 
proteins. Examples of monoclonal 
home pregnancy test kits include 
Advance, Answer Plus, Clearb- 
iue Easy, Daisy 2, e.p.t., Fact 
Plus, First Response and Q Test. 

All of these indicate results by 
color change or color appearance. 
One additional test, Answer, is 
different in that it indicates re- 
sults by hemagglutination inhibi- 
tion. 
\ Hybridoma technology has also 
provided home ovulation predic- 
tion kits. !°,!4 Monoclunal antibod- 
ies specific for luteinizing hor- 
mone (LH) are used to predict 
ovulation by detecting the surge 
of LH_as it appears in the urine. 
Remember that ovulation occurs 
20-48 hours after the LH surge. 
Therefore, the kits can help de- 
termine when a woman is most 
fertile. Representative examples 
of monoclonal antibody home ovu- 
lation prediction kits include An- 
swer Ovulation, Clearblue Easy, 
First Response Ovulation, For- 
tel, OvuKIT, OvuQUICK and 
QTest for ovulation. 


Recombinant DNA technology 


Strategies utilizing recombi- 
nant DNA—a hybrid DNA mole- 
cule that is formed by combining 
pieces of DNA (identified gene se- 
quences) from different organ- 
isms and placing them functional- 
ly into another organism—have 
given us the ability to manipulate 
the genetic information inherent 
within the nucleus of living cells 
and thus produce therapeutically 
useful proteins. }°-'"

genetic code stored in a cell’s nu- 
cleus as DNA is used to produce 
proteins to sustain life: enzymes 
and enzyme regulators to pro- 
duce and/or metabolize other im- 
portant components, hormones 
and hormone-like growth fac- 
tors, chemical messengers such 
as the cytokines, and structural 
proteins. 

This code is transferred to an 
intermediary compound, known 
as messenger ribonucleic acid 
(mRNA), by the process of tran- 
scription. 

The mRNA relays the genetic 
information obtained from the 
corresponding DNA into a pro- 
tein by the process of transla- 
tion. Amino acids are added one 
at a time to make the specific 
protein coded for by the cell’s 
original DNA. 

As the amino acid addition oc- 
curs, the newly synthesized pro- 
tein begins to assume its charac- 
teristic three-dimensional shape. 

In summary, the process to 
produce proteins is DNA-to- 
RNA-to-protein. Therefore, in 
theory, one can produce any pro- 
tein one wants, including a ther- 
apeutically useful protein, as 


long as: 

@ 1) the DNA coding for the 
protein can be isolated or syn- 
thesized; 

@ 2) the mRNA translating the 


-amino acid sequence of the pro- 


tein can be isolated or synthesized 
AND used to “retro-synthesize” 
the corresponding DNA; or, 

@ 3) the amino acid sequence 
of the protein is known, so the 
codon sequence can be deduced 
and method 1) or 2) described 
above applied.'’ 

In recombinant DNA technol- 
ogy, a family of “DNA scissor” 
enzymes called restriction en- 
donucleases or restriction en- 
zymes is used to “snip” DNA at 
precise sites to provide the frag- 
ment coding for the human pro- 
tein of interest. 

Bacterial plasmids, circular 
DNA outside of the nucleus that 
replicate freely within the cell, 
are often chosen to carry the hu- 
man gene back into the organism. 
A restriction enzyme opens the 
plasmid and the human gene is 
glued to it by an enzyme called 
DNA ligase. 

This recombinant DNA mole- 
cule, now containing the code for

the human protein, is inserted back 
into the bacteria. The microorgan- 
ism is then grown in fermentation 
producing the human protein. The 
human protein is isolated from the 
fermentation, purified and formu- 
lated resulting in an rDNA-pro- 
duced pharmaceutical. 

Recombinant DNA methods 
have permitted the large scale 
manufacturing of human versions 
of previously animal-derived 
drugs such as insulin, compounds 
once isolated in minute amounts 
from human cadavers such as hu- 
man growth hormone, and new 
therapies such as epoetin alfa and 
the colony-stimulating factors for 
formerly untreatable conditions. 

The biotechnology-derived 
pharmaceuticals are divided into 
the broad classes of hormones and 
growth factors, enzymes and en- 
zyme regulators, cytokines, and 
vaccines. 

Hormones are substances that 
are secreted by one type of cell 
and act on another type of cell 


36 


within an organism. Enzymes are 
proteins capable of catalyzing a 
reaction. Cytokines are soluble 
proteins that are released by a cell 
and act as intercellular messen- 
gers. And vaccines enable the 
body to resist infection. 

Table 2 lists the FDA-approved 
recombinant DNA products along 
with the lone FDA-approved ther- 
apeutically useful (non-diagnostic) 
monoclonal antibody. 


Natural origin biopharmaceut. 


Again, biotechnology is the 
use of living organisms or their 
components to produce useful 
products. While not specifically 
covered as part of this review or 
included in Table 2, several bio- 
pharmaceuticals not produced 
by hybridoma or recombinant 
DNA technology are available, 
and may be considered biotech- 
nology drugs. 

As selected examples, two pro- 
tein biotech drugs—interferon 
alfa-n3 (Alferon N, Purdue Fred- 
erick) and alglucerase (Ceredase, 


Genzyme)—aren’t made by re- 
combinant DNA technology. 
Both drugs are isolated from hu- 
man cells or tissues not of recombi- 
nant origin. Alferon N is indicated 
for the treatment of genital warts. 
Ceredase is used as enzyme re- 
placement therapy for patients 
with Type I Gaucher disease. | 


Other methodologies 


Recently, biotechnology has 
been appropriately described as 
“the engine of drug development.” 
_ There are other methodologies 
that are being used to affect cur- 
rently untreatable genetic dis- 
eases and to manufacture poten- 
tially useful future biotech drugs. 

Some of the newer technol- 
ogies in pharmaceutical biotech- 
nology may make their biggest 
impact on pharmacy practice by 
significantly changing the way 
drugs are discovered or “de- 
signed” and developed. 


Gene therapy 


Recent advances in genetic 


engineering have made gene 
therapy or gene transplantation 
a reality. Gene therapy is the re- 
placement of a patient’s faulty 
or missing genetic information 
with a healthy gene so that the 
patient can now correctly pro- 
duce an endogenous biochemi- 
eal; in essence, a drug deliv- 
ery technique.”’ The patient’s 
own modified genetic informa- 
tion actually serves as the manu- 
facturer of the biopharmaceuti- 
eal. 


Antisense technology 


The development of technol- 
ogies to study DNA-DNA and 
DNA-RNA interactions has led 
to the formation of what is called 
“antisense technology.””'The 
term is derived from the process 
of transcription. 

When two strands of DNA sep- 
arate during transcription, the 
strand of DNA used as the tem- 
plate for the messenger RNA is 
known as the “antisense strand,” 

Continued on page 37 


DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, February 15, 1993 


Continued from page 36 
while the other strand is the 
“sense strand.” 

Antisense technology is the 
study of DNA-DNA and DNA- 
RNA interactions with the anti- 
sense and sense strands of DNA. 
This has led to a variety of re- 
search with potential uses in diag- 
nostics and therapeutics. 


Pharmacist’s role 


What will be the role of commu- 
nity pharmacists concerning 
these pharmaceutical biotechno- 
logies? Will pharmacists have a 
place in gene therapy and anti- 
sense therapy? 

Opportunities for the commu- 
nity pharmacist in the dispens- 
_ ing and clinical use of new bio- 
technology-derived products 
should exist if the pharmacist 
takes advantage of them. Again, 
to take advantage of the oppor- 
tunities presented by pharma- 
ceutical biotechnology, the 
pharmacist must better under- 
stand the nature of biotechnolo- 
gy-derived products. 


Handling and storage 


To help with that understand- 
ing, Table 3 provides general re- 
marks concerning handling and 
storage of the rDNA-produced 
pharmaceuticals currently ap- 
proved in the United States. 

A brief listing of some possible 
precautions, adverse reactions and 
drug interactions is also provided. 

The preparation and adminis- 
tration of drugs of recombinant 
origin is unlike the more conven- 
tional pharmaceutical prepara- 
tions, yet similar to many other 
biopharmaceuticals. 

The protein nature of hybri- 
doma and recombinant DNA 
technology produced drugs 
makes them subject to the limited 
stability characteristic of pro- 
teins, which will be further short- 
ened upon reconstitution. 

Therefore, proper storage of 
both the lyophilized and the re- 
constituted product is essential. 

Table 3 indicates that many of 
the recombinant DNA-produced 
compounds are stored refrigerat- 
ed at 2-8 degrees Celsius, and to 
avoid freezing or exposure to ex- 
cessive heat, as these conditions 
will decrease the stability of the 
protein with a concomitant de- 
crease in potency. 

An additional concern is the 


continuing education 


fact that most are expensive 
drugs, so special care must be tak- 
en not to inactivate the therapeu- 
tic protein during storage and 
handling. 

Some recombinant DNA-de- 
rived pharmaceuticals, in partic- 
ular the cytokines (interferons, 
colony stimulating factors and 
interleukin 2), are formulated 
with human serum albumin to 
prevent adhesion of the protein 
drug to the glass surface of the 
vial which also results in loss of 
protein. Such drugs shouldn’t be 
shaken to prevent foaming of the 
albumin. 


Dosage forms 


Remember that proteins are 
composed of amino acids joined 
by peptide bonds, and that these 
bonds are acid labile. This limits 
the potential for oral dosage 
forms of rDNA-produced phar- 
maceuticals, and necessitates in- 


travenous, intramuscular and. 


subcutaneous administration of 
these drugs. 


Summary 


Advances in pharmaceutical 
biotechnology and in particular, 
hybridoma methodology and re- 
combinant DNA technology, 
have provided improved pharma- 
ceuticals, novel therapeutic 
agents and unique diagnostic 
products. 

These techniques can furnish 
us with a seemingly futuristic ap- 
proach to shape therapeutic inter- 
vention in the 21st century. 

Yet, as you have seen from this 
lesson, pharmaceutical biotech- 
nology and the therapeutic and di- 
agnostic agents it produces are 
truly practical, easily under- 
standable and not at all magical, 
mystical or foreboding. 

Some of the newer and less-un- 
derstood technologies that make 
up pharmaceutical biotechnology 
are poised to make an impact on 
pharmacy practice by significant- 
ly changing the way pharmaceuti- 
cal companies discover or “de- 
sign” and develop drugs. 

Community pharmacists can 
play a major role in the pharma- 
ceutical care of patients being 
administered biotechnology- 
produced pharmaceuticals if 
they continue to fulfill and ex- 
pand their role as the biotechnol- 
ogy knowledge base of the health 
care team. a

DRUG STORE NEWS, March 1, 1993 


OPINION 


Retailers devote higher priority to shrink 


Shrink has risen up the priority list of chain drug 
operators who must cut costs to stay competitive. A 
bold aggressiveness marks chain efforts today in 
loss prevention, prosecution of thieves both inside 
and outside their companies and the seeking of civil 
recovery. 

Mike Knievel, vp-corporate security at Rite Aid, 
says: “We prosecute where we have a chance to win. 
Jurisdiction determines. 


We make civil demand in 
all states where allowed.” 
Bob Ficken Jr., director 


MARKET of human resources and 
PULSE loss prevention at Drug 
AL HELLER Barn, says: “We prosecute 


all internal theft. When 
[the thefts are] external, 
managers make decisions 
on the fly using their own judgment.” 

In presentations at the recent NACDS Small 
Chain Conference, both agreed that a substantial 
part of the problem is inside, so undue emphasis on 
shoplifters is misdirected. 

Knievel cited a 1992 Ernst & Young survey, which 
showed that in drug stores, employee theft accounts for 
6 percent of the apprehensions and 55 percent of the 
amounts recovered. Overall employee theft accounts for 
7 percent of the apprehensions and 38 percent of the 
amounts recovered, according to the survey. 

Ficken urged pre-employment screening to 
counter this problem. “My average bad hire will cost 
me $3,000 [in losses, training and salary]. If I can 
prevent two bad hires a year, that pays for all my 
pre-employment tests. It is my single biggest loss 
preventer,” he said. 

Intelliview, Charlotte, N.C., administers the com- 
puter-aided telephone interviews for Drug Barn, pos- 
ing 100 questions to job candidates within 10 minutes. 
Speed encourages candid responses, which help flag 
areas to be probed in further interviews. CVS uses 


Greentree for its pre-screening. 

Rite Aid’s Knievel said, “Most people caught steal- 
ing are fairly new employees. But when long-term em- 
ployees steal, they generally steal more.” It’s neces- 
sary to key in on changes in people’s lives, he added, 
noting that corporate personnel such as accounts pay- 
able, buyers, real estate, store planning and payroll 
clerks “get into you for bigger dollars.” 

Knievel also cited stunning findings of a study that 
appeared in the January 1993 issue of Chain Store Age 
Executive, a Lebhar-Friedman sister publication. 
Conducted by Joseph and Edna Josephson, Institute 
of Ethics, the study revealed that out of 8,965 people 
aged 15-30, 33 percent of high school students and 16 
percent of college students admitted having stolen 
from a store within the past year. “Unfortunately, 
that’s)who we hire,” said Knievel. 

If youths pose a double-whammy to drug chains, 
both as store staffers and shoppers, Drug Barn’s 
Ficken offers some tips: 

@ tie store manager bonuses to loss prevention; 

® give immediate cash rewards to hourly employ- 
ees who go out of their way to prevent a shoplift or 
help a customer; 

® interview hourly workers about shrink problems 
in their stores; 

® probe apprehended shoplifters about the way 
they and other thieves work to develop successful 
techniques against them. 

He noted further that electronic article surveil- 
lance has slashed shrink at Drug Barn by 22 percent, 
that Revlon is experimenting with source tagging 
and that cigarettes will be the next category to be 
third-party tagged. 

For his part, Knievel outlined specific strategies to 
counter endless theft opportunities by corporate and 
store staff, including managers. - 

Both agreed that systems to deter theft are the best 
investments. “You don’t want to spend time chasing 
thieves. You want to prevent theft,” said Knievel. 


Just last month, NARD and NACDS put aside de- 
cades of bitter and often counterproductive rivalry to 
cooperate on a number of community pharmacy prac- 
tice issues of concern to both independents and chains. 

The top item on the agenda for the newly-formed 
NARD-NACDS “working group” is the future role 
of pharmacy technicians—an issue that has long 
been a source of friction between chain and indepen- 

dent factions. 


Before we had a chance 
to digest the implications 
of that initiative, the two 
national retail pharmacy 
groups had taken another, 
even bigger step toward 
cooperative action. 

Describing themselves 
as “the nation’s communi- 
ty retail pharmacy coalition,” NARD and NACDS an- 
nounced their agreement on a new series of principles 
for health care reform. 

Behind these dramatic moves toward drug store 
détente: a recognition by chain and independent 
pharmacy leaders that sweeping changes in health 
care are imminent, and that retail pharmacy had 
better speak with a clear, strong voice in order to be 
heard on this issue. 

What common ground can independents and chains 
find on this issue? More than you might guess. 

The new NARD-NACDS coalition has identified 
four “concepts” which both sides agree are “funda- 
mental” to any reform of the current health delivery 


» WASHINGTON 
) PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


NARD, NACDS form pharmacy coalition 


system. 

Here’s what chains and independents want: 

® Coverage of prescription drugs under “any basic 
health care plan.” Since pharmacists are in “a key posi- 
tion” to monitor medication use and decrease overall 
health care costs, the “provision of pharmacists’ ser- 
vices are essential,” NARD and NACDS agree. 

@ An aggressive effort to cut third-party adminis- 
trative fat. Redundant and “unnecessary layers of in- 
termediaries” are clogging the current system, and 
new uniform standards are needed to promote elec- 
tronic claims processing. 

@ Fresh assurance that government is committed to 
preserving “freedom of choice” for patients and pro- 
viders. The best way to ensure a competitive market 
for pharmacy services is to guarantee “the public’s 
free access to community pharmacy and community 
pharmacy’s free access to the marketplace.” 

@ A crackdown on multi-tier pricing by pharmaceu- 
tical manufacturers. Eliminating discriminatory pric- 
ing by drug manufacturers is “essential to the preser- 
vation of a competitive community pharmacy 
marketplace.” All pharmacies, chain and independent 
alike, “must be able to acquire prescription drugs at 
the same price, subject only to economies of scale, in- 
cluding volume.” 

With one swing of the axe, NACDS and NARD 
served notice that retail pharmacy is ready to stand 
up to third-party intermediaries, managed care ma- 
vens, pharmaceutical manufacturers and the federal 
government. 

Not bad for openers.

Teen market basket> — 


An exclusive Drug Store News/‘TEEN magazine study 


n the past several years, chains have been trying to court 
the hae > high-consumption teenage market. 
Chains like Eckerd, Walgreens and Perry Drug have 
enhanced their merchandising presentations of products and 
brands popular with teens, especially beauty care products 
like cosmetic organizers, teen fragrances and body sprays, 
oil free makeups and cleansers, feminine h giene, bath and 
body products with natural ingredients and lipglosses. 

At the same time, they are also finding the space to mer- 
chandise new lines dedicated to teens like Almay’s teen treat- 
ments and cosmetics, Del Labs Natur- 
istics and Natural Glow, and the new 
skin treatment line from Cover Girl. 

They are reacting to what Jay Cole, 
publisher of "TEEN magazine, amajor

But in spite of all the interest in and attention being paid to 
teens, many teens still say that they don’t know much about 
drug stores, and don’t often think of them as a place to shop. 

Research shows that teens do the bulk of their shopping 
in food stores, department stores or in specialty shops. 
Many also buy their cosmetics from the Mary Kay or Avon 
lady who services their mothers. 

However, as philosophers and athletes often remind us, 
whatever can be interpreted as a problem can also be inter- 
preted as an opportunity: a challenge 
to overcome. 

And that is how Drug Store News 
sees the teen market. As a challenge. 
An opportunity. A group to be court- 
ed, charmed and won over. 

But to court or charm someone, you 
first have to get to know them. That 
means teens need to be given a chance 
to speak for themselves about what it’s 
like to shop in drug stores. 

So with the help of "TEEN maga- 
zine and BKG Youth, the country’s 
leading youth marketing company, 
Drug Store News organized the chain 
drug industry’s first Teen Market 
Basket Study. 

We wanted to see if, given some 
discretionary money to spend, teens 
Source: U.S. Census. | would think to go to a drug store as a

2000 vs. 1990 


However, as attractive as retailers 
nn they find the market, they also report that teens are 
“fickle” and hard to pull into a store’s franchise. 

“We try to market to teens,” says Perry Drug’s vp of mer- 
chandising Steve Lund, “but they’re constantly changing, and 
what’s ‘in’ one day, is ‘out’ the next. Also teens don’t respond to 
ads the way adults do, so it’s not that simple to reach them.” 

Even chains that advertise in teen magazines report that it’s 
difficult to judge how successful their marketing efforts have 
been. Many chains are still experimenting with a variety of dif- 
ferent strategies to reach this market, ranging from direct mail 


place to shop and, if they did go to 
one, what they would buy and how they would like the ex- 
perience. 

We asked BKG Youth to pick out six typical teens from 
markets around the country and, in partnership with "TEEN 
magazine, we gave six of these young women $100 to spend in 
a local drug store. 

How our teens shopped; what they bought; what they 
thought of drug stores, and some suggestions on how drug 
stores can improve their image with teens, is the subject of 
this special report.

Teen market basket 


Chains work harder to target fickle teens 


rug chains like teens. They 

like knowing the market is 

projected to grow 15 percent 
by the year 2000. They’re delighted 
to hear that teenagers have twice as 
much discretionary income to spend 
today than they had just 10 years ago 
and that their total spending influ- 
ences are over $130 billion. And it 
doesn’t bother them at all to know 
that teens spend about 50 percent of 
their welt income on products 
that make them look good. 

What drug chains don’t like is not 
knowing exactly how to reach teen- 
agers or how to talk to them when they 
do reach them. 

“The toughest thing about teens,” 
says Steve Lubin, divisional mer- 
chandise manager for cosmetics at 
Walgreens, is “they’re fickle. If you 
find something that really works, 
overnight it changes.” 

“They’re a. tough market to hit,” 
says Steve Lund, vp of merchandis- 
ing for Perry Drug. “We’ve tried us- 
ing coupon books to reach them, but 
I’m not sure that works with teens 
and it’s hard to measure its effective- 
ness. They’re also always changing, 
so it’s hard to know what they want.” 

At Harco Drug in Tuscaloosa, Ala., 
Jim Harrison, assistant to the presi- 
dent, also says the market has tremen- 
dous potential but is “hard to reach.” 


How do you target teens? 


Lund thinks the answer may have 
something to do “with getting involved 
in the schools. If you can somehow get 
your business associated with the 
schools, that might do it,” he says. 

Perry Drug is currently working on 
developing a magazine rack that they 
could position in the cosmetic section 
where teens like to browse. Susan 
Lund, cosmetic buyer at Minneapolis- 
based Snyder Drug, has looked at a 
similar type of rack developed by Condé 
Nast, but she has to overcome the prob- 
lem of finding the space for it if Snyder 
decides to do it. 

Snyder is also testing “Club Teen” 
which it promotes through a local high 
school. Paul Mohlke, who manages the 
Ames, Iowa store where the test has 
been underway since April of last year, 
says it has worked out very well. 
Mohlke says his store currently has 
more than 300 active club members, and 
they are shopping the store every two or 
three weeks spending an average of be- 
tween $5 and $10 per visit. . 

“It’s nice to see teens coming in,” 
says Mohlke. “It’s worked very well 
for us, and I think at some point we'll 
be expanding the test.” 

Other chains like Walgreens have 
tried to reach out to teens by buying 
some media segments targeted to 
teens. Walgreens, Rite Aid, Eckerd, 
Harco and many other chains try to 
court teens by carrying lines they like, 


relationship based on glitz. They want 
meanin ad talk, straight talk, and be- 
cause they are so concerned about their 
appearance, they want to be told how a 
product can help them, and where they 
can easily buy it.” 

“If you want to court teens, you have 
to show respect for them as custom- 
ers,” says Theresa Sutton Fryback, a 
spokesperson for Caboodles, Inc., the 
country’s leading brand of cosmetic 
box organizers. “You can’t talk down 
to them, whether it’s in your product, 
your advertising or your promotions. 
Today’s 12 year old is very sophisticat- 
ed, and many 16 year olds think of 
themselves as 34 year olds.”

dent and intelligent,” says Lene Espo- 
sito, vp of new products and creative de-

Contrary to some adults’ expecta- 
tions, price also counts with teens. 
Fifty percent of the 12-15 girls that 
‘TEEN surveyed reported that when 
it comes to buying a cosmetic prod- 
uct, price is a major consideration. 
One-third, 36 percent, of all girls 12- 
15 also say that it’s the brand name 
that attracts them. 

The story doesn’t change much 
when it comes to older teens. Among 
16 to 19 year olds, 59 percent said ac- 
tual usage motivated their decision to 
repurchase, while 58 percent said it 
was the product’s price that influ- 
enced them. Twenty-six percent said 
it was the brand name that attracted 
them.

K&B shopping spree 


Charlotte is a Louisiana girl, so it was 
almost inevitable that she choose to 
spend her $100 spree money at K&B. 

A frequent drug store shopper, Char- 
lotte goes to her local K&B an average of 
three to four times per week, and once 
there she spends approximately a half 
hour shopping and Breviin 

“It’s “| to get there,” she says, 
“since it’s close to my home.” Although 
her parents introduced her to K&B, 
she began going to there alone by the 


time she turned 10. 

By the time she was done, she had

makeup. Also, Clearasil, Scope 
mouthwash, Oral-B toothbrushes, An- 
acin aspirin, Sure deodorant, TDK 
blank tapes and tracing paper. 

Most everything Charlotte pur-

tried before and needed or wanted 
more of. She said that she purchased 
these items because she had seen them 
advertised on television or because she 
liked their packaging. 

Advertising and promotion 

Brochures and pamphlets that come 
in the mail is how Charlotte finds out 


about sale and special items that are 
available in her local drug stores.

the magazine section and the adver- 
tisements in the news aper to see if 
there are any good eats 

Signs in the window or announce-

get Charlotte’s attention. 

However, she is familiar with this 
store, so she said she would definitely 
come back. To attract more teens, 
Charlotte recommends that drug 
stores sponsor teen events such as a 
baseball team or a dance. A student 
discount could spark interest. “With 
a student or high school I.D., the 
store could take 10 percent off pur- 
chases,” she suggests.

adults, so they’re not too helpful.”

Manufacturer's perspective for teens 


to teens feel their best ideas come 
from talking to and listening to 
teens, they often believe that retailers 
who want to attract teen shoppers 
should take a similar approach. 

“Price isn’t really an issue with 
teens,” says Lene Esposito, vp of 
new products and creative develop- 
ment for Cabot Laboratories Inc. in 
Central Islip, N.Y. 

“They will pay more for a product 
that promises to meet their needs. 
They’ll also appreciate it when the help 
in a store pays attention to them. I’ve 
been in some stores where I’ve seen 
clerks ignore a teen in jeans and sneak- 
ers to serve a woman in a business suit, 
even though the teen was there before 
the woman. It isn’t 
fair and teens know 
it. That can hurt a 
store’s business 
with teens.” 

Donna Shapiro, 
who handles con- 
sumer marketing 
for White Plains, 
N.Y.-based Tam- 
brands, points out 
that it’s important 
to keep in touch 
with teens on an 
“on-going basis” 
because’ _ teens 
change constantly.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


PayLess opens first tobacco-free store 


SAN LUIS OBISPO, Calif. — PayLess Drug Stores will not 
sell tobacco products in its new store here, which opened in late 
February. San Luis Obispo, in central California, has a city ordi- 
nance against smoking in any public buildings or businesses, al- 
though tobacco products may be sold. According to PayLess 
president and chief executive officer Tim McAlear, other retail- 
ers have been asked by city officials not to carry tobacco prod- 
ucts, but PayLess is the first major chain to comply. 
The ak PayLeen site faced an obstacle several months ago 
when the chain announced its intention to open in a former Vons 
et. Local groups protested the loss of a grocery store, 
but PayLess arranged for a local chain, Scolari’s Market, to build 
on an adjacent site. Construction of the supermarket will begin at 
a future date after the existing building has been razed. 


Medicine Shoppe to buy 8 pharmacies 


ST. LOUIS — Medicine Shoppe International has agreed to 
acquire eight retail pharmacies from Fidelity Prescriptions and 
Complete Home Care of Dayton, Ohio. The eight Dayton-area 
locations do a combined business of $10 million. 


Charboneau, Heller fo speak at PLMA 


MIAMI — Gary Charboneau, senior vp of sales and marketing, 
Duane Reade, and Al Heller, executive editor, Drug Store News, 
wills on New Directions for Drug Chains during the Private 
Label Manufacturers Association 1993 Annual Meeting and Lead- 
ership Conference Mar. 25-28 at the Doral Resort here. The theme 
is “Uncharted Waters, Untapped Opportunities.” They'll address 
the crowd of an anticipated 200 store brand manufacturers and 
trade executives on Saturday morning, Mar. 27. 


Gary’s denies rumors of sale of stores 


EAGLEVILLE, Pa. — Raymond Hoy, director of marketing 
at I Got it at Gary’s, said that rumors circulating about the sale of 
the five-unit deep discounter are completely untrue. He believes 
that rumors may have started when local trade toe heard of the 
chain’s newest location in Abington, Pa. He said Gary’s has no in- 
tention to sell or to restructure the the business in any way. 


O&M to open DC in Birmingham, Ala. 


RICHMOND, Va. — Owens & Minor plans to open a custom 
distribution center in Birmingham, Ala. in June. No site has been 
selected yet and the size of the center is yet to be determined. 

The Birmingham market had been serviced previously by 
O&M’s DC in Atlanta. The new DC will allow the distributor of 
medical and surgical supplies to expand its service in the Bir- 
mingham area. 


Revco raises funds for McDonald House 


TWINSBURG, Ohio— Revco D.S. said it contributed $270,000 
to 33 Ronald McDonald Houses through its annual sale of Holida 
Nutcrackers. The seven-SKU line of nutcrackers are sold eac 
Christmas season at costs ranging from $5.99 to $9.99, with $2.50 
from the sale of each device going to local Ronald McDonald 
houses. The houses provide temporary shelter for families of chil- 
dren receiving treatment for serious chronic illnesses.
