Alliance building sparks 


By James Frederick 

ORLANDO — To hear dis- 
tribution people tell it, it’s 
only a matter of time before 
the last walls of suspicion 
crumble between retailer and 
supplier and the two sides 
merge into a seamless, com- 
puter-charged sales machine 
running directly on consumer 
input. That, at least, was the 
underlying consensus among 
many of the participants at the 
fourth-annual NACDS Distri- 
bution & Logistics Conference 
here last month. 

In the words of conference 
attendee Don Smith of Confab 
Companies, “It will no longer 
be ‘buy and sell’ between re- 
tailer and supplier; it will just 
be ‘sell.’ The consumer is the 
one we all have to satisfy.” 

Distribution and logistics 
managers from a dozen-and-a- 
half major drug chains met with 
nearly 200 of their counterparts 
during the three-day event. 
That included operations, logis- 
tics and service executives 
from many of the industry’s 
biggest supplier companies, as 
well as computer, logistics, 
trucking and warehouse sys- 
tems vendors. Their chief pur- 
pose: to find new ways to im- 
prove distribution efficiencies, 
reduce costs and respond more 
quickly to consumer demand. 


‘A complete re-evaluation’ 


Indeed, conference partici- 
pants arrived at the Stouffer 
Orlando Resort Feb. 17-19 with 
a sense of mission, even urgen- 
cy. Said John Gleeson, Wal- 
greens’ vice president of mar- 
keting systems and services, 
“This isn’t just a logistics ren- 
aissance. . . this is a complete 
re-evaluation of the way our in- 
dustry does business.” 


Most of his coun- 
terparts on the 
trade floor and in 
conference semi- 
nars agreed. Retail 
attendees seemed 
keenly aware of the 
need to cut inven- 
tory and distribu- 
tion costs in an era 
of super-competi- 
tion, and they spent 
the better part of 
three days putting 
into practice this 
year’s conference 
dictum: “Nurturing 
Alliances Creates 
Distribution Solu- 
tions.” 

“Communication 
[between retail 
buyers and suppli- 
ers] is key,” said 
conference co-chairman Ron 
Miller, senior vice president of 
distribution and logistics for 
Rite Aid, in opening remarks. 

“The times are changing, 
and we’re seeing a glimpse of 
the possibilities” that alliances 
can foster, Miller said. He 
foresaw a time when retailers 
and vendors could “do away 
completely” with the adver- 
sarial wall between the two 
sides and “become true part- 
ners” in moving product from 
factory to store. “If retailers 
and suppliers can truly learn 
to communicate, we could all 
focus our efforts. . .on lower- 
ing costs,” added Jim Whit- 
man, vice president of indus- 
try affairs for NACDS. 

Perhaps no group of retailer 
executives is better equipped 
to see the advantages to infor- 
mation-sharing and _ alliance- 
building with wholesalers and 
manufacturers than are the in- 
dustry’s distribution and lo-

DRUG STORE NEWS, March 15, 1993 


OPINION 


Grocery chains innovate non-food marketing 


Food store and drug chain executives sound amazing- 
ly alike when voicing concerns about low-cost competi- 
tion, fast-changing consumers and tough markets. 

I’ve been on the road quite a lot lately, mixing visits 
at drug chains across the country with meetings 
among supermarket presidents. This whirlwind of 
travel has been invaluable for the chance to hear som- 
ber thoughts on key issues from some of the nation’s 
most influential retailers. 


At the FMI Annual Mid- 
winter Conference, for ex- 
ample, I spoke at length 


MARKET with four enlightened gro- 
PULSE cery chain presidents: Don 
AL HELLER Gallegos of King Soopers, 


Colorado; Dennis Eck of 
Vons, California; Dan Jo- 
sephs of Dominick’s, IIli- 
nois, and Jeff Gietzen of D&W, Michigan. 

Their chains stand among the most innovative in 
pursuing non-food business (translation: core drug 
store categories). They stand out in their ability to 
bring winning non-food strategies and customer ser- 
vice programs to chains in a trade class that largely 
values the power of food’s fast turns (sell the goods be- 
fore you have to pay for them) above nearly all else. 

When D&W’s Gietzen talks about competitor Meijer, 
Inc., for instance, it is with the same sense of respect 
voiced by F&M’s Frank Newman, Perry’s Jack Robin- 
son and Arbor’s Gene Applebaum. All these Michigan 
retailers understand they can’t simply compete with 
Meijer on price, but they can win share in other ways. 

For Gietzen, it means living by his D&W theme, “Dol- 
lar’s Worth, the best combination of service, quality and 
price.” He caters to unique cultural segments within his 
markets, aims to be first with new ideas and items, and 
to be different in many departments. An internal study 
showed HBC sales pick up $1,000 per week when phar- 
macy is added to a store, so D&W is now halfway toward 
installing them chainwide. Impulse perishables line 
store perimeters. Lucrative floral centers are boutiqued 
with greeting cards. 

At Vons, chief operations officer Dennis Eck runs in- 
tegrity audits on sanitation, prices, bar codes, in-stocks. 
“We’re no longer a tonnage business,” says Eck. “We’re 


an SKU business on five times more items than we used 
to be. It adds complexity. Consumers want simplicity.” 

One current challenge: give consumers unobstruct- 
ed grasp of products at 70-inch shelf height. “That is 
very comfortable,” he adds, noting that Vons surveys 
hundreds of older people by neighborhood to learn 
what they want: a full range of products, but simpli- 
fied with shelf tags, smaller sizes at waist level and 
pharmacy positioned as a health care center. 

Avoiding the trap of diminished square-foot perfor- 
mance of larger stores, Eck, in developing a 75,000- 
square-foot combo, stayed with miniaturization tech- 
niques. “Don’t let air expand to fill the container. Look 
to add new sales opportunities,” he says. Some re- 
sults: new party, home organization and business ser- 
vice centers, and expanded floral. 

Perishables get plenty of space at Dominick’s, but 
nonfoods are also important across the chain’s five for- 
mats. “We made a mistake earlier when we let Wal- 
greens open pharmacies next to us,” Josephs said can- 
didly. But he likes efforts by Bob Storch, formerly of 
Revco, to raise the performance, negotiating clout 
and professionalism of the chain’s pharmacies. “With- 
in two years, we should have 35 to 40 pharmacies out 
of 86 Dominick’s” with expanded HBC, said Josephs. 

He also said Dominick’s is adding microlabs “even 
though photofinishing customers shop promos, and 
it’s hard to build a loyalty.” Video rental is in 30 stores, 
which carry 800 to 3,000 titles each, depending on size. 
“We want store visits and the complete shopping 
trip,” Josephs said. 

Under Gallegos, King Soopers has innovated in 
books and magazines, where TV monitors play CNN, 
attract men and children, and leave women to shop. 
The chain sells stamps at every checkstand, has added 
UPS and shoe repair, and may try dry cleaning. 

Gallegos has raised store manager pay to end fric- 
tion with pharmacists. Store signs read, “Guest Ser- 
vice,” and he visits each store quarterly unannounced. 

On food sales at drug and discount stores, he says: 
“They’re high-consumable, high-turn items. It 
doesn’t keep women out of the supermarket. I haven’t 
lost the trip, but we’re splitting the sale.” 

These sound bites from exceptional retailers show 
how innovation can bolster chains against tough odds. 


Here in Washington, almost everybody is gunning 
for the drug industry and the heaviest fire is coming 
from the White House. 

The first shoe hit the floor last month when the pres- 
ident launched a blistering attack on “spiraling” prices 
for vaccines charged by “major drug manufacturers.” 

Next came a series of shots at the pharmaceutical 
industry in the “Vision for Change in America” eco- 
nomic stimulation pro- 


posal that Clinton un- 
veiled during his State of 
the Union address. 

Buried in the fine print 
of that plan is a proposal 
to repeal provisions of 
OBRA ’90 that prohibit 
states from adopting re- 
strictive Medicaid for- 
mularies—a change that could cut Medicaid spend- 
ing for branded drugs by $70 million in four years. 

The Administration’s plan would also sharply reduce 
the industry’s cherished tax subsidy for Puerto Rican 
operations, and direct FDA to boost “user fees.” 

Not all the flak is from the White House, however. 
Congressional criticism of the drug industry is up, too. 
House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee 
chairman Henry Waxman (D-Calif.) has scheduled a 
series of hearings into new charges that wasteful in- 
dustry research and development practices are driv- 


WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


Pharmaceutical manufacturers under fire 


ing up drug prices by encouraging the development of 
duplicative “me too” drugs. 

Meanwhile, Rep. Fortney “Pete” Stark (D-Calif.), 
the chairman of the House Ways and Means Health 
Subcommittee, is talking up a Canadian-style pre- 
scription drug price control plan that would prevent 
manufacturers from raising prices more than two 
points faster than the annual increase in the Consum- 
er Price Index. 

On the other side of Capitol Hill, Senate Aging 
Committee chairman David Pryor (D-Ark.) is 
charging that 19 of the nation’s 31 largest pharma- 
ceutical manufacturers raised outpatient drug 
prices at double the rate of inflation last year. In re- 
sponse, Pryor is proposing to go beyond the Clinton 
plan to limit the industry’s Section 936 tax credits— 
and abolish them altogether. 

The embattled pharmaceutical industry can’t 
count on getting much sympathy from retail phar- 
macy. Drug store industry outrage over the multi- 
tier pricing practices of many manufacturers has 
never been greater—and the complaints are not 
coming only from independents. 

Eliminating the “discriminatory pricing practices 
by manufacturers of prescription products” was one 
of four “fundamental concepts” of health care reform 
agreed to by the new NACDS/NARD coalition. 

This is not going to be a good year for brand name 
pharmaceutical manufacturers.

CLINTON ATTACKS 
SCRIPT ‘PRICE GOUGERS’ 


President Clinton’s vow to 
curb “drug price gouging” 
by pharmaceutical manu- 
facturers is one campaign 
promise the Administration 
appears ready to keep. 

First step, according to 
the president’s new econom- 
ic recovery plan, calls for re- 
pealing the OBRA 90 rules 
prohibiting drug formular- 
ies by state Medicaid pro- 
grams. Estimated savings: 
$70 million over 4 years. 

Next, the Administration 
wants to raise “user fees” 
that manufacturers pay the 
FDA to review new drugs. 
Look for the White House 
to put even more pressure 
on pharmaceutical makers 
when Hillary unveils the 
Administration’s health re- 
form plan. 


CONGRESS EYES SCRIPT 
PRICE CONTROL BOARD 


One option already un- 
der debate in Washington: 
outright federal price con- 
trols on drugs ala Canada’s 
tos igo price review 

oard. 

A new study prepared for 
House Health Subcommit- 
tee Chairman Pete Stark 
(D-Calif.) by Minnesota 
pharmacy professor Ste- 
phen Schondelmeyer con- 
cludes that limiting pharma- 
ceutical price increases to 
the rise in the Consumer 
Price Index plus 2 percent 
would cut U.S. prescription 
drug spending by $78 billion 
over the next decade.

editor’s note 


A kinder, gentler 
profession? 


Drug store News For the Pharmacist re- 
cently attended conferences by two diver- 


heartily endorses the new NACDS Nation- 
al Council of Chain Practitioners as an orga- 
nization whose time has come (see page 59). 

The leaders of these organizations are 
to be commended for putting aside turf 
concerns in the interest of the good of the 
profession. 

All these similarities, partnerships and 


gent trade associations. I was struck by 


be merging or at least distinctions blurring. 

The first conference was the NARD Mul- 
tiple Locations Conference held in Acapul- 
co in January; the second was the NACDS 
Small Chain Conference last month in Or- 
lando. While subgroup membership is a 
matter of degree (NARD defines multi-unit 
as 2 or more—indeed, one attendee boasts 
70 units—and NACDS considers owner- 
ship of 4-50 stores with less than $100M in 
sales to fit their criteria), the similarities be- 
tween the two groups was striking. 

The seminar offerings were similar—in- 
novative ways to expand your pharmacy 
services, e.g., home infusion therapy, 
home health care and long-term care—and 
the conversations and concerns at small 
group discussions were déja vu. And now 
NACDS and NARD are even joining forces 
with the new community practice joint ven- 


endorsements. .

becodtie a inifiod profession, and good- 
ness knows what will happen then!

OBRA report: Three months post-implementation 

Pharmacy groups urge a delay in enforcement of new Medicaid 
Drug Utilization Review and patient counseling requirements un- 
til all the groundrules are firmed up. Here are the open issues yet 
to be resolved. See page 19. 


Daily duties make techs distinct from clerks 
While state regulations differ as to what’s allowed, certain func- 
tions are prohibited by all. See Technician Training page 26. 


How to communicate pharmacy price increases 


Increasing prices are a way of life. Customers don’t like them, 
and how you handle them can mean the return of a satisfied patron. 
See Ask the Expert page 48. 


NACDS & NARD form health care coalition 


After 60 years of sometimes intense confrontation between 
chain and independent practitioners, a new spirit of cooperation 
surfaces. Issues like third party, feocdes-el dhsice and discrimi- 
natory pricing find common ground. See page 60.

Written offers to counsel 


Theres less consensus 
among pharmacy practitioners 
on the question of whether 
pharmacies should be allowed 
to make the offer of counseling 
via signs, bag stuffers or other 
written notices. 

According to a recent APhA 
survey, at: least seven states 
including Maryland and Virgin- 
ia—have adopted legislation or 
regulations allowing pharma- 
cists to make written offers to 
counsel, and some chain drug 
industry officials are urging the 
HCFA to encourage such “flex- 
ibility’ in other states. 

Rite Aid government vice 
president James Krahulec, for 
one, told federal regulators that 
“The mandating of an oral pre- 
sentation by the pharmacist, on 
each and every prescription 
concerning the fact that coun- 


seling is available, is unproduc- 
tive and costly.’ 

Outside of the chain drug in- 
dustry, however, there seems 
to be little support for written 
offers of counseling. 

John Gans, APhA executive 
vice president, told Medicaid 
officials that the use of “posted 
signs in lieu of an oral offer to 
counsel is “unacceptable, © 
while NARD said it is “abso- 
lutely unconscionable for [the] 
HCFA to allow written material 
alone to be substituted for the 
oral provision of information.

states to decide is whether coun- 
seling must be offered only to pa-

to those with refills as well.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Kuske departs PayLess 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. -— Jerry Kuske has resigned his pe 
tion as senior vice president of operations for PayLess Dru 
Stores. In a restructuring move July, Kuske was shif 
from senior vice president of merchandising and marketing to 
the operations post. At press time, PayLess officials were un- 
available for comment. 


Cardinal to acquire Solomons stock 


DUBLIN, Ohio — Cardinal Distribution has announced its 
agreement to acquire all of Savannah, Ga. -based Solomons 
stock in Spex for 849,364 Cardinal common shares, worth 
about $23.5 million. Solomons, which serves Georgia, South 
Carolina and Florida and has annual revenues of about $180 mil- 
lion, will retain its management and will be operated as a sepa- 
rate entity. The acquisition was expected at press time to be 
completed by the end of April. 


Exclusively HBA set for Sept. in Detroit 


CHICAGO — This year’s Exclusively HBA show is planned 
for Sept. 21-23 at Detroit’s Cobo Convention Center. Nearly 
400 branded, private label and ethnic HBA suppliers represent- 
ing about 85 percent of sales in the consumer products category 
are expected to exhibit at the show. The show will be attended 
by buyers from all classes of trade from the United States, Cen- 
tral and South America and other countries. 


Med. Shoppe to buy eight pharmacies 


ST. LOUIS — Medicine Shoppe International has si an 
agreement to purchase eight retail pharmacies from Fidelity Pre- 
scriptions and Complete Home Care, Inc. in Dayton, Ohio. The 
pharmacies will be franchised under the Medicine Shoppe name. 

The acquisition is part of an effort by the franchise pharmacy 
company to bring profitable independent pharmacies into the 
franchise organization. 


June AHBAI conference in Hilton Head 


CHICAGO — The American Health and Beauty Aids Insti- 
tute will host its 1993 Mid-Year Business Conference, themed 
Focus 2000: Strategies for Future Growth, June 12-15 at the 
Hyatt Regency Hotel in Hilton Head, S.C. 

Participants will explore the importance to the African- 
American consumer and will learn how to increase overall store 
profitability by meeting the total needs of this target market. 


Buttrey names two to exec positions 


GREAT FALLS, Mont. — Edward C. Agnew has been 
named chairman and chief executive officer of Buttrey Food and 
Drug. Agnew, who has been p=esident and chief executive offi- 
cer of the company since 1990, will replace Peter J. Sodini as 
chairman. Sodini will remain on the company’s board. 

In a related move, Joseph H. Fernandez will become presi- 
dent and chief operating officer and will become a member of the 
company’s board of directors. Most recently, Fernandez was 
executive vice president and chief operating officer of Kings Su- 
per Markets Inc.

Phar-Mor’s new format features a roomier interior and a dramatically enlarged greeting cards depart- 
ment, as well as new items in cosmetics, bath/body, housewares and HBA. 


By James Frederick 
BOARDMAN, Ohio — Phar-Mor took the 
wraps off its latest retailing concepts in early 
March with the grand reopening of one of its 


highest-volume stores. 


The store marks the culmination of months of 
intensive redesign efforts by Phar-Mor as it 
sheds unwanted merchandise categories, em- 
phasizes faster-turning basic products and 
widens aisles to allow for easier shopping. 

The effort took place in the pressure-cooker 


chain’s new approach. Gone or severely cur- 
tailed are sportswear, home/office equipment 
and large-scale electronics. 

'n their place are far larger selections of greet- 


ing cards, cosmetics, HBA and Rubbermaid; 


of bankruptcy and corporate downsizing, as 
Phar-Mor has scrambled to control costs, tar- 


get unprofitable stores and revitalize its busi- 
ness. In the process, the chain has slowed the 
erosion of its market share, cut its store base 
from 310 to 224 and changed the way it has done 


business for years. 


Phar-Mor also added a few promising new cate- 
gories like body/bath, dramatically enhanced its 
Movies and Music department for video rentals 
and CD sales and consolidated tobacco, photo- 
processing, lottery and other services in a front- 
end convenience center with its own checkouts. 


A new look

Debt offering to finance Big B expansion 


By Mike Troy 

Big B is looking stronger 
than ever with nine consecu- 
tive quarters of increased 
earnings, annual sales that 
surpassed the $500 million 
mark for the first time, the re- 
cent acquistion of 45 Treasury 
Drug stores and a debt offer- 
ing that will reduce the retail- 
er’s interest expenses. 

At press time, a date had 
not been set for the securities 
offering, and Big B president 
and chief operating officer, 
Arthur “Mack” Jones, de- 
clined to comment on the 
Treasury acquisition, citing 
Securities and Exchange 
Commission regulations. 

However, information in the 
company’s prospectus indicates 
Big B will pay approximately 
$16.5 million for Thrift Drug 
inc.’s 45 Treasury stores, 39 of 
which are located in the Atlanta 
area. Another $5 million will be 
needed to convert the stores to 
the Big B format. 

The Birmingham, Ala.- 
based retailer currently has 
64 stores in the Atlanta mar- 
ket. An additional $9 million 
will be spent on POS system 
improvements. 

unding for the acquisition 
will be provided by a $35 mil- 
lion (convertible subordinated 
debentures) debt offering. 
The proceeds will be used to 
reduce existing bank debt 


which consists of a $50 million 
revolving credit facility ($27.1 
million outstanding) and a $15 
million line of credit ($5.1 mil- 
lion outstanding). Those lines 
of credit will then be tapped to 
finance the Treasury acquisi- 
tion, store conversions and 
POS system upgrades. 


Thrift leaves Atlanta 


Thrift Drug, a subsidiary of 
J.C.Penney, decided to aban- 
don the Atlanta market to con- 
centrate on its stronger mar- 
kets in the mid- Atlantic area. 
“In Atlanta, there are already 
so many drug store players and 
we didn’t have the share of the 
market that we do in most of 
our other trading areas,” said 
Thrift spokeswoman Trish Or- 
chard. “So, when a buyer be- 
came available, it made sense 
to sell the stores so we could 
strengthen our position in oth- 
er markets.” 

Thrift continues to seek a 
buyer for 19 Treasury Drug 
stores remaining in Georgia 
that Big B opted not to pur- 
chase. “We have had some in- 
terest and we will continue to 
pursue those that are interest- 
ed,” Orchard said. 

Just a few years ago, Big B 
barely had a toehold in Atlan- 
ta. The retailer jumped in fully 
in 1989 with the 85-store Reed 
Drug Co. acquisition. Now, 
with 45 Treasury stores, Big B 


has roughly as many stores in 
Georgia, the majority of which 
are in Atlanta, as it does in its 
home state of Alabama. 

By the end of 1995, Big B 
plans to have nearly 400 
stores. The Treasury buyout 
boosts the retailer’s store 
count to approximately 350. 
Then, plans call for an addi- 
tional 10 to 12 new store open- 
ings in fiscal 1994 and 15 to 20 
new stores in fiscal 1995. Ad- 
ditional growth is anticipated 
through the acquisition of in- 
dependent drug stores. 

uture expansion is expect- 
ed to come in the five South- 
eastern states, Alabama, 
Georgia, Mississippi, Tennes- 
see and Florida, that comprise 
Big B’s operating region and 
can be served by the chain’s 
new 440,000-square-foot dis- 
tribution center.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 5, 1993 


New directions for drug chains. 

That was my assignment from Brian Sharoff, presi- 
dent of the Private Label Manufacturers Association, 
when he asked me to deliver a speech before his Annu- 
al Leadership Conference in late March. 

The request wasn’t gratuitous. He felt some of his 
manufacturer members haven’t been focusing on this 
trade class, and needed to be updated on how chains 
are turning themselves 


into more distinctive, via- 
ble competitors. 

The good news is that I 
had plenty to say. Going 
beyond surface headlines 
about scandals and bank- 
ruptcies, the industry is 
operating smarter, more 
efficiently and with a 
greater flair for experimentation than in many years. 

Market realities have reined in efforts to diversify 
out-of-field and have chains focusing on their core 
strengths of health and beauty care and convenience. 
Diversification today often means institutional and 
mail order pharmacy, and experimentation means 
new store formats that include nutrition centers, ex- 
ercise gear and bath and body boutiques—all of which 
reinforce drug stores’ distinctive wellness image. 

Some points from my address to private label exec- 
utives—increasingly critical partners in the genera- 
tion of gross profit dollars for large and small chains— 
underscore the resilience of this trade class: 

@ While drug chains aren’t revered for their innova- 
tion, they are highly adaptive. They. . .are now doing 
what they do best: delivering health care economically 
and conveniently to the masses. Chain pharmacy ac- 
counts for 60 percent of all prescriptions dispe:sed 
. . about 5 percent of the nation’s health care costs, 
and is arguably the most cost-effective deliverer of 
health care. 

e@ Drug chains are disciplining themselves to be- 
come lower-cost operators. Walgreens slashed $53 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


OPINION 


Drug chains show off their resilience 


million of inventory from its distribution centers since 
rolling out its Strategic Inventory Management Sys- 
tem. Happy Harry’s cut half its inventory costs since 
it began using E-III buying software. 

e@ Headquarters staffs are thinning, and senior 
chain executives have more hands-on responsibility 
for category management. One example: Eckerd elim- 
inated 600 headquarters positions in recent months. 

®@ Deep discounting isn’t dead. From F&M in Michi- 
gan to Marc’s in Ohio to I Got It At Gary’s in Pennsyl- 
vania, the formula is working—though the business 
will settle in at 22 percent margins rather than 17 per- 
cent where it began. 

@ There are more total drug stores today—about 
51,000—than there were in 1982—about 49,000. 
Chains own about 22,000 of them, or 40 percent of the 
units now, up from 33 percent then. And drug chains 
account for nearly $52 billion in annual sales, or 67 per- 
cent of total drug store sales of $77 billion. 

@ Customers are using drug stores in new ways. 
Extra services, such as automated teller machines, 
faxes and shipping services, are especially important 
to younger consumers, noted a NACDS/Peter Hart 
survey. Overall, availability of full prescription re- 
cords, direct billing of insurers and pharmacist consul- 
tations ranked high. 

@ In the drug store of the future, pharmacy is the an- 
chor. Drug stores are also the best-positioned trade 
class to benefit from the growth in Rx-to-OTC switches. 
Drug stores will reinforce their wellness image by de- 
veloping nutrition centers, exercise gear sections and 
other related areas. Photofinishing will grow increas- 
ingly important since it builds store visits and reinforces 
professional quality image. Beauty care boutiquing will 
expand, as drug stores encroach further on department 
store turf. Consumables will continue to be a strategic 
weapon to capture the fill-in visit between supermarket 
trips, following the leads of Walgreens, Longs, Osco and 
Revco. Stationery and greeting cards will be an essen- 
tial part of the drug store mix, helping to meet the com- 
plete shopping needs of families. 


Hillary Clinton’s White House task force on health 
care reform is closing in on a series of proposals that 
are likely to rely on direct federal price controls to re- 
duce spiraling costs. 

Pharmacy leaders here in Washington recognize 
this and appear ready to help the Administration 
hammer out the details of a new system of health 
care price controls that now appears to be all but in- 

evitable. 


A few years ago, the 
specter of outright gov- 
ernment price controls on 
pharmacy products and 
services would have 
prompted howls of protest 
from drug chains, inde- 
pendents, hospital phar- 
macists and other practi- 


p WASHINGTON 
\ PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


tioner greups. 

Today, pharmacy leaders have an even more impor- 
tant worry: the prospect that pharmacy services may 
not be included in the new federal health plan—at all! 

Incredible as it sounds, top policy officials at APhA, 
NACDS and other groups believe that Hillary’s task 
force just may come up with a plan to reform the na- 
tion’s health care delivery system that excludes cover- 
age of prescription drugs. 

If that happens—if Washington chooses to ignore 
the role that pharmacists can play in improving pa- 
tient care and reducing health costs—the objective of 
health care reform will be undermined. 

For pharmacists, the consequences could be even 
more serious. To be left out of the first meaningful re- 


Will health plan squeeze out pharmacists? 


form of American health care in generations would be 
an ominous turning point for the profession. 

Virtually every segment of pharmacy now recog- 
nizes this danger. 

The No. 1 recommendation to the Clinton Adminis- 
tration from the newly forged NARD-NACDS 
‘Health Care Reform Coalition’ emphasizes “the ne- 
cessity of including pharmacists’ services in any 
health care plan.” 

A separate and even more broadly based coalition of 
national pharmacy organizations assembled by APhA 
delivered a similar message during recent meetings 
with White House health reformers. 

Speaking on behalf of hospital and consultant phar- 
macists as well as academics and pharmacy regula- 
tors, APhA’s coalition said that prescription drugs 
and pharmacists’ services ’should be a core benefit un- 
der health care reform.” 

To be sure, not all segments of pharmacy agree on 
all aspects of health reform. 

Retail pharmacy groups maintain that the focus of 
prescription cost containment by federal health re- 
formers should be on eliminating the multi-tier pricing 
practices of pharmaceutical manufacturers. 

Representatives of institutional pharmacy—a 
prime beneficiary of these unfair and discriminatory 
pricing practices—would like the government’s cost 
control emphasis to be placed elsewhere. 

It’s important that disagreements over cost con- 
tainment issues don’t undercut pharmacy’s consensus 
on the most significant issue of all—ensuring that 
pharmacy practitioners play a role in the emerging 
health reform program.

simple but profound truism was uttered more than two years ago by former 
Walgreen president and chief operations officer Fred Canning, as the nation’s 
economy was beginning its slide into stubborn, protracted recession. 

Given all that’s happened since, Canning’s summation of the strengths of drug 
store retailing rings even truer today. Drug chains have weathered the long slide in 
consumer spending—and the painstakingly uncertain recovery that has followed— 
by adhering to their basic strengths, shedding costs and servicing customers. 
They’ve taken some of the sting out of shrinking gross margins by adding technol- 
ogy, buying smarter and promoting higher-gross private label. And they’ve contin- 
ued to explore promising new products and categories. 

On the following pages, we present Part I of Drug Store News’ Annual Report on the 
Chain Drug Store Industry, with an in-depth look at the product categories that drive the 
business. In the next issue, we'll examine the key players that make up that business.

ANNUAL REPORT PART | EXECUTIVE COMMENTS 


Drug chain executives brace for the future 


Vern Brunner 
executive vp- 
marketing 
Walgreens 


Marketing and merchandising in the 
drug store industry will continue to be 
challenged by the low-inflation envi- 
ronment of recent years. Managing 
sales and profits during low-inflation 


_ periods isn’t easy, wut it can be done 


through the use of technology. 

With scanning, we can now get an- 
swers to questions we’ve been asking 
for years. Scanning will allow market- 
ing departments to recognize trends at 
the individual store and market level 
and capitalize on them. 

We'll have the ability to develop the 
merchandise mix of our stores by their 
location. That’s been done for years in 
a general way, but information from 
scanning will take that process one 


step further. 

e challenge is to merchandise to a 
specific store’s market, while at the 
same time, maintain the general corpo- 
rate image. A customer who shops us 
in Chicago should be able to walk into a 
Walgreens in Phoenix and still recog- 
nize us. 

Marketing departments also need to 
more effectively utilize their advertis- 
ing dollars. That money must be used 
to promote specific store and market 
needs, not just the chain in general ona 
national basis. 

Finally, stronger partnerships with 
vendors can lead to more efficiency in 
business as well as generating “real” 
category growth. 


Stephen Lund 
vp-merchandising 
Perry Drug Stores 


I’m sure I’m not the first drug store 
executive to state that retailing—in 
particular, chain drug retailing—is not 
as easy as it once was. 

With the introduction into the mar- 
ketplace of retailing concepts such as 
category killers, warehouse clubs, 
deep discounters and hypermarkets, 
the old days of buying an item at the 
best cost, selling it for a reasonable 
price, paying the expenses and taking 
the profit to the bank are gone. 

Chain drug retailers are confront- 
ed with ever-decreasing market 
shares of [HBA] and OTC products. 
Other general merchandise product 
sales are also finding their way to oth- 
er retail outlets. 

Generally these lost revenues are 
—— offset by significant increases 
in pharmacy sales. Unfortunately, 
these pharmacy sales are producing 
lower gross margins. So, what is a re- 
tailer to do? 

1) Emphasize core drug store cate- 
gories: 

Product selection and merchandis- 
ing approaches must show the custom- 
er immediately what the real focus in 


‘the store is. . .pharmacy. 


2) Be aggressive in marketing: 

With so many retail options avail- 
able to the consumer, marketing ap- 
proaches must leave the customer with 
no doubt as to what you're offering 
them in distinctive benefits. 

3) Offer fair pricing: 

Although drug stores have the bene- 
fit of convenience over other retail out- 
lets, there is a limit to what most cus- 
tomers will pay for convenience. 

4) Take care of your customers: 

The retailing giants are finding ways 
to make their customers feel good 
about shopping in their stores. Cer- 
tainly we can and must do the same. 

5) Control expenses: 

The salvation of chain drug retail- 
ing will be to shave expenses directly 
in relationship to the increase in 
pharmacy business, with its corre- 
sponding decrease in gross margin. 
Increased use of technology is s kes 
to expense reduction. 

This may seem a very simplified ap- 
proach to returning chain drug retail- 
ing to profitability. But simplicity may 
be what we need, and it may work. 


Markus Ernst 
executive vp 
Arbor Drug 


Too many in our industry fear the 
community drug store is marked for 
extinction, given the tremendous com- 
— challenges we face today. 

m combo supermarkets and mass 
merchandisers with pharmacies to cat- 
egory killers, deep discounters and 
even direct mail operators, new retail- 
ing formats certainly abound. 

ifty years from now, there will be 
other new formats and new players on 
the scene. Where will the deep dis- 
counters or category killers be? I don’t 
know. But I do Enow that the commu- 
nity drug store will be there, thriving 
as it does today. 

For other retail formats, pharmacy is 
often an accommodation to their busi- 
ness. Phe somata! core business. To- 
day’s informed, discriminating consum- 
er continues to prefer the traditional 
drug store format, which has always 
been Arbor’s competitive edge. 


As drug stores, we must never lose 
our health care focus. We must also 
learn to use the latest technology, com- 
bined with attention to the needs of 
customers, to make the shopping expe- 
rience more convenient. 

The winning drug store operators 
are focused on long-term strategies, 
particularly advanced systems, in ad- 
dition to emphasizing health care, 
trust and superior customer service. 

The community drug store is not an 
endangered species. We will not only 
ig il but also prosper, as long as we 

isten closely to consumer messages. 
The keys are a strong health care iden- 
tity combined with convenience, 
speed, selection and quality staffing. 

While the future of all retailing 
pg to be ever challenging, we 

lieve there will be even greater op- 
Shag ag for “customer-driven” 

rug store chains.

ANNUAL REPORT PART | OVERVIEW 


ou call this a recovery? | 
The economy spent 1992 try- 
ing to get out of its sickbed. And 
despite recent positive signs—an up- 
tick in employment, rising gross do- 
mestic product and home ie a de- 
cent last-minute Christmas season, an 
energetic new administration in Wash- 
ington—the people who are paid to 
read economic tea leaves and predict 
the future are still divided about the 
health of the patient. 

So, too, are the nation’s consumers, 
who are still worried enough about their 
jobs and their futures to keep their 
spending habits on a short leash. 

Indeed, many households in the 
Northeast, in the industrial Heart- 
land, in Washington State and in Cali- 
fornia, among other regions, are still 
reeling from massive cutbacks in 


aerospace, steel, automobiles, de- 


fense, computers and other indus- 
tries. They’re in no mood to go on 
spending sprees. 

Chain drug retailers know all about 
it. Along with their counterparts in 
general merchandise and supermarket 
retailing, they’ve spent the past two 
years waiting out the longest reces- 
sion—and the ugliest, most uncertain 
economic recovery—since the 1930s. 

Competition for dwindling con- 
sumer dollars has intensified in every 
category. New competitors continue 
_ to multiply. Margins continue to 
shrink—not only in front-end catego- 
ries under assault by Wal-Mart, 
Kmart, the wholesale clubs and oth- 
ers, but also in core areas like pre- 
scriptions, as low-margin third-party 
payments come to dominate the phar- 
macy landscape. 

The recession of ’91-’92 was the final 
coda to the free-spending ’80s. It has 
been particularly unkind to debt-laden 
drug chains born or bought in the lev- 
eraged buyout binge of the last decade 
and to those whose historically high 
operating costs left them stranded like 
dinosaurs in tar when consumer spend- 
ing and profit margins receded. 

n the process, the weakest and 
most debt-heavy chains have gone 
under, sold out or fled for the protec- 
tion of the bankruptcy courts. The 
others have attacked their cost struc- 
tures in operations, distribution, in- 
ventory and labor to stay ahead of the 
profit squeeze and position them- 
selves for this new and unforgiving 
era of retailing.

U.S. to enter free trade

being pushed and pulled into a world 
economy. 

Free trade with Canada is a reality; 
free trade with Mexico is on the hori- 
zon. (See International Retailing 
column, page 34.) Europe is coalesc- 
ing, however haltingly, into a unified 
world power in manufacturing, ex- 
porting and consumption. Japan re- 
mains a fast-growing economic su- 
perpower, despite recent troubles, 
and other Pacific Rim nations like Ko- 
rea, Taiwan, China and even Viet- 
nam are exploding as exporters.

get its market act together. 

All of them represent competition 
for American goods and American 
jobs. Meanwhile, demand here at 

ome for many U.S. products re- 
mains weak. That keeps U.S. indus- 
tries in a cutback mode while they 
scramble to develop the technologies 
and innovations to compete interna- 
tionally. 

Coupled with fundamental economic 
shifts are changes in consumer demo- 
graphics and behavior. 

or one thing, population growth 
will remain slow, depriving retailers of 
one traditional way to pump sales for 
the foreseeable future. 

On the behavior side: not only are 
consumers more cautious and value- 
conscious, but they are also more will-

On the retailing horizon 


What this means for the nation’s 
‘retailers is that change is now a con- 
stant. In the words of retail consul- 
tant Willard Bishop, drug chains and 
other mercHants will face “relentless 
margin pressure” as new forms of 
competition spring up, prices stay 
down and prescription drug spending 
by public and private insurers re- 
mains under assault. He predicts 
“relatively slow growth” for retailers 
through 1994, followed by a period of 
faster growth and higher inflation in 
the mid-1990s. 

After that, said Bishop: a time of 
“moderate, sustained growth,” mod- 
erate inflation and a “rebirth” for re- 
tailers that remain flexible and innova- 
tive. “Traditional retailers will 
continue to lose ground,” Bishop said 
at the International Housewares Expo 
in January. “Every retailer needs to 
manage their business like a leakin 
bucket. The successful retailer wi 
continue to put more water in the top 
than is leaking out the bottom.” 

To succeed, he said, retailers will 
have to take sales from their competi- 
tors. They’ll have to make “superior 
use of technology.” They'll have to cre- 
ate “unique merchandising excite- 


ment” in their stores, coupled with a - 


“dynamic pricing strategy.” And 
they’ll have to develop ways to focus 
their store marketing and merchandis- 
ing to target their consumers with real 
precision. 

Many drug chains have been doin 
just that. Internally, chains like Wal- 
"eta American Drug, PayLess, 

evco and many others have spent 
huge sums on technology to combat 
shrinking pharmacy margins and 
growing competition. They’re har- 


58 


nessing that technology to attack 
costs, move product more efficiently 
into their stores and buy smarter. 
They have little choice, given the 
enormous impact of low-cost, super- 
efficient retail powerhouses like Wal- 
Mart, Kmart, Sam’s Wholesale Club 
and Target Stores. 

At store level, drug chains are 
adapting automation to get a clearer 
handle on what customers want to buy 
from them and who those customers 


are. POS information is giving them a 
tool to move faster into and out of prod- 
uct categories, to react to trends and to 
test new ideas. 

In short, the industry is in a mood 
to try whatever works to get and hold 
their customers. Chains like PayLess 
and Phar-Mor have installed new 
bath boutiques, capitalizing on rapid, 
20 percent growth in the bath catego- 
ry last year. Thrift, Osco, PayLess 
and others have brought in full health

a 


Although fragrance sales stalledin 
‘92, some chains reported success 
with prestige brands and upscale 
lines of fragranced bath products. 


ragrance sales in chain drug sales 

were soft in 1992. But sales for 

gift sets featuring fragranced 
bath products had double-digit in- 
creases, and some buyers think the 
two trends may indicate a shift in the 
way consumers are buying gifts for 
special occasions. 

Chain buyers said their fragrance 
sales in 1992 were either flat or down, 
with only a few chains reporting moder- 
ate gains in the low single-digit rates. 

The economy was blamed for part of 
the problem. But buyers also felt that 
consumers seemed to be buying less 
fragrances this year and more of other 
types of products such as clothing, 
bath sets and candy. 

“It’s been a tough year for fra- 
grances,” says Detroit-based F&M’s 
cosmetics director Pat Gardocki. 

Kathy Covault, merchandise mana- 

er of cosmetics for Columbus, Ohio- 

ased Drug Emporium, agreed, add- 
ing that she has seen less of a demand 
for fragrance products in ’92. 

“Our fragrance sales were flat,” says 
Mary Hoepfner, who buys cosmetics 
for Detroit-based Perry Drug Stores. 
“It’s partly the recession, and partly 
because there wasn’t much happening 
in the category this past year. Truly 
Lace was the only launch to do any- 
thing in the women’s fragrance catego- 
ry last year.” 


Some scents strong 


Coty was the only manufacturer to 
launch strong new fragrances—Truly 
Lace and Gravity—to the mass seg- 
ment. As one buyer for a major chain 
put it, “without exciting new products 
and exciting promotions to support the 
fragrance category, it’s getting harder 
and harder to generate growth.” 

Gravity, launched last fall, started 
off slowly as most men’s fragrances do. 
By mid-February, buyers were saying 
it was turning into a success. “Not a 


gang-buster fragrance” as one buyer 
put it, “but a good selling item.” 
Most buyers described Truly Lace, 
Coty’s newest woman’s fragrance, as 
the best launch in the mass fragrance

78 DRUG STORE NEWS, April 5, 1993 


Moisturizers aren’t merely moistur- 
izing anymore. Added benefits offered 
in new lines, products carrying an ad- 
vanced formulation cachet and niche 
items are making skin care products 
more attractive to consumers. 


ueled by an aging baby boomer 
population, skin care products 


that employ advanced formula- 
tions, therapeutic products and niche 
items that fill consumers’ individual 
skin care needs will continue to be the 
stars of the skin care segment. The 
area, according to one manufactur- 
er’s estimate, is growing 10 percent 
annually. 

Overall at drug chains in 1992, face 
cream sales leaped ahead 8 percent and 
hand and body preps grew 4.7 percent. 

Manufacturers are introducing 
items that mimic department store 

roducts and are capitalizing on the 
essons learned in department stores: 
that consumers are interested in high- 
er performance products that utilize 
the latest technology to provide new 
solutions for skin care. In short: Sci- 
ence sells in skin care. 

More and more high-tech upscale 
products are being offered through 
drug stores. Manufacturers have tak- 
en hold of that theme in their consumer 
advertising. For example, Jergens’ 
ads are tagged with the slogan “Jer- 
a You Can Touch.” 

onds’ new ads for its five-SKU mois- 
turizer line will also focus on the high- 
tech theme. 


ANNUAL REPORT PART | TOILETRIES 


Upscale, advanced formulas 
reap super sales for skin car 


Neoreric Cosmetics Inc.’s two- 
SKU Alpha Hydrox line, cited by re- 
tailers as asurprise winner in the cat- 
egory, continues to appeal to 
consumers despite a higher retail 
ticket of $7.99 to $9.99. 

“The products are not as irritating 
as Retin A and I think they are appeal- 
ing to the same customer,” said 
Pharmhouse buyer Jerry Biarsky. 
“The company is planning to introduce 
a full line of products, which I expect 
will do very well.” 


Advanced formulations sell 


Manufacturers are beginning to use 
alpha hydroxy acid (AHA), which has 
become a hot button in skin care, in 
some skin care formulations. Alpha 
Hydrox is one line utilizing the tech- 
nology. Revlon plans an introduction 
of a line called Results, which will use a 
patented molecular complex formula 
similar to AHAs. 

Pond’s new five-SKU line of facial 
skin care products includes Dramatic 
Results Capsules, which contains lip- 
ids and AHAs to instantly smooth 
away fine dry lines. The company 

lans to put $30 million in advertising 
ehind the line. 

Capsule products containing lipids, 
once available only to department 
stores, will be introduced by a number 
of other manufacturers. 

Michelle Jones, buyer at Perry Drug 
Stores, said she'll wait to see how 
Pond’s capsules move before stocking 
similar products from other manufac-

Planograms are critical 

There are constant pressures to 
maximize return on investment in a 
climate of new product proliferation 
and shrinking shelf space. Yesterday, 
planograms were an optional way to 


describe a shelf-set. But today, they — 


are critical to success. 


They are the blueprint 

Space management is becoming more 
than a tool for matching space to 
movement. Planograms are built to 
handle increasingly more complex 
product assortments, micro-marketing 
needs and merchandising looks. 
Planograms are the blueprints upon 
which vendors and retailers build 
profitable partnerships to attract the 
consumer and meet their demands. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 5, 1993 


Not all planograms work 
Anyone can place products on a shelf. 
Few can build planograms that meet 
complex merchandising objectives 
that get implemented. Planograms 
cannot reflect a single point of view. 
They must blend market data, vendor 
and retailer merchandising philosophy 
and common sense.

quantities of information and build 
merchandising solutions that are 
objective, cohesive and innovative. 
Most important, our solutions stimu- 
late the consumer.

Chains promote 


The popularity of ethnic cosmetics 
contrasted with a slowdown in hair 
care sales to produce a slight overall 
category gain. Bright spots: relaxers 
and styling aids, especially gels, 
spritzes and sheens. 


ith the exception of cosmet- 
ics, the ethnic beauty care 
category sustained only 


slight growth in drug cnains for 1992. 
Ethnic edged ahead 0.6 percent to 
$314.8 million this past year. 

Because of new introductions, eth- 
nic cosmetic sales were up over 30 per- 
cent in many chains this past year, but 
ethnic hair care, which is still the heart 
of the category, was either flat or up in 
low single-digit rates for the year. 


Fighting the competition 


As drug chains move through 1993, 
they are recognizing the need to fight 
harder against intensifying competi- 
tion from beauty and barber stores, 
dollar stores and mass merchandise 
chains. 

Their strategy is to enhance their 
merchandising presentations and to 
advertise the department more ag- 
gressively to increase its visibility. 

In addition to advertising ethnic 
beauty care in local newspapers and 
radio, more chains are now also fea- 
turing ethnic items in their chainwide 
circulars. 

Chains are partnering with manu- 
facturers to create local in-store 
events, such as radio remotes, con- 
tests, sampling, even cosmetic make- 
overs, all designed to increase the visi- 
bility of the department and highlight 
the sales and services that drug chains 
can provide. 

They are also carefully monitoring 
their product mix, trying to stay on top 
of new hot items and growth segments 
while cutting back or eliminating slow 


Chains are doing more pro- 

motions and experimenting 

vigorously with the types of 
promotions they do.

hoto processing means double ex-

nience and professional image.

notes that drug stores were down 1.3 
percent (units) in rolls. 

To keep dollars up, drug chains of- 
fered more value-added promotions 
rather than make deep cuts in process- 
ing prices. In-store labs also boosted 
photo processing revenue. 


Film, camera sales 


Total rolls purchased were down 
about 1.8 percent in units. But 35mm 
print color and black and white were 
up about 1.9 percent. “All of the de- 
cline is in cartridge and slide film,” 
says Harrand. The good news was that 
higher-price-point 35mm film contin- 
ues its upswing, adding dollars to the 
category despite weak unit figures. 

To add excitement, manufacturers 
are devising new 35mm film types—like 
Konica’s new Super XG, Polaroid’s 
3omm HD, Fuji’s SuperG, Kodacolor 
Gold Plus—for finer grain, more satu- 
rated color, or with Konica’s new Baby 
Film, a specially calibrated film speed 
designed to photograph children.

ANNUAL REPORT PART I/GREETING CARDS 


Greeting cards expand into new ex- 
pressive styles and hit more niche 
markets—and with good margins, 
too, which add more luster to this 
growing drug chain core category. 


ustomers browse and buy in the 

greeting card department, en- 

riching the drug store shopping 
experience. That’s because the cus- 
tomer is engaged: he or she is looking 
for just the right image and message, 
the personal expression. 

ees days, there might even be an 
electronic interactive unit like the 
American Greetings CreataCard, 
launched in 1992, or Hallmark’s Per- 
sonalize it! or the new Print a Little 
Message from Recycled Paper Greet- 
ings—all designed to customize cards 
with an individualized message and 
image. 

Greeting cards made a good show- 
ing in drug chains in 1992, with a 6.6 

ercent increase to $899.3 million. 

otal U.S. card sales continued to 
climb, to $5.3 billion, compared to $5 
billion in 1991, according to the 
Greeting Card Association. as in- 
creases in card prices (as units held 
steady) were accepted by consumers 
who find cards are a bargain in place 
of gifts in tight times, or who want to 
stay in touch when travel and long 
distance phone calls can strain a fru- 
gal budget. 

For the retailer, margins of around 
50 percent and turns in the range of 
five-plus help offset other low-margin 
traffic builders, from soft drinks to 
Huggies. 


More choice 


Alternative cards were a growth 
area for many drug retailers in 1992, 
like Troy, Mich.-based Arbor Drug, 
where executive vice president Mar- 
kus Ernst notes that customers re- 
spond to relationship-specific cards 
such as for a niece’s husband. The 
success of alternative card lines is 
Spawning more choices. Gibson will 
expand its Life As We Know It alter- 
native card line in 1993, for example. 

Manufacturers like Recycled Pa- 
per Greetings note that blank card 
sales rose in 1992, a further indication 
that consumers want to add a person- 
al touch.

tailored to a chain or specific locations 
for peak seasons and everyday. 


Selection means sales 


To maximize selection, more manu- 
facturers are offering flexible, cus- 
tomized packages to avoid wasting 
display space with slow movers and 
thereby beefing up inventory turn. 
More drug chains are refixturin 
card departments to dense up and of. 
fer more facings in less space. Gib- 
son’s new Card Express fixture is one 
such modular display device offering 
installation choices. 

Selection is the key to greeting card 
sales. As point-of-sale (POS) scanning 
reaches more categories, greeting 
card segments will become more fine- 
tuned and out-of-stocks will be avoid- 
ed. Fixturing, POS scanning (not yet 
universal but growing) and the part- 
come of representative servicing all 
contribute to category sales increases 
by keeping stock fresh and avoiding 
out-of-stocks. 

For customers, finding what they 
want in a social expression purchase 
reinforces the chain drug image of 
neighborhood and lifestyle conve- 
nience—a critical plus for rug chains 
when competing against market-grab- 
bing mass merchants.

the office monster category killers,

ucts, school supplies (both basic and 
fashion), new writing implements, 
and arts and craft kits as well as mail- 
center growth. 

The stationery department ad- 
vanced 5.4 percent overall to $2.6 bil- 
lion at drug chains in 1992. 

A well-organized, focused statio- 
nery assortment helps busy shoppers 
meet their needs. A chain like Troy, 
Mich.-based Arbor wii ingyen a 
stationery department ere you'll 
find, pulled together, the key items. 
It’s convenient,” says Markus Ernst, 
executive vice president and chief op- 
erating officer. 

Stationery grew in 1992, he notes, 
—— in home office and Back To 
School, where both kids and adults like 
color and novelty—whether it’s pens 
or color presentation folders. 

For adults, products are geared to 
do a job with personal style—like 
Mead’s Cambridge line of organiza- 
tional Lae and day planners or Stu- 
art Hall’s Executive Suite office prod- 


ucts in soft colors for women. 
Buyers also report that consumers

ANNUAL REPORT PART | STATIONERY 


like to try new writing instruments,

nomic design comes at an affordable

Value added 


Lynn Santulli, stationery division 
manager for distributor N.W. Cash, 
says that in 1992, she noticed another 
trend: good movement in mid-sized 
multi-packs in pens and pads. “At re- 
tail, most consumers don’t have a place 
to put 11 legal pads. The trend is to 
threes and sixes,” she said. 

Whether it is multi-packs or a pre- 
mium in, consumers are on 
the lookout for value-added products. 
An extra feature—a pen included 
with a planner or a dispenser pack- 
aged with tape—give consumers a 
reason to buy, and not just for a rock- 
bottom price. 

Consumers still want a touch of post- 
1980s luxury, too. That means afford- 
able fashion with themes that cele- 
brate the earth or crystal tints to help 
at the task done decoratively in a 

ome office. Fashion thrives, despite 
budget concerns. Imitation stone and 
rock designs, for e le, are making 
inroads in everything from writing im- 
plements to desk accessories. 

Paper products may be at the heart 
of recycling efforts, yet buyers say 
vendors seem to be reducing their re- 
cycled stationery offerings, a trend 
found in other categories as well. One 
buyer notes that his chain’s sales in re- 
cycled stationery were flat in 1992 
compared with 1991. One problem, he 
says, is that consumers are confused 
by terms like recycled and post-con- 
sumer waste. 


Mail aid 


Drug chains’ corner convenience 
means service features, including 
postage stamps and other mailing ser- 
vices. The trend in drug chains and 
food/drug combos is toward providing 
an all-purpose fax/photocopy/informa- 
tion/mail center—or some variation to 
help consumers get through their 
checklists. And it’s an opportunity to 
sell products ranging from tape to pad- 
ded mailers, styrofoam packing pea- 
nuts to collapsible boxes.

Dakota, greeting s are adjacent to 
its service/mail center, which provides 
a place for customers to address cards, 
buy postage and mail them on the spot. 

ood/drug combos are setting the

ike Vons new super combo in Simi

packaged with tape.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 5, 1993 


ANNUAL REPORT PART | HOUSEWARES GENERAL MERCHANDISE 


Chains take lean approach to housewares 


out of the massive housewares 

industry. But previous efforts 
by drug chains to pare their general 
merchandise inventories and selec- 
tion yielded an unexpected benefit, 
by decreasing their exposure to the 
downturn and shielding them from its 
worst effects. 


Sharp on selection, price 


Most drug chains weathered the 
downturn by staying sharp on selec- 
tion and price, according to buyers 

lled by Store News. The result: 

ousewares sales rose 1.3 percent at 
drug chains to $2.58 billion in 1992. 

“Only the essential basics are selling 
at this point,” with “an awful lot of [dis- 
counting],” reported Thrifty Corp. 
housewares buyer Mike Roberts. 
Thrifty, he added, was able to main- 
tain a steady housewares business 
through the recession, without having 
“to kill its margins,” by “being in stock, 
relying on convenience and promot- 
in lug 
Other chain drug buyers echoed that 
approach. Ontario’s 118-store Big V 
Peanuaiee Co., for instance, stayed 
“aggressive” on price, kept its house- 
wares selection close to low-priced ba- 
sics and cut its SKUs in all GM catego- 
ries “drastically” over the past year 
and a half, according to vice president 
of marketing Gary Goyeau. 


Stay with the basics 


Nevertheless, the chain continues to 
make a strong “statement” in the cate- 
gory by staying in stock on key items, 
merchandising them creatively and 
promoting aggressively. What keeps 
the category profitable, Goyeau indi- 
cated, is being “very selective” in 
items and price points. 

Agreed Gerald Proulx of LaVer- 
diere’s Super Drug Stores in Water- 
ville, Maine, “We feel the emphasis is 
going to be on basics. . . with the focus 
on convenience and impulse sales. 
We're trying to find products we can 
merchandise around Wal-Mart.” 

Nevertheless, said Proulx, the 
chain always comes up with a few 
“hot items” from the annual NHMA

Closer to suppliers 


Some drug chains are also forging 
new, stronger alliances with a few of 
their key housewares vendors. Both 
Thrifty and Phar-Mor, for instance, 
have installed “Everything Rubber- 
maid” departments in some of their 
stores, giving the vendor enough 
space and selection for a complete as- 
sortment of household products, as 
well as more input into the merchan- 
dising process. 

“We sat down with Rubbermaid in 
negotiations, and added more than 250 
items to the mix,” said Rich Juliano, 
senior vice president of merchandising 
for Phar-Mor. “We now have almost 
560 total [Rubbermaid] items in the de- 
partment. . . and the selection is con- 
stantly turning.” 

Other chains indicate they are also 
moving toward closer, more strategic 
relationships with their suppliers. 

At the recent housewares show, 
Longs Drug Stores general merchan- 
dise manager Barry Renner indicat- 
ed the chain’s merchandisers and 
buyers were trying to forge new links 
directly with vendors, and he said 
suppliers were increasingly able to 
demonstrate “flexibility” in meeting 
them halfway. 


Convenience, 
kids, ethnic 
markets drive 
hosiery sales 


n chain drug stores, the hosiery se- 
lection can be a lifesaver for a female 
shopper—and often she’s in a hurry. 
She wants a selection and easy-to- 
identify packaging to help her quickly 
choose a pair for work tomorrow, a 
shade to match a party dress to wear to- 
night or a fast replacement for today. 
siery manufacturers like No Non- 
sense and L’eggs offer space-saving dis- 
plays with broad assortment plus easy- 
to-choose packaging. In 1992, L’eggs 
rolled out its more compact packaging 
which uses less material a provides 
clearer information for the consumer. 

POS scanning and service represen- 
tatives both help the retailer avoid out- 
of-stocks and help maintain customer 
confidence. That’s especially important 
as styles and demographics change. The 
big boom in sheer pantyhose which 

eaked in 1983 has diversified into dif- 
erent hosiery segments since then. 
Sheers have declined since 1983, but 
opaque pantyhose sales have nearly 
doubled in the one decade. And in re- 
cent years children’s tights and socks 
have really accelerated. 

In 1992, according to a study by Port 
Washington, N.Y.-based MPD Group’s 
consumer purchase panel, conducted for 
the National Hosiery Manufacturers 
Association, the total nylon leg category 
(excluding socks and Seiow the knee) 
was down 3 percent in retail dollars in 
all trade classes for the year. 

But segment winners included be- 
low-the-knee, for a total of $135 million

multi-ethnic customer base, where the 
shopper may want a fashion tint or a 
more natural hosiery shade to enhance 
her own skin tone. And she may be 
brand loyal to an ethnic hosiery line, too. 

The affordable-brand hosiery found in 
drug stores is being challenged these 
days by private label pantyhose. Some 
chains like Newport Beach, Calif.-based 
Horton & Converse carry an upscale 
line—H&C carries Hanes in two of its 
stores and reportedly does well with it. 
It remains to be seen whether the up-

more high-end brands in the mix.

Trading card scarcity puts margins on the rebound 


here is no shortage of 

young sports fans to fuel 

sales in the trading card 
category—but they aren’t the 
only consumers. In the peak 
— for trading cards, specu- 
ators drove up numbers by 
gobbling new releases and 
even driving prices above sug- 
gested retail. 

In the 1990s, however, ex- 
cessive production created a 
glut and weakened the catego- 
ry. Add a player strike in 1992 
to confuse the licensing pic- 
ture and it wasn’t a great year 
for trading cards. 

That’s changing, say manu- 
facturers and buyers. The in- 
dustry has begun to tighten up 
production and cut back on the 
size of different series. This 
year, for example, Topps’ pre- 
mium line Stadium Ctub will 
appear in three series for a to- 
tal of 750 cards, down from 900 
last year.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Discounters target big Midwest markets 


CHICAGO — Two major discount chains are striking into 
new markets in a oe and north central regions, and both 
campaigns involve pharmacy expansion. 

Target Stores has launched a major assault on the Chicago 
market with the simultaneous gpa of 11 Target Greatland 
stores in mid-March. All 11 of the giant discount combination 
stores—which ave more than 100,000 square feet—feature 
pharmacies and full drug store departments. Target said it will 
open another seven Chicago stores this year, and said the region 
could support as many as 40 stores. 

Grand Rapids, Mich.-based Meijer, meanwhile, is actively 
scouting store sites in northeastern Ohio for its giant, 200,000- 
square-foot hypermarkets. The 70-store chain could open as 
many as a dozen stores, all of which would contain pharmacies, 
in the greater Cleveland area, according to Meijer spokesper- 
son Jennifer Downs. 


David Panasci: President of Fay’s 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — David Panasci has been named presi- 
dent and chief operating officer of Fay’s Inc. The position had 
been assumed by Fay’s chairman and chief executive officer 
Henry Panasci Jr. since Dan OQ’ left Fay’s in September. 
Previously, David Panasci was president of Fay’s 34-unit Paper 
Cutter division. 


American Greetings buys Magnivision 


CLEVELAND — American Greetings has agreed to acquire 
Magnivision, the leading manufacturer and distributor of non- 
_ prescription reading glasses in the United States and 15 other 
countries. Magnivision, a Florida-based and privately held com- 
pany, was acquired in a stock swap transaction and will become 
part of the Consumer Products Divisicn of American Greetings. 


Revco names head of managed care 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has named outsider Mi- 
chael Green to the new post of director of sales, managed care. 
Green, 40, will take charge of the sales team for retail and mail 
service ee, reporting to vice president of managed care 
Gerald in. Green served since 1989 as director of sales for 
Cole Vision Corp. in Cleveland. 

Revco’s Paget iy care he gong include prescription benefit 
programs for plan providers and employers, including third- 
— payor card programs, mail-order pharmacy and reim- 

ursement of health insurance claims. 


PLMA hosts ist Asian private label show 


_NEW YORK — The Private Label Manufacturers Associa- 
tion will sponsor its first World of Private Label in Asia trade 
show Jan. 26-27, 1994 in the Hong Kong Convention Center. It 
will be the first trade show in Asia developed exclusively to pro- 
mote the private label business. 


Rite Aid, Pharmacy Express ink pact 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Rite Aid has signed on Pharmacy Ex- 
press to provide customers in the Buffalo market with free home 
delivery service for prescriptions and HBA items. Rite Aid 

to test the service in the market, then review the service 


or possible chain-wide rollout.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 26, 1993 


OPINION 


Is there a crisis in new product development? 

Of all people, new product managers at packaged 
goods firms think so. 

In an astonishing criticism of their own companies, 
63 percent of marketers don’t think their management 
has a clear, strategic focus on the role of new products. 
And, contrary to all the hype surrounding new prod- 
ucts, 72 percent feel their management is more com- 

mitted to established 


brands. 

These are some key 
findings of the latest In- 
novation Survey con- 
ducted by Group EFO 
Ltd., Weston, Conn. 

These insights mean a 
lot in today’s retail envi- 
ronment, in which chain 
operators climb over each other to get any kind of edge 
in the delivery and support of sigrificant new prod- 
ucts. After all, being first in the market is a pretty 
good image to have. 

Indeed, the best practices of category management 
and planogram development include dedication to new 
products: quick cut-ins, secondary displays and pro- 
motions, and often higher level communications than 
just buyer to sales rep. From the retailer’s point of 
view, one big advantage of partnering with suppliers 
is the ability to learn more—more quickly—about new 
products, and obtain more manufacturer support. 

New product information tops the list of our own 
readership surveys when we ask what people want. 
That’s why we’ve developed monthly customized New 
Product Watch charts with Towne-Oller. And that’s 
why we value our ongoing relationships with Nielsen 
Marketing Research and Information Resources, and 
are proud to run special features provided by them. 

So what gives? Are retailers being sold a bill of 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


Where is the commitment to new products? 


goods by manufacturers? Or, in their zeal to secure 
any kind of competitive edge, are retailers pinning too 
much hope on new products? Good grist for discussion 
and a special feature in an upcoming issue. 

Meanwhile, let the survey findings help put new 
products in perspective. 

@ Only 8 percent of new product projects initiated 
by major companies reportedly survive to reach the 
market. Only 17 percent that enter the market suc- 
ceed. 

@ 90 percent of new product managers polled said 
their corporate management is the single factor that 
makes or breaks a new product effort. Group EFO 
Ltd., a private consulting firm headed by Ed Ogiba, 
derived this from 166 managers surveyed at 112 
leading manufacturers and retailers. To corrobo- 
rate the surprising findings, the firm went back to 
probe in-depth with 15 randomly selected respon- 
dents. Their anecdotes told of individual executives 
who'd override a year of consumer testing in favor of 
personal preference. 

@ While 63 percent of new product managers said 
they sought “30 percent or more of sales in the next 
five years to come from new products,” almost all of 
the probed respondents said they had set that goal 
and it wasn’t shared by management. 

@ 53 percent of managers said their best market- 
ing people weren’t assigned to new products. Just 40 
percent of companies said they have any managers 
devoted solely to new products. 

@ 28 percent rated their new product approach as 
proven or relatively successful. Over half the re- 
maining 72 percent raised serious doubts about their 
process’s ability to deliver desired results. For in- 
stance, 68 percent questioned their ability to identi- 
fy new sources of business. And 78 percent rated 
their process poorly for uncovering hidden product 
appeals or consumer benefits. 


Here’s the latest competitive nightmare for the 
U.S. drug store industry: the spectre of off-shore 
mail-order dispensaries flooding the U.S. market with 
cheap foreign drugs. 

Independent druggists already are worried sick 
over “unregulated” mail-order pharmacies crossing 
state lines here in this country. Wait until they find 
out that the new North American Free Trade Agree- 
ment just might open the 


floodgates for a vora- 
cious new species of 
cross-border mail order 


2 WASHINGTON prescription piranha! 
, PERSPECTIVE Says who? Says pharma- 
KEN RANKIN cy leaders in Texas, who 


have long complained of 
Mexican pharmacies 
that cater to border-hop- 
ping Americanos seeking over-the-counter drugs 
which, in this country, are either available only by 
prescription or outlawed altogether. 

Officials of the Texas Pharmaceutical Association 
expressed those concerns openly during last month’s 
APhA Annual Meeting in Dallas. 

In a resolution aimed at prompting an APhA re- 
sponse to the prospect of international mail-order dis- 
pensing, the TPA’s delegate warned that NAFTA 
may indeed increase the cross-border trafficking in le- 
gitimate prescription drugs. 

As a result of the elimination of international trade 
barriers between the U.S., Canada and Mexico, 
NAFTA is likely to increase “pressures to import sub- 


One if by land, two if by sea. . . 


stantial quantities of drugs for resale in the U.S., both 
through legitimate as well as gray market outlets,” 
the TPA told APhA’s House of Delegates. 

“Given the significantly lower prices at which (phar- 
maceutical) products are available in Mexico and Can- 
ada, it is not inconceivable that mail-order operators 
could spring up across the borders designed to service 
American health‘care plans,” the Texans argued. 

The economic implications of the TPA’s internation- 
al mail-order prescription scenario are staggering. 

Suppose, for example, that NARD and NACDS 
succeed in convincing Clinton Administration health 
reformers to outlaw discriminatory pricing by U.S. 
pharmaceutical manufacturers. That victory would be 
hollow if NAFTA enables foreign mail services to sell 
prescription drugs in this country at prices below 
what U.S. retailers pay for those products. 

But there are also concerns that transcend econom- 
ics. How safe are the pharmaceuticals being marketed 
in Mexico, Canada or other foreign countries? 

According to the TPA, there is reason for concern 
that drugs produced for sale in other countries may 
not be chemically or therapeutically equivalent to 
those marketed for use in the U.S. 

Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Drug Quali- 
ty director Charma Konnor raised even more ominous 
concerns about foreign drugs during the APhA meet- 
ing. Outright counterfeiting of prescription drug 
products is a growing concern at the FDA, she said, 
adding that on the international market counterfeit 
pharmaceuticals are already “a very serious prob- 
lem.”

Chains in the balance: 
bay's pressures & 
to : orrow's challenges 


elcome to the rest of the 20th Century, and hold onto your busi- 
ness. It’s going to be a wild ride. 
Thus far, the 1990s have been like the sobering morning af- 
ter that followed the relatively freespending, fast-lane economy of the 
1980s. And like their discount store and supermarket counterparts, 
chain drug retailers now find themselves charting unfamiliar wa- 
ters. To many, the passage is already a stormy one. 

Over the past year, the industry has been rocked by financial scan- 
dal, ever-increasing competition, tight consumer spending, corpo- 
rate restructurings and a few high-profile bankruptcies. It has wit- 
nessed takeovers and sudden management changes. It has had to 
adapt to new federal dispensing guidelines and counseling mandates 

under OBRA ’90, and to the steadily increasing clout of third-party 
_. prescription payment programs that have squeezed margins in the

tion review requirements

stressed. Computer systems

e Intense competition in

others to decide our fate.

built. With the increased use 
of technology and information 
availability, we must empow-

cisions at store level and in- 
volve field people more in 
corporate decisions.

acquisition activity 


flurry of buyouts during the 

past 12 months saw more more 

than 1,300 drug stores change 

hands as retailers’ quest for market 
dominance continued. 

The most significant acquisition of 
the past year occurred last summer 
when Los Angeles-based investor 
group Leonard Green & Partners ac- 
quired 620 stores from Pacific Enter- 
pane retail subsidiary Thrifty Corp. 

reen and partners also acquired PE’s 
42-unit Bi-Mart membership/discount 
store subsidiary. 

PE’s liquidation of its Thrifty opera- 
tions allowed PayLess to increase its 
dominance in the northwest through 
the acquisition of Thrifty’s 126-store 
Pay ’n Save division. With the Pay ’n 
Save acquisition and the purchase of 51 
Osco stores the previous year, Pay- 
Less has grown to 554 stores. 


Significant others 


The Thrifty deal was clearly the 
year’s largest, but a string of smaller 
acquisitions were significant from 
the standpoint that they helped 
chains solidify their existing market 
presence.

market, for example, the Jack Eckerd 
Corp. assured its dominance by pick- 
ing up the 13-store Fort Worth-based 
Town and Country chain and then a 
month later landing 16-store Dallas-

share—and in competi- 

tion with pharmacy and 
HBA encroachment by mass 
merchant and food/drug com- 
bo operators—several drug 
store chains launched innova- 
tive new formats in 1992 and 
early 1993. 

A key component of the pro- 
totypes is greater space and 
visual commitment to health 
and nutrition, plus enlarged 
pharmacies designed to com- 
ply with federal patient coun- 
seling requirements. 

Core categories like greet- 
ing cards and photofinishing 
command more space in some 
new formats, as do cosmetics 
and fragrance departments, 
which are presented as up- 
scale boutiques in markets 
where price is less important 
than convenience, service 
and selection. 

Here are some new format 
highlights: 

®@ Osco Drug: An enlarged 
pharmacy and patient lounge 


: n the race for market 


with consultation area demon- 
strates Osco’s concentration 
on health care in its “Vision 
Store” prototype, launched by 
American Drug Stores in 
Phoenix last year. Osco’s new 
stores (and remodels) include 
a nutrition department with 
over 2,000 SKUs ranging from 
juices and whole-grain cereals 
to four vitamin lines. 

The focus is on core catego- 
ries—pharmacy, greeting 
cards, photo finishing, cos- 
metics—and cuts back on 
some general merchandise. 
An upscale fragrance and cos- 
metics department commands 
the central service island. 
Overall, the prototype is 
smaller: down to 15, or 
16,000 square feet from 18,000 
to 19 square feet. 

* PayLess Drug Stores: 
Health and fitness is also dorn- 
inant in the new PayLess ret- 
rofitted test store early this 
year in Rohnert Park, Calif. 

The mix reduces general 
merchandise categories along 


mare peer, Tr 1 
ndgetngen el [ale = 


with fewer but more dramati- 
cally themed and serviced de- 
artments, such as wellness/ 
itness and party/social ex- 
pressions, in addition to other 
regular departments such as 
photofinishing. 
The new layout opens with 
a dramatic bath and body set 
located between cosmetics 
and pharmacy/OTC. The ad- 
jacent health and fitness sec- 
tion includes high-ticket ex- 
ercise equipment, workout 
wear, fitness tapes, nutri- 
tional products, health foods 
and vitamins. 
® Thrift Drug: Thrift’s new 
prototype in Princeton, N.J., 
creates specialty stores within 
a store. It offers more trained 
staff in serviced departments, 
such as bath and body and cos- 
metics. Thrift’s bath and body 
care department offers up- 
scale brands, while its 
“Healthy Choices” depart- 
ment combines nutritional 
foods and health books. 
Other departments offer 
upgraded product in a bou- 
tique presentation, includin 
jewelry, sunglasses re 
ilo The —- card 
epartment has been expand- 
ed to include more alternative 
lines. The prototype interior 
is more spacious, with wider 
aisles and a layout dividing the 
store into two halves. One side 
is traditional OTC and HBA 
on steel shelving; the other 
uses customized fixturing in- 
cluding wooden hutches and 


glass showcases. 
® Austin Drug: Austin also
