DRUG STORE NEWS, April 26, 1993 


ANNUAL REPORT PART 2 @ CHAIN PROFILES 


EERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreen 
Co. lived up to its role in 1992 
as the undisputed heavy- 
weight champ of drug retailing. Year 
after year, in up and down economic 
times, the chain continues to smash old 
performance records and deliver con- 
sistent growth in sales and earnings. 
Indeed, the chain again made more 
money last year—more than $220 mil- 
lion in net earnings on sales of $7.5 bil- 
lion—than at any time in its history, 
despite a recessionary climate that 
chilled growth and froze profits at 
many retail companies. What’s more, 
it did so while adding a record 128 new 
and acquired stores, remodeling an- 
other 118, continuing its rollout of the 
SIMS Strategic Inventory Manage- 
ment stem and completing a chain- 
wide scanning installation project with 
a price tag of more than $100 million. 
Walgreens isn’t immune to the con- 
sumer spending slowdown; Christ- 
mas, for instance, was a “nail-biter” 
until sales picked up in the final week, 
according to chain president L. Daniel 
Jorndt. But the chain’s consistent 
strategy of constantly re-evaluating 
and improving every facet of its busi- 
ness has given it an edge in a tough 
market. The numbers tell the story: 
same-store sales up 7.5 percent in fis- 
cal ’92 and 8.1 percent in the first quar- 
ter of fiscal 93; 118 million scripts 
filled; $446 in sales per square foot. 


Markets infiltrated 


Walgreens has also solidified its po- 
sition as the leader in a dozen top drug 
store markets: Chicago, Houston, 
Phoenix, Ft. Lauderdale, St. Louis, 
Minneapolis/St. Paul, San Antonio, 
Cincinnati, Louisville, Ky., Milwau- 
kee, West Palm Beach, Fla. and Nash- 
ville, Tenn. according to chairman and 
chief executive Charles R. bps eo 
III. “And we're a close second in . 
‘eoheay Pete, San Francisco, Miami, 

ew Orleans and Orlando,” he added. 

Instead of coasting on its momen- 
tum, the chain’s success seems to have 
bred a deeply rooted culture of tough- 
minded self-renewal at all levels. To 
outsiders, it looks as if Walgreens’ offi- 
cers and managers are keenly aware of 
the danger of complacency that years

of market leadership can bring, and de-

company, Walgreens is constantly 
looking over its shoulder. 

“It’s not easy staying in first place in 
this competitive retail world, but we’re 
doing it,” said Jorndt at the company’s 
packed annual meeting in January. 

‘And we'll continue to do it because we 
don’t take anything for granted. Noth- 
ing. We know that — No. 1 means 
fixing things before they break, cutting 
costs during profitable times, giving up 

rofitable businesses which aren’t our 

usinesses any longer—like we did with 
restaurants a few years ago,” he said. 
“Above all, we know that staying No. 1 
takes renewal and flexibility. . .tough 
decisions. . .leaving safe waters for un- 
known ones.” 

Thus, Walgreens has spent more 
than $700 million on new and remod- 
eled stores, advanced technology and 
distribution centers over the past five 
years. Another $200 million will be 
plowed back this year, mostly for new 
and remodeled stores. 


The SIMS advantage 


Last fall, the chain topped off a $120 
million rollout of scanning to all stores. 
The aim: to speed transactions, boost 
productivity, eliminate price sticker- 
ing and allow for faster, more accurate 
price changes. And in the words of the 
company’s most recent annual report, 
“Scanning also provides the vital link 
to our [SIMS] project, perhaps the 
most ambitious technological project 
undertaken by a drug store chain.” 

SIMS’ aim: to unite all elements of 
the purchasing-distribution-sales cy- 
cle into one “tightly integrated pro- 
cess.” According to company reports 
and officials, the automated buying 
segment of the system will have cut 
$80 million out of warehouse inven- 
tories alone by next fall, with addition- 
al savings coming later in store inven- 
tories. SIMS is now in well over 200 of 
Walgreens’ nearly 1,800 stores, with 
new installations picking up. 

“With [SIMS], we’re managing the 
process of inventory flow as well as the 
product,” notes the company’s annual 
report. “We are ‘seeing into’ the entire 
pipeline, from vendor merchandise or- 
der to cash register 
sale.”

Pharmacy stressed 


Meanwhile, Walgreens has pushed 
ahead with its strategic emphasis on 
pharmacy as “the engine that drives 
the train,” in Jorndt’s words. 

“We owe a lot to our pharmacies and 

harmacists for [our] advances,” added 

algreen. “Pharmacy sales i 
16.2 percent last year and are now 37

Company executives acknowledge

Infiltration yet to come 


On the expansion front, Walgreens 
entered Indianapolis with seven stores 
last fall, putting it back into the key 
Midwestern hub for the first time since 
1935. The chain also entered new mar- 
kets like Grand Rapids, Mich., Green 
Bay, Wisc. and Baton Rouge, La. It 
added another 14 units in Chicagoland, 
boosting home-market strength to 271 
stores. And it opened an eighth distri- 
bution center in Lehigh Valley, Pa. 

This year, Walgreens will open 130 
new stores, including its first units 
in the Pacific Northwest with an entry 
into Spokane, Wash. The chain is also 
readying a massive first assault on an- 
other major market, as yet unnamed. 

“We continue to expand in existing 
markets, but must also reach into new 
large and mid-sized cities,” said Jorndt.

AK BROOK, III. — American 

Drug Stores, the chain drug 

division of retail giant Ameri- 
can Stores, has emerged in the 1990s a 
stronger and more focused drug retail- 
er than at any time in its history. 

For one thing, the company’s 741 
Osco and Sav-on drug stores turned in 
a solid performance in fiscal 1992. 
Sales were up more than 7.5 percent, 
breaking the $4 billion mark. Same- 
store sales gained nearly 3 percent, de- 
spite the large mix of general merchan- 

ise in many Sav-on units, the general 
state of the economy and the down- 
ward same-store sales trend in Ameri- 
can Stores’ other two divisions, Jewel 
Companies and Lucky Stores. 

Osco and Sav-on also combined to 
rack up impressive profits, with operat- 
ing earnings up 13.6 percent to mil- 
lion for the year ended Jan. 30, 1993. 
Comparable-store operating earnings 
grew even better, up 14.1 percent over 
the previous year. Said American 
Stores president and chief executive of- 
ficer Vic Lund, “As in prior quarters, 
higher operating profits in our drug 
store operations played a significant role 
in our excellent performance.”

developments as well. One of the big-

Southern California to the Sav-on for-

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 26, 1993 


n 1992, the Jack Eckerd Corpora- 

tion underwent, as many retail- 

ers did, a year of change and un- 
certainty. 

To maintain its status as one of the 
nation’s leading drug chains and en- 
sure long-term profitability, Eckerd 
exposed itself to intense internal scru- 
tiny that resulted in a major restruc- 
turing. Six hundred positions were 
eliminated, several senior executives 
departed and operating regions and 
districts were realigned. The dust has 
nearly settled since last August when 
most of those events took place, and 
the difficult aspects of the restructure 
are EY behind Eckerd. 

“As far as I’m concerned we have 
been going forward all the time,” said 
Eckerd president and chief executive 
officer Stewart Turley. “We deter- 
mined some time ago that we wanted 
to reduce our overhead and reduce our 
expense base in order to be more com- 
ae Ee in the marketplace and still 

old margins. In order to accomplish 
this we felt we had to make some fun- 
damental changes in the structure of 
the organization.” 

mg resulting from the restruc- 
ture will take an estimated 12 to 18 
months to fully implement, but “the 
magnitude of the changes will certain- 
ly be alot less going forward than it has 
been in the past,” according to Turley. 


Consolidating operations 


Eckerd announced several months 
ago it will consolidate its Florida 
warehouse operations. A recently ac- 

uired 600,000-square-foot facility in 

rlando is being refurbished and out- 
fitted with new equipment, with op- 
erations phased in over the summer. 
In the coming months, plans also in- 
clude the completion of a chainwide 
store reset project, eo of its 
point-of-sale system and the upgrade 
of 600 pharmacy computers. 

“Last year we reset about 850 stores 
and this year we will reset another 800, 
so we will in effect have done a reset in 
all of our stores within the last year,” 
Turley said. “We are not experiment- 
ing with a lot of layout changes. The re- 
set is what I would call fine tuning. It is 
not aremodel, but we are making some 
interior store changes.” 

Eckerd stores now have a new skin 
care section, two “ateore iy runs rather 
than three, an enlarged OTC depart- 
ment and repositioned checkouts.

AMP HILL, Pa. — Rite Aid 

had an active 1992 on many 

fronts: The chain moved into 
Maine with a key acquisition; won a 
lawsuit that brought business back 
into stores; moved into new headquar- 
ters, and began installing a satellite 
communications system. 

The chain reported drug store sales 
for the fiscal year ended Feb. 27, 1993 
at $3.83 billion, an 8.6 percent increase 
over year-earlier sales of $3.53 billion. 

Rite Aid picked up 34 of Hannaford 
Bros. Co.’s 41 Wellby Super Dru 
stores last May, when Hannaford sol 
its chain drug division. The acquisition 
put Rite Aid in Maine for the first time 
with 27 stores. 

The balance of the stores were in 
New Hampshire, and the purchase 
strengthened Rite Aid’s presence in 
the state where Rite Aid x oper- 
ated 12 locations. Now that all loca- 
tions bear the Rite Aid name, the move 
strengthened Rite Aid’s presence in 
New England. 

It wasn’t long after entering the 
Maine market that Rite Aid embarked 
on a legal battle with the state. The 
chain filed suit against the state of 
Maine, the Department of Financial 
and Administrative Services and 
Medco Containment Services, charg- 
ing that Medco, the company selected 
to administer the state employees’ pre- 
scription program, violated state law 
by failing to allow local pharmacies to 
participate fully in the program. 

B ber, Rite Aid had emerged 
as the victor after a Maine state court 
ordered that the chain be permitted to 
dispense long-term prescriptions to 
Maine state employees.

Out of bankruptcy, 
Revco roars back to life 


WINSBURG, Ohio — Some- 

times, bankruptcy really works. 

In Reveo’s case, Chapter 11 of 

the federal bankruptcy code did what 

it was designed to do: provide protec- 

tion from a slew of creditors while the 

company overhauled its business and 

figured out a way to pay its bills. Revco 

D.S. is a textbook case of how to do 
bankruptcy right. 

The chain roared out of Chapter 11 
last June ready to take on the world— 
without the court’s protection for the 
first time in nearly four years. It was 
ready because its officers, store man- 
agers and employees had essentially 
rebuilt the company from ground up, 
and its creditors, lenders and le 
overseers had allowed it the financial 
muscle to do the job — In return, 
those creditors and lenders got control 
of a revitalized, viable drug chain posi- 
tioned to compete in the ’90s. 

The Revco that emerged from Chap- 
ter 11 bore almost no resemblance to 
the company that staggered into the 
courts four years earlier. For the first 
time since its highly leveraged and ul- 
timately disastrous buyout in late 
1986, the company has a healthy bal- 
ance sheet. Its finances were reorga- 
nized to cut its massive debt load and 
interest obligations; since then, Revco 
has completely refinanced the $433.2 
million in debt with wnich it emerged 
from Chapter 11 through a combina- 
tion of new stock and note offerings 
and new bank borrowings at lower in- 
terest rates. 

The recapitalization—completed 
early this year—cut Revco’s debt and 
interest payments, and strengthened 
its equity/debt ratio. 

Revco’s operating systems have 
also been completely overhauled. 
The chain is one of the first to roll POS 
scanning systems to all 1,150 of its 
stores. Data captured by the scan- 
ners is now feeding into the buying 
and distribution systems, enabling 
the chain to get a better handle on 
consumer demand and adjust its mer- 
chandise mix, ads, item movement 
and order quantities for a more tar- 
geted, store-specific approach. The 
eventual goal: a true perpetual inven- 
tory system that provides just-in- 
time goods automatically. 

Also revamped was the chain’s phar- 
macy a system. Under its Pre- 
scription Access Link (PAL) program, 
Reveo went on-line with a new, inter- 
active pharmacy system and modern- 
ized its third-party billing and patient 
adjudication systems. In the process, 
the chain dramatically cut its billing 
cycles and nonpayables.

resources to development of a new

chusetts-based Thayer Pharmacies 
operation and bought 10 Fay’s stores 
in Pennsylvania. 

“We are concentrating on building 
markets where we have the most sig- 
nificant penetration,” said CVS a. 
ident and ceo Harvey Rosenthal. “In 
California our share was too low; we 
do best in markets where we have a 
high share.” He said that in the 25 
metro markets in which CVS oper- 
ates, the chain holds the No. 1 spot in 
18 markets. 

All Thayer Pharmacies have been 
renovated and are operating under the 
CVS name. CVS says the company is 
pleased with the stores’ performance. 


Bolstering Peoples presence 


The chain also focused on strength- 
ening the Peoples stores CVS had ac- 
quired in the Wachinnton, D.C., mar- 
ket about two years ago. The chain has 
shown steady improvement and Ro- 
senthal says the groundwork has been 
laid to make Peoples a successful part 
of the CVS chain. 

“Remodeling the Peoples stores 
was a major effort for us last year. It 
took a long time since many of those 
stores had not been renovated for a 
long while,” said Rosenthal. With the 
renovation of the stores nearly com- 
plete, CVS can now see a positive im- 
pact on sales. 

“The good news is that renovated 
stores are out-performing the other 
stores. We’ve worked hard on the ser- 
vice end of the business—speeding up 
checkouts and upgrading pharmacy

Thrifty Drug downsizes, aims for turnaround 


OS ANGELES — Thrifty Corp. 

and its Thrifty Store chain 

underwent a whirlwind of owner- 
ship change, remodeling and store clos-

1998. Just as the downsizing neared

architect of this change—ceo and chair- 
man William Yingling—resigned, re- 
portedly to pursue other interests. Dur- 
ing this eventful year, the chain also saw 
three stores destroyed in the April, 
1992. riots in Los Angeles. 

The management-led buyout of 
Thrifty Corp., headed by Leonard 
Green & Partners along with a number 
of Thrifty executives, was announced 
in May of 1992. The change met with 
the approval of many analysts, who 
viewed Green’s aggressive turn- 
around record as a possible cure for 
Thrifty’s ills under former parent com- 
pany Pacific Enterprises. 

But most industry observers 
agreed it would be tough to revive the 
sluggish drug store chain in a reces- 
sionary economy and fight to keep 
market share against formidable new 
competition, especially in the eco- 
nomically-troubled Southern Califor- 
nia market.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 26, 1993 


ANNUAL REPORT PART 2 @ CHAIN PROFILES 


F&M a bright spot among deep discounters 


ARREN, Mich. — 
Age has its advan- 
tages. F&M Dis- 


tributors, the granddaddy of 
deep-discount drug store 
chains, is a case in point. 

Tracing its business back to 
the first off-price drug store 
opened by Fred and Margaret 

ohen in 1955, F&M Distribu- 
tors can rightfully call itself a 
retail pioneer. And unlike 
many younger siblings in this 
relatively young industry, 
F&M has sailed through the 
past two years of economic 
slump with solid earnings. 

In general, 1992 and early ’93 
have been a dismal time for off- 

rice drug chains. Industry 
eader Phar-Mor is in bank- 
ruptcy, still reeling from mas- 
sive losses related to last year’s 
financial scandals and a too-rap- 
id growth strategy. No. 2 Drug 
Emporium is fighting to reas- 
sert its position and profitabili- 
ty after a series of fiscal losses, 
and has abandoned its strategy 
of decentralized management 
and merchandising. 

Recession and debt loads 
have also helped push two oth- 
er quality operators—A.L. 
Price/Freddy’s and Drug 
Barn—into Chapter 11. 

F&M, meanwhile, posted 
record net earnings of $10.3 
million for the fiscal year end- 
ed Jan. 30, 1993, and sales of 
nearly $740 million, up 10 per- 
cent from the previous year. 

The chain has bucked the 
tide by sticking close to operat- 
ing — hammered out 
over d es of slow, careful 
expansion. That expansion has 
been accelerated since the mid- 
1980s by chain president Frank 
Newman, but F&M’s growth 
strategy is still a model of pru- 
dent, frugal investment and 
precise site selection. 

The 116-store chain concen- 
trates its stores and its growth 
in five of the nation’s top mar- 
kets: Detroit, Chicago, Wash- 
ington/Baltimore, Minneapo-

sales-per-square-foot aver-

30,000 square feet of selling

standards of some competi- 
tors. And its SG&A expense 
structure, at 15.5 percent of 
sales, is the envy of most re- 
tailers. 

Last year, F&M capitalized 
on its age record by go- 
ing public. In the process, the 
chain netted $33.5 million to 
pay down debt and fund ex- 
pansion. On tap: as many as 18 
new stores in the next year.

Walgreen: another 
DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreen Co. again reported record 
sales and earnings for the second quarter and first half of fiscal 
1993, extending a long-running winning streak in a sluggish 
economy. 
Walgreens drove sales ahead 10.8 percent for the quarter 
ended Feb. 28, to $2.26 billion. Net earnings advanced 9.2 per- 
cent to $84.2 million. Factoring out a one-time charge to redeem 
$100 million in 9.5-percent sinking fund debentures, the chain’s 
earnings would have risen 14.6 percent. 
For the first six months, sales rose 11.4 percent $4.17 billion, 
and net earnings were up 10.5 percent to $124.5 million. 
Pharmacy sales again led the way, rising 15.1 percent for the 
quarter and 14.5 percent for the half. Same-store pharmacy 
sales rose 11.3 percent. Anticipating that “major health care 
— will be forthcoming,” chairman and ceo Charles R. rapa

ANNUAL REPORT 


Pharmacy maps out 
health care reform . . . 
But is anyone listening? 


By Ken Rankin 


year ago the nation’s community pharmacists were 
struggling tounderstand and adjust to a series of chal- 
lenges from Washington, academia and the marketplace 
that threatened to reshape the practice of pharmacy well 
unto the next century. 

Today those same challenges—the impact of new OBRA 
90 patient counseling/DUR requirements, the competitive 
pressure from mail order pharmacy services, and the push 
forauniversal six-year Pharm.D. degree—continue to cast 
a long shadow over the future of community pharmacy.

OTCs are ace in the hole for pharmacy 


By Mike Troy 


ver-the-counter medi- 
cines are proving to be 
the ace up the sleeve 


of drug stores in the poker game 
of retailing. Although only 
modest sales gains were posted 
in 1992, drug stores remain the 
dominant trade class in many 
categories and are well-posi- 
tioned for future gains. 

OTCs are one of drug stores 
strongest suits in the face of 
mounting regulatory mandates, 
shrinking prescription margins 
and heightened competition 
from other trade classes. As 
those forces gnaw at profits, drug 
stores can find solace in the fact 
that OTCs offer high per-square- 
foot and per-transaction profits. 
Not only that, but two of the 
most significant trends driving 
sales growth in many OTC cate- 
gories will continue for the fore- 
seeable future. 

American’s desire to self- 


medicate in light of enormous 
health care costs combined 
with: the nation’s aging popula- 
tion will provide a steady 
stream of customers that have 
grown up with and feel comfort- 
able in the drug store format. 
Surveys repeatedly place 
pharmacy as the most trusted 
profession, and the pharma- 
cist’s opinion on proper OTC 
use is highly sought after. One 
conservative estimate indicates 
pharmacists make an average of 
15 OTC recommendations dai- 
ly, and 90 percent of the time 
the recommendation is fol- 
lowed. That’s a lot of clout, and 
the pharmacist’s importance in 
counseling will only increase as 
self-medication trends contin- 
ue and OBRA '90 requirements 
become fully effective. 
Virtually every OTC catego- 
ry, including such things as di- 
gestive products, incontinence- 
related items, analgesics, skin 
care, diabetes, feminine hy-

Family planning category 


he family planning cate- 

gory has seen its share of 

ups and downs in recent 
years, but it continues to be one 
of the drug store’s strongest 
OTC categories. 

Condom sales went through 
the roof a few years back, ta- 
pered off and now appear to be 
rebounding. Technological 
breakthroughs have improved 
+908 accuracy and ease-of-use of 

pregnancy and ovulation 
in to. Ae personal lubricants 
and moisturizers are gaining a 
base of regular users. 

Different segments of the cat- 
egory stand to benefit in vary- 
ing degrees from consumer con- 
cerns about sexually 
transmitted diseases, aging 
populations and manufactur- 
ers innovative marketing ap- 
proaches. 


Condoms largest segment 


Condoms comprise the larg- 
est segment of the family plan- 
ning category, accounting for 
roughly $183 million in sales at 
drug stores during the past 12 
months, according to Towne- 
Oller. That represents a 10 per- 
cent increase compared to the 
same time period a year earlier. 

Manufacturers contend 
condom sales still have a long 
way to go, considering recent 
studies that reveal the alarm- 
ing rates at which high risk 
groups indicate they engage in 
unprotected sex. One recent 
survey indicates that 66 per- 
cent of heterosexuals with 
multiple partners do not regu- 
larly use condoms. 


The increase in condom sales 
that has taken ore has also 
helped pull ales of personal lu- 
bricants higher, making it one 
of the category's fastest growing 
segments. As with condoms, 
the need for proper education 
remains strong. Research by 
Johnson & Johnson, makers of 
K-Y brand jelly, indicates that 
oil-based lubricants such as pe- 
troleum jelly, hand and body lo- 
tions and oils can damage latex 
condoms and diminish their ef- 
fectiveness in preventing sexu- 
ally transmitted diseases and 
unplanned pregnancy. 

To get its point across, in 
Pesos J&J initiated a nation- 
wide a campaign showing a 
large sewing needle piercing a 
condom package with the tag 
line, “This is what series 
jelly can do to a condom.” 

According to J&J, roughly 50 

ercent of condom users use ad- 
Hitional lubrication. In fact, one 
out of three women report us- 
ing a lubricant to relieve vaginal 
dryness during intercourse. 

Another factor boosting the 
sales of lubricants and moistur- 
izers is the aging of America and 
the increase in the number of 
post-menopausal women. 
Women in this age group tend 
to experience vaginal dryness 
and personal lebelcank and 
moisturizer sales in part are re- 
flecting the demographic shift.

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, April 26, 1992 


STD increases prompt new labeling 


No discussion of the family 
planning category would be 
complete without exploring the 
impact of sexually transmitted 
diseases (STDs). 

The shift in public attention 
to AIDS has de-emphasized 
the dangers of non-AIDS 
STDs, even though on gt 12 
million Americans eac year 
contract these diseases. Con- 
sider the following: 

® More than 30 million 
Americans have the virus that 
causes genital herpes and 
300,000 to 500,000 new cases 
develop each year. 

@ Chlamydia has risen to epi- 
demic proportions and causes 
about four million new infec- 
tions annually. 

® Syphilis cases increased 
from about 70,000 to 136,000 
between 1986 and 1988 and 
continue to increase. 

@ Drug-resistant strains of 


otc merchandiser 


gonorrhea increased from 11,000 
cases in 1986 to 35,000 in 1990. 
Left untreated, non-AIDS 
STDs can cause serious infec- 
tions and complications such as 
infertility, blindness, neurologic 
damage and cancer. Concern 
that consumers might confuse 
certain birth control methods as 
offering protection against STDs 
has generated a new round of la- 
beling requirements by the 
FDA. One specific incident in- 
volved a girl who died of AIDS 
who thought the birth control 
pills she was taking would pre- 
vent her from contracting STDs. 
The new labeling should start 
appearing on contraceptive 
packages in about six months. 
They will be required to have a 
statement about STDs on the 
package with a message that 
products such as birth control 
bills, implantable contraceptives 
and IUDs are intended to pre- 


vent pregnancy, but will not pre- 
vent the transmission of STDs. 
Natural skin condoms will 
also be required to carry a state- 
ment advising consumers that 
they should use latex condoms 
instead of natural skin condoms 
to reduce the risk of STDs. New 


labeling requirements for s er- 
micides, cervical ca 
phragms and sponges olga yet 
to be determined by FDA. 

More information on STDs 
can be obtained by calling the 
American Social Health Associ- 
ation at (919) 361-8400.

false information about the health of 
the company.

eral court here alleging that they were 
deceived about Phar-Mor’s financial 
condition prior to investing in $155 mil- 
lion worth of notes issued by the compa- 


NACDS attendees poised 


ny, which is now in Chapter 11. Among

By James Frederick 
YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Taking 
the wraps off its long-awaited business 
plan, Phar-Mor said it will sell off or 
close 64 stores, lay off 4,100 workers 
and speed up its investment in POS, 
pharmacy and warehouse technology. 
“We’ve made the tough decisions 
about store consolidation and over- 
head reductions,” said chief executive 
officer Tony Alvarez. “Now, we can fo- 


‘cus on investing in our core stores and 


building on our strengths.” 

Phar-Mor said it will shrink to a core 
base of 168 “established, gt onal 
ly concentrated, profita le deep-dis- 
count drug stores” in 23 states. That 
will mean the elimination of 64 more 
stores and 3,600 more store-level jobs, 
capping a drastic downsizing program 
that began last summer after the com- 
pany announced a major financial scan- 
dal and fled into Chapter 11 bankrupt- 
cy protection. 

tores to be closed are scattered

part of its new core network of 168 
stores. 

Phar-Mor also said it will also cut an- 
other 522 jobs in corporate, distribu-

The store closings and staff reduc- 
tions will cut corporate overhead and 


s, boost technology 


distribution costs roughly 30 per-

clude the downsizing process begun

filed for Chapter 11 after uncovering

Those accusations led the chain to 
take $499 million in charges against 
earnings and to overhaul its manage-

New franchise program for Med Shoppe 


ST. LOUIS — Medicine Shoppe International has developed 
a new multiple-store poets which allows franchisees to open 
up to eight Medicine Shoppe units over a three-year period in a 
specified territory. The program includes a scaled origination 
fee, which allows MSI to structure a development opportunity 
for franchisees from the start rather than adding expansion 
agreements later. The program allows franchisees to better 
strategize long-range p g on market share development. 


Five such contracts have already been signed. 


Rite Aid’s Grass to get Scopus award 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Alex Grass, chairman of the board and

Award of American Friends of the Hebrew University at a Phar- 
maceutical and Mass Merchandising Division dinner in Manhattan 
this month. The award will be given to Grass in honor of his dedica- 
tion and commitment to advancing higher education at the School 


of Pharmacy at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

ANAHEIM, Calif. — Catalina Marketing 
Corp. is expanding its in-store electronic 
Checkout Coupon program into drug stores, 
beginning with 10 selected Thrifty Drug Stores 
in Southern California and 10 Longs Drug 
Stores in Northern California. 

Catalina’s system uses scanner technology 
to target consumers and distribute coupons at 
the checkout based on consumer purchase be- 
havior. Three different types of incentives can 
be triggered by a consumer’s purchase: it can 
generate a coupon at point-of-sale for 1) the 
same product in a different size; 2) for a differ- 
ent product from the same manufacturer or 3) 
for a competing oho ta & 

According to Catalina, this is the only tech- 
nology of its kind in supermarkets and drug 
stores. Another type of in-store coupon distri- 


Catalina enters drug store coupon market 


bution system uses a blinking light on a shelf 
unit to alert a customer to take a coupon. 

Any retail operation with scanners is a po- 
tential outlet for this type of program, noted 
Tommy Greer, chairman and chief executive 
officer of Catalina Marketing. The Catalina 
Marketing Network for drug stores will be the 
same as that used in supermarkets. The system 
is installed in 5,600 supermarkets across the 
country, including Giant, Dominick’s, Kroger, 
Winn-Dixie and Cub Foods. 

According to Catalina, the leading coupon- 
printing categories in the drug store arena in- 
clude candy, cough and cold medicines, soft 
drinks and oral hygiene. The company expects 
that the addition of drug stores to its network 


will attract new manufacturer clientele from 
the HBA product categories.

and renew its market leader- 
ship position in ter De- 
troit after being edged out last 
year by rival Arbor t_>

resident and chief executive 
ill Edwards to the

well as inventories. It is essen- 
tially a stores-for-debt swap, 
which would effectively cancel 
the $3.6 million which ALP still 
owes Perry for the original pur-

Perry was one of three cred- 
itors which forced the off- 


Perry, ALP/Freddy's 
agree to debt ‘swap’

OPINION 


‘The Annual’ reflects chains’ changing roles 


a 


When drug chain chief executive and chief operat-- 
ing officers roost in Palm Beach for the NACDS Annu- 
al Meeting, the intensity of one-on-one sessions belies 
the calm splendor of The Breakers. 

The mood of the Annual has turned increasingly 
dramatic over the years, as executives work the con- 
ference more urgently to refine their retailing vi- 
sions, build credibility for their chains, improve 
partnerships with sup- 


pliers and acquire fresh 
knowledge that can 
make them more com- 


MARKET petitive against an on- 
PULSE slaught of threats. 
AL HELLER Health care reform 


and the radical changes 
that may bring to retail 


pharmacy, not surpris- 
ingly, was uppermost in the thoughts of presidents 
and chairmen. “It’s terrible that we [drug chains] have 
become a distribution process. It bothers me that 
we’ve done such a [blankety-blank] job of delivering 
pharmacy care that drug stores aren’t perceived as an 
essential part of the U.S. health care system,” said 
Don Beeler, chief executive of Snyder, in one of a se- 
ries of face-to-face meetings I held with top-tier exec- 
utives at the Annual. 

He spoke with great apprehension about clinical 
settings becoming a major threat to drug stores.” 

Beyond this threat, the aggressive pursuit of phar- 
macy by other trade classes has PayLess chief execu- 
tive officer Tim McAlear saying, “we must reinvent 
what a drug store will be in order to survive going into 
the next century. 

“We have to get away from the mass merchandise 
line mentality and get into bridge lines of merchandise 
between discount and department stores,” he added. 
PayLess, a chain unafraid to experiment, has been 
testing new department sets with varied results. 


“People focus on bath care because it’s the prettiest, 
but party goods, greeting cards and the nutrition cen- 
ter are yielding more productive returns so far,” he 
said. At the same time, the chain is phasing out domes- 
tics and apparel and scaling back peripheral hard 
goods to make room for more core areas. 

PayLess will unveil its prototype in Sandy, Utah, 
on May 26 with a new level of store staff: wellness 
consultants “who can explain bee pollen and the use 
of different garlics to consumers who aren’t in the 
cult. They’ll be akin to cosmeticians,” said McAlear, 
who considers his chain’s 75 percent to 25 percent 
full-time to part-time store staff ratio as an invest- 
ment. “Shoppers can go anywhere to buy Head & 
Shoulders. We need to be dedicated to making peo- 
ple look good and feel good.” 

For her part, Margaret, Urquhart, corporate vice 
president of marketing at Hook-SupeRx Inc., spoke 
with great animation of chief executive Phil Beek- 
man’s plan to move beyond old concepts and build a 
single corporate vision for its three retail operations: 
Hook’s, Brooks and SupeRx. “This has almost taken 
on a life of its own. The ranks are the driving force now 
for the consolidation,” she said, noting the process 
should take 18 to 24 months. 

At Ulta®, principal Dick George has unveiled an 
8,500-square-foot prototype in Minneapolis. Plans are 
set to take the unique beauty store format into Dallas by 
late summer and Atlanta in the fall, as the chain expands 
from seven stores now to 17 by the end of the year. 

Perry chief operating officer Andy Giancamilli 
spoke about how the chain is using technology to cut 
operating expenses, and will be full scanning by Au- 
gust. Pharmacy, which accounted for 51 percent of 
sales in the latest quarter, is being-strengthened: four 
stores already have redesigned pharmacy counters 
that ease consultation, and the chain will soon launch a 
professional image ad campaign encouraging people to 
see their pharmacists. 


NACDS/NARD’s secret plan to save pharmacy 


For months now, representatives of the nation’s 
chain and independent drug stores have been meeting 
behind closed doors with top White House officials in a 
concerted effort to influence the Clinton Administra- 
tion’s health care reform plan. 

Working under the umbrella of their newly formed 
Community Retail Pharmacy Coalition, staffers from 
NACDS and NARD have reached consensus on a se- 
ries of “principles” that 


both organizations be- 
lieve the Clinton sup- 
porters shouid follow in 
hammering out the new 
health proposal. 

But other more specif- 
ic—and potentially more 
controversial—propos- 
als have also been ad- 
vanced by NARD and NACDS during their secret 
meetings with Clintgn health reformers. Indeed, the 
two associations have already presented White House 
officials with a detailed plan for universal third-party 
prescription drug coverage to be included in the Ad- 
ministration’s health reform package. 

What do retail pharmacy leaders really want in the 
Clinton Administration’s soon-to-be-announced 
health care reform program? Neither NARD nor 
NACDS is willing yet to disclose the substance of the 
plan that they proposed to the White House. Not even 
to their own members. 

But some of the details are beginning to dribbie out. 
One important element involves across-the-board 
price controls on pharmaceutical manufacturers. Spe- 
cifically, NARD and NACDS want drug product costs 
capped at the Average Manufacturers’ Price (AMP), 


we WASHINGTON 
B, PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


with future price increases limited to the annual rise in 
the Consumer Price Index. 

Citing an economic analysis prepared for the coali- 
tion by Washington, D.C.’s Policy Research Group, 
NARD and NACDS say such a price control mecha- 
nism would generate at least $24 billion in savings dur- 
ing the first five years of the Administration’s new 
health reform program. 

At the same time, they contend that the AMP re- 
quirement would also eliminate price discrimination 
against retail pharmacies by effectively punishing 
drug manufacturers who engage in such practices. 

Additionally, NACDS and NARD are urging 
Clinton supporters to adopt health reform policies 
that will result in “enhanced professional pharmacy 
services”—a move that the Research Policy Group 
study suggests will “save” another $27.3 billion over 
five years. 

At this point, representatives of the coalition aren’t 
saying which pharmacy services they have asked 
Washington to “enhance.” The pharmacist’s product 
selection role would be broadened—but it’s not clear 
whether NARD and NACDS have proposed federal- 
ly-mandated therapeutic substitution, expanded 
DUR requirements, universal patient counseling or 
other measures. 

On the reimbursement front, the coalition’s plan 
calls on the government to pay each pharmacy’s usual 
and customary charge, capped at the 90th percentile. 

Although retail pharmacists have long advocated 
such a “marketplace pricing” system in order to raise 
third-party reimbursement levels, the new NACDS- 
NARD study contends this approach would actually 
lower total payments for pharmacy services by $100 
million to $200 million annually.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 24, 1993 


OPINION 


It’s time for a hard look at brands 


How important are coupons to consumers? How do 
coupons affect buying habits, induce product trial and 
erode brand loyalty? In what categories are they most 
effective, and for which demographic groups? 

These questions interest marketers on the supplier 
and retailer sides, as trade executives increasingly 
view consumer pull as the preferred way to move 
products through the distribution pipeline. 


4 >: 


Jeff Nedelman, vp- 
communications at the 
Grocery Manufacturers of 
America, issued a state- 


MARKET ment on couponing that is 
PULSE meant to strengthen the 
AL HELLER position of brands: “Both 


national manufacturers 
and retailers have, in one 
sense, helped create a 
temporary situation that has led to ‘brand switching.’ 
Depending on the Sunday coupon section or the sale at 
the local store, consumers are now switching from re- 
tailer to retailer and from brand to brand in an effort to 
get the best quality at the lowest cost.” 

Has the trade gone overboard in this effort? 

The dollar value of coupon redemptions across the 
nation has soared 7 percent to $4.7 billion in 1992. This 
level is twice the $2.3 billion redeemed in 1985—re- 
flecting aggressive efforts by manufacturers and 
chains to show value while keeping base prices high. It 
also shows consumers’ increased responsiveness 
‘uring a tough economic period. 

Brands have other challenges facing them too. 

Shoppers seeking value in tight times are also stick- 
ing more with private labels. The bad news for brand 
marketers is that consumers are expected to stick 
with private labels once economic pressures ease, be- 
cause their quality and packaging are vastly im- 
proved. And private label companies are starting to 
elevate their status from just being contractors for 


chains; more are becoming strategic partners discuss- 
ing logistics, EDI and other cost-effective measures. 

Moreover, branded suppliers have to whittle SKU 
duplication to drive down distribution costs. In doing 
so, they’ll limit the number of me-too items on shelves 
that don’t add to retailers’ variety image. Findings ofa 
new Food Marketing Institute study, sponsored by 
Frito-Lay and conducted by Willard Bishop Consult- 
ing, Barrington, Ill., support this conclusion. 

The study found that retailers can reduce SKUs 
from 5 percent to 25 percent without hurting sales or 
how shoppers perceive a store’s variety. 

There are significant implications to this finding: in- 
ventory investment, store size, operating costs might 
all be lowered. 

If put into practice, the efficiencies it will bring to con- 
ventional formats will make them better able to compete 
with wholesale clubs and other limited selection stores. 

Just as chains have taken an axe to costs throughout 
their networks, they also need to think about SKU- 
cutting: sever the needless line extensions and me-too 
mimics; slice away an overabundance of package sizes; 
reward distinctive items and market leaders with 
high-profile footage. 

I feel that retailers need to apply fresh logic to their 
assortments. They need to look beyond GMROI and 
other key performance measures. They must review 
product benefits, and ask themselves how particular 
items meet different consumer needs. They must look at 
their mix through customers’ eyes, and assess how well 
the overall store variety fits tetal shopping require- 
ments. They must balance image and performance. 

At the same time, suppliers must critically review 
their brand lineups and decide which items are worth 

supporting. They are responsible for helping to cut out 
brand clutter, streamline their mix, and help make 
themselves and retailers earn greater total returns. 

That is, after all, the essence of partnership and 
serving the ultimate consumer. 


Health care reform: First the good news. . . 


First, here’s the good news for pharmacy from the 
health care reform front: “Prescription drugs abso- 
lutely will be covered” under the Clinton Administra- 
tion’s soon-to-be-announced program. 

So says APhA past president Marily Rhudy, a To- 


peka, Kansas independent pharmacist who has helped 


to formulate the still-secret White House plan. 
Rhudy is one of two pharmacists on a 47-member 
White -House health pro- 


fessionals advisory group 
appointed to review the 
Administration’s reform 
plan before it is released 
to the public. 

The reason Rhudy is so 
sure prescription drug 
coverage will be part of 
the President’s new pro- 
gram is that she got the word directly from First 
Spouse Hillary R. Clinton and White House Health 
Reform Task Force director Ira Magaziner. 

“They realize that cutting prescription drug cover- 
age out of the plan wouldn’t save them money,” she ex- 
plained. “First of all it’s a relatively small part of the 
health care pie, and secondly, they recognize that pre- 
scription drug coverage actually saves money down 
the line.” 

The bad news from Washington is that if Rhudy is 
right—if pharmacy groups have convinced the White 
House to cover prescription drugs under the President's 
new health reform plan—the retail drug store industry 
may not like what it sees in the proposal at all. 

So says Senate Aging Committee chairman David 


h WASHINGTON 
\ PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


Pryor (D-Ark.), retail pharmacy’s best friend on Capi- 
tol Hill and a long-time political ally of the Clintons. 

During NARD’s annual legislative conference in 
Washington last month, Pryor warned independent 
druggists that the White House reform plan may in- 
clude a number of provisions that retail pharmacy will 
find objectionable. 

Sen. Pryor did not offer any examples of these ob- 
jectionable provisions, but it doesn’t take much imagi- 
nation to come up with a health reform scenario that 
community pharmacy would find indigestible. 

How about prescription drug coverage built around 
a “managed competition” model that allows participa- 
tion by only the lowest-bidding pharmacy providers? 

Or what about a plan that offers a big competitive 
edge to mail order pharmacies, or HMO drug dispen- 
saries, or dispensing physicians? 

What if the Clinton Administration ignores the 
advice of groups such as NACDS, NARD and APhA 
and designs a universal prescription drug benefit 
that fails to utilize che full professional capabilities 
of pharmacists? 

Even optimistic health reformers such as Rhudy ac- 
knowledge that pharmacy’s role under the Adminis- 
tration’s new drug program is far from clear. 

One possible new role for pharmacists may in- 
volve service on the new government drug formu- 
lary panels that the White House is expected to pro- 
pose, Rhudy said. 

“Just who will serve on these formulary committees 
is uncertain,” she said, “but it could be a great oppor- 
tunity for pharmacists on the state and federal levels 
to weigh in on these decisions.”

Vons’ operating earnings increase 


ARCADIA, Calif. — The 
Vons Companies announced a 
6 percent increase in operat- 
ing earnings for first quarter 
1993, or $15.9 million up from 
$15 million a year ago. Reve- 
nues dropped 5.8 percent to 
$1.19 billion compared with 
$1.27 billion in the first quar- 
ter of 1992, while same-store 
sales decreased 8.3 percent in 
the first quarter. 

Chairman and ceo Roger 
Stangeland explained that im- 
shi operating earnings re- 

ect tight margin and expense 
management. “Our contempo- 
rary store base, which offers 
customers a broad selection, 
has allowed us to expand our 
gross margin by improving 
the mix of the products we 


sell,” said Stangeland. 

Gross margin improved 50 
basis points to 25.3 percent of 
sales in the quarter compared 
with 24.8 percent in the com- 
parable quarter last year. 

The drop in sales was attrib- 
uted to a combination of fac- 
tors, including the recession 
throughout the company’s 
various regions, competitive 
store openings and remodels, 
increased promotional activi- 
ty and negative publicity sur- 
rounding the Foodmaker food 
poisoning epidemic. 

Vons is the largest super- 
market operator in Southern 
California and operates 346 
stores under the Vons, Pavil- 
ions, Tianguis and Williams 
Bros. names.

[news trends] 


APhA endorses NARD/NACDS reform plan... 


Under pressure from state pharmacy association executives and their community pharmacist mem- 
bers, APhA’s Board of Trustees voted to endorse the principles of health care reform advanced earlier 
this year by the NARD/NACDS “Community Retail Pharmacy Health Care Reform Coalition.” Although 
that endorsement appears to knock APhA off the fence on the sticky issue of outlawing manufacturer 
prescription price discrimination against community pharmacy, it hasn't yet created much unity in orga- 
nized pharmacy’s response to the emerging Clinton Administration's health reform plan. 


... But retail pharmacy isn’t reciprocating 


Ron Ziegler, NACDS president, and Charles West, NARD executive vp, expressed appreciation for 
APhA’s “general support” of the coalition’s health reform principles, but told John Gans, APhA exec vp, 
that isn’t enough. In a “Dear John” letter to Gans, West and Ziegler called on APhA to advocate the “leg- 
islative remedy to discriminatory pricing by pharmaceutical manufacturers’ that the coalition secretly 
provided to the White House earlier this year. That “Dear John” letter also rebuffed Gans’ plea that 
NARD and NACDS endorse the health reform principles endorsed by APhA’'s separate coalition of hos- 
pital and consultant pharmacists. The hang-up, according to West and Ziegler: background statements 
which “cloud your position on the key issues of discriminatory pricing and open access.” 


Pharmacy techs eye greater responsibilities 


With OBRA ’90 patient counseling requirements adding to the workload of pharmacists, pharmacy 
boards in a number of states are under pressure to relax restrictions on the use of prescription depart- 
ment ancillary personnel. Just last month, Louisiana pharmacy technicians were granted new “count 
and pour” authority, and some pharmacy groups are eyeing even broader responsibilities for support 
staffers. A resolution slated for debate by hospital pharmacists at ASHP’s annua! meeting in Denver next 
month calls on the association to “foster dispensing of medication using qualified technicians to verify 
the work of other technicians.” 


Here’s fresh proof of Rx price discrimination .. . 


An OBRA '90 mandated study by the General Accounting Office found that institutional pharmacies 
are able to buy pharmaceuticals at discounts off of average wholesale price (AWP) up to three times 
greater than those available to retail ‘serbllgee In areport to Congress on prescription drug purchas- 
ing by pharmacies in Maryland and Illinois, GAO found that hospital pharmacies “paid an average of 30 

ercent less than AWP” for pharmaceuticals, and that some were able to purchase drugs for 42 percent 


low AWP. In contrast, GAO said, “retail pharmacies routinely pay prices that average about 13 per- 
cent below AWP.” 


o 


... And more evidence of pharmacists’ value 


Government officials concerned about rising health costs should take note of a recently completed 
NARD membership survey examining the types of interventions independent pharmacists perform for 
their patients. “In 18 percent of the prescription cases, and 42 percent of OTC cases, pharmacist inter- 
ventions led to the patient not receiving a medication,” NARD said. This is “an extraordinarily important 
observation relative to current concerns over health care cost containment.”

Placing the 
responsibility 
where it belongs 


It seems that there are far too many 
hoops to jump through when providing 
professional continuing education pro- 
grams. Two of the hoops that providers 
such as Drug Store News must clear are the 
determination of how much credit to award 
readers of home study CE programs, and 
topic selection. 

It is interesting to note that home study 
CE is not big among physicians. One rea- 
son is that doctors have a process which al- 
lows them to get credit for just saying they 
read professional journals 2 hours a week. 
Why can’t pharmacy treat pharmacists as 
the most honest and ethical professionals 
that they are (Gallup, 4 years running) and 
trust them for similar reportin 

Or, if that’s too close to abandoning man- 
datory CE, at least solve the dilemma of de- 
termining how much credit to award by al- 
lowing pharmacists to state how long it took 
them to complete a home study program, 
and give them that amount of credit. This 
would, in effect, tailor the lesson to the stu- 
dent. For example, it may take a new grad- 
uate 30 minutes to complete a lesson on 
pharmacokinetics, but someone who grad- 
uated 20 years ago might need 3 hours to 
understand the same lesson. So is it fair that 
both get a certificate for 2 hours of study, as 
they do by today’s standards? 

Another concern is topic selection. Ide- 
ally, CE should be chosen not for ease of 
completion, but for its educational value to 


the individual. When someone tells me 
about the pharmacist who sits through a 
live CE presentation reading a newspaper 
because they are obviously just there for 
the certificate, or . pharmacist complains 
about “hard” CE questions because they ve 
had to think, I know that these are the ex- 
ceptions rather than the rule. Our profes- 
sion is so dynamic and there are so many re- 
sponsibilities growing around the provision 
of service, its scary to think that any phar- 
macist would waste a CE learning opportu- 
nity and refuse to learn so ing. 

Of course, providers need to take re- 
sponsibility, too, for the quality of the pro- 
a offered. We can’t make you learn, 

ut our goal in selecting the material we of- 


cist participants for choosing appropriate 
topics and learning. |

Profitable niches drive eye care sales 


By Mike Troy 


ontact lens care products may no 

longer be ringing up double-digit 

sales increases, but the nearly $1 
billion category is far from dead for retailers 
with the flexibility to fine-tune their prod- 
uct mix. 

Growth in the number of lens wearers 
has slowed and is projected to remain at 
about 25 million through the year 2000. 
However, manufacturers see the category 
churning as more wearers switch from hard 
to soft or disposable lens types. Retailers in 
touch with these trends and the demo- 
graphics of their store or stores can create 
opportunities by focusing on key category 
segments. 

The most significant of these segments is 
in the one step or multi-purpose cleaners 
used by soft lens wearers. Soft lens users ac- 
count for roughly 75 percent of all lens 
wearers, and products for their care gener- 
ate about $824 million of the $966 total lens 
care category sales as measured by Infor- 
mation Resources Inc. 

The total lens care category grew by 9 
percent during the 12 months ended Jan. 
31, but soft lens daily cleaners and disinfec- 
tants increased by 16 percent. Soft lens 
rewetting drops increased a whopping 20 
percent. These segments have benefited 
ete a massive migration of hard lens wear- 
ers to soft lenses. An estimated 50 percent 
of today’s soft lens wearers at one time wore 
hard lenses. 

“The category is not what it used to be four 
or five years ago, but there are pieces of it that 
are growing and can give retailers the dou- 
ble-digit growth they used to see,” said Mar- 
vin Morrison, director of national accounts 
with Alcon Laboratories, manufacturer of the 
chemical disinfectant Opti-Free. 

“We still think it is a growing market al- 
though not growing as rapidly as it once 
did,” said Gayle pone product manag- 
er of the chemical disinfectant Renu, manu- 
factured by the Bausch & Lomb lens care 
division. 

Of the 25 million Americans that wear 
contact lenses, about 20 million of those 
wear soft contact lenses. Lens care product 
manufacturers say they don't expect the 
wearer base to increase significantly by the 
year 2000. In fact, some expect the number 
of wearers will remain rom eae at about 


25 million.

Types of contact lenses 


Each type of contact lens has benefits and 
drawbacks that appeal to different users. 
The following terms are used when discuss- 
ing lens types. 

@ Hard or rigid lenses—developed over 25 
years ago, their usage has declined with the 

advent of more eye-friendly lens types. 

Hard lenses are durable but they limit oxy- 
gen to the cornea. 

® Rigidgaspermeableor RGPlenses—sim- 
Jar characteristics to hard lenses except they 
allow a to reach the cornea and in some 
case may be worn overnight. 

© Soft lenses—made of plastic materials that 
incorporate wate. and allow for softness and 
flexibility as well as the transmission of oxy- 
gen to the cornea. The fastest growing wear- 
er group, comprising an estimated 75 per- 
cent of all lens wearers. 


@ Disposable lenses—typically they come in 
a six pack and can be worn one or two weeks 
before being discarded. These soft lenses do 
not need inke cleaned or stored in a solution, 
although some wearers clean them anyway. 
® Extended wear lenses—this type can be 
either soft or RGP and can be worn, as the 
name implies, for extended periods of time. 
Unlike disposable lenses, extended wear 
lenses require periodic cleaning.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 7, 1993 


Retailers and brand marketers ought to regard cou- 
pons as increasingly powerful strategic weapons. 
More people are redeeming them, more are trying 
new products because of them, and more feel that cou- 
pons save them money. . 

A by-product of the recession, greater coupon use Is 
evident across all demographic groups in a 1993 study 
of primary grocery shoppers by Carolina Manufactur- 
ers Service (CMS) of Win- 


ston-Salem, N.C., a man- 
ufacturer’s agent in 
marketing information 


MARKET and coupon redemption. 
PULSE Temporary phenome- 
AL HELLER non or not, consumers are 


paying more attention to 
coupons than ever before. 
Marketers can enter this 
window of opportunity to induce product trial, incre- 
mental purchases and other productive behavior. 
Coupons can yield these benefits while maintaining a 
product’s price integrity. 

Consumers have exceedingly positive views of 
coupons: more than 80 percent say they encourage 
trial of new or different brands; even 66 percent of 
non-coupon users acknowledge this. More than 40 
percent of coupon users will buy a new brand only 
with a coupon. 

Moreover, 86 percent of respondents believe that 
coupons save them money; close to half of non-coupon 
users recognize this. Just 38 percent of consumers are 
skeptical enough to say that coupons raise the price of 
products. 

More than one coupon user in four buys products 
that aren’t needed right away in order to put coupons 
to work. 

The only apparent downside to consumers—who 
get something for nothing with coupons—is the time 


OPINION 


A lesson for marketers seeking redemption 


and effort it takes to use them. Slightly more than half 
of consumers feel that coupons lengthen shopping 
time. And 78 percent agree that coupons are easy to 
forget to take to the store. 

Not surprisingly, 38 percent of those surveyed 
said they are redeeming more coupons this year 
than last. Another 51 percent said they use the same 
amount. The heaviest usage climb is among young 
shoppers, aged 18 to 29, of whom 52 percent said 
that this year more is better. Indeed, twenty-some- 
things prefer to get their coupons in-store more than 
any other group. Coupon usage also picked up more 
in larger households. 

Heavy coupon users place an even greater empha- 
sis on double couponing and sales at the store, CMS 
reported. 

Shoppers prefer to get their coupons in freestand- 
ing inserts: 89 percent said this, compared with 80 per- 
cent who cited in-pack or on-pack; 77 percent, direct 
mail; 76 percent, retailer circular; 73 percent, handout; 
64 percent, magazine. 

In actual distribution, CMS reports 86 percent of 
coupons appear in FSIs. An overwhelming 87 percent 
of health and beauty care coupons appeared in FSIs in 
1992, up from 77 percent in 1988. 

Expiration periods are generally shortening, with 
26 percent expiring within two months and another 
58 percent becoming invalid after three to five 
months. Average face values are rising, to 52 cents 
in 1992. 

Coupons redeemed are most often valued at 25 to 34 
cents and 50 to 74 cents; combined they account for 
half of the coupons turned in, with the higher value 
coupons continuing their popularity upswing. The 75 
cents to $1 range has rapidly gained share the past 
three years. 

Chain and brand marketers seeking redemption 
should heed these consumer shifts in setting strategies. 


It hardly seems fair. Attorney General Janet Reno 
is still reeling from the political backlash over the 
Waco standoff, and she now must face an even more 
formidable adversary: NARD. 

The confrontation between President Clinton’s 
AG and independent pharmacy isn’t being played 
out in a compound in Texas, but in a courtroom in 
Washington. 

At issue: whether the 


Justice Department’s 
Drug Enforcement Ad- 
ministration may legally 
increase the federal 
“user fees’’ on retail 
pharmacists, drug 
wholesalers and others 
registered with the agen- 
cy to distribute con- 


trolled substances. 

It is not that NARD believes drug stores should 
be exempted from rising taxes. One of the unpleas- 
ant facts of life in the 1990s is that we’re all going to 
have to “contribute” more to the federal goevern- 
ment to reduce the budget deficit, finance the Clin- 
ton Administration’s health reform package and pay 
for all the other ongoing and new spending programs 
that Congress creates. 

How much more we will be asked to contribute to 
government is, of course, an important consideration. 
But it’s not the only one. In some respects, it’s almost 
more important to ensure that the new, additional tax 


Janet Reno and the wrath of NARD 


burden is spread equally and equitably. 

That is where Reno incurred the wrath of NARD. 
The DEA’s proposal wouldn’t raise user fees for 
Controlled Substance Act registrants by a digest- 
ible 10 percent or 20 percent. It calls for quadru- 
pling those fees! 

NARD, NWDA and the American Medical Associa- 
tion cried foul. Along with Capitol Hill independent 
pharmacist Edward Dillon, the three groups filed suit 
against the DEA, Reno and the Justice Department to 
obtain a federal court injunction against the proposed 
new charges. 

According to NARD, the proposed new fees would 
impose “an unconstitutional tax on DEA registrants 
to support activities not related to their regulations.” 

Moreover, the rule creating the new, higher user 
fees is “arbitrary and capricious” because “it does 
not provide adequate information on government 
figures and the programs the fees will support,” 
NARD argued. 

The effort by NARD, NWDA and the AMA to block 
the unjustified increase in DEA user fees is important 
for all taxpayers—not just those in the drug distribu- 
tion chain. 

Over the next couple of years, Washington will be 
seeking to impose a variety of new taxes on all of us. 
None of those tax hikes is going to be popular, and 
some of them are certain to be unfair. 

NARD, NWDA and AMA have served notice on 
the Clinton Administration that inequitable tax initia- 
tives will draw a strong challenge.

Future opportunities 


By Mademoiselle’s reckoning, half 
of all females between 18 and 29 spend 
more than $200 a year on beauty care 
products, and 78 percent spend more 
than $100 a year. 

But Mademoiselle confirms what a 
lot of chain drug store cosmetic buyers 
already suspect: that druy chains are 
missing an opportunity to generate 
even better sales with twenty-some- 
thing shoppers. 

Yes, some twenty-somethings cer- 
tainly do shop drug stores, but Made- 
movselle’s most recent beauty care sur 
vey finds that only 37 percent of all 
twenty-somethings buy their cosmet- 
ics in drug stores. 

This compares to 52 percent of twen- 
ty-somethings who are buying cosmet- 
ics in department and specialty stores.

First step in courting busters: Discover their niche 


As drug chains 
begin to grapple 
with the problems 
of marketing to 
specific niches like 
twenty-some- 
things, executives 
are working harder and hard- 
er to understand the custom- 
ers that they are trying to 
woo. In the case of a segment 
as diverse as twenty-some- 
thing busters, that is not ex- 
actly easy. 


Diverse segment 


“Busters are an attractive 
marketing opportunity, but 
what different products or 
merchandising techniques 
can we use to attract them?” 
asks Walgreens’ cosmetic di- 
visional merchandise manag- 
er Steve Lubin. 

“The buster generation is a 
pretty wide group. We hope 
that by carrying products 
that appeal to a broad selec- 
tion of consumers, we’re able 
to satisfy their needs asa seg- 
ment within that group.” 

“In cosmetics, it seems that 
the group is s read between 
Maybelline and L’Oréal, so we 
feel we have a mix that ap- 
peals to their needs. We're 
trying to read the trends and 
position ourselves behind the 
trends, but we do not want to 
make merchandising changes 


reacting just to 
fads,” he said. 
Steve Lund, vice 
president of mer- 
chandising for De- 
troit-based Perry 
Drug, says that 
one of his upcoming projects is 
to look at busters to try to 
identify what they like. 


Developing strategies 


“Busters are a great oppor- 
tunity,” he says, “but we must 
learn more about how they 
shop our stores and how we 
can communicate with them.” 

“We’re not sure how you 
talk specifically to busters,” 
says tephanie Hayter, cos- 
metic buyer for New York- 
based Genovese Drug. 

“We offer value and conve- 
nience, but we offer that for 
everybody. I don’t know how 
we'd segregate different prod- 
ucts or brands for busters.

Trendier, more ‘fun’ categories 
appeal to busters 


SS may not know 
anu ing they’d like to know 
about twenty-somethings, but 
they do know they want to 
woo this market, and they are 
deciding that the best way to 
do that is by getting hip. 

For some chains, that 
means expanding into fun and 
trendy categories that appeal 
to sophisticated, fashion-con- 
scious consumers. 

For others in trend-setting 
markets like New York’s 
Greenwich Village, it means 
becoming part of the “in 
crowd by getting mentioned 
regularly in the magazines 
and publications twenty- 
somethings read. Some New 
York chains, such as Ricky’s, 
do that by creating a “glitzy 
aura” that attracts even show 
business celebrities into their 
makeup departments. 


Value, selection score 


More conventional Manhat- 
tan chains like Luv’s and 
Duane Reade go after twenty- 
something shoppers by offer- 
ing great prices on popular 
brands including professional 
hair care products, cosmetics 
and cosmetics accessories. 

New York-based twenty- 


10 


somethings told Drug Store 
News they like Luv’s because 
it’s clean and well-stocked. 
They like Duane Reade be- 
cause it offers great prices and 
selection and it’s convenient. 

California-based twenty- 
somethings single out Longs 
for its “fun departments, help- 
ful cosmeticians, clean stores 
and colorful merchandising.” 

In the Midwest, Snyder 
Drug gets nominated as a 
good drug store to shop be- 
cause it, too, has fun depart- 
ments, including an exten- 
sive gift department. 


Fun is important 


Drug chain executives tell 
Drug Store News that they 
know twenty-somethings like 
fun and fashionable products 
to “play with.” 

So across the nation, chains 
that can’t go all-out hip are 
trying to at least give twenty- 
something shoppers some- 
thing different. 

In Wilsonville, Ore., Gor- 
don Barker, executive vice 
pee of PayLess Drug 

tores, says his company is 
trying to create a “new type of 
drug store to appeal to women 
in their 20s and early 30s.” 


Barker says the newest pro- 
totype, being tested now in 
the Rohnert Park, Calif. 
store, includes a lot of depart- 
ments that were added to at- 
tract younger consumers in- 
terested in beauty, fashion 
and fitness. 

That store has a huge bou- 
tique bath set, an extensive 
“te! and lotion department, a 
health food department, an 
exercise and sports clothing 
department and an expanded 
assortment of department 
store cosmetic and skin treat- 
ment lines. 

Barker says PayLess will 
refine these concepts before 
introducing them in its next 
prototype store opening early 
this summer in Sandy, Utah. 

“Our feeling,” says Barker, 

‘is that with this prototype, 
we have created a perfe ect 
match for twenty-somethings 
and women in their early 30s.’ 


Classy advertising 


Aware that younger women 
want what Barker calls “the 
beauty they associate with de- 
partment and specialty stores 
combined with the conve- 
nience and value of drug 
stores,” PayLess has also 


with older people—prescrip- 

tions are our No. 1 business. 
“But from a growth per- 

spective, that’s coming more 


and more from a younger 


crowd. This is the age group 
that’s spending more of its 
money on hair, styling and 
makeup. We try to court that 
group by carrying and adver- 
tising the new beauty prod- 
ucts that drive that business.” 


Play up brands busters want 


“Busters may be different 
from boomers,” said the cos- 
metic buyer for one large 
chain that is headquartered 


in the Midwest. 

“As far as we can tell, bust- 
ers and boomers are buying a 
lot of the same products,” 
said the buyer, “so we don’t 
think we should merchandise 
any differently. 

“But we have to find a way - 
to identify those products 
that have a high appeal to 
busters. Then [we must] con- 
centrate some of our ads and 
our in-store displays on fea- 
turing these products, espe- 
cially in neighborhood stores 
where we might have a large 
concentration of people in 
their teens and 20s.” 


Product ingredients and packaging matter to busters, who tend to 
read labels, compare benefits and smell the different fragrances.

Niche marketing 


At Ohio-based Revco, cos- 
metic buyer Judy Wray says 
she tries to merchandise to 
specific niches by tailoring se- 
lect in-store cosmetic events 
and featuring merchandise to 
the demographics of a given 
neighborhood. At Christmas, 
for example, she’ll ask stores 
that have high concentrations 
of 40- to 50-year-old custom- 
ers to build displays for fra- 
grances that are favorites of 
that age group, like Old Spice 
for men and Tabu for women. 

Wray calls this merchandise 
strategy “product segment 
merchandising.” To make her 
stores more appealing to twen- 
1 demmoinge as and other young 
shoppers, she recently expand- 
ed her mix of professional nail 
care products, and now, she is 
reviewing the newest collec- 
tions of cosmetic organizers. 

“Through their stytes and 
their advertising, the manufac- 
turers are clearly trying to ap- 
peal to the twenty-something 
market,” she said.

What do busters want? 


One of the first studies to ex- 
amine twenty-something atti- 
tudes and shopping prefer- 
ences—the Roper one done for 
Mademoiselle—found that 
younger women are more likely 
to splurge on fashion accesso- 
ries, even expensive accesso- 
ries like designer lipsticks, skin 
creams, wrinkle creams and 
handbags, than older women. 

Four out of every 10 women 
in the Roper study reported 
that it was “somewhat” to “ex- 
tremely” important to be able 
to buy a better brand of lip- 
stick. Only 38 percent of older 
women gave that answer. 

Possibly because twenty- 
something women are so de- 
manding or discriminating, 
they tend to stick with a prod- 
uct they like once they find it. 

According to Mademoiselle, 
98 percent of twenty-some- 
things feel this way, and 82 per- 
cent say that if a beauty care 
product works, the price 
doesn’t matter to them. 

The Mademoiselle/Roper 
study also provided some in- 
sight into the mindsets of 
twenty-something women, 
describing them as “career- 
minded, independent and fi- 
nancially stable.” Research- 
ers reported that they are 
“better informed, more real- 
istic about health, fitness and 
personal grooming and very 
brand conscious.” 

Over half of this market, 54 
percent, is still single and a 
whopping 55 percent say they 
still live with their parents.

plans to promote in schools,

Where do twenty-some- 

things shop for beauty care? 
at makes them choose 
one store over another’? 

What do they buy once 
they’re in the store? 

hat better way to find out 
than to ask twenty-some- 
things these questions direct- 
ly. So with the help of Made- 
moiselle magazine, that’s 
what Drug Store News did. 

In the fall, we’ll be publish- 
ing the results of a joint Drug 
Store News/Mademoiselle 
survey focused on 500 twenty- 
somethings and their atti- 
tudes toward shopping for 
cosmetics in drug stores. 

Honest and direct, twenty- 
somethings seem to enjoy 
having the chance to discuss 
what they like and don’t like 
about shopping for cosmetics 
in drug stores. 

For example, 15 twenty- 
somethings surveyed by Drug 
Store News informed us that 
the best stores they shop are 
clean, well laid out, have a 

ood selection of products, 
aks plenty of fun products 
(like cosmetics, hair accesso- 
ries, eting cards, stuffed 
animals and small gifts), have 
pee rices, carry well-known 

rands, have testers, good 
displays and knowledgeable 
people on hand to help them 
make the right decisions. 

Twenty-somethings also 
told us they like to save money 
and they like shopping in 
stores a sales clerks un- 
derstand the products. 

“I’m a good shopper. I know 
what I need,” says 28-year-old 
Cindy Edelstein. “I like it 
when a store lets me look and 
play with the products, then if 

do have a question, it’s nice 
to know there’s someone there 
who will have an answer.” 

Lipsticks and nail polish, 
the two beauty care products 
that twenty-somethings say 
they most often buy in a drug 
store, generate impulse sales 
because they are colorful. 
They also stand out because 
they are often displayed in 
eye-catching pre-packs on 
counters and tables. 

But only one in four twenty- 
somethings said they buy per- 
fume or cologne in a drug 
store. 

Twenty-somethings told 
Drug Store News they would 
think of drug store cosmetic 
departments more often if 
they received flyers or direct 
mail, especially if these ads 
were in color. 

Wendy Bringentoff, 26, of 
California, said she might pay 
more attention to drug store 
ads if they “didn’t advertise so 
many things. It’s hard to fig- 
ure out if they do have some- 
thing you might like.”

What does it take to make a buster happy? 
Alice Johnson, who spent $50 in a drug store while 
modeling for this story, just liked being able to touch, 
smell and feel the products. 


Bringentoff also responds 
to bright, colorful ads. She 
says magazine ads for brands 
like Revlon and Maybelline 
appeal to her because they are 
bright and colorful. 

“If a drug store had a cou- 
pon associated with their ad, I 
might try that.” 


Why Jill Mittler prefers 


department stores 


Jill Mittler, a 23-year-old 
media assistant for Coca-Cola 
USA, regularly shops her 
neighborhood drug stores in 
Atlanta for hair care and as- 
sorted toiletries, but she buys 
most of her cosmetics in a de- 
partment store. 

“T’m really concerned about 
my skin,” she explained, “so I 
don’t like to buy something in 
a package. I like stores to have 
testers so I can see what the 
color will really be like, and I 
like having someone in the de- 
partment to help me. 


“ In a drug store, you’re on 
your own, but in a department 
store, they have people to help 
you and if you test something 
on your skin, they have tissues 
to wipe it off.” 

Mittler associates fun shop- 
ping with the malls, not with 
the two drug stores she shops 
regularly for toiletries. 

‘Eckerd is cut and dried,” 
she says. “They usually have 
what you need, but it’s not a 

lace to go and browse or to 
ook for something new.” 

“Drug Emporium has good 
prices, and you can find some- 
thing new like bath products 
and shower gels, but I’ve nev- 
er really gone into their cos- 
metics department. Maybe 
because I’ve never seen any 
ads for their cosmetics depart- 
ment and I just never thought 
of trying it.” 

Mittler, however, has been 
in one drug store that she says 
was “the best drug store I’ve 
ever been in.” 


Daria Fabian and Al- 
ice Johnson spent 
much of their time 
shopping for bath 
care products, care- 
fully checking the 
prices and the quali- 
ty. Kim Bladridge, 
meanwhile, couldn't 
resist the eyelashes. 


It was an independent store 
in Connecticut (where she 
went to college), and she liked 
it because it was a mini spe- 
cialty store. One half of the 
store was like a Hallmark card 
shop with cards, nice gift 
items, stuffed animals and 
other “fun” things. The other 
half was a full-service dru 
store. “That store was fun. If 
had something like that near 
me, I’d shop it.”

Twenty-something New Yorkers call Ricky’s a “hip” drug store. 


Translation: lots of bulk displays, beauty care products stacked 
from floor to ceiling. Neon graphics. Color as far as the eye can 
see. Testers and trendy products everywhere. 


Ricky’s scores again with the massive presentation it gives to profes- 
sional hair care. Positioned in the front of the store, across from cos- 
metics, the selection and prices delight busters like Alice Johnson.

Why Cindy Edelstein 
says ‘yes’ to some stores 
an ‘no’ to others 


In Manhattan, 28-year-old 
Cindy Edelstein, a magazine 
writer and marketing consul- 
tant who has her own busi- 
ness, the Jeweler’s Resource 
Bureau, says she wouldn't 
think of buying cosmetics in a 
“boring” drug store. 

“I don’t want to walk the 
aisles if a store doesn’t look 
nice,” says Edelstein. 

“I may shop it for conve- 
nience items like a shampoo or a 
snack, but I won’t browse or 
spend much time in cosmetics. 
Also I won’t browse if the aisles 
are too tight or too crowded. 
It’s just too uncomfortable.” 

But Edelstein told Drug 
Store News she will happily 


spend hours shopping a drug 
store “from shelf to shelf” as 
long as it’s “exciting, fun and 
trendy,” stocked with “the 
newest products and lots of in- 
teresting things like fresh- 
smelling soaps, hair accesso- 
ries, body lotions, etc., priced 
reasonably.” 

Edelstein prefers to buy 
cosmetics in Ricky’s, a five- 
unit health and beauty aids 
chain based in New York City. 
Edelstein considers Ricky’s 
the “prototypical drug store 
for twenty-somethings.” 

“It’s very hip. Very glit- 
tery. Very funky. I forget it’s 
a drug store. And it’s got great 
prices.” 

“What I look for is a store 
that has the latest items, 
trendy items. Ricky’s is a 
small store, but they give me a 
great selection. 

“They have every hair styl- 
ing product you can imagine, 
from Redken to Paul Mitchell. 
And they carry Aura, which is

a reasonably priced alterna- 
tive to Aveda. 

“Most of the drug stores I 
know don’t try to romance you 
in cosmetics. I fall in love my- 
self, and that’s why I buy so 
much, but they don’t do much 
with their merchandise to 
make me notice things. I sel- 
dom notice the wall. I usually 
look at the displays. 

“A store like Ricky’s is dif- 
ferent. It’s a very exciting 
store to shop, and they always 
seem to have new items way 
ahead of everyone else.” 


Why Wendy Bringentoff 
says testers are important 


Twenty-somethings like to, 
in their words, “play” with a 
cosmetic before buying it. 
They like to rub it on their skin 
to see if the color and the tex- 
ture pleases them or not. 

In California, 26-year-old 
Wendy Bringentoff, a former 
investment banker who is

might wind up spending $30 to

“Because I’m able to try so 
many things, I wind up shop- 
ping longer and buying more.” 

Bringentoff sometimes 
buys cosmetics in Longs, a 
chain she thinks has the best 
drug stores she’s ever seen. 

But she still makes the bulk 
of her cosmetics purchases in 
Nordstrom’s and she buys her

cause I’ve gotten spoiled. 
They’re expensive but I’m 
happy with the products.” 

endy likes stores that 

keep their stock up, “like 
Longs,” and she likes stores 
that offer a wide variety of 
supplemental cosmetic or

sponges, “the little accesso- 
ries you can’t find in a depart- 
ment store. Longs does that, 
and it’s helpful to me.” 


Wendy says that if drug 
stores could provide more ser- 
vice, as well as a more upgrad- 
ed image, she would gladly 
shop them more often. 

“It’s true that my generation 
probably has more money to 
spend,” she said. “But that 
doesn’t mean we don’t want to 
spend it intelligently. The more 
we can save, the more we have 
left to spend on other things. I 
can go into a department store 
and buy four or five items and 
spend over $100 on cosmetics. 
In fact, about two-thirds of my 
regular department store bill is 
for cosmetics. I’d like to be able 
to save money by shopping 
drug stores if they just had 
more to offer. 

“The aisles shouldn’t look 
like junk. They should make 
their displays. .. more excit- 
ing. The better stores I’ve been 
in have products stacked ev- 
erywhere from top to bottom. 

“That’s why I shop for cos- 
metics in a department store. 
You pay for the attention, but 
they're trained to see what’s 
best for you and you know you 
can usually depend on their 
recommendations, and once 
they’ve sold you something 
that’s right, you stick with it. 

“Only if I were extremely 
bored and had nothing better 
to do would I look at the drug 
store wall,” said Bringentoff, 
“because it’s so bland. 

“If I’m shopping a drug 
store, I usually go in, get what 
I want and get out. If I see a 
bright display with a super- 
model on it, that could catch 
my eye, but the wall doesn’t 
interest me.”

ty-something mar-

as a struggling,

They may not have children

their futures to worry about, 
and today’s stagnant economy

chain managed to equal last 
year’s earnings fc deigoone
