NEWS IN BRIEF 


PayLess, Lederle help smokers quif 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — One thousand smokers in 
Utah who want to quit will get free ProStep nicotine 
atches in a — sponsored jointly by PayLess 
Drax Stores, Le erle Laboratories and the Utah De- 
partment of Health. 

The drug store chain recently announced that it would 
stop selling cigarettes and other tobacco products in all 33 
Utah PayLess Drug Stores. Priority will be given to smok- 
ers who meet income, medical and insurance guidelines. 
Those who ify will save $180 on the six-week therapy. 

Vince Di agEl0, vice president of PayLess’ southern 
region, noted that as tobacco-free stores this “makes our 
pharmacies the perfect places to distribute the ProStep 
stop-smoking patches.” 


Contest heats up for French distributor 


ORANGE, Calif. — A bidding war is underway to ac- 
quire French distributor Office Commercial Pharmaceti- 
que. Suitors in the escalating contest are Gehe AG, a Ger- 
man distributor, and a newly formed joint venture of 
Bergen Brunswig Inc. and its co-bidder, Cooperation 
Pharmaceutique caise. 

Gehe AG has just upped its bid to 985 French francs 
(ex-dividends) vs. the joint Bergen-CPF bid of 865 
French Francs (with dividends). A Bergen Brunswig 
spokesperson told Drug Store News that Bergen is re- 
viewing its bid. 


O&M buys Ohio/Pa. wholesaler 


RICHMOND, Va. — Owens & Minor has aquired Ly- 
ons Physician Supply Company, a wholesaler that has 85 
percent of sales in medical and surgical supply sales to hos- 
pitals in northern Ohio and western Pennsylvania. 

The purchase of Lyons Physician Supply, which has 
annual sales over $30 million, gives Owens & Minor a 
stronger presence in areas the wholesaler has targeted 
for expansion, namely the Ohio Valley, Great Lakes re- 
gion and western Pennsylvania. 


Ssnyder’s caps buyout of rival 


MINNEAPOLIS — Snyder’s Drug Stores has complet- 
ed its purchase of hometown rival Snyder Bros. 

The deal adds 19 stores to Snyder’s network, bringing 
the total store count up to 82 stores. Most of that new mus- 
cle is in the chain’s home market of Minneapolis/St. Paul, 
where 18 of the former Snyder Bros. units are located and 
where Snyder’s already operated 42 stores. 

The co plans to convert the newly acquired stores 
to its own logo and format within 90 days. Combined reve- 
nues for the two chains total roughly $190 million, accord- 

to Snyder’s spokesperson Mary Gustafson 


_ The employees of Snyder Bros. have done an extraor- 
dinary job throughout this transition period,” said Sny- 


der’s chairman, president and chief executive officer Don 
Beeler. “They are — people and we are pleased to 
have them join the Snyder’s organization.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 21, 1993 


OPINION 


Which is more fun: listening to your teen’s Metallica 
records cranked way up, having root canal, or selling 
products into national chains? 

Tough choice. But there are plenty of people who’d 
say the pain lasts longest in the latter. 

To help shed light on some winning strategies for 
marketing successfully into major retailers, the Uni- 
versity of Arkansas hosted a conference last month in 

Little Rock. Eckerd 


Drug, Sam’s Wholesale 
Club, Woolworth, Ace 
Hardware and J.C. Pen- 


MARKET ney were among chains 
PULSE that presented. 
AL HELLER - Today’s tenor, of 


course, is that retailers 
have largely won back ne- 
gotiating leverage with 
suppliers as they’ve become smarter interpreters of 
product movement information. Chain merchants are 
looking to tailor mixes to match store demographics, 
eliminate costs of product distribution, secure allow- 
ances that tie into their marketing approaches, and 
are looking for more strategic partnerships with cate- 
gory leaders. 

Retailers are more demanding because they have to 
be to survive: their competition is better. The drug 
chains, discounters, combos and wholesale clubs are 
vying for a customer base that is increasingly reluc- 
tant to spend—and so same-store growt” is exceed- 
ingly difficult to come by. 

Welcome to a piece of the suppliers’ world, in which 
they have to satisfy increasing demands by chains, be- 
come increasingly resourceful in meeting those 
needs—and fend off their own category competition at 
the same time. 

One of the most telling sheets was part of a presenta- 


Suppliers face more savvy retailers 


tion by Mark Steiner, director of merchandise procure- 
ment and analysis at Eckerd Drug Company. The sheet, 
titled Supplier Performance Measures, lists criteria 
Eckerd uses to assess companies selling into the chain. 

Financial concerns include: item level and line per- 
formance compared with the category; sales, gross 
profit and inventory turns; terms, co-op and miscella- 
neous allowances; quick response/EDI; returns policy 
and alliance building. 

Logistics demands are stringent: 


Standard 
Quantitative Criteria Margina! Optimal 
Order lead time (# days) ..... 14 <7 
On-time delivery .......... 95% 100% 
Line item fill rate ......... 96% 98% 
Total order fillrate ........ 97% 99% 
Inventory turns* .......... 14 >18 
DC service level* .......... 95% 99% 
(*Quick Response suppliers.) 


Eckerd also looks at the quality of packing and pal- 
letizing products and the use of preferred carriers. 

Clearly, the more prepared a supplier is and the more 
he knows about the chain’s markets and business proce- 
dures, the greater the chain’s willingness to partner. 

Indeed, retailers told me time and time again at the 
recent NACDS Annual Conference that they resent 
when suppliers don’t do their homework and learn the 
basics of the chain’s business. All who spoke on this is- 
sue felt they could shortcut by dealing primarily with 
suppliers who take the time to understand and meet 
their specific needs. 

That’s why on the eve of Marketplace—which prom- 
ises to be the biggest show ever put on by NACDS, 
with more than 560 booths and 3,060 registrants—sup- 
pliers must dig in, study the chains they’re selling into 
and impress the hell out of them. 


execs centralize on pharmacy policies 


President Clinton isn’t the only important govern- 
ment official who’s scurrying back toward the middle 
of the road—influential state pharmacy regulators 
from across the country also appear to be drifting to- 
ward a more centrist position on issues affecting the 
practice of pharmacy. 

That shift was apparent at last month’s meeting of 
the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy 

where delegates ap- 


proved a series of resolu- 
tions that may signal 
more realistic regulation 
of the drug store indus- 
try in the future. 

Case in point: the regu- 
latory status of pharmacy 
technicians. For years 
now, pharmacy board offi- 
cials in many states have been resisting efforts by 
drug chains and progressive independents to secure 
rule changes facilitating the use of support personnel 
behind the prescription counter. 

If there ever was a defensible basis for outlawing 
the use of pharmacy technicians to perform routine 
prescription department tasks, it evaporated earlier 
this year with the start of OBRA ’90. With the law’s 
new patient counseling responsibilities now taking up 
a significant part of the the pharmacist’s work day, the 
need for ancillary personnel to assist behind the pre- 
scription counter is greater than ever. 

NAPB delegates recognized that and approved a 
series of resolutions supporting a new regulatory 
agenda that should enable pharmacists to make great- 
er use of technicians. 

Among other things, the NABP delegates called for 
the creation of a new system of pharmacy board regis- 
tration of technicians in each state, as well as changes 


WASHINGTON 
\ PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


in the group’s Model State Pharmacy Practice Act to 
facilitate this registration process. 

In addition, the state regulators endorsed a national 
system for verifying the qualifications of pharmacy 
technicians, and requirements that would hold phar- 
macists directly responsible for the actions of ancillary 
personnel working for them. 

In a separate arena, the NABP’s members are ex- 
pressing new reservations about the effort to estab- 
lish a six-year Pharm.D curriculum as the sole entry- 
level degree for future pharmacists. 

At last year’s NABP meeting, state pharmacy board 
executives voted to endorse the mandatory Pharm.D 
degree unconditionally. This year, the delegates back- 
pedaled. The group’s change of heart reflects a growing 
recognition among many pharmacy practitioners that 
they will not be “grandfathered” into the new degree. 

In a resolution passed by the ’93 NABP delegates, 
the group’s continued support for the all-Pharm.D 
concept will be “contingent upon the establishment of 
an equitable mechanism for degree exchange.” 

If pharmacy regulators and academics are unable 
to hammer out such a mechanism, the resolution di- 
rects NABP to “reconsider” its support for the uni- 
versal Pharm.D. 

To be sure, some of the resolutions adopted by the 
delegates will prove to be controversial. On the sticky 
issue of therapeutic substitution, for example, the 
state pharmacy board execs agreed to push for new 
laws and regulations to facilitate “therapeutic inter- 
change by pharmacists in all practice settings.” 

In addition, the NABP delegates endorsed the cre- 
ation of a “third class of drugs”—former prescription 
products switched to OTC status which would be 
available only from a licensed pharmacist “with appro- 
priate patient consultation in order to protect public 
health and safety.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 21, 1993 


Osco, Sav-on top 
American performers 


SALT LAKE CITY — American Stores’ drug store division 
again led the way in same-store sales and earnings gains in the 
first quarter of fiscal 1993, ended May 1. 

Sales for Oak Brook, Ill.-based American Drug Stores were 
up 7.9 percent to $1.03 billion for the period, with same-store 
revenues rising 2.5 percent. By contrast, American Stores’ food 
store operations suffered slight declines in same-store results 
due to poor weather, tough competition and a halting economic 
recovery. Total sales for the company’s 931 supermarkets— 
which operate under several banners, including Jewel Food 
Stores, Acme Markets and Star Markets in the East, and Lucky 
Stores in the West—were basically flat. . 

American Drug’s Osco and Sav-on divisions combined for $43 
million in operating profits during the quarter, marking a 4.0 per- 
cent rise from the same period last year. As a percent of sales, op- 
erating profits for the company’s 745 drug stores dipped slightly to 
4.19 percent because of higher operating expenses. 

Said American Stores president and chief executive Vic 
Lund, “Our drug stores, . . achieved steady results despite rel- 
atively low drug price inflation.” 

Overall, American Stores recorded $41.5 million in net earn- 
ings for the quarter vs. $18.3 million the wtoary year. Results 
were one by nonrecurring gains in the most recent period 
related to debt restructuring and early retirement charges, and 

by a one-time loss in the first quarter of 1992 related to the sale 
of 74 Jewel-Osco combos in the Southwest and Florida. 

Operating earnings for the company’s supermarkets were down 
slightly to $118.1 million for the quarter, primarily because of the 
impact of a price reduction program in Western stores which 
kicked off in February. Southern California has been under in- 
creasing competitive pressure as layoffs in defense and other in- 
dustries have taken their toll, and as competition from recent en- 
trant Smith’s Food & Drug and other sources heats up. 

Nevertheless, said Lund, “We are extremely pleased with 
the progress of our price reduction program in our California 
and Nevada Lucky stores. As expected, this important pro- 
gram impacted first-quarter profits. . . (but) is having a favor- 
able effect on sales. Like-store sales in our Southern California 
stores were at their best level in nine quarters.” 

During the quarter, American Drug opened eight new stores 
and closed four older units. Three other stores were remodeled 
in line with the new Osco Vision prototype. 


Belt-tightening helps 
Arbor maintain momentum 


TROY, Mich. — Holding 
the line on costs, Arbor Drugs 
again reported record results 
for the third quarter ended 
April 30. 

The 135-store chain racked 
up a 16.4 percent gain in net 
earnings for the period, to $3.9 
million, on sales of $133.6 mil- 
lion. Sales were up 10.5 per- 
cent, with same-store results 
gaining 5.2 percent. 

Arbor chairman, president 
and chief executive Eugene 
Applebaum credited disci- 
plined expense control and 
strong pharmaceutical unit 
sales growth for the strong 
performance. 

For the nine months, net 
earnings rose 10 percent to 


$12.9 million, with sales up 
12.8 percent to $398.2 million. 
e are very pleased with 
our record results. . . particu- 
larly in view of the inclement 
weather during much of Febru- 
ary and March,” said Apple- 
baum. “Our strategic focus on 
health care and everyday con- 
venience, combined with the 
operational excellence of our 
organization, continues to gen- 
erate record sales and profits.” 
Applebaum added, “It is 
especially gratifying to note 
that Arbor can achieve 
strong net income increases, 
in spite of the lower sales in- 
creases which have resulted 
from a declining rate of phar- 
maceutical inflation.”

Quick facts on beverages and snacks 


@ Americans now consume, on average, 48 gallons of soft drinks per 
person each year. That marks a dramatic jump in consumption from 
years past: in 1980, for instance, per-capita soft drink consumption was 
34.2 gallons. In 1970, it was only 22.7. Americans consume more soft 
drinks than they do water or any other beverage—and nearly double 
what the average Canadian drinks. (Source: John Maxwell, Wheat First 
Securities; PepsiCo Inc.). 


© Beer edges out soft drinks in U.S. retail dollars, at roughly $49 billion in 
1991 sales. Soft drinks are close behind, soaking up $48 billion in sales 
last year. (Source: Miller Brewing Co., Beverage World magazine). 


e Drug stores gained a full point of market share in the fight for carbon- 
ated beverage sales between March 1991 and March 1992. Also gain- 
ing: discount stores. Both segments took share from supermarkets and 
mom-and-pop grocers. (Source: Nielsen Marketing Research.) 


® The United States annual per-capita consumption of snack chips has 
risen more than three pounds in the past five years, to 16 pounds of 
crunch per consumer in 1992. (Source: PepsiCo/Frito-Lay.) 


® Bottled water sales have flattened in the ‘90s, but total industry 
growth over the past five years is pegged at more than 42 percent. So- 
called New Age beverages are still on a sharp growth climb, rising 14- 
16 percent a year. (Source: Beverage Marketing Corp., Beverage Aisle 
magazine).

have touched this product.

when women ask themselves 
these questions, they tend not 
to buy the product. 

In a department or special-

test a shade, she uses a sam- 
ag Many women say they 
ike the security of knowing 
they’re buying a product no

DrSN GALLUP REPORT 


Where do women shop for cosmetics & fragrances? 


When drug store retailers 
ask the question “where do 
most women buy their cos- 
metics and fragrances,” they 
are closing in on one of the big- 
gest opportunities facing 
chain drug stores in the 90s: 
women who love cosmetics 
and fragrances but don’t usu- 
ally buy them in drug stores. 

Chain drug executives know 
that many women fall into that 
category. Their challenge is to 
understand why those women 
shop where they do and to find 
ways to lure them out of de- 
partment and specialty stores 
and into drug stores. 

The easiest part of the puz- 
zle is quantifying how many 
women do shop drug stores, at 
least some of the time, for cos- 
metics and fragrances. 

The Gallup Consumer Beau- 
ty Care Purchase study, spon- 
sored by Drug Store News for 
the past five years, tracks 
where women most often buy 
cosmetics and fragrances and 
how their patterns have 
changed over the years. 

This year, Gallup discovered 
that 49 percent of all women 
said they most often buy fra- 
grances ina why or spe- 
cialty store. That inane 
was up from the 46 percent who 
said the same in 1991. 

That one statistic gives 
drug retailers a lot to consid- 
er. For example: 

@ Since half of all women aren’t 
buying their fragrances in drug 
stores, there is a tremendous 
opportunity to develop the fra- 

ce business. 

@ But the opportunity is not 
being mined. Despite the in- 
dustry’s recent upgrades in 
both cosmetic departments 
and product mix, less women 
buy fragrances in drug stores 
now than two years ago. 

Drug stores still lose cosmet- 
ic shoppers to other channels. 
In 1991, Gallup found that 22 
sae of all women surveyed 

ought fragrances in drug 
stores. In 1993, that percent- 
age dipped to 18 percent. 

Two key questions emerge: 
why are women shopping lo- 
partment and speciality stores 
most often for cosmetics and 
fragrances, and what can drug 
stores do to lure those shoppers 
into their departments?

assortment, pleasant ambiance, as well as sharp prices. 


Core shoppers are boomers 


Baby boomers, women 30 
to 44, were the most likely to 
shop drug stores for fra- 
grances. Gallup found 22 per- 
cent of boomers bought their 
fragrances in a drug store 
most often, while 44 percent 


shopped a department or spe- 
cialty store “most often” for 
fragrances. 

ince 86 percent of all bust- 
ers use a perfume or a cologne 
and 65 percent of all busters 
who use fragrances apply it at 
least once a day, drug stores 
not reaching this market are 


missing a great opportunity.

opportunity to boost cosmet- 
ic sales among tie twenty- 
something shoppers. Accord- 
ing to Gallup, one third of 
women between 18 and 29 
shop drug stores most often 
for cosmetics.

tial customers.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 21, 1993 


When Gallup asked women 
to name what was very impor- 
tant to them in the stores they 
shopped for fragrances, bust- 
ers were more concerned than 
boomers or pre-boomers 
about brand variety, person- 
alized service, product com- 
parisons and the availability of 
someone to introduce them to 
new and trendy items within 
the category. 


What women shoppers want 


Both busters and boomers 
were also more interested 
than pre-boomers (women 
over 45) in incentives like free 
samples, competitive prices 
on fragrance brands and the 
availability of department 
store brands. 

Busters (80 percent) and 
pre-boomers (79 percent) 
were allied in their demand 
for “courteous, friendly” 
sales people to assist them. 
That aspect was not as impor- 
tant to the boomer shopper; 
by comparison 66 percent of 
that age group rated courte- 
ous sales people as very im- 
portant to them. 

The findings clearly suggest 
that drug stores can enhance 
their — to all women, but 
especially to twenty-some- 
things, by positioning their 
fragrance departments as 
“fun places” to shop. 


Filling the niche 


In merchandising fra- 
grances, drug chains should 
try to create the impression 
that they carry a lot of differ- 
ent brands, even department 
store brands. Advertisin 
should send that message, an 
the store should follow 
through by staffing the de- 
partment with knowledgeable 
‘sig le who help customers 

ind the fragrance that is just 
right for them. 

Store advertising should 
concentrate on letting cus- 
tomers know what’s new, 
what’s trendy and what may 
be an especially good value. 
That message can hb sup- 
ported at the store level by 
the cosmetician. 

Value should prove to be a 

articularly strong incentive 
or twenty-something shop- 
pers, since they are not as sat- 
isfied as the other groups with 
the value they are getting 
from stores they are buying 
fragrances from. 

Only 70 percent of twenty- 
somethings rated their regu- 
lar store as excellent or good 
on competitive prices. 

In comparison, 84 percent 
of pre-boomers and 79 percent 
of boomers said the stores 
they shopped for fragrances 
could be rated excellent or 
good on delivering competi- 
tive prices. 

For more details on what 
consumers say drug stores are 
doing right and what they may 
be doing wrong, see the conclu- 
sion of this Special Report in 
our July 5 issue.

fragrances 


Eight out of every 10 women use fragrances. But women buy most of their fragrances in either department or specialty stores. 


Drug chains’ challenge: lure fragran 
shoppers away from department stores 


rug stores trying to lure women into 
their cosmetic department should nev- 
er overlook the power of fragrance. 

Nearly eight out of every 10 women use a fra- 

ance, according to the emacs of this year’s 

allup Beauty Purchase Survey, and the ma- 
jority of fragrance users, 64 percent, spritz 
themselves at least once a day. 

Denartment store fragrances are, and al- 
ways have been, very popular. Nearly half (49 
percent) of the women in the Gallup survey said 
they prefer a department store or specialty 
store brand. 

It’s always been hard for mass brands and 
mass retailers to compete with the expensive 
advertising that supports the department 
store fragrance business. Most chains can’t 
give their shoppers the same kind of sophisti- 
cated service and merchandising that depart- 
ment stores provide. 

But women resent the high prices they have 
to pay for department store brands, and there 
are also many who hate the hassle of getting to 
and from a department store. 


An opportunity for mass 


In the past, drug stores have always tried to 
go after these mers i by stressing their low 
everyday prices on fragrances. Their ads often 
mention the convenience aspect of their stores. 

The strategy has continued to work to some 
degree. According to Gallup, two out of every 
10 fragrance users are loyal to a mass brand 
they gongs in a neighborhood store. 

Stil, drug stores report that their fragrance 
sales have been soft for the last several years,

DRUG STORE NEWS, 


Falsely labeled knock-offs of 
French Transit’s Crystal Body 
Deodorant threaten the niche 
the product has created. 


BURLINGAME, Ca.—French 
Transit, Ltd. has created a niche 
in the deodorant category out of a 
crystal-like stone made of mineral 
salts which is made in France. 

Since it’s introduction in 1984, the 
company’s Crystal Body Deodorant, 
a 100 percent natural product made 
of nothing but natural mineral salts, 
has singlehandedly created a new 
upscale niche in the category, has 
garnered support from health pub- 
lications and has 
even been 
recommended 
by physicians 
for patients with 
sensitive skin. 

But success has 
had its down 
side for the 
company. In the 
past two years, a 
wave of inferior 
knock-offs have 
been brought to 
the market. 
French Transit 
president Jerry 
Rosenblatt fears 
that those prod- 
ucts may undercut the solid repu- 
tation of his product and erode the 
niche Crystal Body Deodorant has 
created. 

“The knock-offs could really harm 
the category if consumers have a 
bad experience with one of those 
products,” said Rosenblatt. A bad 
experience may be likely, he says, 
since none of the knock-offs contain 
potassium, the mineral salt that 
makes the product effective. 

When moistened and spread under 
the arm (or on the feet), the palm 
sized crystalline stone leaves an 
invisible trace of mineral salts on 
the skin. Rather than clogging the 
pores the way antiperspirants 


work or masking the odor 

as other deodorants do, Crystal 
Body Deodorant actually eliminates 
odor by killing the bacteriathat 


causes odor.” said Rosenblatt. 


More than market 


encroachment | 

French Transit has had an indepen- 
dent lab do tests on all knock-off 
products on the market and found 
that not one contained potassium, 
although two claimed to. Many 
contained nothing but.aluminum. 
Other products’ were found to 
contain careinegenic materials. 

“These knock-off products are 

, imported from 

ee theOrient and 
either.do not 
label their 
ingredients or 
falsely state 
them,” said 
Rosenblatt. This 
is a clear viola- 
tion of FDA regu- 
lations, but since 
manufacturers 
are not required 
to send their 
packaging to the 
FDA, the pack- 
aging often goes 
undetected for 
some time 
by the agency. By falsely 
stating their ingredients, the 
products are guilty of false adver- 
tising and are involving stores in 
liability to the consumer. 

“These products are trying to blur 
the distinction between Crystal 
Body Deodorant and their prod- 
ucts,” said Rosenblatt. “They are 
surviving off the marketing and 
advertising French Transit has done 
to create the category and maintain 
the demand for the product. Many 
of the products are packaged to 
resemble our product and that 
confuses customers.” 

Rosenblatt said that along with the 
glowing letters the company has

Buyers: Beware 

Buyers should be cautious when 
looking at products that claim to 
have the same benefits as Crystal 
Body Deodorant. “With any prod- 
uct, any time-you're looking at a 
knock-off, you're looking at an infe- 
rior product,” said Rosenblatt. 

“Buyers have to be careful and 
think about what they are offering 
to their customers. Many of these 
products imported from the Orient 
aren't tested and can be very harm- 
ful to consumers. These fly-by-night 
operations could be out of business 
tomorrow, and stores can be left 
with a tremendous liability from 
consumers,” he said. 

What's his advice to buyers? 
“You can't just buy on price. Ask 
for proof of ingredients and be very 
wary of any thing that looks like a 
knock-off. Buy the real thing.”

Grim statistics in toiletries 


One of the drug store indus- 
try’s best category segments 
so far this year, according to 
IRI, is shaving lotion, up 15 
percent for the 13 weeks end- 
ing March 28, 1993. 

hat picture gets grim 
when you consider that mass 
merchandisers grew the cat- 
egory by 42 percent. While 
drug store sales of skin care 
products were up 5 percent in 
the same period, they were 
up 30 percent in mass mer- 
chandiser stores. Hair spray 
was down 12 percent in drug 
stores; the category was up 
13 percent in mass stores. 


Lower prices win 


The statistics don’t even 
Surprise most chain drug 
store merchandisers any- 
more. They know that they 
are losing sales to the mass 
channel primarily because of 
price, and they know that the 
mass merchants are able to 
‘poste so. low because they 

ave the technology in place 
that lets them operate more 
efficiently. 

As drug chains face the fu- 
ture, they are adopting a wide 
variety of strategies to fight 
for their share of the business. 

Some chains are trying to 
build sales by discounting 
prices on front-end merchan- 
dise including cosmetics and 
fragrances. Others are in- 
vesting more hours in the de- 
partment to better provide 
customer service and are re- 
modeling and expanding 
their mix to compete more di- 
rectly with depa~tment 
stores. 

More than ever, drug chains 
today are working frantically 
to develop the space allocation 
and inventory management 
programs they need to save 
money. 

The multi-purpose ae is 
very clearly articulated: 

@ Reestablish the cosmetic 
profitability by 
lucing inventories and in- 
creasing turns. 
@ Manage the product assort- 
ment so that space and inven- 
tory dollars are allocated to 
the most productive SKUs. 
@ Create and maintain the op- 
timum assortment and ambi- 
ence that will generate im- 
pulse sales from existing 
customers while drawing new 
consumers, particularly quali- 
ty-conscious department 
store shoppers and price-con- 
scious mass merchandise 
shoppers, back into chain drug 
stores.

— The Ultimate Breath Freshener 


The breath freshening “sensation of the ‘50s” is 

back by popular demand. Johnny Carson talked 

about it in one of his last monologues, Stephen

Rx BOARD SUPPORT 
WAVERS ON PHARM.D. 


State pharmacy regulators are 
backpedaling from their earli- 
er support for a mandatory 
Pharm.D entry-level degree. 
Delegates to the National As- 
sociation of Boards of Phar- 
macy (NABP) meeting in Bal- 
timore—many of whom favor 
“grandfathering” B.S. phar- 
macists under the new de- 
gree—voted to make their con- 
tinued support for the all 
Pharm.D “contingent upon 
the establishment of an equi- 
table mechanism for degree 
transfer.” 

If that doesn’t happen, the 
resolution directs NABP to 
“reconsider” its endorsement 
of the universal Pharm.D con- 
cept. NABP delegates also 
adopted new positions on such 
sticky state regulatory issues 
as pharmacy technicians, 
compounding, and therapeu- 


tic substitution. See story page 
60. 


SURPRISE: PHARMACISTS 
ARE HAPPY ON THE JOB! 


Nine-out-of-10 pharmacists 
today are “happy with their 
choice of pharmacy as a ca- 
reer” and over half (5! per- 
cent) are “completely satis- 
fied” in their professional 
work. So says a new Schering- 
Plough survey of 400 pharma- 
cists in retail stores, hospitals 
and HMOs. 

“The highest level of com- 
plete satisfaction (55 percent) 
was found among pharmacists 
working in chain and indepen- 
dent pharmacies,” research- 
ers said. See story page 338.

Generics poised 
for explosive growth 


W ith quality issues largely resolved, FDA has stepped 

up attention to generic drug approvals. Combine 
this with a large number of major branded pharmaceuti- 
cals about to lose patent protection and the nation’s focus on 
cutting health care costs, and you have the formula for an 
explosion in generic drug sales in the coming years. Our 
Annual Generic Report begins on page 19.

Albuterol Sulfate Inhalation Solution 0.083% * 
("Potency expressed as albuterol) 
BRIEF SUMMARY: Please see package insert for full prescribing information 
DESCRIPTION: Each mL of Albutero! Sulfate Inhalation Solution (0.083%) contains 0.83 mg of albuterol (as 1 mg 
of abuterol sulfate) in an isotonic, sterile, aqueous solution containing sodium chloride, edetate disodium, sodium 
citrate and hydrochloric acid to adjust the pH between 3 and 5 
CONTRAIMDICATIONS: = Albutero! Sulfate inhalation Solution is contraindicated in patients with 4 history of 
hypersensitivity to any of its components. 
WARMINGS: As with other inhaled beta-adrenergic agonists, Albutero! Sulfate Inhalation Solution can produce 
paradoxical bronchospasm, which can be life threatening. /f it occurs, the preparation should be discontinued 
immediately and alternative therapy instituted 
Fatalities have been reported in association with excessive use of inhaled sympathomimetic drugs and with the 
home use of nebulizers. It is, therefore, essential that the physician instruct the patient in the need for further 
evaluation if his/her asthma becomes worse. In individual patients, any beta-adrenergic agonist, including 
albuterol solution for inhalation, may have a clinically significant cardiac effect. 
immediate hypersensitivity reactions may occur after administration of albuterol as demonstrated by rare cases of 
urticaria, angioedema, rash, bronchospasm, and oropharyngeal edema 
PRECAUTIONS General: Albuterni, as with all sympathomimetic amines, should be used with caution in patients 
with cardiovascular disorders, especially coronary insufficiency, cardiac arrhythmias and hypertension, in patients 
with convulsive disorders, hyperthyroidism or diabetes mellitus, and in patients who are unusually responsive to 
sympathomimetic amines 
Large doses of intravenous albutero! have been reported to aggravate pre-existing diabetes mellitus and ketoacidosis 
As with other beta-agonists, inhaled and intravenous albuterol may produce a significant hypokalemia in some 
patients, possibly through intracellular shunting, which has the potential to produce adverse cardiovas-cular effects 
The decrease is uSually transient, not requiring supplementation 
information for Patieats: The action of Albuterol Sulfate Inhalation Solution may last up to six hours and 
therefore it should not be used more frequently than recommended. Do not increase the dose or frequency of 
medication without medica! consultation. If symptoms get worse, medical consultation should be sought promptly 
While taking Albuterol! Sulfate Inhalation Solution, other anti-asthma medicines should not be used unless 
prescribed 
Drag lateractions: Other sympathomimetic aerosol bronchodilators or epinephrine should not be used 
concomitantly with albuterol 
Albuterol should be administered with extreme caution to patients being treated with monoamine oxidase inhibitors 
or tricyclic antidepressants, since the action of albuterol on the vascular system may be potentiated 
Beta-receptor blocking agents and albuterol inhibit the effect of each other. 

and impairment of Fertility:  Albutero! sulfate, like other agents in its 
Class, caused a significant dose-related increase in the incidence of benign leiomyomas of the mesovarium in a 2- 
year Study in the rat, at oral doses corresponding to 10, 50 and 250 times the maximum human nebulizer dose. In 
another study, this effect was blocked by the coadministration of propranolol. The relevance of these findings to 
humans is not known. An 18-month study in mice and a !ifetime study in hamsters revealed no evidence of 
tumorigenicity. Studies with albuterol revealed no evidence of mutagenesis. Reproduction studies in rats revealed 
no evidence of impaired fertility 
Pregnancy: Teratogenic Effects: Pregnancy Category C: Albutero! has been shown to be teratogenic in 
mice when given subcutaneously in doses corresponding to the human nebulization dose. There are no adequate 
and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Albuterol should be used during pregnancy only if the potential 
benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. A reproduction study in CD-1 mice with albuterol (0.025, 0.25 and 2.5 
mg/kg subcutaneously, corresponding to 0.1, 1, and 12.5 times the maximum human nebulization dose, 
respectively) showed cleft palate formation in 5 of 111 (4.5%) of fetuses at 0.25 mg/kg and in 10 of 108 (9.3%) of 
fetuses at 2.5 mg/kg. None were observed at 0.025 mg/kg. Cleft palate also occurred in 22 of 72 (30.5%) of fetuses 
treated with 2.5 mg/kg isoproterenol (positive contrc:). A reproduction study in Stride Dutch rabbits revealed 
Cranioschisis in 7 of 19 (37%) of fetuses at 50 "g/kg, corresponding to 250 times the maximum human nebuliza- 
tion dose 
Labor aad Delivery: 0a! albuterol has been shown to delay preterm labor in some reports. There are presently 
no well controlled studies which demonstrate that it will stop ,;eterm labor at term. Therefore, cautious use of 
Albuterol Sulfate Inhalation Solution is required in pregnant patients when given for relief of bronchospasm so as 
to avoid interference with uterine contractibility 
Nursing Mothers: | is not known whether this drug is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for 
tumorigenicity shown for albuterol in some animal studies, a decision should be made whether to discontinue 
nursing or to discontinue the drug, taking into accord the importance of the drug to the mother 
Pediatric Use: Safety and effectiveness of albuterol solution for inhalation in children below the age of 12 years 
have not been established 
ADVERSE REACTIONS: = The results of clinical trials with Albutero! Sulfate Inhalation Solution in 135 patients 
showed the following side effects which were considered probably or possibly drug related 
Central Nervous System: tremors (20%), dizziness (7%), nervousness (4%), headache (3%), insomnia (1%) 
Gastrointestinal: nausea (4%), dyspepsia (1%) 
Ear, Nose and Throat: pharyngitis (<1%), nasal congestion (1%) 
Cardiovascular: tachycardia (1%), hypertension (1%) 
Respiratory: bronchospasm (8%), cough (4%), bronchitis (4%), wheezing (1%) 
No clinically relevant laboratory abnormalities related to Albutero! Sulfate Inhalation Solution administration were 
determined in these studies

of patients treated with isoproterenol during clinical trials of three months, the following moderate to severe reactions

NEW YORK — Longtime 
Generic Pharmaceutical In- 
dustry Association (GPIA) 
president Dee Fensterer is 
resigning from the organiza- 
tion in order to “seek new 
challenges,” she told GPIAs 
board of directors. 

However, Fensterer has 
agreed to assist the GPIA 
during a transition period, 
and has left open the date of 
her departure. 

Fensterer has been a key 
figure in the explosive 
growth of the generic drug 
industry for more than a 
decade. 

Said William Haddad, 
GPIAs chairman, “No sin- 
gle person has done more to 

efine the generic pharma- 
ceutical industry and re- 
duce the cost of pharmaceu- 
ticals to all Americans than 
Dee Fensterer. 

“She has helped to chart 
the course not only of the 
GPIA, but [also] of the entire 
industry,” he added. 


Congressional battles 


“Her leadership,” Had- 
dad continued, “helped the 
industry to win the impor- 
tant battles in Congress, in- 
cluding Waxman-Hatch and 
Process Patent legislation, to 
survive the generic scandal 
and to shape itself into the 
current GPIA, whose mem- 
bers account for 40 percent 
of prescriptions dispensed in 
the United States.” 

Fensterer has been in- 
strumental in giving voice 


to leave 


Fensterer 


and respectability to the ge- 
neric industry, both to the 

ublic at large and in the 
halls of federal and state 
government. 

She recently addressed 
the White House Task 
Force on Health Care Re- 
form in efforts to assure 
pharmaceutical benefits for 
all Americans, to encourage 
cost-cutting through in- 
creased reliance on gener- 
ics, and to establish a single 
reimbursement price for 
multi-source drugs. 


White House statement 


In a statement to the 
GPIA’s board, Fensterer 
said, “The association needs 
to prepare for the long and 
difficult political fight that 
will erupt when the Con- 
gress and the country debate 
President Clinton's program 
for national health coverage. 
The organization needs 
someone in place in time to 
assist that struggle.” 

She added: “Waxman- 
Hatch has taken hold; FDA 
is routinely approving multi- 
source products; generic us- 
age after patents expire will 
soon be universal; and 
GPIAs role as the spokes- 
person for the industry is 
well established. 

There is a growing team of 
one leaders who 
are leading the charge for 
low-cost pharmaceuticals; 
and this administration is 
firmly committed to the use 
of generic drugs.”

BENZONATATE CAPSULES USP 100 mg 


(SOFT GELATIN CAPSULES) 


DESCRIPTION 

Benzonatate, a nonnarcotic oral antitussive agent, is 
2,5,8,11,14,17,20,23,26-nonaoxaoctacosan-28-yl-p-(buty- 
lamino) benzoate; with an average molecular weight of 603. 


HNH — )— COOCH.CH.(OCH.CH.) OCH 


— wd, 


Each softgel (soft gelatin capsule), for oral administra- 
tion, contains 100 mg benzonatate. In addition, each cap- 
Sule contains the following inactive ingredients: gelatin, glyc- 
erin, purified water, methylparaben, propylparaben and D&C 
Yellow No. 10. 


CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY 


Benzonatate acts peripherally by anesthetizing the 
stretch receptors located in the respiratory passages, lung 
and pleura by dampening their activity and thereby reducing 
the cough reflex at its source. It begins to act within 15 to 20 
minutes and its effect lasts for 3 to 8 hours. Benzonatate 
nas no inhibitory effect on the respiratory center in recom- 
mended dosage. 


INDICATIONS AND USAGE 


Benzonatate is indicated for the symptomatic relief of 
cough. 


CONTRAINDICATIONS 
Hypersensitivity to benzonatate or related compounds. 


PRECAUTIONS 


Information for Patients: 


Release of benzonatate from the softgel in the mouth 
Can produce a temporary loca! anesthesia of the oral 


2OF TGELS 


mucosa and choking could occur. Therefore, the softgels 
should be swallowed without chewing. 


Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of 
Fertility: 

Carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, and reproduction studies 
have not been conducted with benzonatate. 
Pregnancy: 

Pregnancy Category C. Animal reproduction studies 
have not been conducted with benzonatate. It is also not 
known whether benzonatate can cause fetal harm when 
administered to a pregnant woman or can affect reproduc- 
tion capacity. Benzonatate should be given to a pregnant 
woman only if clearly needed. 


Nursing Mothers: 

It is not Known whether this drug is excreted in human 
milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk cau- 
tion should be exercised when benzonatate is administered 
to a nursing mother. 


ADVERSE REACTIONS 

Sedation, headache, mild dizziness, pruritus and skin 
eruptions, nasal congestion, constipation, nausea, gastroin- 
testinal upset, sensation of burning in the eyes, a vague 


"chilly" sensation, numbness in the chest, and hypersensitiv- 


ity have been reported. 


OVERDOSAGE 


No clinically significant cases have been reported, to our 
knowledge. The drug is chemically related to tetracaine and 
other topical anesthetics and shares various aspects of their 
pharmacology and toxicology. Drugs of this type are gener- 
ally well absorbed after ingestion. 

Signs and Symptoms 

If softgels are chewed or dissolve in the mouth, oropha- 
ryngeal anesthesia will develop rapidly. CNS stimulation 
may Cause restlessness and tremors which may proceed to 


clonic convulsions followed by profound CNS depression. 
Treatment 

Evacuate gastric contents and administer copious 
amounts of activated charcoal slurry. Even in the conscious 
patient, cough and gag reflexes may be so depressed as to 
necessitate special attention to protection against aspiration 
of gastric contents and orally administered materials. 

Convulsions should be treated with a short-acting barbitu- 
rate given intravenously and carefully titrated for the smallest 
effective dosage. 

Intensive support of respiration and cardiovascular-renal 
function is an essential feature of the treatment of severe 
intoxication from overdosage. 

Do not use CNS stimulants. 


DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION 

Adults and Children over 10 years of age: Usual dose is 
one 100 mg softgel t.i.d. as required. If necessary, up to 6 
softgels daily may be given. 


HOW SUPPLIED 

Each yellow softgel is imprinted with " P’ 4600" and 
contains 100 mg of benzonatate and is available in bottles of 
100's (NDC 10888-4600-1) and 1000's (NDC 10888-4600-3). 

The softgels should be protecteu from light, moisture and 
humidity, and stored at controlled room temperature 15” - 30 
C (59° - 86’ F). Dispense in a tight, light-resistant container 
as defined in USP/NF. 

Caution: Federal law prohibits dispensing without pre- 
scription.

NARD survey: Pharmacists make a difference 


In what may be the first wide- 
spread study of patient interven- 
tions by community pharma- 
cists, researchers tor NARD 
found that the nation’s pharma- 
cists are in a pivotal position to 
curb runaway health care costs. 

But in addition to saving mon- 
ey for patients, third-party plans 
and taxpayers, the NARD find- 
ings also suggest that pharmacist 
interventions can save lives. In 
one case history released by the 
researchers, a newborn infant 
was —— from potentially se- 
vere liver damage by a quick- 
thinking Colorado pharmacist. 

In another, an intervention by 
a Wisconsin pharmacist helped 
doctors identify and treat a pa- 
tient with —— bacterial 
pneumonia. And a Pennsylvania 
woman seeking the pharmacist's 
advice on OTC eye drops was re- 
ferred to an eye doctor for a de- 
tached retina. 

“Such problems present 
themselves daily to pharma- 
cists, who must then intervene 
on their patient’s behalf,” ac- 
cording to NARD. 

The new study data “clearly 
illustrates the on (ie of pharma- 
cists professional interventions 
in preserving patients health 
ae well-being and reducing 
health care costs by identifying 
dangerous drug interactions 
and adverse reactions. 

The association's membership 
survey on interventions is part of 
a larger study being undertaken 
by NARD to document the “di- 
rect and indirect economic ind 
social value of pharmacists pro- 
fessional services.” 

“Had patients bought their 
rescriptions from a volume- 
riven pharmacy, such as a mail 

order io. it is highly unlikely 
these interventions would have 
occurred,” NARD maintained. 


Problem interception 


The survey, which drew re- 
sponses from hundreds of 
NARD members across the 
country, found that patient in- 
terventions are commonplace 
in the community pharmacy 
setting, and that they meas 4 
a wide range of potential medi- 
cation problems. 


58 


Of the more than 1, 100 inter- 
vention reports submitted to 
the NARD researchers, one-in- 
five (21 percent) involved incor- 
rect dosage. Other frequent 
reasons for interventions in- 
clude concerns over drug-drug 
interactions (13 percent), drug 
allergy/prior adverse reaction 
(12 percent) and side effects/ 
toxicity (10 percent). 

Other factors prompting 
pharmacists to intervene in the 
patient's prescription drug 
therapy tadlude duplicate ther- 
apy (7 percent), under - or over- 
utilization (7 percent), an incor- 
rect drug (6 percent) and mis- 


discontinuation of another 
medication (6 percent). 

— the researchers 
found that 18 percent of the in- 
terventions resulted in the 
pharmacist not filling the pre- 
scription with any drug. 

To underscore this point, 
NARD cited a case history in- 
volving Southhampton, Pa. in- 
dependent John Sherpin. Upon 
receipt of a prescription for Ca- 
tapres from a patient suffering 
from high blood pressure, 
Sherpin noticed that the man 
was also taking Minipress, Al- 
domet, Altace, Calan SR and 
Procardia XL.

pin’s conclusion and supplied 
the patient with several samples 
of Catapres. The patient col- 
lapsed within hours and was hos- 
pitalized for several days due to 
the improper medication. 


OTC interventions, too 


NARD’s survey also revealed 
that pharmacists frequently in- 
tervene in patients non-pre- 
scription drug therapy. 

In 58 percent of the OTC in- 
terventions reported to NARD, 
the pharmacist recommended 
an over-the-counter product 
and counseled the patient on its 


proper use, the researchers 
said. But in more than 4-out-of- 
10 these interventions the pa- 
tient was advised by the phar- 
macist not to purchase any OTC 
medication. 

In 22 percent of the cases, the 
patient was cautioned against us- 
ing an OTC drug because of con- 
cerns over drug interactions or 
contraindications, NARD said. 
In 15 percent of the interven- 
tions the pharmacist concluded 
that no OTC products were ap- 
propriate to treat the problem 
and that the patient should see a 
physician. In another 5 percent 
of the OTC interventions, the 
patient was advised that the 
problem was “self-limiting” and 
that no non-prescription medica- 
tion should be purchased. 

Pharmacists responding to 
NARD’s survey reported that 
some patient interventions are 
almost daily occurrences. “One 
such intervention, preventing an 
aspirin and Coumadin interac- 
tion, has become almost rou- 
tine,” NARD officials said. 

According to Albert Fuchs, 
owner of Pottstown, Pa.'s 
Downtown Prescription Cen- 
ter, cardiologists will often pre- 
scribe Coumadin for arthritis 
patients who are already tak- 
ing eight aspirins a day.” 

This combination of two anti- 
coagulants can lead to excessive 
bleeding from minor incidents, 
Fuchs says. “For instance, if pa- 
tients brush their teeth too hard 
and scratch their gums, they 
could bleed profu Ay’ 

Other problems that prompt 
interventions by pharmacists are 
considerably “more ominous,” 
NARD said. Fort Collins, Colo. 
pharmacist Barbara Wilkins re- 
ported receiving a prescription 
instructing her to compound a 
suspension from Nizoral tablets. 
The prescription called for one 
teaspoon by mouth twice daily— 
a dose acceptable for a child old- 
er than four years. 

In discussing the medication 
order with the patient, however, 
Wilkins discovered that the drug 
was for a newborn infant. Had 
the dosage not been adjusted, 
the infant could have suffered 
liver damage, NARD said.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Pay 'n Saves go public as PayLess 


HONOLULU — Former Pay ’n Save stores on Oahu 
and five outer islands celebrated grand openings as Pay- 
Less Drug Stores here in mid-June. Signs were changed 
for the occasion on all 15 stores, where instead of ribbon- 
cutting ceremonies local customs were celebrated with the 
“untying of the meile lei” and blessings of the stores, along 
with live remote radio events and the appearance of Miss 
Hawaii in some locations. 


Genovese names two vps 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Genovese Drug Stores has ap- 
pointed Susan Crickmore vice president of human re- 
sources and Stephen Poolner vice president of pharmacy 
operations. Poolner will oversee the chain’s pharmacy op- 
erations, its mail order operations and third-contracts, 
freeing director of professional relations Tom Esposito to 
concentrate on retail pharmacy operations. 


Arbor to open four units. . . 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor Drugs will raise store count to 
140 units with the opening of four new stores by the end of 
August, chairman and chief executive Eugene Applebaum 
said, All four of the store sites are in Arbor’s core market 
area of metro Detroit. 

Two of the new stores opened in June, including a sixth 
Arbor store in Westland, Mich., within a former Richard- 
son’s Drug store. The chain in June also converted a former 
Richardson’s store in L pene Mich. to the Arbor format. 

In August, Arbor will open its first store in the densely 
a suburb of Hamtramck just north of downtown 

etroit and a second unit in the suburban town of Novi. 


.. while Perry rolls new stores 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Trading competitive salvos with 
hometown rival Arbor Drugs, Perry Drug Stores has tak- 
en the wraps off a new store site and a remodeled unit of its 
own in metro Detroit. 

In late May the chain signed a lease for its first store in 
the close-in urban community of Highland Park, marking 
its 144th unit in the seven-county metro area surrounding 
Detroit. The 10,800-foot store will open in October, not far 
from the site of a new Arbor store in nearby Hamtramck. 

Three weeks later, Perry marked the grand reopen- 
ing of a remodeled and enlarged store in suburban St. 
Clair Shores. 


Brunswig drops European firm bid 


ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen Brunswig Corp. and _ its 
French co-bidder dropped out of the race to acquire Ku- 
rope’s largest drug distributor, Office Commercial Pharma- 
ceutique. German drug distributor Gehe AG topped the Ber- 

en Brunswig bid (made jointly with Cooperation 
Prasnecontione Francaise) with a bid of 985 French francs/ 


share against Bergen’s bid of 865 French francs/share.

By Allene Symons

cluding brand extension, corporate, character, 
fashion, nostalgia, entertainment, sports, graph- 
ics and lifestyle properties, representing a $62.2 
billion industry in the United States and Canada. 

Panelists speaking at the 13th annual Licens-

from classics to opportunistic properties.

sent a timeline/marketing plan, indicating the 
licensees on board. This allows space and sales 
promotion to be properly planned. Next,

tailer by the licensor and licensees.

Kinney draws 5,000 at 
first annual HBA expo 


ae 


WATERTOWN, N.Y. — Kinney Drugs’ first Health and 
Beauty Expo, held here this spring to celebrate the chain’s 
90th year, drew 5,000 attendees and some major exhibitors. 

Procter & Gamble, Kimberly-Clark, Revlon, Maybelline 
and Coty were just a few on hand to promote their products to 
consumers. Many suppliers distributed coupons redeemable 
only at Kinney stores as well as free product samples and in- 
formation. Revion and Maybelline gave free makeovers. 

Kinney, based in Gouverneur, N.Y., gave out free health 
informaiion, and held free demonstrations of step aerobics 
and karate. Blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose checks 
were just a few of the screenings available to attendees. The 
chain also sponsored a brown-bag medicine review with a 
Kinney pharmacist. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, July 5, 1993 


When Genovese enters Manhattan for the first time 
next month, will it be like a breathtaking tour of Juras- 
sic Park? Or will the largely suburban chain have 
learned enough about the distinctive shopping pat- 
terns of the density capital to avoid culture shock? 

Much like the earnest paleontologists in the hit 
movie, Genovese has scored hits in the digs of New 
York City boroughs and suburbs. Indeed, the chain 

has consistently regis- 


tered good results in 
competitive markets 
against Pathmark, 
Rockbottom, Kmart 
and now CVS. 

But how can the 


AL HELLER 
chain really prepare for 
the live animal? Can 


we. 
Genovese outmaneu- 


MARKET 
PULSE 


ver the local inhabitants on their turf to succeed with 
its first store on 2nd Avenue and 67th Street? 

Can Genovese overcome what Allan Patrick, execu- 
tive vice ppresident of merchandising, advertising 
and store operations, concedes is “no name recogni- 
tion among Manhattanites.” Patrick is optimistic be- 
cause of the chain’s history: “When we open a store, 28 
to 30 percent of the trading area shops us on a weekly 
basis,” he says. 

And it seems as if the chain has prepared about as 
well as anyone could. Before redesigning the former 
Gristede’s supermarket site into an 8,000-square-foot 
(selling space) Genovese—which is one-third smaller 
than a typical Genovese—management ran a focus 
group to learn about Manhattan shoppers. 

The biggest difference is shopping frequency. Man- 
hattanites stop into stores every day or every other 
day compared with once every 10 or 11 days at the typ- 
ical Genovese. Store draw is about four to five blocks, 
not several miles as in outlying areas. 

Smaller households mean smaller package sizes, 
but no less variety. That affected the chain’s approach 
to store design and shelving. 

Core planograms are being collapsed: 12-foot sec- 
tions become nine feet and four-foot sections go down 


OPINION 


Will Genovese like New York City digs? 


to three feet. Gravity-feed sloped shelves keep prod- 
uct neat and fronted, help minimize shrink by making 
sweeps more difficult, and allow enough height to fit in 
an additional shelf. “We didn’t eliminate any items,” 
said Patrick. 

Overall, the store has more in common with the 
6,000-square-foot Genovese Express format than the 
chain’s conventional layout. And the chain is import- 
ing lessons learned from its Express store in Queens 
about how to manage within a smaller cube. 

To keep the store well-stocked, the chain’s distribu- 
tion center will deliver goods three times a week. 

Three senior managers will run the 24-hour store 
with more autonomy than most on authorized items. 
“They'll be able to call a lot of audibles,” said Patrick, 
“as long as they tell the buyer [so they’re covered on] 
scanning documentation and liability.” 

Despite high household income of more than 
$50,000 in this Manhattan neighborhood, shoppers are 
still concerned about price. “They want all the tradi- 
tional drug store departments plus ease of shopping. 
Appearance, convenience and service are also impor- 
tant,” he said. 

To satisfy them, the store has: 

@ A 24-hour pharmacy. (The store is near New 
York and Memorial Sloan-Kettering Hospitals, but 
those doctors probably won’t prescribe for outside 
pharmacies, so the chain will promote its services to 
community physicians. ) 

@ A one-hour minilab. 

@ Looked into a house charge card. (“People crave 
familiarity,” says Patrick.) 

@ Lots of cat food and toys for pet-owning apart- 
ment dwellers. 

® Some upscale bath, body, fragrance and cosmet- 
ics. (“The doors really aren’t open to us, though we 
have some lines,” he says.) 

Genovese will probably never match Duane Reade’s 
sales per square foot of $1,200, but to avoid being eat- 
en in Manhattan, it must perform better than its 
chainwide $465 pace. It will, although with costlier 24- 
hour operations. 

This will be fun to watch. Anyone up for a sequel? 


Freedom of pharmacy choice alive in Fla. 


Are mail-order prescription drug services accept- 
able substitutes for face-to-face interaction with 
warm-blooded pharmacists in real chain or indepen- 
dent drug stores? 

The managed care mavens here in Washington 
seem to think so. 

If Patient A really has a question about her medica- 
tion, she can call an 800 number and speak to a phar- 
macist long distance. 


If the wrong drug is 
inadvertently deliv- 
ered to Patient B, he 
can just mail it back and 
wait a few more days 
for his prescription. 

And if the physician 
makes a prescribing er- 
ror that results in an in- 
correct dosage form or strength, too bad for Patient C. 
After all, a community pharmacist might not have 
caught that mistake, either. 

Of course, not everybody sees it that way. Critics of 
mail-order pharmacy contend that patients deprived 
of free access to the pharmacy of their choice are likely 
to receive a lower level of care. 

Legally, that’s a tough case to make. But it’s getting 
easier thanks to a Florida judge who ruled that mail- 
order drugs are no substitute for the services of a com- 
munity pharmacist. 

At issue in the case: whether an employee entitled 
to prescription drug benefits under Worker’s Com- 


> WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 
m® KEN RANKIN 


pensation may be required to obtain pharmaceuticals 
through a mail-order pharmacy. 

In declaring such restrictions on a patient’s freedom 
of choice of pharmacy “unreasonable and contrary to 
the intent of the workers’ compensation act,” the Flor- 
ida judge held that retail pharmacists do indeed pro- 
vide benefits that mail dispensaries can’t match. 

Unlike a mail-order prescription service, she said, 
“a community pharmacist who provides all of the 
claimant’s prescription medications will have a com- 
plete patient profile on the claimant for all medications 
being taken... ” 

As a result, the community pharmacist “is in a bet- 
ter position to advise the [patient] on the interaction 
and contraindications of any of the medications, in- 
cluding over-the-counter medications purchased at 
the pharmacy.” 

Although the judge acknowledged that employers 
have an interest in holding down the cost of employee 
health care benefits, she concluded that this interest is 
“outweighed” by the patient’s “need to receive his 
medications from a community pharmacist.” 

Those are encouraging words for drug chains and in- 
dependent pharmacists concerned over the growing 
competitive threat posed by mail-order dispensaries. 
But they aren’t the last words we'll hear on this subject. 

At this point, no one can say how much weight the 
Florida ruling will have in other legal challenges to re- 
strictions on the public’s right of free access to commu- 
nity pharmacy. 

But it is a start. »

Rite Aid reports 
strong first quarter 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Rite Aid Corporation’s sales and earn- 
ings for the first quarter ended May 29 grew 8.1 percent to $1.06 
billion from the $984.05 million reported for the comparable 
quarter last year. Net income advanced 3.5 percent to $34.16 
million vs. $33.01 million last year. 

Chain drug store division revenues rose 8.3 percent to 
$999.54 million compared to $922.82 million, and net income 


grew 4.2 percent to 


1.66 million versus $30.36 million. Same- 


store sales increased 4.1 percent for the 13-week period. 
At the end of the quarter, Rite Aid operated 2,600 drug 
stores, a net gain of 27 stores for the first quarter.

is attributed to the one-time

associated with the chain’s 
new accounting standards for 
post-retirement benefits.

associated with the closing of 
nine Paper Cutter stores in 
_ the Philadelphia market were 


charged against net earnings.

ee with $1.54 million 
for the same period last year.

DrSN GALLUP REPORT | shopper preferences 


Women want service at cosmetics/fragrance dept. 


he Gallup findings sug- 
gest the more stressful 
the world becomes, the 
more women are exposed to 
tension, pressure, deadlines, 
even hostility in the workplace 
and the world at large, the 
more they seem to appreciate 
friendliness and civility wher- 
ever they encounter it. 

Whether a woman was 
shopping for cosmetics or fra- 
grances, the presence of cour- 
teous, friendly salespeople 
was of paramount importance, 
and Gallup determined that 
women think drug stores do a 
better job than either depart- 
ment/specialty stores or door- 
to-door marketing companies 
in providing this service. 

e Performance Index for 
drug stores on courteous, 
friendly service was 148 based 
on the responses of women 
who shopped for fragrances. 
It rose to 183 based on the re- 
sponses of women who 
shopped for cosmetics. 

In contrast, the perfor- 
mance rating for women who 
shopped for cosmetics in de- 
partment/specialty stores was 
137. It was 144 for women who 
bought cosmetics from door- 
to-door companies. 

Friendly service was so im- 
portant to cosmetic shoppers, 
it achieved a Value Index of 


208, 103 points above the aver- 
age index. 


Service a competitive edge 


However, there’s a paradox 
in the Gallup findin Al- 
though women think the ser- 
vice people in drug stores are 
friendlier and more courteous 
than the service people in oth- 
er types of establishments, 


Women think it’s 
important for 
stores to have 

someone on hand 

to help them find 
something. 


they don’t seem to find them 
particularly knowledgable or 
skilled about products or 
product recommendations. 
The findings show that most 
women believe that the people 
who work for department and 
specialty stores, as well as the 
women who sell door-to-door 
cosmetics, are much more 
adept at recommending a 


beauty care product that is 
right for the shopper’s individ- 
ual skin and color types. 

The drug store performance 
ratings fall off sharply when 
Gallup asks about service skills 
related to training and product 
knowledge, such as the value of 
having someone in the store 
who can help shoppers compare 
product benefits or introduce 
them to new products just com- 
ing into the cosmetic and fra- 

ce marketplace. 

This shift in gradings 
seems to suggest that drug 
stores aren’t taking full ad- 
vantage of the marketing op- 
portunities afforded by the 
presence of friendly sales 
people in their stores. 

For example, when fra- 
grance-buying consumers 
were asked how they evaluat- 
ed drug stores on their ability 
to ap ess someone who could 
he P them find what they were 
looking for, they gave drug 
stores a performance index of 
just 92. 

That is a missed opportuni- 
ty, because women think it is 
important for stores to have 
someone on hand to help 
them find something. Ac- 
cording to Gallup, fragrance 
shoppers give this attribute a 
value rating of 140 while cos- 
metic shoppers gave it a val-

for delivering variety.

brands stocked.

with convenient store locations, are clear drug store strengths.

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 5, 1993 


fter waiting for tech- 
nology and consumer 
demand to ripen into 
new opportunities, the na- 
tion’s drug chains are wading 
rapidly into the one-hour pho- 
tofinishing business. Indeed, 
drug, supermarket and dis- 
count store chains are provid- 
ing the only real growth in 
one-hour labs in the United 
States, even as installation of 
stand-alone and camera-store 
one-hour centers “has kind of 
slowed to a crawl,” in the 
words of one photo industry 
executive. 

Examples of the chain drug 
industry’s growing love for in- 
store labs abound. Among 
them: 

@ Raleigh, N.C.-based Kerr 
Drug this summer will roll mi- 
crolabs into 25 of its 93 stores in 
North Carolina after a success- 
ful test of the Qualex Expres- 
Stop one-hour program, featur- 
ing Noritsu processors. The 
chain’s one-hour business at its 
test site “took off,” said vice 

resident of marketing Biil 

axley, and “gross profits are 
running quite well.” 

e Longs Drug Stores, 
whose units, the company 
claims, “sell more photofin- 
ishing per store than do any 
other drug retailers in the 
U.S.,” is building on its early 
lead in West Coast in-store 
labs. “We currently operate 
18 mini-labs and over the 
next 12 months we intend to 
expand in this area,” Longs 
recently reported. 

@ Alabama’s Harco Drug 
has opened minilabs in four of 
its stores. “Two of them are 
doing well, and two are just 
OK,” reported vice presi- 
dent of purchasing Jim Harri- 
son III at the spring buying 
show of the Chain Drug Mar- 
keting Associates. 

= Eckerd Drug, the chain 
drug leader in one-hour, now 
operates well over 300 Ex- 
press Photo labs in its stores. 

@ The Osco Drug division of 
American Drug Stores has 
made complete photo service 
centers and one-hour labs a 
core perimeter department in 
its new Vision prototype 
stores. American Stores’ new 
Jewel-Osco super-combo for- 
mat also features: a one-hour 
lab at the front of the store. 

® Drug Emporium’s new 
prototype store in Heath, 
Ohio, features the chain’s first 
in-store lab. The one-hour ser- 
vice is offered at the store’s 
front-end service counter, ad- 
jacent to the registers, where 
Signage alerts customers to 
the program. 

@ [ Got It At Gary’s, which 
first ion into one-hour 
microlabs with a single-store 
lab in 1991, has added Qualex 
ExpresStop centers in two 
additional locations in Penn- 
sylvania. 

@ New Orleans’ K&B and

One-hour labs: A developing process 


One-hour photofinishing labs are gaining credibility as a valuable service and marketing component. 


ee 


Drug stores are implementing photo centers with quality customer service in mind. 


Waterville, Maine’s La- 
Verdiere’s Super Drug 
Stores both opened their 
first in-store labs last 
year, with promising re- 
sults. 

@ London Drugs, the 
broad-based, high-vol- 
ume operator based near 
Vancouver, B.C., al- 
ready has one-hour labs 
in all 42 of its stores. 


Building sales 


The reason for the 
new flurry of one-hour 
photofinishing installa- 
tions is simple. In-store 
photofinishing labs, be 
they mini or micro, are 
fast gaining credibility 
as a valuable service 
and marketing compo- 
nent of a peace, chain 
drug photo depart- 
ment. The one-hour 
labs can pump incre-

mental, high-margin 
one-hour developing 
revenues into a drug 
store’s photo business, 
but equally important, 
they add the kind of di- 
mension and service 
visibility that can push 
overall photofinishing 
sales higher. 
LaVerdiere’s is a case 
in point. The 68-store 
chain opened its first 
one-hour lab last year, 
installing Konica micro- 
lab equipment in an out- 
lying store and later 
moving the lab to a more 
urban, higher-income 
LaVerdiere's location in 
Brunswick, Maine. 
After roughly six 
months in Brunswick, 
the microlab’s one-hour 
sales are now “better 
than the original loca- 
tion,” although not yet 


“up to our original expecta- 
tions,” said Nancy Belanger, 
LaVerdiere’s photo manager 
and buyer. But the real pay- 
off, she said, is in the “better 
identity” the in-store lab and 
service counter brings to the 
store’s overall photo depart- 
ment. 

“Overnight processing 17 
that store is up phenomenal- 
ly,” Belanger said. 

The lab’s total contribution 
to photo revenues in the Bruns- 
wick store are a key reason why 
LaVerdiere’s is expanding the 
one-hour business. “In the last 
couple of days, we’ve commit- 
ted to opening at least two 
more labs,” Belanger said in 
mid-June. 

At Kerr Drug Stores, the 
ability of one-hour service to 
push up overall volumes was 
also a key factor in the decision 
to expand in-store labs, said 
Baxley. “It brings a lot of at- 
tention to the department,” he 
said. Indeed, photofinishing 
revenues were up sharply in 
the chain’s highest-volume 
store after Kerr began pro- 
moting one-hour service in the 
store, he said. 

I Got It At Gary’s found 
similar results. “By offering 
on-site, one-hour processing, 
it allows us to grow our total 
share of the photo processing 
market,” said chain marketing 
director Raymond Hoy. 

One big caveat: demograph- 
ics are important. Both retail- 
ers and photo experts warn 
that in-store labs work best in 
an urban, higher-income set- 
ting. Said LaVerdiere’s Be- 
langer, “The lab failed miser- 
ably at its first location, which 
was a rural store. We moved it 
to an upscale, tourist area of 
Brunswick. 

“You need to look at the 
cleintele in an area to see if 
they’re abie to bite the bullet 
and pay the extra price for 
one-hour,” she added. 

Kerr’s Baxley agreed. “It 
was disappointing in a rural 
setting,” he said. 

Ted Fox, group executive 
for marketing information 
for the PMA, advised that 
drug chains use the old real 
estate adage of “location, lo- 
cation, location,” when se- 
lecting a site for a one-hour 
lab. The in-store service 
should usually only be of- 
fered in high-traffic loca- 
tions, and it should be used to 
attract new customers rather 
than “robbing customers 
from your captive wholesale 
lab,” he said. 

A successful one-hour pro- 
gram also depends on “total 
commitment” from the top of 
the organization down, es on 
dedicated service people in the 
store, Fox said. He also ad- 
vised that stores that offer one- 
hour “consider actively target- 
ing commercial accounts” in 
their area to pump volumes.

Longs shows off new concepts 


By Allene Symons 
WESTLAKE, Calif., —

its most advanced store de- 
sign in this affluent suburb 
north of Los Angeles. The new 
location includes a bath and 
body department showcased 
in tall, elegant custom fixtures 
and a new approach to mer- 
chandising the pharmacy 
counter area. 
Another unusual feature for 
this chain is a modified 45-de- 
ee angle store layout. The 
iagonal plan appears on each 
end of the store in cosmetics 
and photo/electronics depart- 
ments, while the main store 
retains the traditional grid 
layout. The visual effect is 
more spacious than most 
Longs stores: aisles are 1 foot 
wider. (See photos, page 19.) 
This 278-store chain, based 
in Walnut Creek, Calif., 
would not call its bright, new 


store a prototype—its stores 
are unique, although most 
share some similar features 
such as right-side cosmetics, 
center-rear pharmacy and a 
lateral, center bargain alley. 

The store opening drew 
Longs managers from 
throughout the state who 
were welcomed by president 
Steve Keath in an enthusias- 
tic opening ceremony, fol- 
lowed by a crush of grand- 
opening customers. 

The large store is the third 
Longs in the Conejo Valley 
and the 27th store in the 
West Los Angeles district. 
This location’s selling space 
adds up to 19,000 square feet, 
but the total footage is 31,000 
square feet since it houses a 
Longs regional training cen- 
ter plus the store’s own ware- 
house area.

anchored by the cosmetics 


service counter, is now home 
to toiletries such as skin care 
(this was located in the rear) 
and franchise lines of pegged 
cosmetics were moved next 
to the bullpen and removed 
from the wall. The toiletries, 
once a draw to the back wall 
of the store, have been re- 
placed by another traffic-lur- 
ing category, diapers and 
baby wipes. 

To accommodate the wall- 
high pegged selection on a 
lower gondola, the fixture has 
a lower-than-usual base. Both 
new adjacencies allow cosme- 
ticians to assist customers and 
do stock work without leaving 
the service area.

PayLess Medicaid error 


WILSONVILLE, Ore. — PayLess Drug Stores has en-

billing system.

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 26, 1993

EDITORIAL 


Fresh thinking was the star at Marketplace 


The best part of any convention or trade show for me 
is sitting down one-to-one with trade executives to re- 
new friendships and advance business relationships. 

Away from the din of the 602-booth NACDS Mar- 
ketplace in San Diego—yet close enough to keep our 
adrenaline racing—retailers and manufacturers 
swapped views with me and a few of my staff editors 
on wide-ranging topics and strategies that will impact 
our business significantly 


in coming years. 

My privilege as an edi- 
tor is to hear the concerns 
of trade executives from 
all over the country. I get 
the macro view. 

My responsibility to 
people I meet with is to 
play back how trends that 
concern them are manifested elsewhere, and to share 
how other chains and suppliers are viewing and meet- 
ing similar challenges. 

For readers, I cull what is most relevant and share 
some of the most enlightened opinions. These are 
meant to be directional and a service to readers. 

Here is some of what I brought back from San Diego: 
@ Cleveland is fast becoming a hotbed of retail compe- 
tition. Market sources speculate that Walgreens is 
eyeing 20 sites there in anticipation of a change in 
state liquor laws that would give the chain a ground 
floor opportunity in a business it knows well. Mean- 
while, Revco has picked up six additional sites around 
Cleveland as a defensive move. 

One problem all will have here is an escalation in the 
price of pharmacists, as Wal-Mart, Target, Meijer, 
Kroger, Walgreens and others vie for their services. 
® Private label is quite the rage, but at London Drug 
in British Columbia, Canada, Len Marks, vice presi- 
dent of general merchandise and pharmacy, keeps 
“positive vendor relations” in mind when merchan- 
dising store brands. “We only use compare and save 


MARKET 
PULSE 
AL HELLER 


signs under our house labels—not under the national 
brands. And we don’t run any big circular ads for pri- 
vate label.” | 

On a separate matter, by law in his province, over- 

the-counter medicines must be merchandised within 
25 feet of pharmacists for hearing and visual contact 
with customers. The chain has designed pharmacy al- 
coves and encourages pharmacists to come out from 
behind the counter, further giving a store-within-a- 
store effect and raising its professional image. 
@ Lewis Drug in Sioux Falls, S.D., takes its conve- 
nience image seriously, says general merchandise 
manager Doug Gravning. “Five minutes. Five Lewis 
bucks,” he says, referring to the reward to customers 
who have to wait on a checkout line that long. He’s 
only given out a handful so far, but the statement visi- 
bly demonstrates the chain’s commitment to customer 
satisfaction. 

More on the convenience premise: Lewis has taken 
its first step into one-hour photofinishing, offers video 
rentals at $2 per day for new releases and 99 cents for 
hot hits, and has reset and expanded its greeting cards 
and party goods section. 

On the value of helium: Lewis sells mylar balloons at 
$1.95 on a 54-cent cost. To get additional sales, the 
chain attaches candy and toys to these popular items. 
@ Andy Streifel, vice president of merchandise at 
PayLess, says of his chain’s willingness to invest: 
“We'll take our short-term lumps to position ourselves 
for the long term in HBA, OTC, wellness and nutrition 
to make our feel good-look good statement.” By this 
September, all stores will have 40 feet of bath, 40 feet 
of hair (up from 22 to 28 feet) and 44 feet of skin (up 
from 28 feet). 

Moreover, health foods will help build a new cus- 
tomer base, he said. And party goods, a new destina- 
tion section, is already up to nearly 2 percent of total 
store sales. 

For me, fresh thinking and the ability to take intelli- 
gent risks were the stars at the latest Marketplace. 


Pharmacy benefits with third class of drugs 


For generations now, retail pharmacy groups have 
been pressing the FDA to establish a new class of drugs 
available without a prescription—but only from a regis- 
tered pharmacist. 

To date these efforts have been spectacularly un- 
successful. In large part, pharmacy’s failure to gener- 
ate support for restrictions on the distribution of OTC 
drugs has been due to the transparently economic ba- 

sis for their plan. 


L PERSPECTIVE 


Critics of the idea—in- 
cluding OTC drug manu- 
facturers and retailers of 
HBC products outside of 
the drug store industry— 
have been able to portray 
the scheme as nothing 
more than an attempt to 


WASHINGTON 


KEN RANKIN 


create a “druggists mo- 
nopoly” in the sale of nonprescription medicines. 

Anybody who ever rolled the dice and landed on 
Boardwalk knows what happens when somebody gets 
a monopoly. Prices go up sharply. 

That’s the last thing federal health officials here in 
Washington want to hear. Today the emphasis through- 
out the Clinton Administration is on reforming the 
health delivery system to hold down runaway costs. 

So why is the “third class of drugs” issue suddenly a 
hot button again in 1993? 

Why did the state pharmacy regulators at this 
year’s National Association of Boards of Pharmacy an- 
nual meeting vote to support national standards limit- 
ing the sale of certain OTCs to pharmacists? 

And why is APhA back beating the drum for a 
“third class of drugs” with such renewed vigor these 


day? Perhaps it’s because pharmacy’s braintrust be- 
lieves it can convince Hillary Clinton & Co. that a new 
pharmacist-only standard for certain OTCs will actu- 
ally reduce the nation’s health care costs. 

The plan backed by APhA, for example, would es- 
tablish a “transitional class” of drugs to which pre- 
scription products would move before being made 
available over-the-counter on an unrestricted basis. 

When an pharmacy drug such as ibruprofen is 
switched to OTC status, the cost of that product to 
consumers and third-party payors falls dramatically. 
More importantly, overall health costs decline even 
more because a visit to the doctor is no longer neces- 
sary to obtain the medicine. 

Although the FDA does have an Rx-to-OTC switch 
program in operation, scores of prime candidates for 
the switch remain available only via pharmacy be- 
cause the FDA is nervous about allowing their unre- 
stricted OTC sale. 

Seldane, for example, is “widely used, advertised 
directly to the consumer and enjoys a reputation as a 
highly safe and effective product,” APhA says. But 
reports to the FDA “of adverse events make reclassi- 
fication” of Seldane to unrestricted OTC status “high- 
ly unlikely.” 

A third “transition” drug class—such as those in 
place in most other industrialized countries—would 
enable drugs such as Seldane to be sold without a pre- 
scription because the pharmacist would monitor the 
patient’s therapy. 

The bottom line: potentially massive savings in 
health care costs. At least that’s the bottom line that 
advocates of a pharmacist-only class of drugs are 
sending to Clinton health reformers.
