DRUG STORE NEWS, July 26, 1993 


Walgreen scores 
another record quarter 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Extending its long winning streak, 
Walgreen Co. racked up record sales and earnings for the third 
quarter and first nine months of fiscal 1993. 

Net income advanced 13.8 percent for the quarter ended Ma 
31, to $64.4 million. Sales rose 10.6 percent to $2.08 billion, wit 
same-store results up a healthy 5.8 percent for the quarter. 

For the first nine months of the fiscal year, net earnings in- 
creased 11.6 percent to $188.9 million, with sales up 11.1 per- 
cent to $6.26 billion. Same-store sales rose 6.6 percent for the 
nine months. 

Pharmacy again led the way at Walgreens, with prescription 
sales gaining 16.3 percent for the quarter and 15.1 percent for 
the nine months. Same-store pharmacy sales were up 11.1 per- 
cent for the quarter and 11.2 percent for the first three periods. 

“We continue to perform consistently well in the extremely 
competitive retail arena and to invest heavily in the expansion, 
technology and customer service that will ensure our leadership 

ey into the next century,” said chain president L. Daniel 
ornat. 

Walgreens entered a new market, Spokane, Wash., with 
three Walgreen RxPress stores in June. “These 1,600-square- 
foot stores, linked by satellite to the entire Walgreen chain, fill 
prescriptions and stock 650 of the most coe ar OTC health 
items,” said chairman and ceo Charles R. Walgreen III. “The 
three Spokane stores bring the total number of RxPress units to 
14.” He said the Spokane stores were “doing very well.” 

As reported earlier, Walgreens is also negotiating for leases 
in the greater Cleveland market. The chain will open 20 units si- 
multaneously in the Cleveland/Akron/Canton area by the end of 
1994, making it “Walgreens’ most aggressive entry into a new 
market, other than by acquisition, in our 92-year history,” said 
the chairman.

L__exitor’snote 


The grass isn’t 
always greener 


En route to a business meeting across the 
country in late June, I was able to skim 
chraeih half a dozen popular news and 
business publications. 

Featured as the cover story in several, 
and as smaller news items in others, was 
the dismal situation facing many of this 
country's displaced white collar workers 
and others who are unemployed. Major 
corporate cutbacks, the stagnant econo- 
my, the trade imbalance—wherever the 
experts lay the blame, one thing is for 
sure: the gloom and doom has not affected 
pharmacy. 

Our profession certainly faces its share 
of challenges, but for the most part, phar- 
macy remains a growth industry. Demand 
for new pharmacists remains strong and I 
have met many students who had little 
difficulty securing employment. In fact, 
most had several attractive offers from 
which to choose. 

The fact is, pharmacists fill an incredibly 
valuable role in society that stands to gain in 


stature and responsibility with reform of 
the nation’s health care delivery system. 


You can complain about the long hours, 
sore feet and no lunch breaks, but those 


things seem to pale in comparison to the 
plight millions of other well-educated and 
ormerly well-paid workers who no have 
nowhere to ply their trade. 

I know Thanksgiving isn’t until Novem- 
ber, but on a half-empty plane 35,000 feet 


over Oregon, the grass looks greener than 
ever on the pharmacy side of the fence.

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, July 26, 1993 


By Mike Troy 


harmacies have long 
been the most popular 
place where parents 
sought lice treatments for their 
children. Drug store pharma- 
cies, in icular, account for 
about 75 percent of sales in the 
roughly $85 million category. 

To strengthen their position 
in the category, a number of 
chain stores are working 
closely with the National Pedic- 
ulosis Association to distribute 
an educational brochure called, 
“Don't Let Your Child Become 
an Egghead.” 

National chains such as 
Brooks, CVS, Eckerd, Hook, 
Osco, PayLess, Peoples, Rite- 
Aid, SupeRx, Thrifty, Wal- 

ns and Wal-Mart will be 
istributing the brochure to 
customers in September as part 
of National Pediculosis Preven- 
tion Month. 

“We are totally psyched 
about the involvement of the 
drug chains,” said NPA presi- 
dent and executive director 


otc merchandiser 


Deborah Altshuler. “This is a 
huge milestone for our organi- 
zation because the stores have a 
brochure to distribute that is 

repared by us, an indepen- 
feat, nonprofit group, rather 
than promotional materials 
from manufacturers.” 

The brochure provides infor- 
mation for parents who want to 
keep lice out of their children’s 
hair. It also points out that pedi- 
culicides are pesticides and 
must be used appropriately and 
carefully so as to avoid prob- 
lems. 

If they are consulted, phar- 
macists can play an important 
role in ensuring products are 
used correctly, according to 
Altshuler. 

“There are a lot of ways for 
pharmacists to be involved in 
this category and we look to 

harmacists as one of the first 
ines of defense and to help de- 
tect infestations in communi- 
ties,” Altshuler said.

Outbreak prevalence 


Although head lice are preva- 
lent throughout the year, cer- 
tain climates and months of 
year see a greater incidence of 
outbreaks. 

“As a general rule, the West 
and South tend to show higher 
sales of lice treatments and I be- 
lieve that has to do with the 
va weather, oe 
said. “Hispanics, as a popula- 
tion, also tend to have a her 
infestation rate than the general 
population. This has to do with 
the fact that [Hispanics] tend to 
reside in warmer climates, and 
have larger families. Lice has 
nothing to do with cleanliness.” 

Certain times of the year, 
such as the fall when children 
return to school and after 
Christmas vacations, also are 
the times when outbreaks are 
common.

Parent Kmart may sell 
PayLess Drug Stores. The 
outright sale of Less or 
other Kmart specialty units 
is seen as a move to tighten 
the discount giant’s strategic 
focus and enhance flagging 
shareholder value. 


By Allene Symons 
TROY, Mich. — Kmart is 
seeking a suitor for 560-store 
PayLess Drug Stores, its 


wholly-owned chain drug sub- 
sidiary. Such an outright sale, 
rather than a long-discussed 
IPO strategy or corporate re- 
structuring, is anew and more 
radical plan but only one op- 
tion, say Kmart officials. 


Industry and media esti- 
mates set the price tag at 
around $1 billion for the Wil- 
sonville, Ore.-based drug 
chain, which posted sales of 
$2.3 bilion an operating in- 
come of $113 million in 1992. 

PayLess officials declined 
to comment, but Shawn 
Kahle, Kmart director of cor- 

rate communications, told 

Store News: “We are 
confirming that Merrill Lynch 
is involved,but we are not con- 
firming anything in the discus- 
sion of price and we are not 
locking in a time frame.” 

The news marks a change 
since Kmart’s annual meeting 
in May. At that time, the fu- 


Bill’s will mark the first chain acquisition by Longs and signals 
Longs’ desire to enrich its market and grow its third-party clout.

This is my farewell column. 

After nearly eight years of close ties to the retail drug 
industry and 12 years at this publishing company, | 
have resigned to become chief editor of Non-Foods Mer- 
chandising, the leading publication for health and beau- 
ty care and general merchandise in supermarkets. 

I will miss the day-to-day involvement with this in- 
dustry, which embraced me, helped me feel I was an im- 

portant part of it, and add- 


ed to my knowledge of 
critical retail issues like no 
other body of people. 
Since the drug and su- 
permarket industries are 
so closely aligned, I’m 
sure to see many in the 
trade often at conventions 
and market visits. I’m 


glad for that. 

Changes I’ve seen over the years position this trade 
class better than ever, with a heightened focus on core 
areas of the store that keep drug chains distinctive in 
the marketplace and add to their convenience image. 

At the same time, operators are experimenting 
with new ways to meet the fast-changing needs of con- 
sumers. They’re using technology better and have 
grown more enlightened in their dealings with manu- 
facturers and reps. These advances make the industry 
stronger and more competitive. 

As I depart, I am excited to tell about two projects 
in particular that I’ve helped set in motion. First, 
Drug Store News’s joint survey with Marketing Cor- 
poration of America, the mega-consulting firm based 
in Norwalk, Conn. , will detail for the first time today’s 
real trade practices between retailers, wholesalers 
and manufacturers. Pricing and promotion strategies, 
cost reduction efforts, the uses of private label, scan- 
ning data and consumer research will all be covered 
when results are released in the second October issue 
of DrSN. Category management, relationships with 
trade counterparts and customer satisfaction strate- 


OPINION 


Successful road forks into two bright futures 


gies will also be reported. 

It’s an exhaustive study, with 225 respondents al- 
ready. The findings will set benchmarks for the indus- 
try and better enable trade executives to establish new 
directions that make sense fur today’s marketplace. 

Second, DrSN will launch a trade conference and 
exposition in October 1994 on store-specific market- 
ing. The show, to take place in Chicago, is tied directly 
to an evolution in shopping demographics that is im- 
pacting on retailers and suppliers alike. 

For example, by the year 2010: 

@ 47 percent of the U.S. population will be non-fam- 
ily, single-parent households. 

@ 40 percent will be over 45 years old. 

® Minorities will account for one-third of the U.S. 
population. 

These changes cause chains to alter their product 
mix, pricing and marketing so each store maximizes 
its potential. And suppliers need to market products 
along demographic segments and custom-tailor mixes 
by market. 

This exclusive DrSN event will be a retail first. The 
conference and expo will be a unique event that could 
add significantly to the profitability of each store. 

As the industry moves ahead and I advance in my 
career, Drug Store News and Drug Store News For the 
Pharmacist will also go on as the industry’s paceset- 
ting publications. I am extremely proud of the talent- 
ed and dedicated editorial staff I regrettably leave be- 
hind. We were more than co-workers; we were great 
friends and will continue to be so. We shared a vision 
of how our biweekly tabloid and monthly magazine 
should serve the industry, and we often worked be- 
yond reason to deliver the best we could. | 

So thanks to J. Roger Friedman, Jay Forbes and Jill 
Manee, who provided the environment in which I 
could grow and refine my talents. And a special warm 
“so long” to my staff, who gave all of themselves when- 
ever I asked—and that was often. These editors will 
continue to serve this industry well and deserve all 
the professional cooperation and respect you can give. 


The Department of Labor (DOL) spent just four 
months writing final regulations implementing the new 
“Family and Medical Leave Act” which took effect na- 
tionwide on Aug. 5. But it’s likely to take years of litiga- 
tion and consternation for employers, employees and 
the courts to sift through all the implications of that law. 

On the surface, at least, the ground rules seem clear 
enough: starting this month, drug chains and large in- 
dependents (those with 50 


or more employees on the 
job for at least 20 months) 
will be required to offer 
workers up to 12 weeks of 
unpaid leave annually in 
the event of a “serious” 
personal or family illness, 
or the birth or adoption of 
a child. Even part-time 
employees are eligible if they’ve worked at least 1,250 
hours during the past 12 months. 

If the new law works as well as its supporters hope, 
drug stores and other businesses will be able to pro- 
vide their employees with an extra measure of securi- 
ty and flexibility at very little additional cost. 

Unfortunately, however, the DOL’s hastily ham- 
mered out regulations appear more likely to promote 
abuse of the system, costly scheduling problems for 
employers and a potential medical liability nightmare 
for the drug store industry. 

The real problems are not likely to involve the “fam- 


Industry cautiously eyes DOL Leave Act 


ily leave” requirements, but rather the “medical 
leave” provisions. 

Although the law permits workers to take medical 
leave only for “serious health conditions,” the new 
regulations suggest that virtually any illness may be 
“serious” enough to qualify for leave benefits. Even 
a common cold could be declared a “serious health 
condition” if the worker makes at least one visit to a 
“health care provider” and receives a prescription 
for the symptoms. 

Workers are not required to take their leave all at 
once—indeed, the rules permit “intermittent leave” 
benefits of as little as one hour at a time. And empioy- 
ees do not need to provide any notice before taking 
“emergency” leave. 

Separate provisions of the law require employers to 
continue paying health insurance premiums for workers 
on leave and to restore all job benefits to employees re- 
turning from family or medical leave. But the DOL rules 
do not require employees to continue paying their share 
of health insurance premiums while on leave. 

What happens if the company’s health insurance 
carrier refuses to reinstate workers who allow their 
coverage to lapse while on leave? The answer, accord- 
ing to some legal experts who have picked through the 
new regulations, is likely to keep drug chain employee 
benefit managers awake all night. Under the DOL 
rules, they say, the employer could be required to pay 
all future health costs for these uninsurable returning 
workers out-of-pocket.

Targeting Hispanics 


Over the vears, chain drug 
retailers have learned a lot 
about targeting African-Amer- 
ican consumers. Because Afri- 
can-Americans have very spe- 
cific hair- and skin-care needs, 
it has been relatively easy for 


chains to and advertise 
apap formulated specifical-

But as Walgreens ethnic hair

is much more challenging be- 
cause their personal care needs 
are less specific. Many chains 
have been trying to court His- 
panics and Asians by stocking 
darker shades of makeup, hair 
color and hosiery. 

But chains have also 
learned that they can woo His- 
panic customers by making 
simple language accommoda- 
tions, specifically by provid-

products with re pack-

workers who are Spanish or 
who speak Spanish. 

Many chains are also mar-

y to African-American and 

ispanic consumers. The em- 
phasis is on using advertising 
and merchandising programs 
that will let African-American 
and Hispanic consumers know 
that drug chains are eager to 
court their business. 

One example: American 
Drug Stores, which is now us- 
ing the Hispanic and African- 
American yellow pages to en- 
hance its visibility among these 
key consumer groups, accord- 
ing to vice president of adver- 
tising and sales Terry Maloy. 


Community outreach 


Ethnic category buyers are 
also working with distributors 
and manufacturers to create 
promotions and programs that 
offer consumers more than 
just price-off products. 

There is a growing demand 
for community service promo- 
tions that, in the words of sev- 
eral buyers, “put something

the American Health & Beau-

Ads tailored to consumers 


Many retailers have also 
come to realize that it makes 
good economic sense to tailor 
their ads directly to specific 
niches iike African-American 
or Hispanic consumers. 

Scott Wilson, president of

about 84 percent of the ads ina 
esi market ad go to white 

ouseholds. “You can see that

“Tailoring ads to the mar-

tion of shoppers,” he says, 
“and that means they should 
be able to draw more custom- 
ers into their stores.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, August 16, 1993 


TARGETING THE ETHNIC CONSUMER 


ore and more chain 
drug retailers are 
trying to meet the 


diverse needs of ethnic con- 
sumers by tailoring their 
product mix and their adver- 
tising directly to the demo- 
graphics of their individual 
store neighborhoods. 

In some markets, retailers 
find they can court customers 
by carrying regional food 
items in their stores. In oth- 
ers, they’re trying to woo 
consumers with ethnic lines 
of greeting cards or expand- 
ed ethnic hair, skin and cos- 
metic departments. 

Some chains marketing to 
Hispanic customers are mak- 
ing selective adaptations in 
the way they present their 
OTC and pharmacy depart- 
ments. Several retailers not- 
ed that Hispanic shoppers 
feel much more comfortable 
when information on phar- 
macy, OTC products and vi- 
tamins is provided for them 


en Espanol. 
According to operators of 
Hispanic-oriented chains in 


south Florida, Hispanics tend 
to view pharmacists and the 
OTCs they recommend as their 
first line of defense against ill- 
ness. Retailers say stores can 
capture the loyalty of many 
Hispanic shoppers by stocking 
and advertising those OTCs 
they are familiar with from 
their home countries. 

Health brochures in Spanish, 
like those offered in Sav-on’s 
pharmacies in selected loca- 
tions on the West Coast, help 
spark sales. So, too, does Span- 
ish-language store signage. 

Research indicates that 
Hispanics consume more vita- 
mins than the general popula- 
tion. That has led one leading 
vitamin manufacturer, Na- 
ture’s Bounty, to add Spanish 
labeling on 15 of its most popu- 
lar lines. According to Na- 
ture’s Bounty research, be- 
tween 40 and 48 percent of 
Hispanics take vitamins, com- 
pared with 25 to 35 percent of 
the general population. 

In addition, chain mer-

Ethnic hair care 


The biggest product seg- 
ment in the ethnic market is 
ethnic hair care. And this 
year, the strongest growth in 
ethnic hair care is in relaxers, 
hair styling products, prod- 
ucts targeted to children and 
hair coloring products. 

African-American consum- 
ers tend to be very brand loy- 
al, and they tend to support 
well established brands that 
are marketed directly to Afri- 
can-American consumers in 
vehicles like African-Ameri- 
can magazines, newspapers 
and radio stations. 

This past year, some of the 
best sellers in ethnic hair care 
have been Soft Sheen’s Opti- 
mum Care relaxer kits, regu- 


lar and super; Johnson Prod- 
ucts’ Gentle Treatment kits, 
regular and super; Pro Line’s 
preteen Just For Me kit; Lus- 
ter’s PCJ Original and PCJ 
For Kids; and Shark Product’s 
African Pride, a hair styling 
line that has been extended to 
include a No-Lye Condition- 
ing Creme Relaxer. Buyers 
say African Pride and Pro 
Line’s Just For Me are two of 
the best ethnic hair care 
launches of the past year. 

Buyers are also very posi- 
tive about a new men’s hair 
color line recently launched by 
Carson Products: Dark & Nat- 
ural Hair Color For Men. Ac- 
cording to most retailers, 
men’s hair color is an under- 
developed market “just as 
children’s toiletries were until 
Baby Love and Just For Me 
came along,” said one source. 

“Right now, many ethnic 
men buy the Dark & Lovely 
shades targeted to women. 
Now that there are shades 
specifically for men on the 
market, we should see a real 
surge in this category,” said 
the source. Several buyers be- 
lieve the Dark & Natural line 
for men will drive sales in the 
hair color category “dramati- 
cally.” 

Also looking promising is 
Alberto Culver’s introduction 
of TCB Bone Strait to retail. 


Retailers are able to turn greet- 
ing cards into a destination shop 
whenthey carry African-Ameri- 
can or Hispanic lines in ethnic 
neighborhood stores. 


Drug chains certainly want Hispanic customers to feel comfort- 
able in their stores, so they often use Spanish-speaking signs to 
send a welcoming message. 


For the past five years, Bone 
Strait has been selling beauti- 
fully in the salon market. It’s 
targeted to the 70 percent of 
African-American women 
who relax their hair at home. 
The launch is being supported 
with $3 million in advertising 
and promotions that will reach 
90 percent of all African- 
American women aged 18 to 
49 at least four times in the 
next few months. 

With lines like Soft Sheen’s 
Baby Love and Pro Line’s 
Just For Me doing so well, 
wt are hoping mothers 
will be enthusiastically re- 
ceptive to the new Tinkerbell 
from Posner line now being 
shipped in. According to sev- 
eral sources, early sales have 
been very promising. 

Skin care is still a small seg- 
ment within ethnic. But it is a 


definite growth segment that 
Ambi currently dominates.

from J. Strickland, however.

ood and the advanced formu-

Emerging opportunities 


Most ethnic hair care trends 
are born in beauty and barber 
shops and salons. The reason: 
shoppers become familiar 
with new items and trends via 
exposure from hair stylists 
who send them to salons for 
maintenance products. 

Once the product becomes a 
styling basic, consumers like 
to be able to find it at their lo- 
cal drug stores. 

That's one reason why re- 
tailers are excited about Al- 
berto-Culver’s TCB Bone 
Strait, a seven-SKU line that 
helps keep hair relaxed. Re- 
laxed hair styles remain a ma- 
jor look among African-Amer- 
ican consumers, about 70 
percent of whom favor the 
styles at least some of the 
time, studies say. 

Alberto is also working ona 
relaxer kit for the retail mar- 


ket to serve as an anchor to the 
styling products.

heritage that is important to 
the shopper,” explained Merle

ing for Alberto-Culver’s Pro- 
fessional Division. 

TCB Bone Strait will still be

aged in different sizes that dis-

counterparts.

line available through mass 
market stores.

Planograms are critical 

There are constant pressures to 
maximize return on investment in a 
climate of new product proliferation 
and shrinking shelf space. Yesterday, 
planograms were an optional way to 
describe a shelf-set. But today, they 
are Critical to success. 


They are the blueprint 

Space management is becoming more 
than a tool for matching space to 
movement. Planograms are built to 
handle increasingly more complex 
product assortments, micro-marketing 
needs and merchandising looks. 
Planograms are the blueprints upon 
which vendors and retailers build 
profitable partnerships to attract the 
consumer and meet their demands. 


Not all planograms work 
Anyone can place products on a shelf. 
Few can build planograms that meet 
complex merchandising objectives 
that get implemented. Planograms 
cannot reflect a single point of view. 
They must blend market data, vendor 
and retailer merchandising philosophy 
and common sense. 


We stimulate the consumer 
We know how to analyze large 
quantities of information and build 
merchandising solutions that are 
objective, cohesive and innovative. 
Most important, our solutions stimu- 
late the consumer. 


We build the best

Database™, over 90,000 high-quality 
product dimensions and images. We 
add a staff of seasoned, dedicated 
merchandisers and end with dazzling 
graphics to enhance the presentation.

wears many hats 


New technology, more technicians and other chang-s in pharmacy strat- 
egy and structure are all impacting pharmacy operations in the 1990s. Our 
1993 Survey of Pharmacy Operations indicates several emerging trends 
and new directions—from personnel shifts to OBRA counseling strategies 
to home delivery. Our report begins on page 13

Pharmacy operations survey 


Today's dynamic chain drug store environment requires the pharma- 
cist to wear many hats. To see how different retail formats handle the 
new demands, FTP surveyed chains, supermarkets and discounters 
on management, technology, formats and operations. See page 13.

for durable medical equipment and other home health care sup-

pharmacies starting this fall, NARD warns. See page 23.

the responses of several

where significant, differ-

The pharmacist 
as supervisor 


Our survey shows that 


and training role is ex- 
panding in all but the 
smaller pharmacies. Our 
survey shows that today a 
senior pharmacist is likely 
to supervise other phar- 
macists, clerks and phar- 
macy technicians, the 
newest adjunct in phar- 
macy personnel. 

According to our sur- 
vey, 93.6 percent of 
pharmacists supervise 
technicians, while 79.8 
percent supervise clerks 
and 73.4 percent super- 
vise other pharmacists. 
Survey respondents in- 
dicate that they employ 
(on average) one to two 
technicians per store, 
and for deep discount- 
ers, the number rises to 
an average of three tech- 
nicians. 

Among all chains sur- 
veyed, 16 percent report 
that they plan to ee 
more pharmacists. For 
large chains of 50 or more 
stores, the number was 
slightly higher at 17.9 


in 90 percent of all re- Pharmacists are supervising more tiers of subordinates than in previous years, percent. 


S 
the person who super- 
vises pharmacist/managers is a 
pharmacist, too. This is gener- 
ally viewed as a positive re- 
porting structure, as it is likely 
to minimize friction between 
managers and pharmacists 
while it reinforces the impor- 
tance of the profession to a 
greater extent than when 
pharmacy professionals are su- 
pervised by non-pharmacists. 

But pharmacists themselves 
are supervising more tiers of 
subordinates than in previous 
years, our survey shows. The 
OBRA ‘90 requirement that 
pharmacists provide patient 
counseling reduces the dis- 
pensing productivity of a phar- 
macist, especially in a high vol- 
ume setting. As a cost-effective 
solution, more pharmacies are 
adding pharmacy technicians to 
the staff to assist with non-jud- 
gemental functions such as pre- 
paring labels.

ing more technicians, 31 
percent of traditional drug 
stores in our survey said they 
plan to do so. Among the large 
chains, 64.3 percent say their

Once hired, 92.6 percent of 
pharmacists get on-the-job-

of technicians and 87 percent 
of pharmacy clerks—that’s in 
contrast to 75 percent of non- 
pharmacy clerks and 70 per- 
cent of managers. 


Who minds the store? 


@ At store level, the percent- 
age of managers who are phar-

chains, compared with 37.5 
percent at discounters and 17.4 
percent at supermarkets. 

@In field supervision, 64 
percent of supervisors are phar- 
macists at larger chains, while 
at smaller chains 28 percent are 
pharmacists.

® Going up the corporate 
ladder, larger chains (50 phar- 
macies or more) have a higher 
percentage of corporate staff 
that are pharmacists than do 
smaller chains—36.6 percent. 
At smaller chains that percent- 
age is 26.1 percent. 


Wave of technology 


Pharmacy computers aren’t 
just a convenience any more. 
Increasing third-party business 
requires familiarity with elec- 
tronic processing systems as 
more private and government 
insurers move toward paperless 
data interchange. With OBRA 
90, more information is needed 
in a timely manner to promote 
compliance, avoid adverse re- 
actions and detect drug interac- 
tions. Counseling is aided by 
computer-generated printouts, 
not only in English but also—in 
an increasing number of mar- 
kets—in Spanish. 

We asked just how many 
chains provide written counsel- 
ing information, such as these 
computer generated printouts. 
Our survey shows that the ma- 
jority of nf dhesniticr operators do 
provide written patient informa- 
tion with prescriptions (85. 1 per- 
cent), but materials seem to be 
provided selectively. Written in-

formation is given by 62.8 per- 
cent “on new prescriptions only” 
while 13.8 percent responded 
“where required by law only.” 

What type of electronic phar- 
macy support is the most popu- 
lar? Our survey found the great- 
est percentage of respondents 
use PDX (16 percent) computer 
systems, followed by QS1 (11.7 
percent) then 3PM (9.6 percent), 
with Condor and National Data 
tied at 6.4 percent each. 


The POS lag 


Even though high-tech has 
come to the pharmacy, when it 
comes to sales information, drug 
stores lag behind other trade 
classes in the use of scanning 
technology. Only 33 percent of 
all stores in our survey scan at 
point of sale, with all (100 per- 
cent) of responding discounters 
scanning and a significant 82.1 
percent of larger drug chains 
making use of the technology. 

Of the chains that use POS 
scanning, 64.3 percent have all 
stores on the system. When 
others were asked when the 
would be 100 percent up-and- 
bimpien 20.7 percent said by 
the end of 1994, 8.6 percent by 
year-end 1996, 1.7 percent 
each for 1998 and 2000—and a 
whopping 51.7 percent re- 
sponded “don’t know.” 


Do You Scan At Point-of-Sale? 


The advantages of scanning 
technology range from faster in- 
ventory replenishment and po- 
tentially greater turns to more 
control over internal and exter- 
nal shrinkage. 

As electronic ordering sys- 
tems continue to improve, this 
technology offers more oppor- 
tunity for the drug store to max- 
imize market potential by 
avoiding out-of-stocks and tar- 

eting marketing to a neighbor- 
ood s needs. 

Yet another “hat” is placed on 
the head of the supervising 
pharmacist as more sophisticat- 
ed and customized sales reports 
= them to become in- 
volved in analyzing—or be- 
come proactive in customiz- 
ing—-sales and stock reports. 

The trend in more opera- 
tions-savvy pharmacies is to 
keep less inventory on hand and 
rely on “just in time” replenish- 
ment to reduce inventory dol- 
lars. This also points toward 
more sophisticated electronic 
ordering systems and pharma- 
cists skilled in using avail- 
able data to the best advantage. 


Other technology 


Even fairly low-tech tools 
like fax and video kiosks, which 
offer health information and po- 
tential counseling support, are

being used increasingly in the 
pharmacy setting. 
Video kiosks largely serve as 
a marketing tool. Most chains 
report using a kiosk to test cus- 
tomers blood pressure (39.4 
percent), while another 19.1 
rcent use them to dispense 
ealth information. No respon- 
dents say they charge custom- 
ers for the use of blood pressure 
or drug-information kiosk use. 
In our survey, 45.7 percent of 
drug stores reporting said they 
use fax machines to receive pre- 
scriptions from doctors, while 


_ 66 percent use the machine for 


general store purposes. 

With shrinkage a growing 
concern for all retailers, it’s not 
surprising that 68.1 percent of 
drug chains in our survey rely 
on motion detectors and video 
surveillance (56.4 percent) to 
combat shrink, with only 35.1 
percent using electronic article 
surveillance at this time. 


Positioning pharmacy 


A rear pharmacy position has 
been the traditional location for 
most chain drug stores—one 
that faces the customer upon 
entering the store. In merchan- 
dising terms, it also pulls phar- 
macy-destination shoppers to 
the back of the store, giving

In our survey, 81 percent of drug chains

the rear. But, perhaps indicative of relative 
store size differences, 62.5 percent of dis-

47.4 percent of supermarkets, where the

beauty care department. 

Some traditional drug chains are moving 
pharmacy toward the front, however, like 
Wilsonville, Ore.-based PayLess Drug 
Stores. One reason cited is customer con- 
venience: Pharmacy customers, especially 
the elderly, prefer not to walk far from the 
entrance to have a prescription filled in 
their larger stores. 

Other design changes in the wake of 
OBRA '90 find many chains lowering their 
pharmacy counters to make counseling eas- 
ier. OBRA-inspired pharmacy format 
changes also “ae de separate drop-off and 
pick-up windows, with around half of all re-

Longs finalizes Bill’s takeover 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. — Longs Drug Stores has 
completed its acquisition of the 21-store Bill’s Drugs 
chain based in Benicia, Calif. Consolidation of the 
stores will strengthen Longs’ clout in its home mar- 
ket, the San Francisco Bay Area. 

Terry Burnside, former executive vice president of 
operations for Bill’s, will join Longs in the position of 
GM manager, reporting to Dan Wilson, senior vp of 
marketing. “The addition of Terry Burnside to our 
marketing department is part of a change in our orga- 
nizational structure, but it hasn’t been totally defined 
as to what the buying structure will be,” said William 
Combs, vp of administration for Longs. 


Genovese to mark store #100 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Genovese Drug Stores will add 
two new locations in October, bringing its store count 
to 101. The 100th store will be a 15,000-square-foot 
unit in New Jersey; the other location will be a 9,000- 
square-foot store in the New York City borough of 
Queens. The chain is poised to make its first foray 
into Manhattan at the end of October. 


Rx Place is poised for growth 


NEW YORK — Woolworth Corp. is considering 150 
Woolworth mall locations for conversion to Rx Place 
stores or Foot Locker stores, according to William 
Lavin, chairman and chief executive officer of Wool- 
worth Corp. 

Lavin, who took the helm of the chain in July, told 
shareholders in Dallas that the company has “confi- 
dence in the future of the Rx Place pharmacies as an 
important element of our United States general mer- 
chandise strategy...” 


Phar-Mor creates private label post 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Accelerating its new pri- 
vate label program, Phar-Mor has inducted Revco 
D.S. veteran Scott Gorley to assume the newly created 
post of senior director of corporate brands. Gorley will 
take charge of Phar-Mor’s fast-growing line of private 
label products. 

The move signals Phar-Mor’s continuing shift to 
new merchandising and marketing strategies aimed 
at beefing up its bottom line and pulling it out of 
Chapter 11 with a healthy financial structure. A 
pared-down, higher-margin product mix, including a 
newly launched line of house brand items, is part of 
that strategy. 

The off-price chain recently launched its own brand- 
ed line with more than 100 initial HBA items; another 
100 SKUs are being rolled into stores in the coming 
months. Among future private label introductions will 
be general merchandise and food items. 

“Scott’s experience enables us to aggressively move 
forward on our private label program,” said president 
and chief operating officer Dave Schwartz. “In addi- 
tion to the traditional mix of products, we are working 
on a unique, premium quality food line.” 

Gorley will report directly to Schwartz, indicating 
the high priority the chain has given private label. He 
last served as senior beauty products buyer at Revco, 
and prior to that was assistant vice president of buy- 
ing at Perry Drug Stores. 


Perry names pharmacy supervisor 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has named 
Lorie Blair a pharmacy supervisor. Blair, a pharma- 
cist, last served as an assistant store manager, and 
has held several such posts at the chain.

Genovese: Record earnings 
with higher margins, POS 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — An 
adjustment in margins and 
an increase in the number 
of stores capturing item 
movement at the register 
helped Genovese Drug 
Stores reach record sales 
and income in the second 
quarter ended August 13. 

The 101-unit chain re- 
ported sales of $111.43 mil- 
lion for the quarter, an in- 
crease of 6.1 percent over 
the $105.01 million reported 
during the same period last 
year. For the 28-week first 
half, sales increased 4.5 per- 
cent to $254.08 million from 
$243.11 million reported for 


the first half of last year. 

Net income for the quar- 
ter increased 15.6 percent to 
$1.38 million compared to 
the $1.2 million reported for 
last year’s second quarter. 

For the first half of the 
year, net income was up 17 
percent to $2.86 million 
over last year’s $2.45 mil- 
lion. 

Company president and 
chairman Leonard Gen- 
ovese said the increase in 
sales was encouraging, par- 
ticularly in light of the 3.3 
percent sales increase re- 
ported for the comparable 
period last year. 


“We adjusted margins 
minimally and fine-tuned 
our pricing,” added Jerome 
Stengel, vice president and 
treasurer. “Scanning really 
helped our balance sheet. 
We know gross profit on a 
weekly basis now.” 

Genovese opened two new 
locations during the first 
half. One location is a Gen- 
ovese Express, a scaled- 
down version of the chain’s 
prototype. 

The chain plans to open 
four to six stores in the sec- 
ond half of the year, includ- 
ing its first unit in Manhat- 
tan.

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


freshly released report of Gore’s “Na- 
tional Performance Review” (NPR) 
does call for changes in the way gov- 
ernment regulates pharmaceuticals. 

The rules governing the way phar- 
macists and drug wholesalers are re- 
quired to handle controlled sub- 
stances, for example, could be altered 
considerably under Gore’s plan to 
merge the Drug Enforcement Admin- 
istration into the FBI. 

According to the NPR report, “Ma- 
jor structural changes to integrate the 
drug enforcement efforts of the DEA 


and medical de- 
vices? 

Will plans to 
require the 
HCFA to secure competitive bids on 
third-party claims processing con- 
tracts indirectly backfire on pharmacy 
by encouraging more restrictive reim- 
bursement practices? 

Or will the NPR’s suggestion for 
“raising user fees” on regulated indus- 
tries create additional economic bar- 
riers for small firms seeking FDA ap- 
proval for generic drugs? 

The effects of other NPR recommen- 
dations for reinventing government 
are relatively clear. 


Drug industry leaders should find it 


easier to express their concerns to 
Clinton health regulators under 
Gore’s plan to require HHS regulators 
to secure “more input from stakehold- 
ers” (i.e. industry and professional 
groups with a “stake” in proposed reg- 
ulations). 

Drug chains that sell beer, wine or 
spirits should toast the report’s pro- 
posal to repeal the current “Special 
Occupational Tax” (SOT) on alcoholic 
beverage retailers. 

And the NPR’s plan to “integrate” 
Labor Department enforcement of 
wage-hour, child labor and equal em- 
ployment rules is a signal that em- 
ployers should reexamine their compli- 
ance efforts in these areas. 

For many industry retailers, whole- 
salers and manufacturers, however, 
the most radical recommendation in 
the Vice President’s plan to reinvent 
government calls for a defacto privati- 
zation of Federal Occupational Safety 
and Health Act enforcement. 

According to Gore, “no army of 
OSHA inspectors need descend on cor- 
porate America” to ensure compliance 
with federal workplace safety rules. 
Instead, employers—ranging from gi- 
ant, multi-national pharmaceutical 
manufacturers to small, independent 
corner pharmacies—could be required 
to “hire third parties, such as private 
inspection companies” to “certify” that 
each job site is safe. As an alternative, 
businesses could provide special train- 
ing and certification to “non-man- 
agement employees” to their employ- 
er’s workplace for OSHA violations.

Allman receives 1993 Clairol Mentor of the Year award 


Eckerd’s Carol Allman 
has been named as the 1993 
recipient of the annual 
Clairol Mentor Award in the 
field of retail management. 

International cover model 
Cheryl Tiegs presented All- 
man with the award at a re- 
cent luncheon in New York. 
Allman, director of merchan- 
dise for Eckerd, now begins 
a year-long mentoring rela- 
tionship with Rebecca Weil- 
er, one of the 1993 recipients 
of Clairol’s Distinguished 
Aspirant awards. 

Currently in its fifth year, 
the Clairol Mentor program 
is the only nationwide, com- 
pany-sponsored program 
that promotes mentoring 
between successful and as- 
piring women in a variety of 
professions. 

Last year, Genovese’s 
Stephanie Hayter was 
named Mentor in the field 
of retail management. 

Allman now belongs to a 
distinguished group of men- 
tors that includes New York 
District Attorney Linda 
Fairstein; the president of 


Mrs. Fields Cookies, Debbie 
Fields; and Dr. Johnnetta 
Cole, a well-known educator. 

Allman, who selected 
Weiler to be her mentee 
from a field of over 3,000 ap- 
plicants, will spend the year 
providing guidance, support

he children’s toiletries 

department is a hard 

category to decipher. 
Buyers know there’s a mar- 
ket for the merchandise, but 
they don’t know how much 
product to stock, how varied 
a mix they should offer or 
even where they should put 
the department 

To help guide retailers, 
Drug Store News commis- 
sioned a study from Leo J. 
Shapiro and Associates Inc. 
The study found that 

there is a substantial mar- 
ket for children’s toiletries. 
In a survey of 450 heads of 
households, 55 percent of 
the respondents said they 
had purchased some type of 
children’s toiletry product in 
the past. 


The interest is there 


Half (49 percent) of those 
surveyed said they had a 
current interest in purchas- 
ing one or more such items. 
Households which included 
children under 12 had the 
highest rate of positive re- 
sponses to the question; of 
that group, a full 80 percent 
expressed interest in pur- 
chasing one or more kid’s 
HBA items. 

The survey found 
that the market for chil- 
dren’s HBA products knows 
no gender’ boundaries. 
When asked who they might 
buy the products for, re- 
spondents were as likely to 
say a boy (43 percent) as a 
cirl (40 percent). 

According to Shapiro’s 
data, parents with younger 
children (under age 7) are 
attracted to a wider range of 
products than are parents of 
older children. Parents of 
children under 7 had an in- 
terest in, on average, 4.6 of 
the seven products asked 
about (see chart) compared 
to a 3.9 average for parents 
with children between the 
ages of 7 and 12.

Drug Store News, September 27,1993 45 


Perry earnings dip slightly 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores reported a modest 
downturn in earnings momentum for the third quarter as 
tight consumer spending continued to affect the Michigan 
economy. Net earnings for the 215-store chain were $1.9 
million for the quarter ended July 31, compared with $2.1 
million for the same period last year. 

Sales for the quarter rose 2.5 percent vs. last year’s third 
quarter, to $173.6 million. Same-store sales were up a mea- 
ger 0.5 percent. 

“Overall, sales growth slowed because of a relatively low 
rate of inflation and a soft economic environment,” said 
chairman, president and chief executive Jack Robinson. 

Sales for the nine months rose 2.9 percent to $522.3 mil- 
lion, with same-store revenues up 2.2 percent. Net earnings 
for the first three quarters of the current fiscal year dropped 
to $4.1 million vs. $6.2 million last year, reflecting a $3 D 
million, non recurring pre-tax charge taken in the first 
quarter to establish a reserve for the remaining payments 
due from the 1991 divestiture of Perry’s Chicagoland stores. 

Despite softening in sales and earnings, Perry noted 
some positive results. Pharmacy sales rose 8 percent for

Longs reports flat 2nd quarter 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores Corp. 
announced sales of $609 mil- 
lion and net income of $13 
million for the quarter end- 
ed July 29, 1993. Sales for 
the two quarters were essen- 
tially flat at $1.2 billion. 

Net income for the two- 
quarter period was down 
slightly, following the one- 
time cumulative effect of an 
accounting change and a $1 
million pre-tax provision for 
closure of under-performing 


stores. In the first half, 
Longs earned $26.9 million 
as compared to $27.2 million 
for the like period last year. 
According to William 
Combs, vice president ad- 
ministration, “Sates and 
earnings continue to be 
hampered by the depressed 
California economy. We are 
pleased that...our gross 
margins have improved 
from 24.6 percent to 25.5 
percent, and our expenses 
remain under control.” 


Giant Food posts slight increase 


WASHINGTON — Giant 
Food Inc. reported sales for 
the second quarter ended 
Aug. 14 at $795.84 million, 
an increase of 2.2 percent 
over sales of $778.59 mil- 
lion for the same quarter 
last year. 

Gross income was $26.25 
million (3.3 percent of 
sales), an impressive 35 per- 
cent increase over last 
year’s gross income of 
$19.45 million. 

The high gross income is 
attributed to strong sales in 
service areas, such as bak- 
ery and prepared foods. 

Net income was $14.6 
million, compared with the 
$12 million reported one 


year earlier. 

For the 24-week period, 
sales were $1.61 billion, an 
increase of 1.75 percent 
over last year’s sales of 
$1.58 billion for the compa- 
rable period. 

Gross income was $63.06 
million, an increase of 3.92 
percent over the $50.51 mil- 
lion reported for the same 
period last year. 

Giant opened its 156th 
supermarket in June and 
continues work on its first 
Delaware store, which will 
be a 64,000-square-foot 
food/drug combo in a Wilm- 
ington suburb. Of Giant’s 
total store base, 110 are 
combos.

by Barbara White 


DEERFIELD, Il. — Walgreen Co. plans 
to enter the Buffalo, N.Y. market with sev- 
en stores, which will open simultaneously 
sometime in 1994. 

“We are very excited about Buffalo,” said 
Charles R. Walgreen III, chairman. “It has 
what we are looking for in a new market—a 
population base of over one million people, 
drug store-oriented customers and a need for 
our convenience-style stores.” He added that 
the market will expand the chain’s geo- 
graphic coverage in the Northeast. 

Once the chain has opened the initial sev- 
en stores, it will continue to fill out the 


market with additional locations. 

The dates for store openings are not yet 
set, according to Walgreen spokesperson 
Michael Polzin, since leases are now being 
negotiated. 

The chain announced in May its plans to 
inundate the Cleveland market with 20 
stores, which will also open on the same 
day sometime in 1994. Cleveland will also 
represent a new market for the chain, and 
like nearby Buffalo, expansion into that 
market marks Walgreens’ ongoing effort to 
reach into new regions that lie outside its 
current strongholds nationwide. The east- 
ern Great Lakes region is one such area be- 
ing targeted; others include the Pacific

More new vp posts for McKesson 


SAN FRANCISCO — Two new executive sales posi- 
tions and four new executive distribution slots have 
been established in McKesson Drug Co.’s ongoing field 
reorganization, as the nation’s largest drug wholesaler 
continues to consolidate four areas into a simpler, more 
streamlined system of eastern and western operations. 

Robert Straughn has been promoted to vice president 
of sales and marketing-East and Jack Fragie to vice 
president of sales and marketing-West. Straughn re- 
ports to Gary Folsom, executive vice president-East, 
headquartered in Delran, N.J., near Philadelphia. 
Fragie reports to Hubie McMorrow, executive vice pres- 
ident-West in San Leandro, Calif., near San Francisco. 

In four other promotions, Michael Hayes and Robert 
Peck were both appointed vice president of distribu- 
tion operations-East. Donald Walker and Dennis 
Morstad were both named vice president of distribu- 
tion operations-West. Hayes and Peck will report to 
Folsom, while Walker and Morstad will report to Mc- 
Morrow. The six new vice presidential appointees are 
all veteran McKesson employees. 


Arrow opens first drive-through 


PLAINVILLE, Conn. — Arrow Prescription Cen- 
ters, a 48-unit chain of franchised pharmacies based 
here, has opened a new location in New Britain, Conn. 
which includes a drive-through and pick-up window 
for prescriptions. Arrow is also offering a home deliv- 
ery service, a 24-hour emergency hot line and a follow- 
up call within 48 hours of every pediatric prescription 
to better serve customers. 


Giant continues Apples for Students 


WASHINGTON, D.C. — For the fifth year in a row, 
Giant Food Inc. will participate in the Apples for the 
Students PLUS program. Under the program, stu- 
dents collect register tapes, send them to Giant and 
gain points toward school equipment. 

During the past four years, Giant has awarded over 
65,000 computers and related equipment to 2,700 
schools in Maryland, Virginia and the District of Co- 
lumbia. This year, schools can apply register credits to 


textbooks, library books, audio tapes and videotapes. 


Genovese rolls out the carpet 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Genovese plans to add modular 
carpet in 20 new stores and renovations scheduled for 
this year. The first store to get carpeting will be the 
8,000 square-foot Islandia, N.Y. location. 

“We had been using tile but we wanted to change the 
look of the stores,” said Emil Dilollo, director of store 
ayn at the chain. 

The chain plans for a gray carpet with red carpet as 
a border to frame the aisles of the store. Blue borders 
will outline the pharmacy area. 


Vons makes home health care deal 


ARCADIA, Calif. — The Vons Companies launched 
a home health care program with Abbey Home Health 
in 20 Southern California Vons Pavilions locations. 
The program was designed to market home health 
care products and services align the Abbey catalog 
provided in the pharmacy. Two of the Pavilions phar- 
peg offer a kiosk with direct telephone service to

Hair, skin, bath entries abound 
at the Exclusively HBA show 


by Barbara White 


DETROIT — Moderately priced bath 
items, niche hair care products and technol- 
ogy-driven skin offerings were among the 
most exciting new products at this year’s 
Exclusively HBA show, held here Sept. 21 
through 23. 

The show’s more than 300 vendors of- 
fered enough new items to dispel the fear 
that Exclusively HBA follows too closely on 
the heels of the NACDS Marketplace event, 
held annually in June. 


New bath lines hit the mark 


Among bath lines, a trend is surfacing 
with new lines positioned directly against 
specialty and department store brands, but 
which are priced for the mass trade. 

Many lines include more body scrubs, 
which can be used in the shower as well as 
the bath. Retailers said that positioning 
these products toward active consumers 
rather than as luxury items is smart; they 
complain that bubble bath products are great 
in theory, but have slow turns on shelves. 

New introductions offer selling points, 
such as scent layering and product technolo- 
gy, which had previously been ignored at the 
mass level. Some key introductions include: 

@ Lisee and Zenue’s upscale botanical 
products that bridge the gap between spe- 


Revion’s Rich Siporin (left) meets with Kevin 
Browett of Kmart at the Exclusively HBA show. 


cialty/department store lines and those of- 
fered at mass. 

Lisee’s line, which has had strong accep- 
tance from West Coast drug chains, actual- 
ly contains herbs floating in the product. 

Zenue’s 15-SKU shower, face and body 
line, which will retail for between $6.50 and 
$8.50, is positioned against products found 
at specialty stores, such as The Body Shop. 
A $2 million print and television ad budget, 
aimed at the J. Crew and The Gap set, will 
support the line.

New dates set for Exclusively HBA 


DETROIT — In a bid to 
strengthen the Exclusively 
HBA show, its organizers 
have changed the timing of 
the event for next year. 

During the recent Exclu- 
sively HBA, held here Sept. 
21 through 23, show orga- 
nizer and chief executive 
Jay Spaulding announced 
the next show has been set 
for March 23 through 25, 
1994 at McCormick Place in 
Chicago. 

“The earlier time slot [in 
the calendar year] positions 
the show as being a lead-off 
event,” said Spaulding. Next 
year, Exclusively HBA will 
precede the NACDS Market- 
place Conference in June. 

The earlier timing will 
better serve cosmetic buyers 
looking to plan their holiday 


merchandise mix and will co- 
incide with business reviews 
that take place in the first 
quarter, Spaulding said. The 
March time slot will also of- 
fer an opportunity for OTC 
buyers to buy cough/cold in 
the first quarter. 

This year the show at- 
tracted 3,186 attendees, in- 
cluding manufacturers’ 
reps, exhibitors, buyers and 
visitors. Of that number, 
702 were buyers. 

Those numbers were up 
from last year's show, which 
attracted 2,9@u attendees, 
586 of whom were buyers. 

The recent show drew 
more small drug chains and 
wholesalers than large re- 
tail drug operators. Whole- 
salers and small chain buy- 
ers represented 25 percent 


of the buyer attendees at 
the show, according to 
Spaulding. He said the 
breakout of the balance of 
buyer attendees was as fol- 
lows: the discount trade rep- 
resented 24 percent, the 
grocery channel represented 
10 percent, general whole- 
salers, specialty wholesalers 
and service merchandisers 
represented 13 percent and 
other channels (including 
clubs, hypermarkets and 
convenience stores) repre- 
sented 28 percent of those 
buyers in attendance. 

The show attracts a di- 
verse audience, including 
military retail operations 
and retailers from Canada, 
Mexico and abroad. Spauld- 
ing said 15 ceuntries were 
represented at the show.

President Clinton's health plan gets solid industry support 


Continued from page 1 
Congress aatit later this 
month, a final draft of the 
plan, obtained by Drug 
Store News, suggests that 
the Administration archi- 
tects of the plan closely fol- 
lowed the recommendations 
of pharmacy leaders. 

Under the President’s 
proposal, outpatient pre- 
scription drugs will be in- 
cluded as part of the plan’s 
basic “Guaranteed National 
Benefit Package” for all 
Americans. 

Coverage will extend to 
all prescription drugs, bio- 
logical products and insulin 
prescribed for use in an 
outpatient setting, and no 
unreasonable frequency or 
quantity limitations may be 
imposed by health insurers. 

Health plans, however, 
will be “permitted to estab- 
lish formularies, drug uti- 


lization review, generic sub- 
stitution and mail-order 
programs,” and patients will 
be required to participate in 
“cost sharing” through a $5- 
per-prescription co-pay. 

The new Medicare out-pa- 
tient prescription drug 
benefit will carry a $250 an- 
nual deductible and a 20 
percent patient co-pay, with 
out-of-pocket expenditures 
capped at $1,000 annually. 
Both the $250 deductible 
and the out-of-pocket cost 
ceiling will be indexed for 
inflation, and private “Medi- 
gap” insurance policies will 
be allowed to cover these co- 
pays and deductibles. 

Reimbursement for phar- 
macists participating in the 
plan will include a $5-per- 
prescription dispensing fee, 
indexed to rise annually 
along with changes in the 
Consumer Price Index.

Drug product costs will be 
reimbursed at the lower of 
the “90th percentile of actu- 
al charges in a previous pe- 
riod” or the “estimated ac- 
quisition cost” (EAC) plus 
the dispensing fee. 

Non-participating pharma- 
cies—those which decline to 
accept assignment on all pre- 
scriptions—will receive $2 
less per prescription. 


A ‘safe harbor’ 


A key element of the plan 
includes repeal of the in- 
surance industry’s con- 
troversial exemption from 
the federal antitrust laws— 
a move long advocated by 
independent pharmacists 
as essential to eliminating 
so-called “price fixing”’ 
activities by third-party 
pharmaceutical plans. 

This safe harbor, however, 
will not permit pharmacists 
or their associations to collec- 
tively “boycott” prescription 
insurance plans that do not 
establish acceptable 
reimbursement mechanisms. 


“When properly 
utilized, 
community retail 


— 


pharmacists save 
the health care 
syste:a billions of 


dollars...’ 


—West, NARD 


The plan includes a Drug 
Utilization Review compo- 
nent patterned closely after 
the OBRA ‘90 Medicaid 
DUR rules, and “participat- 
ing pharmacists [will be] re- 
quired to offer counseling to 
Medicare customers on the 
use of medications.” 

Although the President’s 
plan avoids direct price con- 
trols on drugs, it does in- 
clude a variety of cost control 
mechanisms, including a re- 
quirement that pharmaceu- 
tical manufacturers offer re- 
bates to Medicare as well as 
Medicaid based on the “Av- 
erage Manufacturer’s Price” 
(AMP) of their products. 

The plan also includes in- 
centives to promote the use 
of less costly generic drugs, 
as well as restrictions on 
the dispensing of new 
pharmaceuticals deter- 
mined to be “excessively or 
inappropriately priced.” 


Key restrictions 


For many chain and inde- 
pendent pharmacists, the 
most significant aspect of the 
package is the proposed new 
restrictions on discrimina- 


tory pricing by pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers. 

“As a condition of partici- 
pation under Medicare and 
Medicaid, manufacturers of 
prescription pharmaceutical 
products sold in interstate 
commerce would have to of- 
fer discounts to all pur- 
chasers of pharmaceuticals 
on equal terms,” Adminis- 
tration health reformers ex- 
plained. These restrictions 
would not prevent manufac- 
turers from offering volume 
discounts or discounts for 
prompt payment, prompt 
delivery or other “differen- 
tial economic advantages 
realized by the manufactur- 
er,” they explained. 

Additionally, the plan 
would allow price differen- 
tials to reward pharmacies 
that employ “mechanisms 
that can influence physician 
prescribing behavior’—a 
loophole that would appar- 
ently enable manufacturers 
to offer special discounts to 
hospitals with formularies, 
or to mail-order providers 
such as Medco with counter- 
detailing operations. 

But even though the Ad- 
ministration’s proposal to 
eliminate prescription price 
discrimination is not air- 
tight, it did draw a strong 
endorsement from _ the 
NACDS/NARD coalition. 


NACDS/NARD endorsement 


“Thanks to the President’s 
plan, the American public 
may get relief from the need- 
less and arbitrary cost shift- 
ing that occurs through drug 
manufacturer discriminatory 
pricing practices,’ NACDS 
president Ronald L. Ziegler 
said. 

Officials at APhA and oth- 
er pharmacy groups partici- 
pating in the “Coalition for 
Consumer Access to Phar- 
maceutical Care” reacted to 
the Clinton plan with far 
less enthusiasm. 

Although they praised 
“the efforts of the Clin- 
tons....to reform our nation’s 
health care system,” repre- 
sentatives of the APhA-led 
coalition said it is “essential” 
to “assure Americans of cost 
saving, quality-enhancing 
services of pharmacists—not 
just drug therapy.” 

APhA leaders are partic- 
ularly concerned over pro- 
visions in the Clinton plan 
which would override state 
freedom of choice laws and 
enable individual health 
plan administrators to lim- 
it the number and type of 
pharmacy providers al- 
lowed to participate in 
their plans. 

Moreover, the White 
House proposal would also 
authorize health plans to 
establish exclusive con- 
tracts designating “single 
source suppliers for phar- 
macy...products and ser- 
vices.”

TRIPLE.A PRODUCT STUDY 


Old favorites dominate HBA, OTC top rankings 


In the health and beauty 
aid categories tracked by 
Towne-Oller & Assoc. for 
Drug Store News’ annual 
“Triple A Product Study,” 
there were few surprises 
this year. Only a handful of 
new products worked their 
way onto this’ year’s 
“Hottest 100” list. 

Nevertheless, the hugely 
successful histamine-blocker 


and decongestant Tavist, 
produced by Sandoz 
Pharmaceutical, made a 
strong initial appearance on 
the Triple A rankings follow- 
ing its Rx-to-OTC switch. 
Other noteworthy 
changes: Several of the 
vaginal anti-fungal products 
slipped a notch or two. Al- 
though ranked highly, they 
no longer occupy the top 


three performance spots as 
they did last year in doilar 
volume rankings. 
Cough/cold and analgesics 
products were well repre- 
sented, reflecting the huge 
sales volume. The cough/cold 
and analgesics categories 
racked up more than $2 bil- 
lion each in annual rev- 
enues. The most conspicuous 
analgesic brand was Mc- 


Neil’s Tylenol, with 11 SKUs 
in the “Hottest 100 By Dollar 
Volume” rankings. 

On the beauty aids side of 
HBA, Gillette Sensor car- 
tridge blades showed no 
signs of slowing. The 
brand’s five-count cartridge 
refills held the No. 4 spot. 
The Sensor brand has been 
a top performer since its 
introduction in 1989. Sensor 


20 


Drug Store News, October 11, 1993 


for Women, introduced in 
1992, also made the chart, 
occupying the 42nd spot. 

Feminine hygiene prod- 
ucts also ranked as top 
performers, but the top 
spots were not dominated 
by one brand. Stay Free, 
Kotex and Always brands 
all occupied slots on the list. 

Despite the new introduc- 
tions in skin and hair care, 
the only skin care entry in 
the “Top 100 By Dollar Vol- 
ume” list was Oil of Olay’s 
4-ounce lotion. 


Hot GM sellers 
gain ground 


The top-ranked GM items 
are consumer grabbers and 
are likely to be found in 
multiple store locations. The 
beefed up visibility pays, 
say buyers and marketers. 

That’s because drug chair 
convenience, backed by in- 
telligent pricing, can tri- 
umph over mass merchants 
when a consumer has an 
immediate need for items 
such as batteries or film. 

In the cameras/film cate- 
gory, Kodak’s 200 ISO color 
35mm film (24 exposure) 
took the lead in dollar sales 
over Polaroid’s 600 Plus 
film for dollar rankings, re- 
versing last year’s one-two 
order. 

Even in an overall flat 
photo category for all trade 
classes, strong sellers, like 
single-use cameras, are con- 
verting more amateur pho- 
tographers to 35mm film. 
One reason is the quality of 
prints and enlargements, es- 
pecially with upgraded film 
from Kodak and Fuji. 

Instant film is still a 
leader for fast fun and im- 
mediate gratification, as 
shown by Polaroid’s 600 
Plus film—which moved up 
a slot in unit sales com- 
pared to last year’s rank- 
ing—and Polaroid’s new 
party film reached the dol- 
lar-ranking chart for the 
first time. 

When it comes to power- 
ing up, this year’s rankings 
again show that batteries 
move best in right-size mul- 
tipacks, with Duracell and 
Eveready/Energizer AA al- 
kaline 4-pazks again hold- 
ing the two top slots in 
units and dollars. 

Although new home 
entertainment technology 
lurks on the horizon, most 
consumers in this recession 
are not rushing out to buy 
pricey experimental hard- 
ware. That bodes well for 
convenient drug chains, 
which aim to push volume 
in blank videotape and au- 
dio cassettes to feed the 
huge base of VHS, cam- 
corder and audio hardware. 

This year, Memorex VHS- 
120 High Standard tape 
again led the rankings.

HOW TO EVALUATE A 
CLEARING HOUSE SERVICE 


“What safeguards protect 
your coupons at the process- 
ing center? 

—NCRS follows a careful 
checks and balance system 
which, along with log num- 
bers and audit trails virtu- 
ally assures no chance of 
coupon loss. 

“Are you Maximizing 
manufacturer support 
monies? 

—NCRS can help you 
maximize available funds. 
For example, the dollars 
supporting in-ad programs 
are not from the same 
“well” as coupon support. 
One is based on sales funds, 
the other on marketing 
funds targeted to build a 
brand name. 

“Is your “clearing house” 
really an authorized agent? 
For the retailer’s protection, 
be sure the clearing house 
actually processing your 
coupons is authorized by all 
of the manufacturers. No 
new authorizations have 
been granted in the past 
few years by the major 
manu-facturers with in- 
house redemption facilities. 
Requirements such as an- 
nual audits are strict to pro- 
tect retailer and manufac- 
turer. 

—NCRS has been autho- 
rized by all manufacturers

for over 22 years. In addi-

controls its own processing 
facilities and is also a 
founding member of the As- 
sociation of Coupon Proces- 
sors. 

“Does this clearing 
house really provide a prof- 
itable program? 

Two issues determine 
price structure in coupon 
redemption: 

1) In the standard 8 cent 
available between retailer 
and processor, how much 
does the retailer get? 2) 
How fast is payment made? 

The industry payment 
average is 45 days—but if 
the retailer is paid faster, 
you benefit from improved 
coupon investment return 
by decreasing the days you 
are financing your coupon 
receivables. 

—NCRS offers the flexi- 
bility of programs to im- 
prove the retailer’s return. 

If your answers to this 
evaluation point to a change 
of clearing house... well, 
change isn’t comfortable. 
But if the goal is bottom- 
line improvement, then look 
at a change of clearing 
house as your pro-active op- 
portunity in a time of limit- 
ed retail options.

Competition tangles ethnic hair care sales 


Buyers agree: Manufacturers need to introduce more new eth- 


HIGHLIGHTS IN ETHNIC MERCHANDISING 


thnic hair care sales 
Heremain flat as 1993 
starts to wind down, 
but chain drug store retail- 
ers are hoping to remedy 
that by becoming more ag- 
gressive with their market- 
ing and pricing strategies. 
Many chain drug ethnic 
product buyers report that 
their major problem has 
been competition from the 
growing number of low- 


priced beauty and barber 
shops (B&Bs), as well as 


nic hair care products to increase sales in the category.

from discounters like Kmart 
and Wal-Mart. 

“Our ethnic product sales 
have been very disappoint- 
ing in the last 12 months,” 
reports Susan Lackey, cate- 
gory manager for Eckerd 
Drug. “We’re seeing the 
competition for this category 
get worse. The B&B stores, 
in particular, are moving 
into many of the shopping 
centers that we're in.” 

Walgreens spokesman 
Michael Polzin calls the cat- 
egory “complex,” and adds 
that most of the growth 
Walgreens is experiencing 
in ethnic is coming from 
opening new stores. 

Some distributors esti- 
mate that B&Bs are now 
capturing as much as 40 
percent of all ethnic beauty 
care dollar sales. That has 
left some chains exploring 
whether their real estate 
departments can develop 
leasing agreements that 
lock B&Bs, like Sally’s 
Beauty Supply, out of the 
malls where the drug stores 
are located. One buyer says 
that such leasing agree- 
ments may not be possible 
to develop in today’s econo- 
my, but that they are worth 
exploring as an option. 


More variety = more sales 


Nonetheless, the problem 
isn’t just competition, say 
distributors who sell to all 
trade classes. The market is 
soft overall; they blame the 
economy and the lack of ma- 
jor new style changes for 
the sluggish sales. 

Towne-Oller, a market re- 
search company that tracks 
HBA sales through mass 
market trade classes, re- 
ports that unit and dollar 
sales for ethnic products are 
both down 1 percent for the 
12 months ended last July. 
The company says that the 
only growth areas are in 
cosmetics, styling products, 
skin care, hair coloring, 
wave products and after- 
shampoo conditioners. 

One big reason is the econ- 
omy. In Hartford, Conn., 
home of Beauty Enterprises, 
a large East Coast distribu- 
tor of ethnic supplies, 
merchandise manager Jim 
Normandin reports that the 
industry will be flat this 
year, partly because of the 
economy and partly because 
of styles. “But when you con- 
sider the state of the econo- 
my, particularly in the 
Northeast, being flat isn’t all 
that bad. It could be worse. 

“There are growth seg- 
ments. In our trading area, 
cosmetics are up 30 percent; 
hosiery is up 10 percent; 
skin care, up 6 percent; and 
conditioners and hair dress- 
es, up 4 percent.” 

Although he says it’s hard 
to be totally optimistic, he’s 
beginning to think the econ- 


omy will pick up. “Only, ev- 
ery time I think that,” he 
added, “someone else an- 
nounces that they’ve just let 
400 more jobs go.” 

Other regions also report 
sluggish sales. Detroit- 
based Standard Distribut- 
ing, the largest ethnic dis- 
tributor in the Midwest, 
reports that the category 
has been basically down 
this year. Nevertheless, 
says Standard president 
Dan Medow, “There...are so 
many new intros coming out 
that we could wind up even 
for the year.” 

Medow agrees that the 
economy has had a major im- 
pact on ethnic product sales, 
but he says that could 
change, “depending on what 
goes on in Washington. Right 
now, everybody's saving their 
nickels to pay for taxes.” 

Gerry Davis, 
president of Los 
Angeles-based 


Paul’s Sundries, 
says his cus- 
tomers are still 


hurting from the 
recession: “Cali- 
fornia’s been hit 
hard by the re- 
cession. We've 
never fully recov- 
ered. We_ see 
[them] suffering; 
many are moving 
away.” 

In the South- 
west, Kent 
Humphreys, 
president of 
Jack’s Service—a 
full service eth- 
nic products 
distributor head- 
quartered in 
Oklahoma City— 


Current 12-month share 


points out that 
although “hair 
care is normally 
recession-proof, 
when the econo-

He adds that ethnic hair 
care manufacturers haven’t 
been introducing new items

“The brands that are doing

HIGHLIGHTS IN ETHNIC MERCHANDISING 


Innovative HBA prepares chains for ‘94 and beyond 


number of major prod- 
uct launches may aad 
new spark to the eth- 
nic beauty care market in 
the second half of 1993 and 
the first half of 1994. 
Carson Products is com- 
ing out with a new men’s 
shaving product called Mag- 
ic Shave Platinum Shave 
Powder, and expectations 
are that it will do quite well. 
“It should do fine,” says 
Dan Medow, president of 
Detroit-based Standard Dis- 
tributing. “It’s a premium 
item, high ticket, an im- 
proved formulation. It’ll 
grow the category.” 
“Platinum is a skin condi- 
tioning shaving cream,” 
says Jim Normandin, mer- 
chandise manager for Beau- 
ty Enterprises. “It’s dif- 
ferent from [Carson’s red 
and blue lines]. It will find a 
home right away.” 


Kids’ toiletries expanding 


Carson Products is also 
introducing a new children’s 
relaxer kit called Beautiful 
Beginnings. Medow is very 
excited about the launch. 
“(The] children’s toiletries 
[category] has been one of 
the few strong growth areas 
in recent months, and I 
think there’s room for a few 
more new items. Beautiful 
Beginnings is unique. It’s 
positioned as less likely to 
irritate the scalp—that’s 
important to mothers.” 

In Los Angeles, president 
of Paul’s Sundries Gerry 
Davis says that since chil- 
dren’s toiletries is one of the 
few ethnic hair care seg- 
ments that has_ been 
expanding, there is “merit” 
in Beautiful Beginnings. 

Davis points out that the 
new product has “a unique 
formula, and Carson will 
support it well. It’ll be on 
television in the major 
metro markets, and it'll be 
in print and on billboards. It 
will be a winner.” 

Johnson Publishing’s 


African-American households 
are heavy users of 
_medicated skin treatments = 


Supreme Beauty Products di- 
vision also has a new chil- 
dren’s relaxer kit, called My 
Raveen Children’s Kit, com- 
ing out. Because Supreme is 
a value-priced line with a 
loyal following among budget 
conscious consumers, buyers 
expect My Raveen to do well. 


Relaxers strong 


The relaxer category al- 
ready has a number of 
strong brands battling for 
share, and now two more 
manufacturers, Luster 
Products and Lustrasilk, 
are preparing to launch new 
entries. 

This year, Luster is intro- 
ducing a new Pink Oil re- 
laxer kit that most buyers 
say will have to be “big” just 
because the Pink Oil name 
and franchise is so strong. 
Next year, distributors say 
Lustrasilk will be launching 
still another new relaxer kit 
of its own. 

“[Luster’s] Pink Oil Mois- 
turizer is No. 1 in its catego- 
ry, and the equity in the 
brand’s name will give an 
instant boost to the new 
items,” says Kent Humph- 
reys, president of Jack’s 
Service. “But there are so 
many relaxers coming out 
and there is only so much 
relaxer business.” 

“Pink Oil is the category 
leader, and [Luster] will be 
trading heavily off the Pink 
Oil franchise,” adds Nor- 
mandin. “It should really 
stand out on the shelf, too, 
since its packaging is pink.” 

“It is going to be a very 
strong launch,” says Medow. 
“It is good to see advanced 
formula products come out. 
There must be new activity 
in a category so the category 
can reinvent itself.” 


Shampoos to launch 


The shampoo/conditioner 
category has seen some ag- 
gressive growth in recent 
years, and now some more 
launches are pending. 


Retailers predict that new product introductions in cosmetics 
will continue to give them an edge in their ethnic mix. 


Along with new Pink Oil 
relaxer kit, Luster is 
launching a Pink Oil sham- 
poo and conditioner. 

At the same time, Soft 
Sheen is launching Care 
Free Curl Gold Shampoo. 
Carson has just introduced 
new 16-ounce sizes of its 
Dark & Lovely shampoos 
and conditioners. 

“Pink Oil will be a big 
launch,” says Davis. “But it 
won't be something that ex- 
pands the market. It’s not a 
new concept.” 

Buyers make the same 
points about Care Free Curl 
Gold Shampoo and Care 
Free Curl Gold Gel Gloss. 
Distributors agree that the 
launch will be good because 
Soft Sheen is a “great com- 
pany and a great marketer,” 
according to one distributor. 


This year, Alberto Culver 
is taking its Bone Strait sa- 
lon line of maintenance 
products for relaxed hair 
and launching it at retail. 


Hair stylers big news 


“That has some definite 
possibilities,” says Humph- 
reys. “Bone Strait did well 
in salons. [t has a good rep- 
utation in salons. Culver 
will put money behind it 
too, so it should do well.” 

“It’s been a popular salon 
item for years,” says the 
ethnic hair care buyer for a 
Midwestern chain. “We 
were able to do some promo- 
tions with [Culver’s] 16- 
ounce Blow Dry, and it is a 
preity solid item. At the 
very least, the line should 
be a modest success.” 

Normandin notes that

Tax adjustment curbs 


Rite Aid net income 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Rite Aid Corp.’s drug store division 
sales grew 5.6 percent during the second quarter ended 
Aug. 28. Sales for the 2,663-unit chain were $973.15 mil- 
lion, vs. $921.60 million for the same quarter last year. 

Earnings dropped to $21.58 million, compared to $24.97 
million for the same period one year ago. 

Sales for the 26-week period advanced 7 percent to $1.97 
billion from $1.84 billion for the first half of the previous 


fiscal year. 


Net income for the half fell to $53.21 million from $55.33 
million reported for the same period last year. 

The drop in net income is partially attributed to a de- 
ferred tax adjustment, which cut net income by $1.75 mil- 
lion for the quarter and year-to-date periods. 

Total a Oe revenues for the second quarter rose 5.7 


percent to 


1.04 billion from $983.4 million. The quarter’s 


earnings declined to $23.6 million compared with the previ- 
ous year’s $27.2 million in earnings. 

For the first half, Rite Aid’s sales increased 6.9 percent to 
$2.1 billion, compared to $1.97 billion. Net income was 
$57.7 million, down from $60.2 million one year ago.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark. — 
What started over a 49-cent 
gallon of milk and the issue 
of pricing below cost now 
threatens to grow into a le- 
gal nightmare for Wal-Mart 
Stores. 

Wal-Mart’s surprise loss 
of a predatory pricing law- 
suit to three Little Rock, 
Ark.-area independent drug 
stores could have major im- 
plications for the way the 
nation’s largest retailer 
prices inventory, executes 
competitive strategy and af- 
fects independent and chain 
drug stores around the 
United States. The ruling 
by Arkansas State Court 
Judge David L. Reynolds 
overturns the giant dis- 
counter’s current pricing 
policies at a Wal-Mart store 
in Conway, Ark. and awards 
damages to competitors who 
claim their business was 
hurt by the store’s pricing. 

“The bottom line of this 
whole thing is [Wal-Mart] is 
not going to be able to price 
below cost, and I think that 
is going to benefit all busi- 
nesses,” said Tim Benton of 
Family Drug Center, one of 
the plaintiffs in the case. 

The judge’s decision also 
left the independent phar- 
macy plaintiffs and their at- 
torney swamped with tele- 


Wal- Mart Strategy broadsided 
by unfavorable court ruling 


phone calls from potential 
litigants. 

“I have had a lot of calls 
from pharmacist associa- 
tions wanting to know how 
to do it,” said Dwayne 
Goode, president of indepen- 
dent drug store plaintiff 
American Drugs. 

In response to interest in 
the case, plaintiffs’ attorney 
Matt Adlong will join Goode 
at the National Association 
of Retail Druggists’ 95th an- 
nual meeting to discuss 
specifics of the case with 
NARD members. 

“The ruling in this case 
certainly gives encourage- 
ment to other small business 
competitors who have been 
victimized by the predatory 


SECOND CLASS 


pricing practices of Wal- 
Mart,” said NARD general 
counsel John Rector. “We are 
really happy about this and I 
think it will stimulate litiga- 
tion in the future.” 

At least 21 other states 
and the District of Columbia 
have statutes similar to 
Arkansas’ Unfair Trade 
Practices Act, but before 
other retailers file addition- 
al suits Wal-Mart plans to 
contest Reynolds’ decision. 

In a statement issued af- 
ter the ruling, Robert 
Rhoads, Wal-Mart’s general 
counsel, said, “We will im- 
mediately appeal, and clear- 
ly expect the Arkansas 
Supreme Court to overturn

Record fall buying show 


by Barbara White 


BOSTON — This year’s 
Chain Drug Marketing As- 
sociates show, held here 
from Sept. 30-Oct. 3, was 
the association’s largest one 
to date. 

The show attracted 192 
exhibitors who featured mer- 
chandise in 226 booths. Of 
the 847 registered attendees, 
76 chains and five whole- 
salers were represented. 

CDMA’s show proved to be 
more than an opportunity for 
mid-sized chains to visit 
booths. It included the debut 
of the Cosmetic Buyers Fo- 
rum, a roundtable meeting 
that was the first of its kind 
in the industry (see related 
story), education sessions, an 
idea exchange and mer- 
chandise presentations. 

In his opening remarks, 
Bill Baxley, vice president 
of marketing at Kerr Drugs 
and CDMA’s education com- 
mittee chairman, told 


boosts CDMA's clout 


CDMA members and guests 
that the “ever-changing 
landscape of the chain drug 
industry” would pose chal- 
lenges to the chain drug re- 
tailers present. 

“As people deal with 
change, they will fall into two 
camps: those who lead and 
those who follow,” he contin- 
ued. “The very fact that you 
are here speaks to your hope 


and vision for the future of 
the chain drug industry.” 
CDMA is strategically po- 
sitioned to assist them in 
that vision, Baxley said. 
Added Allan Patrick, ex- 
ecutive vice president of 
Genovese Drug Stores and 
CDMA chairman, “This is an 
association that’s in touch 
with the needs of our stores.”

ble solutions.
