Drug cosmetic buyer Penny 
Wade and Donna Mc- 
Manus, buyer at K&B, the 
forum aimed an intensive 
series of meetings and sem- 
inars at a single overriding 
objective: to bolster prof- 
itability in the hotly con- 


tested cosmetics/fragrance 
category. As such, it proved 
to be the most ambitious 
category management 
event in CDMA’s history 
and a powerful draw: It at- 
tracted 64 buyers from the 
chain drug, mass merchant 
and combo channels. 

The agenda, based on buy- 


er input, focused on three- 


key issues: service, prof- 
itability and fashion trends. 
Service, as it relates to 
shipping, was the most hotly 
debated topic at the meeting. 
Most buyers present 
were unsatisfied by the 
service they were receiving 
from suppliers. And they 
were concerned that it maar 


their business. 

“Years ago, sales were so 
strong that, in spite of your- 
self, you made money,” said 
Judy Wray, buyer at Revco. 
“Now the only way to make a 
profit is to do business 
cheaper, and I’m doing that. 
When my sales are down, it’s 
because I’m out of stock.” 

Other buyers present be- 
moaned the difficulties out- 
of-stocks create for the cos- 
metics business. 

“The change is that be- 
fore, there weren’t that 
many retailers selling cos- 
metics, and now everyone is 
in the business,” said Karen 
Durham, buyer at Duane

laddin, the NFL, Bar- 

A ney and Thomas the 

Tank Engine—that’s 

just a short list of 1993’s 

hottest licenses. From party 

goods to the photo depart- 

ment, licensed product adds 

excitement to just about all 
drug chain categories. 

For manufacturers, li- 
censes enhance brand equi- 
ty and help offset price 
competition from private la- 
bel. The marriage of strong 
licenses and major brands 
also adds fresh merchandis- 
ing when there are limited 
product introductions. 
What’s more, licensed prod- 
ucts provide value-added 
opportunities like premium 
offers, cross-merchandising 
and store events. 

All these factors helped 
drive licensed product sales 
in the United States and 
Canada to $62.2 billion at 
retail in 1992, according to 
the Licensing Industry Mer- 
chandisers’ Association. 
That’s a whopping figure, 
yet it’s down around 2 per- 
cent from 1991. 

Blockbuster theatrical 
properties—or the lack of— 
can impact that total in any 
year, and 1993 looks strong 
so far. “Aladdin is the 
hottest video release we've 
ever had—better than Beau- 
ty and the Beast,” says Andy 
Streifel, vice president of 
merchandising for PayLess 
Drug Stores. 

Along with the home video 
release, Aladdin licensed 
products can be found in at 
least a half dozen categories, 
from first-aid supplies to 
single-use cameras. Streifel 
adds: “Licensing is getting 
so broad-based that you 
have to be very careful 
about picking what to sup- 
port in your store.” 

That is why licensing 
marketers are courting re- 
tail in this tight economy. 
“You can make all the deals 
in the world, but if you can’t 
get to the retailers and get 
their support, you will lose,” 
said 20th Century Fox 
merchandising president Al 
Ovadia, addressing licens- 
ing executives at the 1993 
Licensing and Merchandis- 
ing Conference this past 
June in New York. 


Gimme support 


In today’s changing retail 
marketplace, the licensing 
industry is looking for new 
niches and new kinds of cross 
merchandising and vendor/ 
retailer partnering. An ex- 
ample is the joint promotion 
of Disney’s Aladdin home 
video and Colgate’s products 
for a $5 mail-in rebate. 

Another cutting-edge

strategy in licensed 
merchandising is “private 
label licensing,” which gives 
big retail customers exclu- 
sivity for a customized seg- 
ment of a big license. 

If they can’t have an ex- 
clusive, then at least drug 
retailers want coordinated 
licensing information. To tie 
in with the home video re- 
lease of Aladdin, for in- 
stance, Sacramento-based 
Raley’s/Bel Air food and 
drug chain is mounting nu- 
merous licensed product tie- 
ins, ranging from food man- 
ufacturer offers to licensed 
clothing and housewares 
such as Zak’s Aladdin juve- 
nile dinnerware. 

Hot video is often a loss 
leader, so it’s ir.portant to 
make up the margin on oth- 
er licensed products. Raley’s 
buyer Dan Black notes that 
with many licenses, a frag- 
mented approach does not 
help the retailer. 

“The trouble is, they don’t 


get all the information on .- 


available licensed products 
to the retailer. If we had an 
authorized list of companies 
with related products, we 
could contact those compa- 
nies and plan a promotion 
in a timely manner. But 
they are always so late in 
relaying the information.”

When it works, licensing 
helps differentiate one 
product from another.

licensed category, like

Licensed cards carry paper profit greeting 


When three elements—brand, licensed 
character and a growing category—all con- 
nect, the result can be a product likely to 
turn shoppers’ heads, like Crayola’s chil- 
drens’ art/activity kits featuring Barney, 
the enormously successful purple dinosaur. 

Licensed products often originate in block- 
buster theatrical releases and popular tele- 
vision programs. A theme park event, like 
the new Disney attraction Toon Town, is 
also an occasion for tie-ins, such as Kodak’s 
Toon Town promotion offering Disney hand 
puppets with a multiple proof-of-purchase. 


Cards, party goods, wrap a must 


The kids greeting card, party goods and 
gift wrap categories are a licensing bonan- 
za. Children’s birthday parties are recur- 
rent events in any young family, and when 
a kid wants Barney, Lisa Frank designs or 
Barbie, nothing else will do. 

Gibson and Cleo’s licenses for greeting 
cards, party and gift wrap cover a range of 
evergreen images. Among them: a range of 
Disney licenses including 101 Dalmatians, 
The Little Mermaid, Pinocchio and Aladdin. 
Images of just-retired NBA superstar 
Michael Jordan, Jurassic Park and new en- 
trants like The Simpsons and World Cup 
Soccer also appear on greeting cards, party 
supplies and wrap. 

American Greetings offers a new Super- 
man line to go with hot properties like 
Thomas the Tank Engine, Rocky & Bull- 
winkle and Opus ‘n Bill. American Greet- 
ings has also originated and licensed out 
characters such as Peppermint Rose, the 
Care Bears, Holly Hobby and Strawberry 
Shortcake, and it just launched its newest 
character, the Birthday Bear. 


Licensing gives manufacturers and retail- 
ers plenty of partnership opportunities, 
such as store events tied to in-store 
merchandising. American Greetings part- 
nered with Thrifty for the chain’s “Redis- 
cover Thrifty” grand reopenings earlier this 
year. These featured store appearances by 
costumed characters such as Ziggy and the 
Care Bears. 

In the same promotion, a “life sized” 
Thomas the Tank Engine (star of the an- 
imated “Shining Time Station” PBS-TV se- 
ries) made store appearances, complete 
with smoke and a whistle for photos of kids 
with their parents. The promotion included 
a free photo with a $5 purchase at Thrifty 
as part of the grand opening celebration. 

At Hallmark, spokesperson Rachel Bolton 
says licensing is becoming increasingly im- 
portant. Indeed, she said, Hallmark has “li- 
censed more in 1993 than in any other year, 
and we expect to see that continue.” 


License sharing 


Hallmark and its Ambassador division 
share many licenses. Among the new li- 
censed patterns are the Coneheads, New 
Yorker cartoons, Star Wars and Elvis. Some 
licenses appear in several lines—greeting 
cards, party, gift wrap and ornaments— 
while others are themed for one or two only, 
as is typical of the licensing business. 

The Hallmark/Ambassador lines feature 
both adult classics like Marilyn Monroe and 
James Dean, and powerful brands and 
properties that can evoke nostalgia, like 
M&Ms, Lifesaver, Tootsie Roll and Looney 
Tunes. Among the company’s hot properties 
that appeal to kids are Barney, Cathy, 
Mary Engelbreit and Barbie. 


Licensea products provide chains with value-added opportunities 


such as premium offers, cross-merchandising and store events. 


Sports get full play in license arena 


Licensed sports merchan- 
dise represents $12.1 billion 
in retail sales (United 
States and Canada), accord- 
ing to The Licensing Letter 
from EPM Communications 
of Brooklyn, N.Y. 

Fuji and Kodak are both 
aggressive in the sports li- 
cense arena. Along with its 
new NFL FunSaver 35, Ko- 
dak is offering a promotion 
tying a two-pack of film with 
collector coins featuring lo- 
gos of the 28 NFL teams. 

Fuji’s NFL licensing deal 
covers blank video and au- 
dio cassettes. Its videotape 
Winning Plays/NFL promo- 
tion offers in-store displays 
for an on-pack ruboff card 
game with a quarter-million 
dollars in prizes. The pro- 
motion offer also features 


premiums with proof-of-pur- 
chase. The company is also 
promoting its sponsorship of 
World Cup USA 94. 

Many licenses are category- 
exclusive, but in sports trad- 
ing cards, this is rare. The 
lack of license exclusivity con- 
tributed to an overcrowded 
sports card market in the last 
two years, but shakeouts are 
trimming the field. 

Spokesperson Brad Bart- 
lett of Score and Pinnacle 
brands trading cards notes 
that one way sports cards 
can reach new segments is 
through a new, higher-price 
niche for cards with top- 
quality design and produc- 
tion values. Another niche, 
he said, is limited-edition 
“chase cards,” which add 
value and collectability. 


Brand strength means 
licensing clout for chains 


The Revlon name is synonymous with beauty, but 
surprisingly, this is the first time in 60 years that the 
company has made a commitment to licensing. “It’s a 
whole new direction for Revlon,” says Lynn Krominga, 
president of Revlon Licensing Division. 

Krominga notes that the new licensees are “a logical 
extension of the Revlon name.” They include: Revlon 
fabric cosmetic bags by RGA; Revlon ophthalmic eye- 
glass frames by Classic Optical; Revlon sunglasses 
and reading glasses by Opti-Ray; Revlon costume jew- 
elry by Allison Reed; Revlon watches by Advanced 
Watch Company; Revlon electrical appliances and 
combs and brushes by Helen of Troy and Revlon hair 
accessories, cosmetics accessories and molded cosmet- 
ic organizers by Philips Industries. 

Revlon is involved in every step of the process from 
design to packaging, merchandising and quality con- 
trol. “What we try to do in all categories is tie into 
Revlon’s beauty and fashion image. In addition, in 
each of our product categories, we try to make the 
product interesting and unique, and not just rely on 
name recognition,” says Krominga. “It’s not a short- 
term licensing program. This is a brand licensing pro- 
gram that should be around for many years.”

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


After expressing some initial con- 
cerns over the “obvious” potential 
“threats” posed by Merck’s takeover of 
the nation’s iargest mail-order phar- 
maceutical provider, top APhA officials 
have openly endorsed a new third-par- 
ty pharmacy network that is being put 
together by Medco’s prescription insur- 
ance subsidiary, PAID Prescript’ons. 

PAID’s new “Coordinated Care Net- 
work” of pharmacy providers is being 
described by the company as “a key 
building block” in the “rationale behind 
Medco’s pending merger with Merck.” 

APhAers are describing the new 
PAID initiative as a real breakthrough 


The APhA has 
decided to “part- 
ner with PAID” in 
developing this 
new network because the Medco sub- 
sidiary “is the first firm to step forward 
with a solid plan that recognizes and 
rewards community pharmacists for 


their pharmaceutical care services,” 
APhA president John Gans explained. 


Is it really a partnership? 


But the APhA’s “partnership” with 
Medco’s PAID is not sitting well with 
representatives of either chain or inde- 
pendent retail pharmacies. Indeed, of- 
ficials at NACDS and NARD have ex- 
pressed concern that the APhA’s 
endorsement of the PAID network im- 
plies that community retail pharmacy 


supports this program. 

In a letter to state pharmacy associa- 
tion execs aimed at clearing up this 
“misconception,” NACDS president Ron 
Ziegler and NARD executive vice presi- 
dent Charles West described the APhA 
as an organization that “lacks a signifi- 
cant community retail pharmacy mem- 
bership base,” has “conflicting member- 
ship interests,” and reacts to “hot-button 
words and phrases we want to hear” 
from third-party administrators. 

A separate letter to PAID Prescrip- 
tions from more than 40 major drug 
chains stressed that the APhA’s en- 
dorsement of the new network will 
have no influence on whether individ- 
ual community pharmacies decide to 
participate in the plan. 

“(The] APhA does not represent the 
consensus viewpoint of chain drug 
stores or community retail pharmacy 
practice,” they told PAID bluntly. 

For his part, Ziegler elaborated on 
NACDS’ concerns during a news con: 
ference in Washington. “This is not an 
association turf war,” he said, but 
rather, a far more important effort by 
drug chains and independents to pro- 
tect themselves from third-party 
“middlemen” such as Medco’s PAID 
Prescriptions. 

Indeed, Ziegler believes that under 
health care reform, the role of third- 
party prescription “intermediaries” 
like PAID and PCS will decline, and 
community pharmacies will set up 
their own networks with third-party 
payors. Stay tuned.

54 Drug Store News, October 25, 1993 


Eckerd reports sales uptick 
after return to Wall Street 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Strong pharmacy sales propelled 
Eckerd Corp. to a 6.7 percent overall sales gain during the 
four-week period ended Sept. 25, the company announced. 
Sales for the four weeks, Eckerd’s first reporting period follow- 
ing its initial public stock offering on Aug. 5, totaled $297 mil- 
lion. Same-store sales grew nearly 5 percent during the period. 

“We are very pleased with our recent and year-to-date 
sales results,” said Stewart Turley, Eckerd chairman and 
chief executive officer. “Similar to others in our industry, 
we are experiencing some softness in front-end sales, re- 
flecting, among other things, substantial deflation in cate- 
gories such as cigarettes and diapers. 

“Our changing sales mix, with substantial gains in third- 
party pharmacy, is generating somewhat lower gross mar- 
gins,” Turley added. “We anticipate third-quarter operating 
profit [for the period ending Oct. 31] will be modestly below 
our plans, yet similar to last year.” 

Pharmacy remains Eckerd’s strong suit. The South- 
eastern chain drug leader posted a 15.1 percent prescrip- 
tion sales gain during the recent four-week period. 

Helping the chain’s ongoing financial performance will be 
a $950 million refinancing and the recent IPO. Both actions 
should prove an enormous, long-term benefit to Eckerd in 
that the company expects to reduce annual interest and 
dividend expenses by $35 million to $40 million. 

A $27.7 million, one-time charge associated with the re- 
financing hurt second-quarter and year-to-date earnings, 
but otherwise Eckerd has shown healthy sales growth be- 
fore and after its return to public ownership. For the six- 
month period ended July 31, sales were slightly more than 
$2 billion, nearly an 8 percent increase from the same peri- 
od the previous year. In addition, same-store sales grew 5.9 


percent for the six-month period.

Gearing up for the graying baby boomers 
The health care industry prepares for the growing number of over-50s

By Paul Amatangelo 


merica is undergoing a revolution, 

from top to bottom. Never before 

has the American society appeared 
as it does now, and more change is certainly 
in store for the 21st century. 

By the year 2000, 76 million baby boom- 
ers, almost a third of the total U.S. popula- 
tion, will be over the age of 50. With longer 
life expectancy and decreasing birth rates, 
the swelling of the over-50 market is only 
expected to continue and accelerate into 
the middle of the next century. 

The baby boomers are probably the first 
generation to truly reap the benefits of ad- 
vanced medical knowledge, which translates 
into increased longevity and better health. 
Within a decade, the baby boomers will 
make the over-50 market the fastest growing 


and most powerful buying block of our times. 
The successful retailer will be the one 
who makes a thorough effort to understand 
the needs, lifestyle habits and financial 
makeup of this over-50 group. With this 
necessary information in hand, retailers 
can develop a strategy on how to best serve 
these distinctive consumers and _ orient 
their business for future growth. 
Americans over 50 currently represent 
only 25 percent of the total U.S. population, 
yet they have a combined annual personal in- 
come of over $800 billion and control 70 per- 
cent of the total net worth of U.S. house- 
holds—nearly $7 trillion dollars. When the 
baby boomers join the ranks of the over-50 
market, these numbers will be even bigger. 


According to Ken Dychtwald, author of 


Age Wave, members of the over-50 popula- 


tion account for a whopping 40 percent of 


DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, October 25, 1993 


total consumer demand today. They watch 
television and read newspapers more than 
any other age segment, and are the biggest 
spenders on travel and recreation. 

Maintaining proper fitness is also impor- 
tant to the over-50 market, as noted in a 
study conducted by Modern Maturity mag- 
azine and the Roper Organization. Of those 
surveyed, 41 percent said that regular exer- 
cise is very important, and eight in 10 say it 
is important to look their best. The median 
age of retirement today is 62. And, they re 
concerned about eating a low fat diet, with 
limited cholesterol a salt intake. 


OTCs and home health care 


Bringing this information even closer to 
home, this segment of the population 
spends more money on health and personal 

Continued on page 4 


3 


MARKETING TO AN AGING SOCIETY 


Health care industry gears up for the graying baby boomers 


Continued from page 3 

care products than any other age group, 
ite more in the ie! store than any oth. 
er buying segment. In fact, over-50s are re- 
sponsible for 37 percent of all OTC medici- 
nal product purchases in drug stores. 

The home health care market has experi- 
enced a 20 percent growth per year from 
1980 to 1990, with sales of home medical 
equipment (which is comprised of items 
such as walkers, wheelchairs and hospital 
beds) in 1980 estimated at 500 million dol- 
lars. The market’s increasing product satu- 
ration has slowed this growth to only 12 
percent per year from 1990 to 1993. 

Already, sales of self-diagnostic kits and 
health care products for preventive medi- 
cal purposes are expected to increase to 
$2.2 billion by 1995. The top 100 HBA 
products of 1992, as reported in Drug Store 
News, were a compendium of diagnostic 
and self-health care products. Those over 
50 account for 29 percent of all HBA dollars 
spent and 39 percent of all OTC sales. 

Obviously, the graying of America will 
have a dramatic impact on all forms of busi- 
ness. Marketing geared toward the tradi- 
tional core of the consumer market, the 18- 
to 35-year-olds, will be a way of the past. 
Emphasis must be placed on the middle- 
aged and the elderly who will soon domi- 
nate the marketplace. 


Age-specific concerns 


In a study conducted by the Bryn Mawr 
School of Social Work, a group of over-55s 
were asked to name their main problems of 
everyday life. The following highlights their 
difficulties, most of which are age-specific: 
1. Opening medicine packages; 

2. Reading product labels; 

3. Reaching high places; 

4. Getting dressed (fastening buttons, 
snaps and zippers); 

5. Cleaning; 

6. Carrying purchases home;

Retailers, manufacturers and pharma- 
cists will likely recognize that they can ad- 
dress many of these probiems. There will 
be a need to virtually redesign America in 
everything from package design to adver- 
wee to dered to modes of product ac-

should be issues that readily come to mind.

that it is to the retailer's benefit to offer 
more boutique-like, customized services 
catering to this market, and their sales staff 
should be appropriately trained. Whether 
a part of the largest chain or an indepen- 
dent, the successful business will be the 
one that builds on the model of the neigh- 
borhood store that offers caring, personal- 
ized service. 

In addition, businesses will be marketing 
to a distinct group of people who, to be 
truthful, have “been around the block a few 
times.” Over-50s prefer informative adver- 
tising that doesn't attempt to hard sell, but 
rather to educate, and that recognizes their 
years of experience and advertising sophis- 
tication. Price is an important factor, but 
convenience and accessibility are more sig- 
nificant attributes. 

Over-50s like to see themselves depicted 
as healthy, active and attractive people, not 
weak, ill or elderly. They respond well to 
intergenerational advertising themes; pro- 
fessional endorsements also carry signifi- 
cant weight. 


Tailored marketing 


Marketing techniques should include 
personal contact wherever possible, with 
lots of clearly presented information and 
avoidance of both age-inappropriate im- 
ages and more commercial media (over 50s 
respond better to print advertising). Pro- 
motional efforts may be enhanced by link- 
ing up with informal and professional se- 
nior-oriented organizations and programs. 
Printed materials should be easy to read 
and handle. 

Recent changes in regulations also point 
to the need for counseling and drug utiliza- 
tion review, as well as category manage- 
ment, exploration of direct mail and the use 
of detailed consumer demographics for in- 
dividual stores. 

Preventive medicine and consumer edu- 
cation of all ages will be the biggest growth 
areas and challenges for the coming years 
and the key elements leading to profitabili- 
ty and success. Part of reducing health care 
costs will be in the optimum delivery of pa- 
tient education and homesself health care 
products and services. 

The future will bring significant ad- 
vances in the prevention and treatment of 
disabling diseases, prolonging life and radi- 
cally changing the means, quality and po- 
tential of later life. If retailers want to grow 
and prosper, they must do their part to un- 
derstand and support the changing pace of a 
more mature consumer market. 


Paul Amatangelo is vice president of 
marketing at Cincinatti-based Kendall-Fu- 
turo, a Lathe provider of health care 
products. ®

The average phar- 
macist in the treat-

from pharmacy school 
at a time when there

training program. 

Because they were asked to send in a re-

there were a total of 631 reports on 487 pa- 
tients. These report forms revealed consid- 
erable variation in the likelihood that a 
pharmacist would identify a problem in 
their targeted patients. Eighteen pharma- 
cists identified problems in each of the 103 
reports they submitted, while 13 pharma- 
cists identified problems in less than 40 
percent of their 169 reports submit‘ed. In

ing physician. Interventions that involved

The types of problems identified and the 
number of patients reported to have the 
problems are shown in Table 1. The largest 
categories of drug-related problems identi- 
fied by pharmacists were those of patients 
experiencing a side effect of a drug and hav- 
ing possible drug-drug interactions. 

Drugs implicated in the side effect cate- 
gory included diuretics, analgesics, antihy- 
pertensives, nonsteroidal antiinflamma- 
tory agents, antidepressants, 
bronchodilators, antianginal preparations, 
antiinfectives and tranquilizers. One phar- 
macist discovered that a patient was experi- 
encing uncontrollable diarrhea and was 
taking Mestinon to treat a new diagnosis of 
myasthenia gravis. The pharmacist deter- 
mined that the diarrhea was likely due to 
the drug and wrote a consult letter to the 
prescribing physician with recommenda- 
tions for changes in therapy. Not only did 
the physician alter the therapy, he called 
the pharmacist to thank her for bringing the 
problem to his attention. 

The drugs most commonly implicated in 
drug-drug interactions were diuretics, di- 
goxin, calcium channel blockers, antihy- 
Sp agents, H2 antagonists, couma- 

in and antiinfectives. 

Drug duplications involved analgesics, 
nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, diur- 


tranquilizers and hypnotics. 

Pharmacists reported an average of 14 
minutes per patient encounter with a stan- 
dard deviation of 13 minutes in time they 
spent on assessment and intervention. When 
B armacists reported assessing therapy but 

iscovering no problems, the average was 
10.2 minutes. When at least one problem 
was identified, the mean rose to 17 minutes. 

Tabe 2 shows how the pharmacists evalu- 
ated the effectiveness of their interventions. 


Summary and implications 


1. The volume of prescriptions filled per 
day and the type of pharmacist setting was 
not related to the likelihood of pharmacist in- 
tervention. It may be that pharmacists atti- 
tudes toward the importance of solving drug- 
related problems overcomes other jo 
related pressures, and these pharmacists 
make time to deal with patient problems. 

2. Drug-related sible can be identi- 
fied by pharmacists. These pharmacists do- 
cumented that they could identify and act 
on a number of important drug-related 
problems. Pharmacists identify medica- 
tion-related problems in about two-thirds 
of elderly patients targeted with study cri- 
teria characteristics. 

3. Pharmacists noted that the majority of 
the time physicians accepted their sugges- 
tions and comments regarding these drug- 
related problems. This finding supports 
physician acceptance of pharmacists ex- 

ertise in drug therapy, and the need for 
tter-coordinated health care for patients.
